resource depletion.name: Resource Depletion
resource depletion.description: Using natural supplies faster than they can recover or be replaced. Examples include pumping underground water faster than rain refills it, or wearing away soil faster than new soil forms. This leaves less available for people and nature in the future.
incoming: Mining and processing draw on materials, land, water and energy. The amount needed depends on technology, recycled inputs and what activities are counted.
Growing battery production can concentrate extraction, water use and waste in mining regions. This can add to local pressure on land and water supplies.
Frequently replacing clothing increases demand for fibres, water, energy and processing chemicals. Resources are used to make replacements while existing clothes may still be usable.
Removing carbon dioxide can require land, water, energy and materials. The demands differ greatly between methods and can create pressure on other resources.
Designing buildings to use less concrete can reduce demand for newly extracted materials. Changing the cement recipe alone does not guarantee lower material use.
Factories that cannot yet replace fossil-fuel heating continue to use fuel and other resources. Cooling water and materials remain part of the demand from these high-temperature processes.

More mining, especially of poorer-quality deposits, can require more rock, water and energy for each useful amount of mineral. Recycling and production methods affect the resulting demand for new resources.
Making new plastics uses fossil raw materials, energy, water and other resources. Reuse and recycled inputs can reduce some of the demand for new material.
Conventional steelmaking uses large amounts of ore, fuel and other materials. More efficient production and recycled steel can reduce demand for newly extracted resources.
outgoing: Producing plant nutrients requires energy and raw materials. Shortages of these inputs can raise production costs and prices paid by farmers.
Shortages of important resources can worsen existing tensions. Conflict risk depends strongly on how resources are shared and whether institutions can resolve disputes fairly.
Pumping more groundwater than rain and other sources replace gradually reduces underground reserves. This can continue over years or decades.

human.summary: Shrinking local water, soil and material reserves can make essential supplies harder or more expensive to obtain. Households and farms with few alternatives are more exposed.
consequences: Falling groundwater can raise pumping costs and make wells less dependable.
Losing fertile soil can reduce harvests and increase spending on farming inputs.

planet.summary: Using water, soil and other reserves faster than they recover can weaken ecosystems that depend on them.
consequences: Falling groundwater can reduce flow to rivers and wetlands.
Damaged soil may support less life and cope less well with drought.

response.defaultDriver: Mining and processing draw on materials, land, water and energy. The amount needed depends on technology, recycled inputs and what activities are counted.
levers: Removing carbon dioxide can require land, water, energy and materials. The demands differ greatly between methods and can create pressure on other resources.
Designing buildings to use less concrete can reduce demand for newly extracted materials. Changing the cement recipe alone does not guarantee lower material use.

measurement.metric: Material footprint and domestic material consumption by raw-material class
measurement.geography: UNSD country, region, or World geography with consumption-based and domestic-use boundaries separated
measurement.cadence: annual

occurrences.title: Global peak water limit of future groundwater withdrawals

carbon emission.name: Carbon Emission
carbon emission.description: Carbon dioxide entering the air when fuels are burned, materials are made or forests are cleared. This gas builds up and holds in heat, contributing to long-term warming. The amount released is different from its concentration already in the air.
incoming: Warming can increase decay, drought, fire and thawing of frozen soils. These changes can release stored carbon or reduce natural uptake, adding to warming that began from other causes.
More flying generally means more jet fuel burned unless efficiency or fuel changes offset it. Burning fossil jet fuel releases carbon dioxide into the air.
Making plastics and related chemicals uses fossil raw materials and energy. Production and some disposal methods can release carbon dioxide.
Power plants that burn fossil fuels release carbon dioxide whenever they run. Continued reliance on them for busy hours keeps those releases going.
Burning natural gas to make electricity releases carbon dioxide. The amount per unit of power varies with the technology and efficiency. The cited assessment reports a range.
Factories continue releasing carbon dioxide while boilers and high-temperature equipment burn fossil fuels. Slow replacement with suitable cleaner systems prolongs those releases.
Chemically changing limestone to make cement releases carbon dioxide. Fuel used to heat the process adds a separate contribution. Both are included when assessing total production emissions.
Keeping coal- and gas-intensive metal-making methods in use continues to release carbon dioxide. Reductions depend on replacing or changing those processes effectively.

Chip manufacturing can release heat-trapping gases through energy use and specialized process gases. These are not all carbon dioxide, so any combined climate total must retain the source's gas accounting.
Backup engines burning diesel or gas release carbon dioxide while running. More frequent or longer use increases that contribution unless efficiency or fuel changes offset it.
If available clean power cannot reach users or be stored, fuel-burning generation may still be needed. The emissions effect depends on which power sources actually run instead.
Salt-removal plants need energy to provide water. Where that energy comes from fossil fuels, operating the plants adds carbon dioxide releases.
outgoing: Carbon dioxide builds up in the atmosphere and makes it harder for heat to escape to space. Continued human releases therefore add to long-term warming. The cited evidence gives estimates and ranges for this relationship.
The ocean absorbs some of the carbon dioxide people release into the air. This changes seawater chemistry and makes the water more acidic.
Carbon dioxide released into the air adds to warming. Warmer air and ocean water increase pressure on the large ice masses covering Greenland and Antarctica.
Carbon dioxide adds to warming. Starting from a warmer climate makes dangerous combinations of high temperature and moisture in the air more likely.
Carbon dioxide adds to warming, changing the moisture in the air and temperature differences between land and sea. These changes can affect when seasonal rains arrive and how heavily they fall.
Carbon dioxide adds to warming and the resulting rise in sea level. This increases the background pressure behind coastal flooding and erosion.

Carbon dioxide adds to warming and changes water conditions in the North Atlantic. Warmer, fresher surface water is less likely to sink, which can weaken the large circulation that carries water through the Atlantic.
Carbon dioxide adds to warming, allowing the air to hold more water vapour. Storms can produce heavier rain when enough moisture and rising air are available.
Carbon dioxide adds heat to the air and ocean. Warmer upper-ocean water can help cyclones strengthen rapidly when winds, humidity and other storm conditions are also favourable.
Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.
Carbon dioxide adds to warming and more dangerous heat. Greater exposure can increase heat-related death risks, especially where people lack cooling and health care.
Warming makes strenuous work outdoors or in uncooled buildings more difficult and dangerous. Workers may need more rest and shorter exposure to avoid heat illness.

human.summary: Releasing this gas adds to warming that can last across decades. The consequences can reach people's health, homes, food supplies and public services.
consequences: Added warming can increase damaging heat, fire, flooding and rising-sea hazards.
Public budgets may face more spending on protection and disaster recovery.

planet.summary: The gas builds up in the atmosphere and adds long-lasting warming. Oceans also absorb some of it, changing seawater chemistry.
consequences: Continued releases increase the warming burden that future ecosystems face.
Warmer and more acidic water can put marine life under pressure.

response.defaultDriver: Existing fossil-fuel equipment, subsidies and long investment cycles can keep emissions high even when cleaner options exist.
levers: Use energy sources that release less heat-trapping gas. Use less energy to do the same job and cut waste.
Combine standards, investment and fair financial support so workers and households can make the change.

measurement.metric: Territorial fossil-fuel and industrial-process carbon dioxide emissions
measurement.geography: global, country, or reporting jurisdiction with inventory boundary declared
measurement.cadence: annual

occurrences.title: Half of world's CO2 emissions come from just 32 fossil fuel firms, study shows

personal conveyance.name: Personal Conveyance
personal conveyance.description: The vehicles people use for their own journeys, such as cars and motorcycles. Burning petrol or diesel releases gases that warm the planet and pollution that affects air quality. The impact depends on the vehicle, its energy source and how far and often it travels.
incoming: Frequent, affordable buses and trains can give people an alternative to private vehicles. The service must connect the places people need to reach.
Safe, connected routes make it easier to walk or cycle for short journeys. This can reduce the need to use a private vehicle.
outgoing: Traffic releases particles and gases that people breathe. Exposure to this pollution can contribute to lung and heart disease, depending on the level and duration.
Car-oriented development often needs large areas of roads and parking. Dark paved surfaces can store daytime heat, although shade, reflective materials and compact design can reduce this effect.

Petrol and diesel vehicles release carbon dioxide as they burn fuel. Electric vehicles shift much of the emissions from use to electricity production, while making vehicles and roads adds separate emissions.

Road-fuel demand can add pressure for palm-oil production where fuel contains palm-based biodiesel. Forest impacts depend on where extra supply comes from, yields and land protection. The link does not apply where palm oil is not used in transport fuel.

human.summary: Daily life built around private vehicles can expose people to exhaust, fuel-price changes and high travel costs. Street design also affects safety and access for people who do not drive.
consequences: People near busy roads may breathe more pollution that harms the lungs and heart.
A fuel-price rise is harder to manage when every essential journey requires driving.

planet.summary: Petrol and diesel vehicles release carbon dioxide as they burn fuel. Electric vehicles shift much of the emissions from use to electricity production, while making vehicles and roads adds separate emissions.
consequences: Car-oriented development often needs large areas of roads and parking. Dark paved surfaces can store daytime heat, although shade, reflective materials and compact design can reduce this effect. Dark asphalt absorbs sunlight during the day and releases stored heat later. Large paved areas can keep nearby places warmer after sunset.

response.defaultDriver: The vehicles people use for their own journeys, such as cars and motorcycles. Burning petrol or diesel releases gases that warm the planet and pollution that affects air quality. The impact depends on the vehicle, its energy source and how far and often it travels.
levers: Frequent, affordable buses and trains can give people an alternative to private vehicles. The service must connect the places people need to reach.
Safe, connected routes make it easier to walk or cycle for short journeys. This can reduce the need to use a private vehicle.

measurement.metric: Personal passenger travel activity by transport mode
measurement.geography: declared route, network, port, airport, metropolitan area, country, or fleet boundary
measurement.cadence: hourly or event-based with monthly and annual rollups

occurrences.title: Our cities are choked by cars – here’s how experts would fix them

compound climate hazards.name: Compound Climate Hazards
compound climate hazards.description: Two or more dangerous conditions happening together or close enough in time to make each other worse. For example, a drought can leave little water available when a heatwave arrives. The combined effects can be harder to manage than either event alone.
incoming: A warmer climate changes the chances and strength of several hazards, including heat and heavy rain. Some can occur together and worsen one another, with different effects in different regions.
Unusually warm water in the central and eastern tropical Pacific shifts winds and rainfall. Some affected regions can then face combinations of heat, drought, heavy rain or fire weather.
Unusually cool water in the central and eastern tropical Pacific changes where rain and storms tend to occur. This produces a different regional mix of wet, dry and hot conditions.
This recurring North Pacific pattern changes the background distribution of ocean warmth and regional weather. It can influence unusual conditions without determining every event.

Long-term North Atlantic temperature patterns vary alongside regional climate conditions. The association does not establish that people control the pattern's phase or that it alone causes a particular event.
Warm and cool phases in the tropical Atlantic are linked with shifts in winds and rainfall. These can influence unusual conditions in connected regions.
Changing temperature contrasts across the Indian Ocean can shift rainfall and warmth in connected regions. The phase and season affect which places are wetter, drier or hotter.
This moving tropical weather pattern influences winds and rainfall over several weeks. It can contribute to unusual conditions but does not uniquely determine them.
Changing North Atlantic pressure patterns help steer storms and warm or cold air. Different phases are associated with different regional temperature and rainfall patterns.
Changes in Arctic pressure patterns influence the movement of cold air and storms across the Northern Hemisphere. The resulting unusual conditions differ between regions.
A recurring Pacific and North American pressure pattern is linked to regional temperature and rainfall differences. Its phase changes which areas tend to experience unusual conditions.
The southern belt of strong westerly winds shifting north or south changes storm routes and rainfall. Regional effects depend on the phase and season.
outgoing: Heat and dry soil together can make it harder for trees to move enough water and keep growing. Earlier damage and pests can add to this pressure and contribute to tree death.
Several hazards occurring together can include an episode of very heavy rain. This describes one part of the combined event, rather than saying that the label itself causes rainfall.
Long-lasting drought can be one part of a sequence or combination of climate hazards. Its causes and effects still need to be assessed for the drying region.
Dangerous heat and humidity can occur together with other hazards. The combined category includes this exposure where high temperatures and moist air coincide.
A cyclone that strengthens quickly can be part of a wider sequence of hazards. This applies only in storm-prone regions with suitable ocean and atmospheric conditions.
Heat and drought can dry vegetation before a fire starts, creating a sequence of connected hazards. Fire still needs burnable material and an ignition source.
Population and Asset Exposure in Floodplains
Repeated heavy rain and flooding can threaten people and buildings on flood-prone land. Exposure depends on what occupies the affected area.
Heat combined with other hazards can increase death risks where people lack protection or health support. Age, illness, housing and opportunities to recover all affect the outcome.
Floods and heat can increase contact with contaminated water when water treatment and sanitation fail. Disease risk depends on the germs present and the protection people have.
Heat, drought and heavy rain can damage crops at different stages of growth. Their combined effect on harvests depends on the crop, timing and farm management.
Several hazards can disrupt food production, income and access at the same time. Conflict, inequality and market conditions can make the resulting hardship better or worse.
Climate hazards can contribute to people leaving unsafe homes or damaged livelihoods. Social, economic and political conditions also determine who moves and who can recover locally.

human.summary: Several hazards arriving together or in sequence can damage homes and interrupt daily life. Repeated losses can make recovery harder than a single event.
consequences: Storms, fires and floods can interrupt roads, electricity and housing.
Schooling, medical care and work may be disrupted during emergencies.

planet.summary: Repeated or combined hazards can change which species survive and how habitats are structured. Recovery becomes harder when disturbances arrive too close together.
consequences: An ecosystem may not return to its earlier condition between events.
Species tolerant of heat, fire or flooding may replace less tolerant ones.

response.defaultDriver: A warmer climate changes the chances and strength of several hazards, including heat and heavy rain. Some can occur together and worsen one another, with different effects in different regions.
levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

measurement.metric: Days with concurrent climate-hazard threshold exceedances
measurement.geography: bounded grid, city, basin, region, or country
measurement.cadence: daily classification with monthly and annual rollups

occurrences.title: Fires, floods and record heat: This is the summer of compounding disasters

el niño.name: El Niño
el niño.description: A recurring climate pattern in which the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean become unusually warm. The change shifts winds and rainfall far beyond the ocean itself. Some regions become wetter while others become drier. The effects vary between events.
incoming: Weaker east-to-west winds over the equatorial Pacific allow warm surface water to move east. This can reinforce warming in the central and eastern Pacific.
Extra heat stored beneath the equatorial Pacific can help prepare the ocean for a warm phase. Suitable wind changes are still needed. Stored heat alone does not guarantee it.
Some eastward-moving tropical storm systems produce bursts of west-to-east wind. These can push warm Pacific water eastward and help a warm phase develop.
outgoing: Unusually warm water in the central and eastern tropical Pacific shifts winds and rainfall. Some affected regions can then face combinations of heat, drought, heavy rain or fire weather.
Unusually warm water in the tropical Pacific changes air circulation. In affected regions, including parts of South Asia, seasonal rains may arrive late, weaken or fall less evenly.
Changes in Pacific ocean temperatures can bring heat, drought or flooding to farming regions. These conditions can damage harvests and interrupt food supplies.
Drought or flooding linked to unusually warm Pacific waters can damage harvests, water supplies and livelihoods. Some households may move when they have few ways to recover locally.
Unusually warm tropical Pacific waters can change winds and reduce rain in some regions. Dry soil, low rivers and depleted reservoirs can keep the effects going after the initial weather change.
Unusually warm tropical Pacific conditions can leave a lasting effect on North Pacific temperatures and currents. These effects contribute to longer-lived patterns alongside the ocean's own changes.
Unusually warm tropical Pacific water changes tropical winds. This can alter the temperature difference between the eastern and western Indian Ocean.
Changes in tropical Pacific storms can send a chain of air-pressure changes toward North America. This can favour particular regional wind and weather patterns.
Unusually warm tropical Pacific water shifts tropical winds and storm activity. This can change the strength and path of the eastward-moving band of tropical rain.
A warm Pacific phase can move heat away from the equator and leave cooler conditions behind. This can prepare the ocean for a cool phase, but the transition is not inevitable.
Some warm Pacific events bring both warmer coastal water and powerful waves that damage kelp. Effects vary greatly by location, and nearby forests can respond differently to the same event.

Warmer central and eastern Pacific water shifts rising air and tropical storms eastward. This can weaken or move the usual east-to-west circulation, but one event does not establish a long-term trend.

human.summary: Changes in tropical Pacific water can shift rain and ocean conditions far away. People may feel the effects through farming, fishing, water supplies and prices.
consequences: Drought can damage crops in some places while floods damage them elsewhere.
Changes in sea temperature and nutrients can disrupt fisheries.

planet.summary: Warm tropical Pacific conditions change the exchange of heat and water between ocean and air. Effects can reach distant marine and land ecosystems.
consequences: Less deep, nutrient-rich water reaching the surface can reduce marine plant growth.
Persistently warm water can increase coral bleaching risk.

response.defaultDriver: Weaker east-to-west winds over the equatorial Pacific allow warm surface water to move east. This can reinforce warming in the central and eastern Pacific.
levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

measurement.metric: Oceanic Niño Index warm-phase anomaly
measurement.geography: Niño 3.4 region with coupled tropical-Pacific context
measurement.cadence: monthly or annual according to source release

occurrences.title: High winds during El Niño could be deadly for England’s stressed trees, say experts

la niña.name: La Niña
la niña.description: A recurring climate pattern in which the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean become unusually cool. It changes winds and rainfall across many regions. The effects differ by place and season, so it does not mean that everywhere becomes colder or wetter.
incoming: Stronger, rather than weaker, east-to-west Pacific winds push warm water west and bring colder water up in the east. That opposite phase of the wind measure supports cooler tropical Pacific conditions.
Less heat stored in the equatorial Pacific makes cold water below the surface easier to bring upward. This favours a later cool phase.
A warm Pacific phase can move heat away from the equator and leave cooler conditions behind. This can prepare the ocean for a cool phase, but the transition is not inevitable.
outgoing: Unusually cool water in the central and eastern tropical Pacific changes where rain and storms tend to occur. This produces a different regional mix of wet, dry and hot conditions.
Unusually cool water in the tropical Pacific changes air circulation and the movement of moisture. Seasonal rains can become stronger, weaker or differently timed, depending on the region.
Changes linked to unusually cool Pacific waters can bring destructive rain to some regions and drought to others. Harvests and fisheries may be affected in different ways across regions.
Unusually cool tropical Pacific conditions can reinforce some cool patterns farther north. The longer-lived North Pacific pattern also has other causes.

Cooler central and eastern Pacific water can strengthen the usual pattern of rising air in the west and sinking air in the east. The response differs between events and does not by itself explain a decades-long trend.

human.summary: Cooler tropical Pacific conditions can shift rainfall so some regions face drought while others receive damaging rain. Impacts differ between places and events.
consequences: Changes in seasonal rain can make water supplies harder to plan around.
Flood losses may increase in some river basins while drought losses rise elsewhere.

planet.summary: Cool tropical Pacific conditions shift seasonal rain and ocean patterns. Different regions can face drying or flooding during the same event.
consequences: Water extremes can strain ecosystems adapted to more usual conditions.
Changes in rain timing can disrupt seasonal growth and breeding.

response.defaultDriver: Stronger, rather than weaker, east-to-west Pacific winds push warm water west and bring colder water up in the east. That opposite phase of the wind measure supports cooler tropical Pacific conditions.
levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

measurement.metric: Oceanic Niño Index cool-phase anomaly
measurement.geography: Niño 3.4 region with coupled tropical-Pacific context
measurement.cadence: monthly or annual according to source release

occurrences.title: Weather tracker: More extreme rain in Japan and a tornado in France

amoc slowdown.name: AMOC Slowdown
amoc slowdown.description: A weakening of the large Atlantic Ocean circulation that carries warm water north near the surface and colder water south at depth. This movement helps distribute heat. A lasting change can affect rainfall, sea levels and marine life. One low reading does not establish a lasting slowdown.
incoming: Carbon dioxide adds to warming and changes water conditions in the North Atlantic. Warmer, fresher surface water is less likely to sink, which can weaken the large circulation that carries water through the Atlantic.
Added ocean heat makes seawater lighter. In the North Atlantic, this can reduce the sinking of water that helps sustain its large ocean circulation.
Fresh meltwater from Greenland makes nearby surface seawater less salty and lighter. This can make it harder for water to sink and may weaken Atlantic circulation.
A lighter, fresher surface layer in the North Atlantic can limit mixing and sinking. This weakens a process that helps drive the ocean's large circulation.
outgoing: The Atlantic overturning system is a major part of ocean circulation. A change in its strength changes how water and heat move within that system.
Changes in Atlantic ocean circulation can raise or lower sea levels along parts of the North Atlantic coast. Flooding there also depends on tides, storms, waves and the longer-term rise in sea level.

Part of the strong northward Atlantic surface current belongs to the ocean's wider overturning circulation. Changes in that wider system can affect it, but winds also drive the current, so the two are not interchangeable.

human.summary: Changes in the large Atlantic circulation can shift regional rainfall, coastal water levels and marine conditions. This creates uncertainty for communities planning food, water and coastal protection.
consequences: Rainfall changes can affect farms and water supplies around the North Atlantic and in the tropics.
Changes in marine food webs may affect fishing livelihoods.

planet.summary: Changes in Atlantic circulation move heat and nutrients differently. Marine habitats and rainfall patterns can change over wide areas.
consequences: Species may face different temperatures, food supplies and currents.
The regional distribution of rain can shift as ocean heat transport changes.

response.defaultDriver: Warming and added freshwater affect the sinking of seawater in the North Atlantic. Planning based only on past conditions can leave communities exposed.
levers: Include a range of possible circulation changes in coastal and water planning.
Improve ocean observations and prepare farming and food supplies for less predictable conditions.

measurement.metric: Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation transport at a declared latitude
measurement.geography: named station, transect, depth layer, ocean region, or quality-controlled analysis grid
measurement.cadence: daily to monthly with annual synthesis

occurrences.title: AMOC: Could the ocean currents system collapse?

wet-bulb heat.name: Wet-Bulb Heat
wet-bulb heat.description: Hot conditions made more dangerous by moist air. When the air is very humid, sweat evaporates less easily, so the body has more difficulty cooling itself. How dangerous the conditions become also depends on how long they last, activity and access to cooling.
incoming: Higher temperatures, when combined with enough moisture, make it harder for sweat to cool the body. The change varies by region. The cited projection concerns tropical conditions rather than every place on Earth.
Moister air makes sweat evaporate less easily at the same air temperature. That reduces the body's ability to cool itself. The danger depends on both heat and humidity.
Carbon dioxide adds to warming. Starting from a warmer climate makes dangerous combinations of high temperature and moisture in the air more likely.
Methane adds to near-term warming. This can increase exposure to dangerous combinations of high temperature and humid air.
Dangerous heat and humidity can occur together with other hazards. The combined category includes this exposure where high temperatures and moist air coincide.
outgoing: Repeated periods of heat and humidity can make work and daily life unsafe. They can contribute to pressure to move, alongside jobs, housing, family ties and other factors.
Hot, humid weather can cause many people to use cooling equipment at once. The resulting jump in electricity demand can strain a power system that has little spare capacity.
High humidity makes it harder for sweat to evaporate and cool the body. During extreme heat, this can increase illness and deaths attributed to hot conditions.
Moist air limits cooling through sweat while a person works. In hot conditions this can reduce safe working time and increase the risk of illness or injury.
Hot, humid conditions make it harder for farm workers to cool down safely. They can also strain crops and animals, reducing food production in exposed regions.
High humidity makes sweating less effective during hot weather. Farm workers may be unable to keep working safely through the hottest hours.
Hot, humid air makes sweat evaporate less effectively, so the body has more difficulty losing heat. Illness risk varies with age, activity, housing, previous exposure to heat and access to cooling.
Hot, humid conditions can stress farm animals and weaken their ability to resist illness. They may also favour some germs and disease-carrying insects.
Hot, humid air makes it harder for livestock and workers to lose body heat. This adds to the strain farms face during hot weather.
Hot, humid conditions can reduce aircraft takeoff performance and the time staff can safely work outside. This can limit airport operations and schedules.
Hot, humid conditions reduce safe working time at ports. They can also strain equipment and the systems keeping refrigerated cargo cold.
More dangerous hot and humid weather increases demand for cooling. More equipment can mean more opportunities for heat-trapping cooling gases to leak unless they are properly managed.

human.summary: Hot, humid air makes sweat less effective at cooling the body. Dangerous exposure can develop more quickly when people are active or have no access to cooler conditions.
consequences: Severe exposure can cause heat illness and put organs under strain.
Farm, construction and delivery workers may have fewer hours when work is safe.

planet.summary: This measure describes conditions that make it harder for people to lose heat. It does not by itself measure damage to ecosystems. Effects on other living things need separate evidence.

response.defaultDriver: Warming raises heat exposure, while unequal shade, housing, cooling and worker protection shape who is harmed.
levers: Provide enforceable work-rest arrangements, shade and access to safe cooling.
Improve efficient cooling in exposed homes and use building and street design to reduce heat.

measurement.metric: Hours above a declared wet-bulb-temperature threshold
measurement.geography: bounded NASA POWER 0.5 x 0.625 degree meteorological grid cell represented by a named point
measurement.cadence: hourly with annual rollups

occurrences.title: Knowledge Nugget | How will heat stress affect children and elderly?

monsoon volatility.name: Monsoon Volatility
monsoon volatility.description: Changes in the timing, strength or reliability of a region's rainy season. Rain may arrive late, fall in intense bursts or stop for unusually long periods. These shifts can disrupt planting and water supplies even when the total seasonal rainfall looks normal.
incoming: Warming changes the temperature contrast between land and sea and the moisture available in the air. This can change a rainy season's timing or intensity, with effects that differ by region and season.
Tropical Atlantic temperature patterns can influence seasonal rains in nearby and connected regions. Whether rain increases or decreases depends on the phase, season and place.
An east-west temperature contrast in the Indian Ocean shifts where moist air rises and rain falls. This can change rainy-season behaviour in particular regions, without one uniform effect everywhere.
A travelling pattern of tropical clouds and winds can influence active and dry spells within a rainy season. The effect depends on its location and the region involved.
Changes in particle-related heating and cooling can alter winds and seasonal rain. The effects on rainy seasons are uncertain and differ substantially by region.
Unusually warm water in the tropical Pacific changes air circulation. In affected regions, including parts of South Asia, seasonal rains may arrive late, weaken or fall less evenly.
Unusually cool water in the tropical Pacific changes air circulation and the movement of moisture. Seasonal rains can become stronger, weaker or differently timed, depending on the region.
Carbon dioxide adds to warming, changing the moisture in the air and temperature differences between land and sea. These changes can affect when seasonal rains arrive and how heavily they fall.
Warming caused by methane can change moisture and air circulation. These changes can affect the timing and variability of seasonal rains.
Removing large areas of forest changes how land stores heat and returns water to the air. These changes can affect winds and seasonal rains, with results depending on where clearing occurs.
Changes in tropical rising and sinking air can shift where rain falls. Some monsoon regions respond, while local weather processes can outweigh the distant influence.
outgoing: Unreliable seasonal rains can disrupt planting, watering and harvesting. Farms that depend heavily on these rains may produce less food.
Repeated failures of seasonal rains, or destructive downpours, can damage crops, homes and incomes. Some people may move when local recovery becomes too difficult.
Changes in seasonal winds can concentrate moisture and rainfall in different places or shorter periods. Some regions may then experience more intense rain events.

human.summary: Unreliable seasonal rains make it harder to time planting, manage reservoirs and prepare for floods. Farmers and households can face losses and changing food prices.
consequences: Rain arriving too early, too late or in uneven bursts can damage harvests.
Flooding and dry breaks can affect the same river basin within one season.

planet.summary: Many ecosystems depend on seasonal rains arriving at a reasonably predictable time. Changes in timing and intensity can disrupt growth and recovery.
consequences: Plants and animals may lose the usual rhythm of wet and dry seasons.
Alternating floods and dry breaks can erode soils and damage freshwater habitats.

response.defaultDriver: Warming and changes over land and ocean affect seasonal rain. Farming and reservoirs can remain planned around older rainfall patterns.
levers: Provide useful local forecasts and access to seeds suited to variable rain.
Improve water planning and fair emergency credit so a failed season does not create lasting debt.

measurement.metric: Monsoon rainfall-gate anomaly and seasonal rainfall variability
measurement.geography: IMD Kerala-onset 14-location rainfall panel represented by declared NASA POWER grid points
measurement.cadence: daily source observations with annual complete-season synthesis

occurrences.title: India’s severe monsoon season causes more than 100 deaths since July

permafrost thaw.name: Permafrost Thaw
permafrost thaw.description: Ground that has stayed frozen for at least two years begins to soften as it warms. The surface can sink, damaging roads and buildings. Previously frozen plant material can also decay and release gases that add to warming.
incoming: Warmer conditions allow more heat into ground that has remained frozen for years. More of it can thaw. The projected amount depends strongly on future emissions and the region studied.
Rapid Arctic warming heats the ground and deepens the layer that thaws each summer. This can accelerate the loss of ground that used to remain frozen year-round.
Severe northern fires remove insulating vegetation and soil and can darken the surface. Frozen ground beneath the burned area may then thaw faster than comparable unburned ground.
outgoing: Melting ice inside frozen coastal ground weakens the land. Waves can then wear it away more easily, especially where less sea ice leaves the shore exposed.
Thawed plant material can decay in wet ground with little oxygen. Microbes can produce methane during this process, and some of that gas can escape into the air.
When ice inside frozen soil melts, the ground can sink and become uneven. More thaw can create additional hollows, ponds and unstable surfaces.
Continued warming can enlarge unfrozen pockets or layers within otherwise frozen ground. These openings can change water movement and ground stability.
Thawing ground exposes long-frozen plant and animal remains to decay. This can release carbon dioxide and, where the ground is waterlogged, methane.
Thawing frozen ground can damage buildings, roads and essential services. People may need to move when repairs or continued protection become too difficult.
Thawing ice within the ground can make land sink or shift unevenly. Buildings, roads and pipes built on susceptible frozen ground can lose support or become distorted.
Thawing ground exposes previously frozen plant material to decay. Where the soil stays waterlogged, this can produce methane that escapes into the air.
Ice in rock cracks can help hold pieces in place. When it thaws, the rock loses support and becomes more exposed to seasonal water and temperature changes.
Thawing ground changes drainage, nutrients and the shape of the land. These changes can favour shrubs in some tundra areas, but not everywhere.
Thawing frozen ground on exposed rocky peaks changes moisture, stability and cold local conditions. Specialised species can lose suitable habitat even as the total area of bare rock grows.

human.summary: Ground that thaws and shifts can damage Arctic homes and essential services. Remote communities may have few alternatives when roads or water systems fail.
consequences: Buildings, roads and storage tanks can lose support as ice in the ground melts.
Damaged drinking-water or sewage systems can increase contamination risks.

planet.summary: Thawing northern soils changes both the shape of the land and the fate of stored carbon. These changes can affect habitats and add to warming.
consequences: Previously frozen plant material becomes more available for decay and gas release.
Melting ground ice can form hollows and ponds that change drainage and habitat.

response.defaultDriver: Rapid northern warming changes ground conditions faster than some buildings and roads were designed to handle.
levers: Include emissions from thawing ground in climate planning and improve local monitoring.
Use foundations and land-use rules suited to the ground, and avoid building on unstable ice-rich sites.

measurement.metric: Annual maximum active-layer thickness above permafrost
measurement.geography: named borehole, CALM grid, region, or permafrost zone
measurement.cadence: annual maximum with continuous temperature where available

occurrences.title: The Nepal and Tibet flood is a warning: melting snow and ice will bring more disasters around the world

rain-on-snow flood risk.name: Rain-on-Snow Flood Risk
rain-on-snow flood risk.description: The chance of flooding when rain falls onto existing snow. Rain and melting snow can send a large amount of water downhill in a short time. The outcome depends on the snow, the ground and how much water rivers and drains can carry.
incoming: Warming can turn some winter snowfall into rain and increase melting. Where rain falls on stored snow, the combined water can raise flood risk, depending on the snow, soil and drainage.
Heavy, relatively warm rain falling on existing snow can combine rainfall with rapid melting. The extra water can increase flood risk in snow-covered river basins.
outgoing: Rain adds weight and liquid water to existing snow and can weaken its layers. On steep slopes, this may trigger a slide of wet snow.

human.summary: Rain adds weight and liquid water to existing snow and can weaken its layers. On steep slopes, this may trigger a slide of wet snow. Avalanches can bury or damage roads, railways, power lines and communications equipment. Repeated closures are especially disruptive where few alternative mountain routes exist.

planet.summary: Rain adds weight and liquid water to existing snow and can weaken its layers. On steep slopes, this may trigger a slide of wet snow.

response.defaultDriver: Warming can turn some winter snowfall into rain and increase melting. Where rain falls on stored snow, the combined water can raise flood risk, depending on the snow, soil and drainage.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.

measurement.metric: Rain-on-snow flood risk
measurement.geography: named snow-covered watershed and downstream forecast reach
measurement.cadence: hourly to event interval

occurrences.title: Heavy rain and snowmelt are hurtling large chunks of ice into northeastern Michigan homes

peak glacier runoff passage.name: Peak Glacier Runoff Passage
peak glacier runoff passage.description: The point after which a shrinking glacier supplies less meltwater over the long term. At first, faster melting may increase the water reaching rivers. Eventually, too little ice remains to keep that supply up, making water less reliable downstream.
incoming: At first, faster melting can send more glacier water into rivers. Continued ice loss eventually leaves less ice to melt, so the long-term water contribution declines in affected river basins.

Earlier snowmelt changes the seasonal mix of snow and glacier water reaching rivers. It can make the loss of late-season glacier support more noticeable, without alone proving that a basin has passed its maximum glacier runoff.
Less stored winter snow can make a river basin more dependent on glacier melt. Once that glacier contribution begins declining, late-season water supplies become more exposed.
outgoing: After a glacier basin passes its period of greatest meltwater supply, the contribution can decline over time. People and power systems relying on that water may face less dependable dry-season flows.
Meltwater carries fine rock and soil into the water below glaciers. How much arrives, and at what depth, depends on the amount of water and how it enters the basin.

Strong seasonal meltwater flows carry fine rock particles from glaciers. The amount and timing of sediment depend on the flow, rather than simply on whether a basin has passed its maximum glacier runoff.

human.summary: After a glacier basin passes its period of greatest meltwater supply, the contribution can decline over time. People and power systems relying on that water may face less dependable dry-season flows.
consequences: Strong seasonal meltwater flows carry fine rock particles from glaciers. The amount and timing of sediment depend on the flow, rather than simply on whether a basin has passed its maximum glacier runoff. Sediment carried into a reservoir settles as the water slows. Continued build-up takes up storage space and can interfere with water intakes.

planet.summary: Meltwater carries fine rock and soil into the water below glaciers. How much arrives, and at what depth, depends on the amount of water and how it enters the basin.
consequences: Strong seasonal meltwater flows carry fine rock particles from glaciers. The amount and timing of sediment depend on the flow, rather than simply on whether a basin has passed its maximum glacier runoff.

levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.

marine pathogen range expansion.name: Marine Pathogen Range Expansion
marine pathogen range expansion.description: Disease-causing germs in seawater becoming active in more places or for a longer part of the year. Warmer water can help some of these germs survive and multiply. This can affect seafood safety, marine animals and people who use coastal waters.
incoming: Prolonged warm seawater can help some disease-causing germs grow in new places or seasons. Salt content, human or animal contact and other local conditions also matter.
Warming coastal water can make more places or longer seasons suitable for temperature-sensitive germs such as Vibrio bacteria. This can affect seafood safety and exposure through contact with water.
Rising seawater can change salt levels in estuaries. This may make particular places more or less suitable for disease-causing organisms, depending on the salt range they tolerate.
outgoing: Some marine germs can cause illness through seafood or contact with open wounds. Their spread can add pressure to coastal health services. This is an infection pathway, rather than heat injury itself.

human.summary: Some marine germs can cause illness through seafood or contact with open wounds. Their spread can add pressure to coastal health services. This is an infection pathway, rather than heat injury itself.

planet.summary: Changing water conditions can alter where disease-causing organisms survive and spread. Effects differ by organism and host, and a wider detected range does not prove disease increased everywhere.

response.defaultDriver: Prolonged warm seawater can help some disease-causing germs grow in new places or seasons. Salt content, human or animal contact and other local conditions also matter.
levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

thermal stratification intensification.name: Thermal Stratification Intensification
thermal stratification intensification.description: Water forming more strongly separated layers, often with warmer, lighter water above colder, denser water. The layers mix less easily. This can reduce the movement of oxygen and nutrients between the surface and deeper water.
incoming: Warming makes surface seawater lighter than deeper water. The stronger separation can reduce mixing and the movement of oxygen between layers.
outgoing: Strongly separated water layers mix less easily, slowing the oxygen supply to the bottom. Oxygen can run low as organisms continue to use it, especially where much organic material is decaying.
Separated layers in warm river-mouth waters can make oxygen shortages worse. Young fish and shellfish may then have less suitable sheltered habitat.
More strongly separated water layers slow the replacement of oxygen below the surface. Low-oxygen conditions are more likely where excess organic material is also using up oxygen as it decays.

When warm surface water mixes less with deeper water, fewer nutrients may reach sunlit waters. At a Gulf of Lions study site, the less productive season also showed a narrower range of food resources used by bottom-living animals.
A stable layer of warm surface water mixes less with deeper water. This limits the movement of absorbed carbon away from the surface and can reduce how effectively the ocean takes up more.
Stronger separation between surface and deep ocean water can keep nutrients below the sunlit layer. Tiny drifting plants may grow less where they already lack nutrients.

human.summary: When warm surface water mixes less with deeper coastal water, oxygen and habitat conditions can worsen. Fishing communities may face less dependable catches and seafood supplies.
consequences: Weak mixing can make low-oxygen conditions and some algae problems more likely.
Young fish and shellfish may lose suitable habitat as oxygen-rich areas shrink.

planet.summary: Strongly separated water layers mix less easily, slowing the oxygen supply to the bottom. Oxygen can run low as organisms continue to use it, especially where much organic material is decaying.
consequences: Separated layers in warm river-mouth waters can make oxygen shortages worse. Young fish and shellfish may then have less suitable sheltered habitat.
More strongly separated water layers slow the replacement of oxygen below the surface. Low-oxygen conditions are more likely where excess organic material is also using up oxygen as it decays.

response.defaultDriver: Warmer surface water can strengthen the separation between layers. Fisheries planning may not keep up with the changing habitat.
levers: Monitor water temperature, oxygen and mixing together.
Reduce excess nutrients entering vulnerable waters and adjust fishing rules to observed habitat conditions.

delta salt intrusion fronts.name: Delta Salt Intrusion Fronts
delta salt intrusion fronts.description: The inland edge of salty seawater moving through places where rivers meet the sea. Higher sea levels or weaker river flows can let salt travel farther upstream. Water used for farming or drinking can then become too salty.
incoming: Higher seawater levels can push salty water farther inland through river mouths and connected underground stores. This is especially important when river flow is too weak to push it back.
Weaker or differently timed river flows provide less fresh water to resist the sea. Saltier water can then move farther upstream.
A long drought reduces river flow and the flushing of river mouths. Saltier water can move farther inland and remain there longer.
outgoing: Saltier water reaching drinking-water intakes can exceed normal treatment capabilities. Utilities may need to change intake locations, blend supplies or use additional treatment.
Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands
Saltwater moving inland can enter shallow freshwater stores near the coast. The layer of usable fresh water may then become thinner.
Salt moving through river mouths can also reach connected underground water. This can make coastal wells and reserves saltier.

human.summary: Salt moving farther up a river mouth can affect water supplies before land is permanently flooded. Households, farms and utilities may need costlier ways to obtain fresh water.
consequences: Utilities may need to blend water or switch intakes when salt levels rise.
Farmers can lose a reliable source of fresh irrigation water.

planet.summary: Saltier water reaching drinking-water intakes can exceed normal treatment capabilities. Utilities may need to change intake locations, blend supplies or use additional treatment.
consequences: Saltwater moving inland can enter shallow freshwater stores near the coast. The layer of usable fresh water may then become thinner.
Salt moving through river mouths can also reach connected underground water. This can make coastal wells and reserves saltier.

response.defaultDriver: Rising seas, low river flow and withdrawals can increase the problem, especially where planning treats it as only a short storm event.
levers: Track salt levels and adjust water intakes and releases before supplies become unusable.
Protect needed freshwater flows and redesign repeatedly exposed intakes where practical.

measurement.metric: Position of a declared salinity intrusion front in a river delta
measurement.geography: declared basin, aquifer, utility, catchment, floodplain, or administrative reporting area
measurement.cadence: event-based to monthly with annual accounting

oceanic upwelling disruptions.name: Oceanic Upwelling Disruptions
oceanic upwelling disruptions.description: Changes in the process that brings deeper, nutrient-rich seawater toward the surface. Winds and ocean currents help drive this movement. If its timing or strength changes, the tiny organisms at the base of marine food chains may receive fewer nutrients.
incoming: Changes in currents can alter when and how strongly deeper water reaches the surface. That changes the nutrient supply supporting marine growth and food chains.
outgoing: When less deep water reaches the surface, fewer nutrients may be available to tiny sunlit-water organisms. Their growth can decline, reducing food at the base of marine food chains.
Some fishing grounds rely on nutrients brought up from deeper water. Changes in that supply can make fish growth and catches less predictable.

human.summary: When deep, nutrient-rich water stops reaching the surface at the usual time, coastal food supplies can change. Fishing communities may face less predictable catches and income.
consequences: Less nutrient supply can reduce the growth of tiny plants at the base of the food web.
Fish catches may arrive at different times or in different amounts.

planet.summary: When less deep water reaches the surface, fewer nutrients may be available to tiny sunlit-water organisms. Their growth can decline, reducing food at the base of marine food chains.

response.defaultDriver: Winds and ocean conditions can shift while fishing seasons and markets remain based on past patterns.
levers: Connect ocean monitoring with flexible fishing decisions.
Prepare ports and coastal businesses for changing catch seasons and support other income options where needed.

measurement.metric: Coastal upwelling transport anomaly
measurement.geography: named station, transect, depth layer, ocean region, or quality-controlled analysis grid
measurement.cadence: daily to monthly with annual synthesis

extreme precipitation intensity.name: Extreme Precipitation Intensity
extreme precipitation intensity.description: How heavily rain or snow falls during unusually strong events. A large amount arriving in a short time can overwhelm drains and rivers. The resulting flood risk also depends on the landscape, soil and buildings in the path of the water.
incoming: Warmer air can hold more water vapour. When suitable storms form, that extra moisture can fall as heavier rain or snow. Warming does not make every place wetter.
A band of tropical storm activity moving eastward changes winds and the supply of moisture. During some phases, it changes the chance and intensity of heavy rain in distant regions.
More moisture in the air supplies more water for rain when air rises and clouds form. Suitable storms and weather systems can then produce heavier rainfall.
Changes in seasonal winds can concentrate moisture and rainfall in different places or shorter periods. Some regions may then experience more intense rain events.
Carbon dioxide adds to warming, allowing the air to hold more water vapour. Storms can produce heavier rain when enough moisture and rising air are available.

A strong, long-lasting stream of moist air can produce heavy rain or snow when mountains or fronts lift it. Without suitable lifting, direction or duration, it may mainly provide useful water rather than an extreme event.
Convective Available Potential Energy and Inhibition Anomaly

More strongly rising air can support heavier rain, but moisture, storm movement and organisation also matter. High potential energy can remain unused, while very moist storms can produce extreme rain with little of it.
Several hazards occurring together can include an episode of very heavy rain. This describes one part of the combined event, rather than saying that the label itself causes rainfall.
outgoing: Intense rain can arrive faster than the ground can absorb it or drains and rivers can carry it away. Water can then rise quickly and flood nearby areas.
A heavy burst of rain can send more water into pipes and treatment plants than they can handle. The excess may back up or spill out.
Very heavy rain can overwhelm airport drains and reduce visibility. Flights and ground operations may be delayed or cancelled.
Heavy rain and runoff can make local surface seawater fresher and lighter. This can briefly reduce mixing with deeper water when winds and currents are weak.
Some storms that produce very heavy rain also support damaging hail. Heavy rain alone does not determine hail size or frequency. Winds and temperatures inside the storm matter.
Heavy rain can send more runoff into pipes that carry both rainwater and sewage. Overflow occurs only where such a combined system exists and the incoming water exceeds its capacity.
Heavy rain or rapid snowmelt can fill cracks in rock. Later freezing and thawing, together with water pressure, can weaken blocks that are already vulnerable.
Heavy rain can wash loose material from glacier-fed rivers and deltas. Short bursts of flow may carry fine particles and larger sediment into nearby coastal waters.
Floods can expose or damage fuel pipes and overwhelm barriers around storage. High flows can also carry an existing spill into a river more quickly.
Heavy rain can wash recently exposed sediment and river-bank material into glacier-fed streams. It can add to the sediment already carried by meltwater.
Heavy rain and flood peaks can increase water force against river banks. Saturated or undercut banks may collapse where they are vulnerable.
Heavy, relatively warm rain falling on existing snow can combine rainfall with rapid melting. The extra water can increase flood risk in snow-covered river basins.

human.summary: Very heavy rain can overwhelm airport drains and reduce visibility. Flights and ground operations may be delayed or cancelled.
consequences: Intense rain can arrive faster than the ground can absorb it or drains and rivers can carry it away. Water can then rise quickly and flood nearby areas. Rapid floods can wash dirt and pollution into water sources or damage intakes. Treatment plants may need extra cleaning steps or temporary interruptions.

A heavy burst of rain can send more water into pipes and treatment plants than they can handle. The excess may back up or spill out. Overflowing sewage systems can expose people to water carrying harmful germs. Outbreak risk rises when treatment and sanitation no longer contain that exposure.

planet.summary: Intense rain can arrive faster than the ground can absorb it or drains and rivers can carry it away. Water can then rise quickly and flood nearby areas.
consequences: A heavy burst of rain can send more water into pipes and treatment plants than they can handle. The excess may back up or spill out.
Heavy rain and runoff can make local surface seawater fresher and lighter. This can briefly reduce mixing with deeper water when winds and currents are weak.

response.defaultDriver: Warmer air can hold more water vapour. When suitable storms form, that extra moisture can fall as heavier rain or snow. Warming does not make every place wetter.
levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

measurement.metric: Annual maximum corrected daily precipitation anomaly
measurement.geography: bounded NASA POWER 0.5 x 0.625 degree meteorological grid cell represented by a named point
measurement.cadence: daily source observations with annual complete-year rollup

tropical cyclone rapid intensification.name: Tropical Cyclone Rapid Intensification
tropical cyclone rapid intensification.description: A tropical storm's winds becoming much stronger in a short time. Warm seawater and suitable air conditions can help this happen. Fast strengthening can leave communities less time to prepare, particularly when a storm is approaching land.
incoming: Warmer ocean and air conditions can provide more energy and moisture to an organized tropical storm. This can favour rapid strengthening, but it does not determine what any individual storm will do.
Unusually warm surface and upper-ocean water can supply energy to a tropical cyclone and limit cooling beneath it. Rapid strengthening still depends on winds, humidity, storm structure and its path.
A deep layer of warm ocean water can keep supplying heat as a cyclone stirs the sea. This reduces cooling beneath the storm and can support rapid strengthening when other conditions are favourable.
Moist air around a cyclone limits the disruption caused by dry air entering it. This helps organised thunderstorms continue releasing the heat that powers the storm.
Carbon dioxide adds heat to the air and ocean. Warmer upper-ocean water can help cyclones strengthen rapidly when winds, humidity and other storm conditions are also favourable.
A cyclone that strengthens quickly can be part of a wider sequence of hazards. This applies only in storm-prone regions with suitable ocean and atmospheric conditions.
outgoing: A storm that strengthens quickly near land can leave less preparation time. Strong winds, heavy rain and high seawater levels may then combine to produce flooding.
A rapidly strengthening cyclone gives ships and ports less time to prepare. Closures, changed routes and delays may increase.
Powerful cyclone waves and currents can break or overturn corals and move reef rubble. Damage depends on the storm's path and the reef exposed to it.

human.summary: A rapidly strengthening cyclone gives ships and ports less time to prepare. Closures, changed routes and delays may increase.
consequences: A storm that strengthens quickly near land can leave less preparation time. Strong winds, heavy rain and high seawater levels may then combine to produce flooding. Coastal flooding can affect cable landing stations and their power or land connections. Shared locations increase the risk of several links failing together, while protection, backup power and separated routes can prevent disruption.

planet.summary: A storm that strengthens quickly near land can leave less preparation time. Strong winds, heavy rain and high seawater levels may then combine to produce flooding.
consequences: Powerful cyclone waves and currents can break or overturn corals and move reef rubble. Damage depends on the storm's path and the reef exposed to it.

levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.

pyrocumulonimbus smoke injection.name: Pyrocumulonimbus Smoke Injection
pyrocumulonimbus smoke injection.description: A very intense wildfire creating a towering storm cloud that carries smoke high into the atmosphere. Smoke reaching these heights can travel far and remain in the air longer. These fire-driven storms behave differently from ordinary low-level smoke plumes.
incoming: Very intense fires can create towering storm clouds. These can carry smoke much higher than ordinary fire plumes, allowing it to travel farther or remain aloft longer.
outgoing: Some powerful fire clouds carry smoke high into the atmosphere, where particles can remain longer. This adds to the particle layer rather than removing its cooling influence, although different smoke components can have different effects.

Some observed high-altitude smoke events temporarily cooled Earth's surface overall. The result depends on particle type, height, lifetime, clouds and the surface below, so the effect is not always cooling.

human.summary: Some observed high-altitude smoke events temporarily cooled Earth's surface overall. The result depends on particle type, height, lifetime, clouds and the surface below, so the effect is not always cooling. Hotter air can make aircraft takeoff more difficult and put extra strain on runways and ground operations. The effects depend on the aircraft, airport and conditions.
consequences: Some powerful fire clouds carry smoke high into the atmosphere, where particles can remain longer. This adds to the particle layer rather than removing its cooling influence, although different smoke components can have different effects. Some airborne particles have partly offset warming by reflecting sunlight. Removing that cooling influence can add near-term warming unless the warming influence of other gases also falls enough.

planet.summary: Some powerful fire clouds carry smoke high into the atmosphere, where particles can remain longer. This adds to the particle layer rather than removing its cooling influence, although different smoke components can have different effects.
consequences: Some observed high-altitude smoke events temporarily cooled Earth's surface overall. The result depends on particle type, height, lifetime, clouds and the surface below, so the effect is not always cooling.

levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

coastal permafrost erosion.name: Coastal Permafrost Erosion
coastal permafrost erosion.description: Waves wearing away shorelines whose ground was held together by ice. As the ground thaws and sea ice provides less protection from waves, the coast can break down faster. Nearby homes, roads and other structures can lose the land beneath them.
incoming: Melting ice inside frozen coastal ground weakens the land. Waves can then wear it away more easily, especially where less sea ice leaves the shore exposed.
A longer open-water season gives waves more time and space to attack Arctic coasts. Shores made of thawing, ice-rich ground can erode especially quickly.
Warmer air and sea water thaw ice-rich coastal ground and make it easier for waves to wear away. The effect is strongest along exposed, vulnerable shorelines.
outgoing: Rapid erosion and collapsing coastal slopes can remove support beneath buildings, roads and pipes. Communities may lose reliable access and essential services.

human.summary: Rapid erosion and collapsing coastal slopes can remove support beneath buildings, roads and pipes. Communities may lose reliable access and essential services. Damage to roads, power lines or utilities in remote polar areas can interrupt essential services. Difficult access and limited alternatives can make recovery harder.

planet.summary: Rapid erosion and collapsing coastal slopes can remove support beneath buildings, roads and pipes. Communities may lose reliable access and essential services.

response.defaultDriver: Melting ice inside frozen coastal ground weakens the land. Waves can then wear it away more easily, especially where less sea ice leaves the shore exposed.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.

measurement.geography: named Arctic coastline
measurement.cadence: event to annual

baseline water stress.name: Baseline Water Stress
baseline water stress.description: How strongly people's water use competes with the available supply. When farms, households and businesses use a large share of that supply, there is less room to cope with dry periods. The needs of rivers and other living systems also matter.
incoming: Irrigated farms draw water from supplies also needed by households, businesses and rivers. Heavy use can leave less available during dry periods.
City growth can increase water demand and pollution both inside and outside city boundaries. Better services, more efficient use and changes in industry can moderate or reverse the increase.
Long dry periods reduce river supplies and the water replenishing underground reserves. Shortages become more likely if demand stays high.
Falling groundwater levels reduce the reserves people can reach and make pumping more costly. Users who depend on wells may then face tighter supplies.
Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.
Less water replenishing underground stores can reduce dependable supplies and increase saltwater intrusion near coasts. Large reserves or lower pumping can protect users from short-term shortages.

Losing forests changes how water enters soil, returns to the air and reaches rivers. This can worsen shortages where those forest functions help maintain dependable supplies, but the response is local.
Poorly managed oil and gas wastewater can contaminate fresh supplies, while extraction also uses water. These pressures matter especially where usable freshwater is already limited.
Irrigation pumping can reduce underground reserves when use exceeds replacement from rain, rivers or managed replenishment. Other users then have less dependable water available.
Large industrial withdrawals can compete with households, farms and wildlife for slowly replaced groundwater. Persistent use above replenishment reduces available reserves.
Public water supplies can strain groundwater when pumping repeatedly exceeds replenishment. Alternative sources and lower demand can reduce the shortfall.
Pumping coastal groundwater faster than it is replaced lowers freshwater reserves and pressure. Less usable water may remain available to local users.
outgoing: When demand approaches available water supply, safely treating and using water again becomes more valuable. It helps most when it replaces water taken from an already stressed source.

When water use is already close to available supply, seasonal or drought-related changes can leave lakes and reservoirs short. Imports, lower demand and careful operation can sometimes keep storage stable.
Limited water can bring animals together around fewer drinking places and make cleaning harder. Poorer water quality and closer contact can increase the spread of disease.
When reliable water supply cannot meet normal demand, utilities may ask or require people to use less. The restrictions depend on local operating decisions.

human.summary: Limited water can bring animals together around fewer drinking places and make cleaning harder. Poorer water quality and closer contact can increase the spread of disease.
consequences: When reliable water supply cannot meet normal demand, utilities may ask or require people to use less. The restrictions depend on local operating decisions.

planet.summary: When water use is already close to available supply, seasonal or drought-related changes can leave lakes and reservoirs short. Imports, lower demand and careful operation can sometimes keep storage stable.

response.defaultDriver: Irrigated farms draw water from supplies also needed by households, businesses and rivers. Heavy use can leave less available during dry periods.
levers: Limit water withdrawals to what the connected water system can support, while protecting essential human and environmental needs.
Reduce pollution and improve storage, drainage or treatment where local evidence shows these are the relevant problems.

measurement.metric: Baseline water withdrawals relative to available renewable supply
measurement.geography: basin, sub-basin, country, or declared service area
measurement.cadence: annual with periodic model revision

groundwater depletion.name: Groundwater Depletion
groundwater depletion.description: A lasting reduction in water stored beneath the ground. This happens when water is removed faster than it is replaced by rain and other flows. Wells can become less reliable, and rivers or wetlands fed by this water can also be affected.
incoming: Pumping water for crops can reduce underground reserves when use exceeds the water that seeps back in. The shortage can build up over years, making wells less reliable.
Long dry periods can reduce the water replenishing underground stores while increasing demand for pumping. Reserves fall faster where withdrawals already approach or exceed replacement.
Irrigation that needs more pumping for the same harvest can drain underground reserves. The effect depends on how much of the extra water returns as usable groundwater.
Pumping groundwater for irrigation lowers reserves when withdrawals keep exceeding replacement. A record of water use alone does not show that an underground store is shrinking.
Pumping groundwater for public supplies can lower water levels if use stays above replacement. Other sources or reduced demand can change that balance.
Factories, mines and power facilities can reduce groundwater reserves when sustained pumping exceeds replacement. The actual balance must be assessed for the underground water body concerned.

Changes in pressure between rivers, lakes and groundwater can move water into depleted underground stores or reduce flow back to the surface. This redistributes water and must be assessed across the connected system.
Utilities using groundwater may pump extra water to replace what leaks from pipes. Reserves decline faster if replenishment cannot keep up.
outgoing: Falling groundwater levels reduce the reserves people can reach and make pumping more costly. Users who depend on wells may then face tighter supplies.
Falling groundwater supplies can force use of poorer-quality water or change how salty water moves. Soil salt levels can rise where irrigation and drainage allow salts to collect.

human.summary: Falling groundwater levels reduce the reserves people can reach and make pumping more costly. Users who depend on wells may then face tighter supplies.
consequences: Falling groundwater supplies can force use of poorer-quality water or change how salty water moves. Soil salt levels can rise where irrigation and drainage allow salts to collect. Too much salt around roots makes it harder for crops to take in water. Harvests can fall or become less reliable, depending on the crop and how the land is managed.

planet.summary: Falling groundwater levels reduce the reserves people can reach and make pumping more costly. Users who depend on wells may then face tighter supplies.

response.defaultDriver: Pumping water for crops can reduce underground reserves when use exceeds the water that seeps back in. The shortage can build up over years, making wells less reliable.
levers: Limit water withdrawals to what the connected water system can support, while protecting essential human and environmental needs.
Reduce pollution and improve storage, drainage or treatment where local evidence shows these are the relevant problems.

measurement.geography: USGS well and aquifer
measurement.cadence: weekly
