heat-related mortality burden.name: Heat-Related Mortality Burden
heat-related mortality burden.description: Deaths linked to exposure to high temperatures. The risk depends on more than the temperature: age, health, housing, length of exposure and access to cooling all matter. Estimates need to distinguish deaths caused or contributed to by heat from deaths occurring for other reasons.
incoming: Power disconnection can remove cooling or interrupt essential home medical equipment during extreme heat. This can increase the risk of death, especially for people with limited alternatives or existing illness.
Higher temperatures and more intense hot periods increase the risk of heat-related deaths. Actual harm depends on health, housing, exposure and access to protection and care.
Failures in transport, water or health services can prevent people from getting protection during extreme heat. Several failures together can increase the risk of death.
Heat warnings can help prevent deaths when they trigger contact with vulnerable people, access to cooling and health-service preparation. An alert alone is not enough.
City plans can help prevent heat-related deaths when forecasts trigger funded action. This includes reaching vulnerable people, opening cooling spaces and protecting outdoor workers.
Making safe indoor temperatures available to people at greatest risk can help prevent heat-related deaths. Cooling must remain affordable and available when needed.
Insulation, shade and ventilation can reduce dangerous indoor heat when upgrades suit the local climate and allow heat to escape. Lower exposure can reduce estimated heat-related death risks.
Carbon dioxide adds to warming and more dangerous heat. Greater exposure can increase heat-related death risks, especially where people lack cooling and health care.
Heat combined with other hazards can increase death risks where people lack protection or health support. Age, illness, housing and opportunities to recover all affect the outcome.
outgoing: A surge in heat illness and deaths may occur alongside overwhelming demand for ambulances and hospitals. Death counts alone do not show whether services were overloaded. Their workload and capacity need separate evidence.

human.summary: A surge in heat illness and deaths may occur alongside overwhelming demand for ambulances and hospitals. Death counts alone do not show whether services were overloaded. Their workload and capacity need separate evidence.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

response.defaultDriver: Power disconnection can remove cooling or interrupt essential home medical equipment during extreme heat. This can increase the risk of death, especially for people with limited alternatives or existing illness.
levers: Heat warnings can help prevent deaths when they trigger contact with vulnerable people, access to cooling and health-service preparation. An alert alone is not enough.
City plans can help prevent heat-related deaths when forecasts trigger funded action. This includes reaching vulnerable people, opening cooling spaces and protecting outdoor workers.

measurement.metric: Modelled heat-attributable deaths and fraction of all deaths
measurement.geography: global and WHO region in the current operational release; finer geography requires a separately validated source
measurement.cadence: annual Lancet Countdown release

air pollution health burden.name: Air Pollution Health Burden
air pollution health burden.description: Illness and deaths linked to breathing harmful particles or gases. Pollution can damage the lungs and heart, with effects depending on what people breathe and for how long. These health effects are not all caused by climate change.
incoming: Traffic releases particles and gases that people breathe. Exposure to this pollution can contribute to lung and heart disease, depending on the level and duration.
Very small airborne particles can reach deep into the lungs. Studies following people over time link greater long-term exposure with a higher risk of death from natural causes.
Larger or longer fire seasons can expose people to more smoke and fine particles. Breathing this pollution can harm the lungs and heart and increase illness and death risks.

Breathing carbon monoxide reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen. Risk depends on the amount breathed, exposure time and the person's condition. Detecting the gas alone does not measure health harm.

Breathing ground-level ozone irritates and damages airways, especially in exposed or vulnerable people. Studies reviewed for World Health Organization guidelines also link short-term outdoor increases with a small rise in daily deaths from all causes.
Pollen can irritate the nose and eyes or worsen asthma in people who are sensitive to it. Outdoor counts do not measure each person's exposure, and many exposed people have no symptoms.
Drifting farm chemicals can reach workers, homes and schools through air or direct contact. Harm depends on the chemical and dose. Detecting drift alone does not establish a health effect.

Windblown mineral particles can worsen air quality near their source and far downwind. Health effects depend on the particles and actual exposure. A visible dust plume alone does not establish illness.
Agricultural burning, ammonia and other farm emissions can contribute to air pollution. Health impacts depend on the pollutants released and people's actual exposure.
Conditions that favour ground-level ozone can increase harmful exposure where the necessary gases and people are present. Actual health burden depends on how much pollution people breathe.
Hospital admissions attributed to wildfire smoke are one measured part of the health effects of polluted air. They do not include every symptom, illness or effect outside hospital care.
Diesel freight releases fine particles and other harmful gases. People near busy freight routes can face greater exposure and related heart or lung risks.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Breathing polluted air can increase heart and lung illness and shorten lives. Families may face treatment costs and time away from work or school.

planet.summary: The main measure here concerns harm to people from polluted air. Effects on plants, water and climate depend on the pollutants and require separate measurements.

response.defaultDriver: Traffic releases particles and gases that people breathe. Exposure to this pollution can contribute to lung and heart disease, depending on the level and duration.
levers: Connect useful warnings with accessible health services and practical protection for exposed people.
Improve access to safe housing, water or cooling where the documented exposure requires it.

occupational heat exposure.name: Occupational Heat Exposure
occupational heat exposure.description: People facing hot conditions while doing their jobs, outdoors or inside warm workplaces. Physical effort can make it harder for the body to cool down. The danger depends on humidity, time spent working, protective clothing and access to rest and cooling.
incoming: Warmer conditions can make jobs in hot environments more strenuous and dangerous. Humidity and physical effort affect how much work can be done safely.
Moist air limits cooling through sweat while a person works. In hot conditions this can reduce safe working time and increase the risk of illness or injury.
City heat plans can protect workers when they include enforceable rules and practical support for safer work. A plan without workplace measures may leave this exposure unchanged.
Warming makes strenuous work outdoors or in uncooled buildings more difficult and dangerous. Workers may need more rest and shorter exposure to avoid heat illness.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: People working in hot conditions may need more rest and may be unable to work safely for as long. Risks depend on the task, humidity, clothing and available protection.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

response.defaultDriver: Warmer conditions can make jobs in hot environments more strenuous and dangerous. Humidity and physical effort affect how much work can be done safely.
levers: City heat plans can protect workers when they include enforceable rules and practical support for safer work. A plan without workplace measures may leave this exposure unchanged.

data centers.name: Data Centers
data centers.description: Buildings filled with computers that store information and run online services. The computers need electricity, and their heat must be removed. Their environmental effects depend on the power supply, cooling system, water use and location.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Large computing facilities use substantial electricity in one place. Added demand can strain local or regional power systems, particularly at busy times.
Connecting large computing facilities requires transformers and substation equipment. This adds demand to a supply chain that may already have long delivery times.
Computing facilities often need to keep operating during power cuts. On-site generators are one common way they provide that backup supply.
More computing equipment increases demand for advanced chips. Making those chips uses energy, water, chemicals and other materials.
Servers, networking and cooling use electricity whose fossil-fuel share produces carbon dioxide. Fuel burned in on-site backup generators adds direct emissions that should be reported separately.

human.summary: Large computing facilities need dependable electricity and cooling. Rapid growth can put pressure on local power, water and land systems.
consequences: New electricity demand may require expensive network upgrades.
Water used for cooling can compete with household, farming or environmental needs.

planet.summary: Computing facilities have a physical footprint through electricity, cooling water and construction. Impacts depend strongly on energy sources and local water conditions.
consequences: Continuous demand can prolong fossil generation where cleaner supply is insufficient.
Cooling can add pressure to water already shared with ecosystems.

response.defaultDriver: Buildings filled with computers that store information and run online services. The computers need electricity, and their heat must be removed. Their environmental effects depend on the power supply, cooling system, water use and location.
levers: As online services grow, plan how to keep their equipment powered and cool. Check that local water supplies can meet its needs.
Use independent routes and tested backups where shared failures could interrupt essential communication.

ai data centers.name: AI Data Centers
ai data centers.description: Computing facilities used to train or run artificial intelligence systems. Powerful processors can use large amounts of electricity and produce heat that needs to be removed. The resulting water use and pollution depend on the equipment, cooling method and energy supply.
incoming: Fast international cable links help move data and deliver computing services between facilities. Data-centre growth also depends on electricity, chips, land-based networks and customer demand.
outgoing: Rapid growth in computing for artificial intelligence can add concentrated electricity demand. Power connections and supply may struggle when this grows faster than the network's capacity or flexibility.
More artificial intelligence computing can increase data-centre electricity use. The associated carbon dioxide depends on how much of the electricity supplied is generated from fossil fuels.

More artificial intelligence computing increases demand for advanced chips and memory. Manufacturers may respond by running existing factories more heavily or building additional production and packaging capacity.
Dense computing equipment produces heat that must be removed. Facilities using cooling towers can consume water that other local users also need.

human.summary: Rapid growth in artificial intelligence computing can add large amounts of electricity demand in one place. Communities may face pressure on water supplies, network capacity and costs.
consequences: Fast power-system upgrades can affect customer bills, depending on how costs are shared.
Water-intensive cooling can add competition in already dry river basins.

planet.summary: Rapid expansion of artificial intelligence computing increases demand for power, cooling and hardware. Environmental effects depend on how that growth is supplied.
consequences: Fossil-fuel generation may continue where new cleaner power cannot keep pace.
Water-intensive cooling can add to stress on rivers and other water users.

response.defaultDriver: Fast international cable links help move data and deliver computing services between facilities. Data-centre growth also depends on electricity, chips, land-based networks and customer demand.

Use independent routes and tested backups where shared failures could interrupt essential communication.

semiconductor fabs.name: Semiconductor Fabs
semiconductor fabs.description: Factories that make the tiny chips used in phones, computers and many other devices. Making these chips needs very clean water, power and carefully handled chemicals. It also creates waste and releases gases. The effects on nearby land, water and air depend on how the factory is run.
incoming: More artificial intelligence computing increases demand for advanced chips and memory. Manufacturers may respond by running existing factories more heavily or building additional production and packaging capacity.
outgoing: Chip factories need very clean water for production and cooling. In places with limited supplies, that use can compete with households, other businesses and nature.
Chip factories use electricity, water, chemicals and process gases and create waste. Together these flows describe the resources used and pollution associated with the factories covered.
Chip factories use large amounts of electricity and some heat-trapping process gases. Carbon dioxide from energy use must be distinguished from other greenhouse gases released during manufacture.

human.summary: Chip factories need reliable electricity, very clean water and careful chemical handling. A disruption at a few concentrated sites can affect many industries.
consequences: Large factories may compete with other users for dependable power and water.
Air emissions, wastewater and workplace chemicals need effective controls.

planet.summary: Making chips uses electricity, very clean water and specialised chemicals. Some process gases add a warming effect beyond the emissions from power use.
consequences: Factories can place large water and energy demands in the same industrial region.
Heat-trapping process gases and local pollutants need separate controls.

response.defaultDriver: More artificial intelligence computing increases demand for advanced chips and memory. Manufacturers may respond by running existing factories more heavily or building additional production and packaging capacity.
levers: As online services grow, plan how to keep their equipment powered and cool. Check that local water supplies can meet its needs.
Use independent routes and tested backups where shared failures could interrupt essential communication.

telecom backbone.name: Telecom Backbone
telecom backbone.description: The main cables and equipment that carry phone and internet traffic between cities and countries. Many local connections depend on this network. Keeping it running requires electricity and reliable physical routes, which can be disrupted by damage or extreme conditions.
incoming: Undersea fibre cables carry information between coastal landing stations and land-based networks. They provide important international connections for calls, data and online services.
outgoing: The equipment carrying internet traffic over long distances needs electricity. Its indirect carbon dioxide emissions depend on the fossil-fuel share of that power supply.
Long-distance data routes connect network operators to facilities where they exchange traffic. Those facilities depend on the routes remaining available.
Mobile networks need wider cable and core networks to carry information beyond a local radio mast. A working mast alone does not provide an end-to-end connection.
Failure of major data routes or switching equipment can interrupt communications used by power, water, transport and emergency services. Alternative paths determine how much service continues.

human.summary: The main routes carrying digital traffic support everyday communication and services. Concentrated failures can disrupt much more than the equipment at one site.
consequences: Broken routes or switching systems can interrupt communication across a wide area.
Operating and expanding networks uses electricity.

planet.summary: Major digital networks need physical equipment, electricity and maintenance. Their wider documented risks also concern disruption to connected human services.
consequences: Moving and switching data uses energy across a distributed network.
Growing traffic requires equipment and supporting facilities.

mobile towers / wireless.name: Mobile Towers / Wireless
mobile towers / wireless.description: Antennas and equipment that connect mobile devices without a cable to each user. The equipment still needs electricity and links to the wider communications network. Power cuts, heat or damaged connections can interrupt service.
incoming: Mobile networks need wider cable and core networks to carry information beyond a local radio mast. A working mast alone does not provide an end-to-end connection.
Places where networks connect allow mobile services to exchange traffic with internet and cloud providers. Independent backup connections help keep that exchange available.
outgoing: Mobile networks use electricity for radio equipment and supporting systems. Fossil-fuel electricity and diesel backup generators release carbon dioxide while supplying that power.
Losing mobile masts, connecting cables or backup power can interrupt public warnings and emergency communication. Distributed equipment still needs reliable supporting services.

human.summary: Mobile service depends on radio sites, connecting networks and power working together. People can lose access even when only the local part fails.
consequences: A power cut can outlast the backup supply at a radio site.
Households still need a working local connection even when major internet routes are available.

planet.summary: Radio sites and connecting equipment extend a physical network across cities and rural areas. Their environmental footprint includes materials, electricity and backup power.
consequences: More sites require more equipment and maintenance.
Backup fuel use can add emissions where normal power is unreliable.

response.defaultDriver: Mobile networks need wider cable and core networks to carry information beyond a local radio mast. A working mast alone does not provide an end-to-end connection.

internet exchange points.name: Internet Exchange Points
internet exchange points.description: Places where separate computer networks connect and pass online traffic to one another. These hubs help information reach its destination. Damage or a power failure at an important hub can affect many services at once.
incoming: Long-distance data routes connect network operators to facilities where they exchange traffic. Those facilities depend on the routes remaining available.
outgoing: Places where networks connect allow mobile services to exchange traffic with internet and cloud providers. Independent backup connections help keep that exchange available.
A large network exchange can become a shared failure point if power, cooling or route options are limited. Several dependent services may be interrupted together.

human.summary: Facilities where networks exchange traffic help calls and online services reach their destinations. A small number of sites can support a large share of local connectivity.
consequences: A shared failure can interrupt several networks at once.
Fast local access to hosted services depends on reliable connections between networks.

planet.summary: Network exchange facilities need power, cooling and buildings. The main effects established here concern communication reliability, rather than a measured direct loss of wildlife or habitat.
consequences: Several networks can depend on the same physical facility.
Reliable local power and cooling are essential to its operation.

response.defaultDriver: Long-distance data routes connect network operators to facilities where they exchange traffic. Those facilities depend on the routes remaining available.

subsea cables.name: Subsea Cables
subsea cables.description: Long communication lines laid on the seabed to carry information between places. They connect to land at coastal stations. If a busy route or landing station is damaged, internet and other communications can be disrupted.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Undersea fibre cables carry information between coastal landing stations and land-based networks. They provide important international connections for calls, data and online services.
Fast international cable links help move data and deliver computing services between facilities. Data-centre growth also depends on electricity, chips, land-based networks and customer demand.
Damage to an undersea cable can interrupt services that depend on it. The disruption is greater where there are few alternative routes, landing points or spare connections.
Submarine Cable Landing-Site Concentration and Exposure
Several cables sharing a landing area, power supply or land connection may fail together. More cables provide protection only when these supporting routes and services are sufficiently independent.

human.summary: International online services rely on physical cables and their coastal connections. Damage can have wide effects where independent routes are limited.
consequences: A small number of damaged routes can interrupt communication and trade.
Repairs can take time and require access, ships and cooperation across borders.

planet.summary: The main documented concern here is dependence on a limited number of physical ocean routes and coastal connections. These records do not quantify a separate direct ecosystem impact.
consequences: A few routes may support a large share of communication.
Repairs depend on physical access and suitable vessels.

response.defaultDriver: Damage can arise from anchors, fishing activity and natural hazards. Concentrating routes without independent backups increases disruption risk.
levers: Provide separate routes and tested backup capacity for essential links.
Maintain repair arrangements and protect exposed cable corridors from relevant local hazards.

food waste.name: Food Waste
food waste.description: Food being lost or thrown away instead of being eaten. The land, water and energy used to produce it are then spent without providing a meal. Food rotting without much oxygen, such as in landfill, can also release a powerful heat-trapping gas.
incoming: Food can be lost at each step from farming to storage, shops and homes. How much is wasted depends on facilities and behaviour, rather than a fixed share of food demand.
Growing cities concentrate food shops, restaurants and households, creating more opportunities for waste. Storage, transport and collection practices determine how much is actually discarded.
Broken refrigeration can leave perishable food at unsafe temperatures. Food may spoil before it can be sold or eaten.
outgoing: Food in landfill can decay with little oxygen and produce methane. The amount released depends on waste handling and whether the gas is captured.

human.summary: Food discarded before it is eaten wastes money and the land, water and energy used to produce it. Preventing waste can improve how much useful food people get from those resources.

planet.summary: Food in landfill can decay with little oxygen and produce methane. The amount released depends on waste handling and whether the gas is captured.

response.defaultDriver: Food can be lost at each step from farming to storage, shops and homes. How much is wasted depends on facilities and behaviour, rather than a fixed share of food demand.
levers: Use farming practices suited to the local soil, water and climate, with protection for workers and livestock.
Keep soils covered where appropriate, limit avoidable nutrient and chemical losses, and manage total water use rather than efficiency alone.

aviation.name: Aviation
aviation.description: Travel and freight carried by aircraft. Burning jet fuel releases carbon dioxide, while other emissions and the clouds aircraft can leave behind also affect the climate. Airports add their own needs for land, electricity and transport connections.
incoming: More demand for passenger or cargo flights can increase aircraft activity and fuel use. Aircraft efficiency, how full flights are and other operating changes affect the size of the increase.
outgoing: Aircraft and cargo can move living organisms to places they would not normally reach. Most do not establish harmful populations, so flight numbers cannot be treated as a count of invasions.
Aircraft release carbon dioxide when they burn jet fuel. The total applies to the flights and fuel use included in the source's accounting.

human.summary: Aircraft release carbon dioxide when they burn jet fuel. The total applies to the flights and fuel use included in the source's accounting. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.

planet.summary: Aircraft and cargo can move living organisms to places they would not normally reach. Most do not establish harmful populations, so flight numbers cannot be treated as a count of invasions.
consequences: Aircraft release carbon dioxide when they burn jet fuel. The total applies to the flights and fuel use included in the source's accounting.

response.defaultDriver: Growing travel demand and dependence on fossil jet fuel sustain emissions, while warming adds operating challenges.
levers: Use local forecasts and aircraft performance limits when planning departures.
Reduce avoidable fuel use and plan airport adaptations around local heat, flood and land constraints.

shipping.name: Shipping
shipping.description: Moving people or goods by water. Vessels need energy, often from burning fuel, and depend on ports and usable routes. Their effects include air pollution, gases that warm the planet and pressure on marine environments.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Delays and detours at sea can make ships arrive together or disrupt planned schedules. Ports may then struggle to unload, store and move the accumulated cargo.
Ship engines can release soot when they burn fuel. Winds may carry some of it to snow and ice, especially in nearby regions.
Sulfur in ship fuel can form sulfur dioxide during burning. Fuel standards and exhaust-cleaning equipment determine how much escapes.
Ship engines can produce carbon monoxide when fuel burns incompletely. A useful estimate needs details about the engine, fuel and how the vessel operates.
Collisions, running aground and fuel transfers can damage a vessel or its fuel lines. Spilled fuel can then enter a river, canal or nearby shore.
Ships running aground or dropping anchors can crush, break or bury corals. The damage is concentrated around the incident and any removal work.

Ships can carry organisms in stored water, on their hulls or with cargo. An introduced species becomes invasive only if it establishes, spreads and causes harm. Transport or detection alone does not prove that.
Ships release carbon dioxide when they burn marine fuel. The total depends on vessel activity and whether the source covers domestic shipping, international shipping or both.

human.summary: Delays and detours at sea can make ships arrive together or disrupt planned schedules. Ports may then struggle to unload, store and move the accumulated cargo.
consequences: Ship engines can produce carbon monoxide when fuel burns incompletely. A useful estimate needs details about the engine, fuel and how the vessel operates. Breathing carbon monoxide reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen. Risk depends on the amount breathed, exposure time and the person's condition. Detecting the gas alone does not measure health harm.

Ships release carbon dioxide when they burn marine fuel. The total depends on vessel activity and whether the source covers domestic shipping, international shipping or both. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.

consequences: Sulfur in ship fuel can form sulfur dioxide during burning. Fuel standards and exhaust-cleaning equipment determine how much escapes.
Ship engines can produce carbon monoxide when fuel burns incompletely. A useful estimate needs details about the engine, fuel and how the vessel operates.

response.defaultDriver: Long-lived ships, trade demand and limited clean-fuel supply keep much shipping dependent on fossil energy.
levers: Use cleaner fuels and equipment that reduce soot and heat-trapping emissions.
Plan routes and speeds to reduce fuel use and protect sensitive polar habitats.

cement / concrete.name: Cement / Concrete
cement / concrete.description: Materials widely used to build roads, bridges and buildings. Making the powder that binds concrete requires high heat and releases carbon dioxide when limestone is processed. Fuel use, quarrying and the amount of material needed all affect the total impact.
incoming: More buildings and infrastructure can increase demand for cement and concrete. Reuse, material-saving design and construction standards can reduce the amount of new material needed.
outgoing: Making the binding ingredient in concrete releases carbon dioxide when limestone is chemically changed. This process release is separate from the fuel burned to heat the kiln.
Conventional cement production releases carbon dioxide both from heating raw materials and from the chemical change in limestone. Both sources matter within the production total.

human.summary: Conventional cement production releases carbon dioxide both from heating raw materials and from the chemical change in limestone. Both sources matter within the production total. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.
consequences: Making the binding ingredient in concrete releases carbon dioxide when limestone is chemically changed. This process release is separate from the fuel burned to heat the kiln. Chemically changing limestone to make cement releases carbon dioxide. Fuel used to heat the process adds a separate contribution. Both are included when assessing total production emissions.

planet.summary: Conventional cement production releases carbon dioxide both from heating raw materials and from the chemical change in limestone. Both sources matter within the production total.
consequences: Making the binding ingredient in concrete releases carbon dioxide when limestone is chemically changed. This process release is separate from the fuel burned to heat the kiln. Chemically changing limestone to make cement releases carbon dioxide. Fuel used to heat the process adds a separate contribution. Both are included when assessing total production emissions.

response.defaultDriver: More buildings and infrastructure can increase demand for cement and concrete. Reuse, material-saving design and construction standards can reduce the amount of new material needed.
levers: Plan electricity supply, networks and demand together so cleaner options remain dependable.
Improve efficiency and maintain equipment, with backup arrangements suited to essential services and local hazards.

steel.name: Steel
steel.description: An iron-based material used in buildings, vehicles and machinery. Producing it can require mining, very high temperatures and large amounts of energy. Its climate impact depends on the production method, energy source and use of recycled metal.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Conventional metal production can rely on large amounts of coal and energy. Replacing that equipment and its supply systems takes investment and suitable lower-emission alternatives.
Sulfur in steelmaking fuels and raw materials can be released as sulfur dioxide. Capture and treatment equipment affect the final amount emitted.
Conventional steelmaking releases carbon dioxide from fuels, processing materials and energy use. The amount depends on the production route and which electricity emissions are included.
Conventional steelmaking uses large amounts of ore, fuel and other materials. More efficient production and recycled steel can reduce demand for newly extracted resources.

human.summary: This material supports buildings and transport, but making it can expose workers and nearby communities to heat and pollution. Replacing long-lived plants also affects industrial jobs and costs.
consequences: Each production stage needs protection suited to its machinery, heat and chemical exposures.
Polluting gases and metals from large mills require controls at their sources.

planet.summary: Conventional production uses coal, high heat and large amounts of mined material. Cleaner processes and recycling can reduce some of this footprint.
consequences: Reported greenhouse-gas totals depend on which production and energy stages are included.
Long-lived furnaces can keep coal-based methods in use for decades.

response.defaultDriver: Expensive, long-lived coal-based plants and weak demand for cleaner steel can delay change.
levers: Use materials efficiently, recover good-quality scrap and expand cleaner production where supplies support it.
Plan clean energy, new equipment and support for workers together, backed by credible product standards.

plastics / petrochemicals.name: Plastics / Petrochemicals
plastics / petrochemicals.description: Materials and chemicals commonly made from oil and gas, including packaging, fabrics and solvents. Making them uses energy and raw materials. Pollution can arise during production, use and disposal, including when waste reaches rivers or the sea.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Making plastics and related chemicals uses fossil raw materials and energy. Production and some disposal methods can release carbon dioxide.
Making and handling petrochemical products can release gases from processing, storage and evaporation. The type and amount depend on the product and pollution controls.

Wear, processing and weathering can release tiny plastic fibres or fragments that enter the air. Plastic use alone does not measure airborne releases, and suspected particles need chemical confirmation.
Making new plastics uses fossil raw materials, energy, water and other resources. Reuse and recycled inputs can reduce some of the demand for new material.
Plastic entering the sea can expose animals to particles and associated chemicals. Effects on feeding relationships depend on particle type, dose and other environmental stresses.

human.summary: Making plastics and related chemicals uses fossil raw materials and energy. Production and some disposal methods can release carbon dioxide. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.
consequences: Making new plastics uses fossil raw materials, energy, water and other resources. Reuse and recycled inputs can reduce some of the demand for new material. Shortages of important resources can worsen existing tensions. Conflict risk depends strongly on how resources are shared and whether institutions can resolve disputes fairly.

Plastic entering the sea can expose animals to particles and associated chemicals. Effects on feeding relationships depend on particle type, dose and other environmental stresses. Changes in feeding relationships can alter which fish are available and when. Fishing businesses may receive a less predictable mix or quantity of seafood.

planet.summary: Making plastics and related chemicals uses fossil raw materials and energy. Production and some disposal methods can release carbon dioxide.
consequences: Making and handling petrochemical products can release gases from processing, storage and evaporation. The type and amount depend on the product and pollution controls.

Wear, processing and weathering can release tiny plastic fibres or fragments that enter the air. Plastic use alone does not measure airborne releases, and suspected particles need chemical confirmation.

response.defaultDriver: Large existing fossil-fuel factories and demand for cheap new plastic make alternatives harder to expand.
levers: Reduce unnecessary material use and make products easier to reuse, collect and recycle.
Use cleaner energy and compare the full emissions of proposed production and recycling methods.

air conditioning / refrigerants.name: Air Conditioning / Refrigerants
air conditioning / refrigerants.description: Equipment that moves heat out of rooms using electricity and circulating cooling gases. Some of those gases strongly warm the planet if they leak into the air. The total climate effect depends on the gas, leak prevention and electricity source.
incoming: Replacing powerful heat-trapping cooling gases, preventing leaks and recovering old gases can reduce emissions from cooling equipment. Safe installation and servicing are part of making this work.
More dangerous hot and humid weather increases demand for cooling. More equipment can mean more opportunities for heat-trapping cooling gases to leak unless they are properly managed.
City growth adds buildings needing cooling and surfaces that store heat. This can increase both air-conditioning use and the amount of cooling gas in equipment.
outgoing: Working cooling systems can help prevent hot conditions from becoming a health emergency. Their protection depends on access, affordability and reliable power.

Older cooling equipment can leak CFCs or HCFCs that damage the ozone layer. This pathway excludes modern replacement gases that contain no ozone-damaging chlorine or bromine, and equipment counts alone do not measure leaks.

human.summary: Working cooling systems can help prevent hot conditions from becoming a health emergency. Their protection depends on access, affordability and reliable power.

planet.summary: Older cooling equipment can leak CFCs or HCFCs that damage the ozone layer. This pathway excludes modern replacement gases that contain no ozone-damaging chlorine or bromine, and equipment counts alone do not measure leaks.

response.defaultDriver: Growing cooling demand and continued use of high-warming gases increase the potential for leaks.
levers: Replace high-warming gases with suitable lower-impact options and improve energy efficiency.
Train technicians, check leaks and recover gases when equipment is retired.

fertilizer production.name: Fertilizer Production
fertilizer production.description: Making substances that supply nutrients to crops. Manufacturing nitrogen-based products often uses fossil gas and large amounts of energy. Production and later use can release pollution, so factory emissions and effects on farms need to be assessed separately.
incoming: Growing more crops increases demand for nutrients to replace those removed at harvest. This can increase the production of manufactured fertilisers.
outgoing: Manufactured plant nutrients can support higher crop yields where soil nutrients limit growth. This makes repeated high-output cropping possible, alongside its other resource needs.
Making and using fertilisers increases the amount of nitrogen and phosphorus available in the environment. Some can escape into rivers and coastal waters if losses are not controlled.
Making nitric acid for some fertilisers produces nitrous oxide as a by-product. This link applies to that manufacturing process, not to every type of fertiliser production.

human.summary: Manufactured plant nutrients can support higher crop yields where soil nutrients limit growth. This makes repeated high-output cropping possible, alongside its other resource needs. Irrigated farms draw water from supplies also needed by households, businesses and rivers. Heavy use can leave less available during dry periods.

planet.summary: Making and using fertilisers increases the amount of nitrogen and phosphorus available in the environment. Some can escape into rivers and coastal waters if losses are not controlled.
consequences: Making nitric acid for some fertilisers produces nitrous oxide as a by-product. This link applies to that manufacturing process, not to every type of fertiliser production.

response.defaultDriver: Growing more crops increases demand for nutrients to replace those removed at harvest. This can increase the production of manufactured fertilisers.
levers: Use farming practices suited to the local soil, water and climate, with protection for workers and livestock.
Keep soils covered where appropriate, limit avoidable nutrient and chemical losses, and manage total water use rather than efficiency alone.

mining / critical minerals.name: Mining / Critical Minerals
mining / critical minerals.description: Extracting raw materials used in batteries, electrical networks and electronics. Mining can disturb land, use water and energy, and leave waste that needs careful management. Its effects depend on the material, location and safeguards at the site.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Extracting minerals directly creates demands for land, water, energy and waste management. Greater activity can increase these pressures in the places where extraction occurs.
Mines can directly remove forest, while their roads and settlements open nearby areas to further clearing. The wider loss depends on local development and forest protection.
Collecting material from the seabed and releasing processing water can stir up fine particles. These form cloudy plumes near the bottom or within the water above it.
Mining and processing can release metals from waste, drainage and disturbed material. Some can enter water, food and animal tissues.

More mining, especially of poorer-quality deposits, can require more rock, water and energy for each useful amount of mineral. Recycling and production methods affect the resulting demand for new resources.

human.summary: Extracting minerals directly creates demands for land, water, energy and waste management. Greater activity can increase these pressures in the places where extraction occurs. Making more batteries requires reliable supplies of mined and processed materials. Constraints and environmental pressures at those stages carry through to battery production.
consequences: Mines can directly remove forest, while their roads and settlements open nearby areas to further clearing. The wider loss depends on local development and forest protection. Clearing forests changes shade, standing water, wildlife and contact between people and insects. In some tropical settings, these changes favour mosquitoes that carry disease, but the effect is not universal.

More mining, especially of poorer-quality deposits, can require more rock, water and energy for each useful amount of mineral. Recycling and production methods affect the resulting demand for new resources. Shortages of important resources can worsen existing tensions. Conflict risk depends strongly on how resources are shared and whether institutions can resolve disputes fairly.

planet.summary: Mines can directly remove forest, while their roads and settlements open nearby areas to further clearing. The wider loss depends on local development and forest protection.
consequences: Collecting material from the seabed and releasing processing water can stir up fine particles. These form cloudy plumes near the bottom or within the water above it.
Mining and processing can release metals from waste, drainage and disturbed material. Some can enter water, food and animal tissues.

response.defaultDriver: Rising demand and limited recovery of used materials increase pressure to open or expand mines.
levers: Check how each mine will use water and deal with waste. Give local people a real say in those plans.
Improve recovery, reuse and recycling, and test new extraction methods against actual local impacts.

measurement.geography: declared facility, industry class, country, trade region, or supply-chain boundary
measurement.cadence: monthly or annual according to production and inventory reporting

urban sprawl / housing.name: Urban Sprawl / Housing
urban sprawl / housing.description: Homes and roads spreading outward over larger areas, often with buildings far apart. This can replace farmland or wildlife habitat and make longer car journeys more likely. Construction and the need to extend services also use materials and energy.
incoming: Growing cities may spread outward into more land when housing, roads and planning favour low-density development. City growth does not always take this form.
Good public transport can support homes and services closer together. Housing and planning policies need to support that pattern for outward spread to slow.
outgoing: Outward housing growth often adds roads and other paved areas. Dark pavement absorbs sunlight and stores heat that is later released into the surroundings.
Building outward can remove trees and cover soil with roads and buildings. Tree cover can shrink if development does not protect existing trees or provide suitable space for replacements.
Outward housing growth can replace vegetation with roofs, roads and other surfaces that store heat. This can increase local warming within built-up areas.

human.summary: Homes spread far from jobs and services can increase travel time, fuel costs and the cost of providing roads and utilities. Effects depend on transport choices and how neighbourhoods are planned.

planet.summary: Outward housing growth can replace vegetation with roofs, roads and other surfaces that store heat. This can increase local warming within built-up areas.
consequences: Outward housing growth often adds roads and other paved areas. Dark pavement absorbs sunlight and stores heat that is later released into the surroundings. Dark asphalt absorbs sunlight during the day and releases stored heat later. Large paved areas can keep nearby places warmer after sunset.

Building outward can remove trees and cover soil with roads and buildings. Tree cover can shrink if development does not protect existing trees or provide suitable space for replacements. Losing trees removes shade and some natural cooling. Neighbourhoods can store more daytime heat and remain warmer at night, leaving less relief for residents.

response.defaultDriver: Growing cities may spread outward into more land when housing, roads and planning favour low-density development. City growth does not always take this form.
levers: Good public transport can support homes and services closer together. Housing and planning policies need to support that pattern for outward spread to slow.

clean electricity.name: Clean Electricity
clean electricity.description: Power produced with little release of gases that warm the planet. It can help cut pollution when it replaces fossil-fuel power or supplies transport and heating. Its wider effects still depend on how equipment is built, where it is placed and how the grid operates.
incoming: Adding wind, solar and other renewable power can increase electricity made with low emissions. The benefit depends on connecting the supply and keeping the power system reliable.
Storing electricity allows power generated at one time to be used later. This can help the system use more wind and solar power when demand and supply do not match.
Moving flexible electricity use to times when cleaner power is available can make it easier to use that supply. The benefit depends on which demand can safely change time.
Closing coal-fired power stations can make room for electricity with lower emissions. Replacement power and reliable service need to be planned together.
Delays in building power lines can keep new low-emissions electricity from reaching users. Generation alone is not enough if the network cannot carry it.
outgoing: Electricity with lower emissions can replace power made by burning fossil fuels. It can also reduce emissions when it replaces fuel burning in transport, heating and industry.
Replacing local fuel-burning power stations with cleaner electricity can reduce nearby air pollution. The improvement depends on which plants reduce output or close.
Heat pumps use electricity to move heat. Their climate benefit grows as the electricity they use is produced with fewer emissions.
Charging vehicles with electricity made using fewer fossil fuels reduces the emissions from driving them. Electric vehicles still require materials, roads and space.
Low-emissions electricity can power electric steel furnaces and the production of hydrogen used in some steelmaking methods. The benefit depends on the whole production process.
Cleaner electricity can reduce emissions from parts of cement production, including some heating and carbon-capture equipment. Other emissions from the raw materials still need to be addressed.
Some methods that take carbon dioxide out of the air need large amounts of energy. Using low-emissions electricity helps avoid creating new emissions that cancel part of the removal.

human.summary: Replacing fuel-burning power with lower-emissions electricity can improve air quality and reduce reliance on fossil fuels. Benefits depend on which generation is actually replaced.
consequences: Nearby communities can breathe less pollution when fossil-fuel plants reduce output or close.
Less fuel use can reduce exposure to sudden fossil-fuel price rises.

planet.summary: Low-emissions electricity can reduce the climate impact of power and the activities that switch to using it. The benefit depends on replacing higher-emissions supply.
consequences: Fewer long-lived greenhouse gases are released when fossil generation is displaced.
Less fossil fuel may need to be extracted and burned.

response.defaultDriver: Projects depend on equipment, skilled workers, land and dependable connections to the grid.
levers: Build generation and networks together, with enough dependable supply to replace high-emitting plants.
Protect communities and habitats when choosing sites and sharing benefits.

measurement.metric: Low-emissions electricity generation and share of total generation
measurement.geography: declared country, balancing area, utility territory, facility class, or project portfolio
measurement.cadence: hourly to annual according to the source release

coal power retirement.name: Coal Power Retirement
coal power retirement.description: Closing power stations that burn coal for good, and replacing the power they provide. This can cut air pollution and releases of carbon dioxide. The change also needs a reliable new power supply and support for workers and local people.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Closing coal-fired power stations can make room for electricity with lower emissions. Replacement power and reliable service need to be planned together.
Closing coal-fired power stations stops their fuel-burning emissions. The overall reduction depends on what replaces their electricity.
Closing coal-fired power stations removes a source of smoke and other harmful air pollutants. Cleaner replacement power helps preserve that improvement.

Replacing coal power with lower-emissions electricity reduces a source of future warming. This can ease future heat-related health risks, alongside the more immediate benefit of less combustion pollution.

human.summary: Closing coal-fired plants can reduce harmful pollution around them. Planning replacement power and support for workers helps communities share the benefits.
consequences: Less coal burning reduces fine particles and sulfur pollution.
Lower exposure can reduce related health burdens.

planet.summary: Retiring coal power can reduce carbon dioxide and other environmental damage when replacement generation is cleaner.
consequences: The closed plant stops its fuel-burning emissions.
Lower coal demand can reduce mining and ash-disposal pressures.

response.defaultDriver: Replacement capacity must provide dependable power when the coal plant closes.
levers: Set closure dates alongside reliable replacement supply.
Fund retraining, pensions and new local opportunities rather than leaving communities to manage alone.

measurement.metric: Coal-fired generating capacity retired
measurement.geography: declared country, balancing area, utility territory, facility class, or project portfolio
measurement.cadence: hourly to annual according to the source release

renewable energy deployment.name: Renewable Energy Deployment
renewable energy deployment.description: Building and using power sources such as wind and sunlight that are naturally replenished. They can replace electricity made from fossil fuels. Grids, storage and careful siting help make that replacement reliable and limit damage to nearby communities and habitats.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Adding wind, solar and other renewable power can increase electricity made with low emissions. The benefit depends on connecting the supply and keeping the power system reliable.
Wind, solar and other renewable sources can reduce carbon dioxide emissions when their electricity replaces fossil-fuel generation. Adding capacity alone does not guarantee that replacement.
New wind and solar plants may generate more power than the network can use at some times. Without enough power lines, storage or flexible demand, some available output must be turned down.
Building renewable power equipment, wiring and storage requires minerals. Rapid construction can increase pressure on mining and processing, depending on material choices and recycling.

human.summary: Wind, solar and other renewable sources can reduce pollution when they replace fuel-burning generation. They also give regions more ways to supply their own energy.
consequences: Avoided fuel burning can improve local air quality.
Wind and sunlight have no fuel price, which can make some operating costs steadier.

planet.summary: Renewable generation can reduce fossil-fuel use and emissions when it replaces existing supply. Siting and the type of technology still matter.
consequences: Power-sector greenhouse-gas releases can fall.
Less continued fossil-fuel extraction may be needed.

response.defaultDriver: Useful output depends on the resource, location, network and ability to handle variable generation.
levers: Coordinate new generation with transmission, storage and demand flexibility.
Choose sites with habitat protection and community participation, while improving approval processes.

measurement.metric: Renewable electricity capacity added by technology
measurement.geography: declared country, balancing area, utility territory, facility class, or project portfolio
measurement.cadence: hourly to annual according to the source release

grid-scale energy storage.name: Grid-Scale Energy Storage
grid-scale energy storage.description: Saving energy for use later across an electricity network. Batteries and other systems can supply power when production is low or demand is high. This helps balance supply and demand, although different technologies store different amounts for different lengths of time.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Storing electricity allows power generated at one time to be used later. This can help the system use more wind and solar power when demand and supply do not match.
Storage can save wind and solar electricity that would otherwise go unused. It can release that energy later, within its capacity and operating limits.
Stored electricity can be released when demand is high and supply is tight. This helps only while enough stored energy and delivery capacity remain available.
Reliable storage can supply electricity during busy hours. Where it can meet the required demand, it can reduce reliance on fossil-fuel plants used mainly at those times.
Building large battery stores increases demand for minerals, processing and manufacturing. The pressure depends on the type of storage, its lifespan and the use of recycled materials.

human.summary: Stored electricity can help bridge gaps between generation and demand. Its protection lasts only within the store's power and energy limits.
consequences: It can make supply more reliable during short gaps.
It may replace some expensive, polluting generation used at busy times.

planet.summary: Storage can help use low-emissions electricity that would otherwise go unused. Its own materials and energy losses still need to be considered.
consequences: Wind and solar output can be saved for later use.
Dependable stored power can replace some fossil generation.

response.defaultDriver: Every system has limits on how much power it supplies and for how long. Energy must first be available to store.
levers: Use a mix of storage suited to the hours or days of flexibility needed.
Require safe operation, responsible mineral sourcing and recovery of materials at the end of use.

measurement.metric: Grid-scale storage power and energy capacity
measurement.geography: declared country, balancing area, utility territory, facility class, or project portfolio
measurement.cadence: hourly to annual according to the source release

demand response.name: Demand Response
demand response.description: Changing when electricity is used to ease pressure on the power system. For example, suitable equipment can run earlier or later instead of during the busiest hours. This can reduce the need to start additional power plants, provided essential needs are protected.
incoming: When electricity demand approaches available supply, moving some use to another time becomes more valuable. Only demand that can safely change should be shifted.
outgoing: Moving flexible electricity use to times when cleaner power is available can make it easier to use that supply. The benefit depends on which demand can safely change time.
Reducing or moving flexible electricity use during busy hours eases pressure on the power system. The benefit depends on how much demand actually changes.
Dependable reductions in busy-hour electricity use can replace some need for extra power plants. The savings must be reliable enough for the system to plan around them.
Fair payments for changing electricity use can help participating households afford their bills. The benefit depends on programme design and whether households can participate safely.
Moving flexible electricity use to cleaner hours can reduce emissions if it actually changes which generators run. Extra use later must not cancel the avoided emissions.

human.summary: Shifting flexible electricity use can help the power system cope with busy hours. People need fair payment and protection against unsafe or unaffordable participation.
consequences: Lower peak demand can reduce some electricity costs.
Reliable flexibility can reduce outage risk when supply is tight.

planet.summary: Moving flexible electricity use can make better use of existing low-emissions supply. Benefits depend on what generation and equipment are actually avoided.
consequences: Fossil plants used mainly at busy hours may run less.
More available cleaner electricity can be used.

response.defaultDriver: Some activities can move to another time. Medical equipment and other essential needs may not be flexible.
levers: Protect essential use, allow people to opt out and reward useful verified changes.
Combine suitable automation with efficient appliances and help for households facing high bills.

measurement.metric: Verified demand-response capacity and dispatched load reduction
measurement.geography: declared country, balancing area, utility territory, facility class, or project portfolio
measurement.cadence: hourly to annual according to the source release

occurrences.title: Small data centers, big impact: How demand response can fuel the energy transition

methane leak detection and repair.name: Methane Leak Detection and Repair
methane leak detection and repair.description: Finding and fixing places where a powerful heat-trapping gas escapes from equipment. Sensors, inspections, aircraft and satellites can help locate leaks. Reducing releases depends on repairs being completed and checked, not just on spotting them.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Finding gas leaks can reduce methane releases when operators repair them and check that the repair worked. Measuring a leak by itself does not stop it.
Finding and repairing gas leaks may also reduce harmful pollutants released alongside methane. Local air-quality benefits depend on what the leaking gas contains.

Finding and repairing methane leaks reduces a gas that contributes to ground-level ozone over wider areas. Repairs may also reduce other ozone-forming gases released alongside it, with benefits unfolding over different times and regions.

human.summary: Finding gas leaks helps only when operators fix them and confirm the repair. This can reduce wasted gas and some harmful pollution near facilities.
consequences: Repairs may reduce hazardous substances released alongside the gas.
Less saleable fuel is lost into the air.

planet.summary: Verified repairs stop some releases of a powerful heat-trapping gas. Detection by itself does not deliver the reduction.
consequences: Successful repairs reduce near-term warming pressure.
Measurements make fossil-system releases easier to check.

response.defaultDriver: Detection depends on instruments, weather and leak size. A scan can miss releases occurring at another time.
levers: Use ground, aircraft or satellite observations together to target inspections.
Require prompt repairs and follow-up measurements showing the release has stopped.

measurement.metric: Methane leak-detection coverage and estimated emissions repaired
measurement.geography: declared facility, industry class, country, trade region, or supply-chain boundary
measurement.cadence: monthly or annual according to production and inventory reporting

occurrences.title: Hunt for methane leaks reveals persistent pollution around French oil and gas sites

refrigerant phase-down.name: Refrigerant Phase-Down
refrigerant phase-down.description: Gradually replacing cooling gases that have a strong warming effect with alternatives that have a smaller one. Preventing leaks and recovering gases from old equipment are also important. The aim is to reduce climate pollution while keeping cooling safe and accessible.
incoming: Building rules can encourage safer cooling gases when they count emissions from gas leaks as well as energy use. Rules that ignore leaks may miss this opportunity.
outgoing: Replacing powerful heat-trapping cooling gases, preventing leaks and recovering old gases can reduce emissions from cooling equipment. Safe installation and servicing are part of making this work.

Cooling can be provided with less climate damage when equipment uses less harmful gases and is efficient. Affordable equipment and trained technicians are needed to make this benefit widely available.

Controls on old ozone-damaging gases reduce new supply, while recovery and destruction prevent releases from existing equipment. Improvement is slow because stored gases can still leak and some remain in the air for many decades.
Stratospheric Ozone Column Depletion and Recovery

Reducing ozone-damaging cooling gases lowers the future supply of reactive chlorine and bromine high in the atmosphere. Recovery is slow and uneven because old equipment, long gas lifetimes and weather still matter.

Using less powerful heat-trapping cooling gases and preventing leaks reduces their contribution to warming. The benefit is measured against what would happen if those releases continued without controls.

human.summary: Cooling equipment can use gases with less climate impact while continuing to protect people from heat. Safe installation, repair and recovery of old gases are essential.
consequences: People can retain access to cooling with fewer heat-trapping releases.
Training and proper servicing can improve technician safety.

planet.summary: Changing cooling gases and managing leaks can reduce powerful heat-trapping releases. Old equipment and discarded gas also need careful handling.
consequences: Lower-impact gases can reduce emissions from each leak.
Good servicing and recovery reduce losses over equipment lifetimes.

response.defaultDriver: Alternatives must match equipment and safety needs, including pressure and flammability.
levers: Train technicians and check leaks during use and when equipment is retired.
Pair lower-warming gases with efficient cooling so electricity use does not erase the gains.

measurement.metric: Hydrofluorocarbon production and consumption under Montreal Protocol accounting
measurement.geography: declared facility, industry class, country, trade region, or supply-chain boundary
measurement.cadence: monthly or annual according to production and inventory reporting

occurrences.title: UK HFC phase down stalls

carbon dioxide removal.name: Carbon Dioxide Removal
carbon dioxide removal.description: Taking a heat-trapping gas out of the air and storing it in plants, soils, rocks or other reservoirs. The benefit depends on how much is removed and how long it stays stored. This has limits and does not replace the need to reduce new releases.
incoming: Some methods that take carbon dioxide out of the air need large amounts of energy. Using low-emissions electricity helps avoid creating new emissions that cancel part of the removal.
Recovering plants and soils can take carbon dioxide out of the air and store the carbon. The benefit lasts only as long as that additional carbon remains stored.
outgoing: Taking carbon dioxide out of the air can balance a limited share of ongoing releases. The removal must be extra, measured and stored for long enough to count as a lasting benefit.
Removing carbon dioxide can require land, water, energy and materials. The demands differ greatly between methods and can create pressure on other resources.

human.summary: Taking carbon dioxide out of the air may help address a limited share of emissions that are difficult to eliminate. The benefit depends on verified, lasting storage and the resources used.
consequences: Reliable projects can address some remaining emissions alongside large emissions cuts.
Long-term monitoring and care can create skilled work.

planet.summary: Removing carbon dioxide can help only when storage lasts and the project avoids creating comparable new emissions. Methods have different land, water and energy demands.
consequences: Verified additional removal lowers the amount left in the air.
Some carefully designed land-based methods can improve soils or habitats.

response.defaultDriver: The climate benefit depends on how much is removed after project emissions and how long it stays stored.
levers: Measure removal and storage separately from emissions cuts.
Require lasting storage and clear monitoring, and avoid using uncertain future removal to delay direct cuts.

measurement.metric: Carbon dioxide durably removed and stored by pathway
measurement.geography: declared facility, industry class, country, trade region, or supply-chain boundary
measurement.cadence: monthly or annual according to production and inventory reporting

occurrences.title: Trawling threatens vital carbon stores in Scotland's sea lochs

building energy efficiency.name: Building Energy Efficiency
building energy efficiency.description: Using less power or fuel to keep indoor spaces comfortable and useful. Better insulation, windows, lighting and appliances can provide the same services with less energy. Results depend on installation, maintenance and how the building is used.
incoming: Rules based on a building's measured energy use can encourage upgrades. Clear targets and deadlines help turn those rules into lower energy use.
Insulation, draught repairs, shading and moisture control can reduce the energy a building needs. The work must suit the building and local climate.
outgoing: Using less energy for heating, cooling and other building services can reduce fuel-burning emissions. The reduction depends on the energy source and actual use after the upgrade.
Buildings that need less heating and cooling use less electricity during temperature extremes. This can reduce pressure during the busiest hours.
Lower energy use can make household bills more affordable. This may reduce the risk of losing service, depending on prices and how upgrade costs are paid.
A building that stays comfortable with less energy is cheaper to cool. This can help more people maintain safe indoor temperatures.
Insulation, shade and ventilation can reduce dangerous indoor heat when upgrades suit the local climate and allow heat to escape. Lower exposure can reduce estimated heat-related death risks.

human.summary: Buildings that need less energy can be cheaper and more comfortable to use. Good design also helps keep people safer during hot or cold periods.
consequences: Lower energy use can reduce bills and exposure to price rises.
Suitable upgrades can keep indoor temperatures safer for longer.

planet.summary: Using less energy for the same building services can reduce fuel use and the equipment needed to supply it.
consequences: Electricity and heating-fuel demand can fall.
Efficient buildings can reduce demand during the busiest hours.

response.defaultDriver: Results depend on the building, installation quality and how equipment is used.
levers: Set useful building and appliance standards and fund improvements in high-cost homes.
Check actual energy use and comfort after work is completed.

measurement.metric: Building final-energy use intensity by building type
measurement.geography: declared country, balancing area, utility territory, facility class, or project portfolio
measurement.cadence: hourly to annual according to the source release

occurrences.title: Scientists put algae to work making fuel. AI reveals which cells are pulling their weight

heat pump electrification.name: Heat Pump Electrification
heat pump electrification.description: Replacing fuel-burning heating with electrical equipment that transfers warmth between places. The same type of equipment can also provide cooling. The climate benefit depends on its efficiency, the equipment it replaces and how the electricity is produced.
incoming: Heat pumps use electricity to move heat. Their climate benefit grows as the electricity they use is produced with fewer emissions.
Building rules can encourage owners to replace fuel-burning heating with efficient electric equipment. This depends on what the rules reward and what support is available.
Improving a building's insulation and shade reduces how much heating and cooling it needs. A heat pump can then meet that demand more easily.
outgoing: Efficient electric heating can replace boilers and furnaces that burn fossil fuels. The climate benefit depends on the equipment's performance and how its electricity is made.
Heat pumps that provide cooling as well as heating can help keep indoor temperatures safe. Protection depends on access, affordability and reliable electricity.
Switching many buildings to electric heating and cooling can increase electricity demand at busy times. Building efficiency and power-system planning help manage the extra load.

human.summary: Efficient electric equipment can provide both heating and cooling. Costs and benefits depend on the building, electricity prices and installation quality.
consequences: Well-suited systems can lower heating costs in efficient buildings.
Replacing fuel-burning furnaces removes that source of indoor combustion pollution.

planet.summary: Efficient electric heating reduces direct fuel burning in buildings. Its climate benefit increases as electricity becomes cleaner.
consequences: Less fossil fuel is burned at the building.
Moving heat can provide heating and cooling efficiently.

response.defaultDriver: Performance depends on climate, equipment sizing, installation and how well the building holds heat.
levers: Match systems to local conditions and improve insulation or electrical supply where needed.
Use efficient equipment and targeted financial support, especially for households with limited income.

measurement.metric: Installed heat-pump stock and annual sales
measurement.geography: declared country, balancing area, utility territory, facility class, or project portfolio
measurement.cadence: hourly to annual according to the source release

occurrences.title: Labour’s energy bills crisis is getting worse. Political honesty is essential

weatherization retrofits.name: Weatherization Retrofits
weatherization retrofits.description: Improving existing homes so outdoor heat, cold and moisture are easier to manage. Work can include sealing gaps, adding insulation and improving shade. Suitable ventilation is also needed to keep indoor air healthy.
incoming: Requirements to improve actual building performance can encourage insulation, draught repairs and shading. Owners need practical ways to fund and carry out the work.
outgoing: Insulation, draught repairs, shading and moisture control can reduce the energy a building needs. The work must suit the building and local climate.
Improving a building's insulation and shade reduces how much heating and cooling it needs. A heat pump can then meet that demand more easily.
Well-designed building upgrades can slow indoor overheating. This can keep temperatures safer for longer, including when cooling is limited.
Upgrades that reduce household energy use can lower bills. More affordable bills can reduce the risk of electricity or heating being cut off.

human.summary: Insulation, draught repairs and other building upgrades can make indoor conditions safer with less energy. The work needs to suit local weather and maintain healthy ventilation.
consequences: Reduced energy needs can lower household bills.
Indoor temperatures may remain safe for longer during outages.

planet.summary: Improving existing buildings can reduce the energy needed to keep them comfortable. Lasting upgrades can also extend their useful life.
consequences: Heating and cooling demand can fall.
Lower demand during extremes can ease pressure on the grid.

response.defaultDriver: A building still needs safe ventilation and suitable moisture control after gaps are sealed.
levers: Prioritize poorly performing homes and check materials, ventilation and installation quality.
Coordinate insulation and sealing with heating or cooling upgrades.

measurement.metric: Building floor area weatherized and verified energy savings
measurement.geography: declared country, balancing area, utility territory, facility class, or project portfolio
measurement.cadence: hourly to annual according to the source release

passive cooling design.name: Passive Cooling Design
passive cooling design.description: Keeping indoor spaces cooler through their design before relying on powered cooling. Shade, airflow, reflective roofs and carefully chosen materials can help. The best combination depends on local weather and the building's use.
incoming: Rules that reward lower cooling demand can encourage shade, ventilation and materials that limit indoor heat. Measured performance helps show whether the design works.
outgoing: Shade, suitable ventilation and reflective surfaces can reduce the heat entering or staying inside buildings. This can lower people's exposure to dangerous indoor temperatures.
Buildings designed to stay cooler need less powered cooling during hot hours. This can ease pressure on electricity supplies.
Designs that limit heat storage and allow heat to escape can keep places cooler after sunset. The result depends on local materials, building layout and airflow.
Shade and other ways of keeping buildings cool can reduce the need for continuously powered air conditioning. This can help people who cannot afford high electricity bills.

human.summary: Shade, ventilation and suitable building materials can reduce indoor heat without relying entirely on air conditioning. They work within the limits of local weather and building design.
consequences: Lower indoor heat can reduce dangerous exposure.
Less powered cooling can lower bills and vulnerability to power cuts.

planet.summary: Designs that limit heat gain can reduce demand for powered cooling. Some also add vegetation when that suits the location.
consequences: Less electricity is needed to maintain comfortable temperatures.
Peak demand during hot hours can fall.

response.defaultDriver: Ventilation may be unsuitable during smoke or when outdoor air is very hot or humid. Design must fit the place.
levers: Include suitable shade and cool roofs in buildings and public spaces.
Protect indoor air quality and assess humidity, security and maintenance alongside cooling.

measurement.metric: Floor area using verified passive-cooling design measures
measurement.geography: declared country, balancing area, utility territory, facility class, or project portfolio
measurement.cadence: hourly to annual according to the source release
