building performance standards.name: Building Performance Standards
building performance standards.description: Rules requiring buildings to meet limits on actual energy use or pollution over time. Owners may need to improve equipment or the building itself. Measuring real results helps show whether those improvements work.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Rules based on a building's measured energy use can encourage upgrades. Clear targets and deadlines help turn those rules into lower energy use.
Building rules can encourage owners to replace fuel-burning heating with efficient electric equipment. This depends on what the rules reward and what support is available.
Requirements to improve actual building performance can encourage insulation, draught repairs and shading. Owners need practical ways to fund and carry out the work.
Rules that reward lower cooling demand can encourage shade, ventilation and materials that limit indoor heat. Measured performance helps show whether the design works.
Building rules can encourage safer cooling gases when they count emissions from gas leaks as well as energy use. Rules that ignore leaks may miss this opportunity.

human.summary: Rules based on real building performance can encourage owners to improve inefficient buildings. Funding and practical delivery determine whether residents benefit.
consequences: Predictable upgrade programmes can support skilled jobs.
Successful improvements can lower running costs and improve comfort.

planet.summary: Rules tied to measured performance can reduce building energy use when owners deliver effective upgrades.
consequences: Actual energy use and operating emissions can fall.
Standards can encourage efficiency and cleaner heating.

response.defaultDriver: Targets must reflect measured performance, building conditions and available upgrade methods.
levers: Phase in clear targets with technical and financial support.
Track real outcomes and protect tenants from displacement or unfair cost increases.

measurement.metric: Building floor area covered by an enforceable performance standard
measurement.geography: declared country, balancing area, utility territory, facility class, or project portfolio
measurement.cadence: hourly to annual according to the source release

public transit expansion.name: Public Transit Expansion
public transit expansion.description: Adding or improving shared transport such as buses and trains. Frequent, reliable services can help people reach work, school and health care with fewer private car journeys. Benefits depend on access, affordability and the energy used.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Frequent, affordable buses and trains can give people an alternative to private vehicles. The service must connect the places people need to reach.
Shared transport can reduce emissions when it replaces more polluting car journeys. The result depends on how vehicles are powered and how many people use them.
Cleaner buses and trains can reduce local air pollution when they replace traffic that burns fuel. The benefit depends on the vehicles used and the car journeys avoided.
Good public transport can support homes and services closer together. Housing and planning policies need to support that pattern for outward spread to slow.
People usually need to walk, cycle or use a wheelchair to reach a bus or train. Better public transport can therefore strengthen the value of safe routes to stops and stations.

human.summary: Frequent and affordable shared transport can help people reach work, school and services without a private car. Benefits depend on useful routes and reliable service.
consequences: Some households can spend less on daily travel.
People unable to drive gain another way to reach essential destinations.

planet.summary: Reliable shared transport can reduce fuel use and space needed for private vehicles. The benefit depends on replacing car journeys and supporting useful development patterns.
consequences: Less driving can reduce transport emissions.
Homes and services can be built closer together around good routes.

response.defaultDriver: A route helps only if it connects useful destinations at suitable times with safe, accessible stops.
levers: Fund frequent, dependable service and safe links to homes, jobs and schools.
Keep fares affordable and prevent improvements from forcing existing residents out.

measurement.metric: Scheduled public-transport service supplied

measurement.cadence: hourly or event-based with monthly and annual rollups

walking and cycling networks.name: Walking and Cycling Networks
walking and cycling networks.description: Creating safe, connected routes for journeys on foot, by wheelchair or by bicycle. These routes can replace some short car trips and make daily destinations easier to reach. Accessibility and protection from traffic are essential.
incoming: People usually need to walk, cycle or use a wheelchair to reach a bus or train. Better public transport can therefore strengthen the value of safe routes to stops and stations.
outgoing: Safe, connected routes make it easier to walk or cycle for short journeys. This can reduce the need to use a private vehicle.
Walking and cycling avoid fuel-burning emissions when they replace motorised journeys. Safe routes help more people make that switch.
More walking and cycling can reduce road exhaust when vehicle journeys fall. A connected network matters because isolated routes may change little traffic overall.

human.summary: Safe, connected walking and cycling routes make short trips easier without a motor vehicle. The network needs to work for the people and journeys it serves.
consequences: More daily journeys can include physical activity.
Households may spend less on transport.

planet.summary: Safe walking and cycling routes can avoid fuel use on short trips. Connected routes also support places where daily destinations are closer together.
consequences: Replacing motor journeys reduces fuel demand.
Less car use can reduce pressure for roads and parking.

response.defaultDriver: A disconnected or unsafe section can make an otherwise useful route unusable.
levers: Build continuous protected links to everyday destinations and public transport.
Provide safe crossings, shade, accessible design and regular maintenance.

measurement.metric: Protected walking and cycling network availability and use
measurement.geography: declared route, network, port, airport, metropolitan area, country, or fleet boundary
measurement.cadence: hourly or event-based with monthly and annual rollups

electric vehicle transition.name: Electric Vehicle Transition
electric vehicle transition.description: Replacing vehicles that burn fuel with ones powered by electricity. This reduces exhaust pollution on the road, while the overall climate benefit depends on electricity and manufacturing. It does not by itself solve congestion or reduce the need for roads.
incoming: Charging vehicles with electricity made using fewer fossil fuels reduces the emissions from driving them. Electric vehicles still require materials, roads and space.
outgoing: Electric vehicles replace oil use with electricity. Their climate benefit generally grows as the electricity supply becomes cleaner, while vehicle and battery production still matter.
Electric vehicles remove exhaust emissions from the vehicles they replace. Pollution from tyres, brakes and electricity or material production still needs attention.
Making more electric vehicles increases demand for battery minerals, processing and factories. Battery size, reuse and recycling affect how much new material is needed.
Many vehicles charging during already busy hours can put extra pressure on electricity supplies. Managing charging times can reduce that pressure.

human.summary: Vehicles powered by batteries remove exhaust from the journeys they replace. They can reduce fuel costs, while tyres, roads and electricity production still have impacts.
consequences: People near streets can face less tailpipe pollution.
Drivers are less exposed to oil-price changes.

planet.summary: Electric vehicles reduce oil use, with larger climate benefits as their power supply becomes cleaner. Battery and vehicle production remain part of the full impact.
consequences: Emissions over a vehicle's life can fall with cleaner charging.
Less petroleum is needed for driving.

response.defaultDriver: Benefits depend on vehicle size, manufacturing, electricity supply and lifetime use.
levers: Improve charging and cleaner electricity together, with battery repair and recycling.
Support smaller vehicles and reliable public transport alongside replacing fossil-fuel cars.

measurement.metric: Battery-electric and plug-in hybrid vehicle stock share
measurement.geography: declared route, network, port, airport, metropolitan area, country, or fleet boundary
measurement.cadence: hourly or event-based with monthly and annual rollups

low-carbon cement and concrete.name: Low-Carbon Cement and Concrete
low-carbon cement and concrete.description: Reducing the gases released when making the materials used to bind and form concrete. Approaches include using less material, changing ingredients and using cleaner heat. The result must still meet the strength and safety needs of the structure.
incoming: Cleaner electricity can reduce emissions from parts of cement production, including some heating and carbon-capture equipment. Other emissions from the raw materials still need to be addressed.
outgoing: Using less cement and replacing part of its most emissions-intensive ingredient can reduce production emissions. Capturing carbon dioxide released during manufacture can address another part of the problem.
Changes to cement ingredients, fuel use and production can reduce carbon dioxide releases. The reduction depends on which methods are used and how well they perform.
Designing buildings to use less concrete can reduce demand for newly extracted materials. Changing the cement recipe alone does not guarantee lower material use.

human.summary: Using less emissions-intensive cement can reduce the climate impact of essential construction. Building design and material choice determine the benefit.
consequences: Infrastructure can be built with fewer production emissions.
New materials can support demand for skilled industrial work.

planet.summary: Changes in cement ingredients, fuel and material use can reduce construction emissions. The method must still meet safe performance requirements.
consequences: Less limestone processing and fuel burning can reduce carbon dioxide releases.
Material-saving designs can reduce demand for new raw materials.

response.defaultDriver: Materials must meet strength and durability needs. Suitable ingredients and carbon-capture infrastructure are not available everywhere.
levers: Allow verified lower-emissions materials in building rules and public purchasing.
Require clear product-level emissions information as well as performance testing.

measurement.metric: Low-clinker cement output and cradle-to-gate greenhouse-gas intensity
measurement.geography: declared facility, industry class, country, trade region, or supply-chain boundary
measurement.cadence: monthly or annual according to production and inventory reporting

near-zero emissions steel.name: Near-Zero Emissions Steel
near-zero emissions steel.description: Making the iron-based metal used in buildings and cars while releasing much less carbon dioxide. Factories can recycle more metal, use cleaner power or change how they process iron ore. The amount saved depends on the fuel, power and materials used.
incoming: Low-emissions electricity can power electric steel furnaces and the production of hydrogen used in some steelmaking methods. The benefit depends on the whole production process.
Steel plants that still depend on coal show where cleaner production is needed. Replacing or upgrading these plants requires a workable plan for equipment, energy and supply.
outgoing: Recycling, cleaner electricity, hydrogen and other production changes can reduce reliance on coal in steelmaking. The right combination depends on the plant and the steel required.
Making steel with very low emissions can reduce carbon dioxide releases when it replaces coal-based production. The full benefit depends on the energy and materials used.
Cleaner steelmaking can require new equipment and more electricity or hydrogen facilities. These changes may increase demand for some minerals even as coal use falls.

human.summary: Cleaner steel production can keep supplying an important material while reducing pollution. Workers and regions need support as plants and skills change.
consequences: Essential industrial capacity can continue with fewer harmful releases.
Recycling, cleaner power and new production methods create demand for different skills.

planet.summary: Cleaner steelmaking can reduce coal use and carbon dioxide releases. Recycling and efficient design can lower demand for new material as well.
consequences: Lower-emissions production can replace coal-based processes.
Good-quality scrap becomes more useful for new steel.

response.defaultDriver: Available cleaner electricity, hydrogen, scrap quality and plant design determine which routes work.
levers: Plan clean power and other needed infrastructure alongside factory changes.
Create credible demand through purchasing standards and support workers during conversion.

measurement.metric: Near-zero-emissions steel production by qualified route
measurement.geography: declared facility, industry class, country, trade region, or supply-chain boundary
measurement.cadence: monthly or annual according to production and inventory reporting

ecosystem restoration.name: Ecosystem Restoration
ecosystem restoration.description: Helping damaged natural places recover their plants, animals and important functions. This can improve water, soil, wildlife habitat and carbon storage. Recovery is more likely to last when the original causes of damage are also addressed.
incoming: Projects that use habitats to protect people can fund their recovery and care. Lasting benefits depend on maintaining those habitats after construction or planting.
outgoing: Recovering plants and soils can take carbon dioxide out of the air and store the carbon. The benefit lasts only as long as that additional carbon remains stored.
Repairing damaged habitats can help native plants and animals recover. Recovery depends on removing the original pressures and maintaining a diverse, connected habitat.
Recovering vegetation and healthier soils can increase the carbon taken up and stored on land. The benefit depends on lasting recovery and protection from renewed damage.
Plant cover and roots help hold soil in place. Restoring them can reduce the amount of fertile ground carried away by wind and water.
Population and Asset Exposure in Floodplains
Restored wetlands, forests and river floodplains can hold or slow water. This can reduce some flood exposure, depending on their location, size and the flood itself.
Healthy habitats provide the living systems needed for natural protection. Wetlands can store floodwater, while trees can provide shade and help cool their surroundings.

human.summary: Repairing damaged habitats can support people who depend on healthy land and water. Benefits depend on lasting recovery and care.
consequences: Farming, fishing and other local livelihoods may gain from healthier ecosystems.
Some projects reduce flooding, heat, erosion or water-quality risks.

planet.summary: Repairing damaged ecosystems can rebuild habitat and the processes that support it. Lasting benefits require the original pressures to be reduced.
consequences: Plants and animals can regain connected places to live.
Healthier soils and vegetation can store carbon and help regulate water.

response.defaultDriver: Recovery depends on removing the original pressure and maintaining suitable habitat under a changing climate.
levers: Protect remaining healthy ecosystems and restore suitable native variety on damaged land.
Respect Indigenous and community rights and fund long-term care and monitoring.

measurement.metric: Ecosystem area under verified restoration with condition improvement
measurement.geography: declared habitat, ecosystem, protected area, watershed, coastline, or analysis grid
measurement.cadence: seasonal or annual with event updates where applicable

multi-hazard early warning.name: Multi-Hazard Early Warning
multi-hazard early warning.description: Alerting people in time to prepare for threats such as floods, storms or dangerous heat. A forecast only helps if the warning reaches people, is understood and can be acted on. Safe places, transport and response plans matter too.
incoming: Missing observations or alerts leave people with less time to prepare. These gaps show where better monitoring, communication and response plans are needed.
outgoing: Better monitoring and accessible alerts can reach people who previously lacked useful warnings. People also need to trust the warning and have practical ways to act.
Earlier warnings give services time to prepare and help people move before danger arrives. This can reduce the number of urgent rescues needed at once.
Heat warnings can help prevent deaths when they trigger contact with vulnerable people, access to cooling and health-service preparation. An alert alone is not enough.
Warnings can reduce unequal disaster losses when they reach vulnerable groups and come with real options for protection. Access to transport, shelter and support matters.
Reliable heat forecasts help cities decide when to activate protective measures. Clear communication helps services and residents act together.

human.summary: Useful warnings give people time to prepare before danger arrives. They protect people only when alerts reach them and practical action is possible.
consequences: Timely preparation can reduce injuries and deaths.
Households and services can protect people and important supplies earlier.

planet.summary: Early warnings can give people time to prevent additional environmental damage during emergencies. They do not remove the underlying hazard.
consequences: Preparation can reduce avoidable spills or damage from an unmanaged emergency.
Earlier action may protect sensitive habitats and essential facilities.

response.defaultDriver: Warnings can fail to reach people or arrive without enough time, trust or means to respond.
levers: Design messages with exposed communities, in accessible formats and local languages.
Connect alerts to funded evacuation, shelter, health and essential-service plans.

measurement.metric: Countries reporting the existence of multi-hazard early-warning systems under Sendai Target G

measurement.cadence: event-based, quarterly, or annual according to reporting

urban heat action plans.name: Urban Heat Action Plans
urban heat action plans.description: Preparing a city to protect people before and during dangerously hot weather. Measures can include warnings, worker protection, shade, outreach and places to cool down. Plans need to reach people who have the fewest ways to protect themselves.
incoming: Growing illness during hot weather shows where cities need stronger preparation. Plans can connect forecasts with cooling, health services and support for people at greatest risk.
Reliable heat forecasts help cities decide when to activate protective measures. Clear communication helps services and residents act together.
outgoing: City plans can help prevent heat-related deaths when forecasts trigger funded action. This includes reaching vulnerable people, opening cooling spaces and protecting outdoor workers.
Coordinating cooling spaces, health services and contact with vulnerable residents can reduce illness during hot weather. The plan needs staff, funding and follow-through.
City heat plans can protect workers when they include enforceable rules and practical support for safer work. A plan without workplace measures may leave this exposure unchanged.
City plans can coordinate cooling spaces, transport and support for people at greatest risk. Protection against electricity shutoffs can help keep home cooling available.

human.summary: A funded city plan can turn heat forecasts into practical protection. It needs to reach people whose homes, work or health leave them most exposed.
consequences: Early action can reduce preventable heat illness and deaths.
Workers, older people, children and people without safe cooling may receive targeted support.

planet.summary: Heat plans can support long-term changes that keep cities cooler. Environmental benefits depend on including measures beyond emergency air conditioning.
consequences: Shade and suitable building design can reduce sudden peaks in cooling demand.
Greener public spaces can provide cooler surroundings.

response.defaultDriver: Protection depends on timely action, accessible services and conditions inside homes and workplaces.
levers: Set local alert triggers and clear responsibilities, backed by budgets.
Protect workers and invest in shade, cooler buildings and accessible cooling during emergencies.

measurement.metric: Population covered by an active heat-action plan meeting declared criteria
measurement.geography: declared household population, jurisdiction, market, institution, or disaster-affected area
measurement.cadence: event-based, quarterly, or annual according to reporting

equitable cooling access.name: Equitable Cooling Access
equitable cooling access.description: Making sure people can keep safely cool, including those with low incomes or unsuitable housing. This can involve shade, better homes, affordable electricity and public cool spaces. Reliable power and efficient equipment help keep protection available during extreme heat.
incoming: Cooling can be provided with less climate damage when equipment uses less harmful gases and is efficient. Affordable equipment and trained technicians are needed to make this benefit widely available.
A building that stays comfortable with less energy is cheaper to cool. This can help more people maintain safe indoor temperatures.
Shade and other ways of keeping buildings cool can reduce the need for continuously powered air conditioning. This can help people who cannot afford high electricity bills.
City plans can coordinate cooling spaces, transport and support for people at greatest risk. Protection against electricity shutoffs can help keep home cooling available.
Losing electricity can stop fans and air conditioning during dangerous heat. Households unable to afford continued service may lose access to safe temperatures.
outgoing: Making safe indoor temperatures available to people at greatest risk can help prevent heat-related deaths. Cooling must remain affordable and available when needed.
Efficient cooling, affordable energy and contact with vulnerable residents can reduce illness during hot weather. These measures work best together.
Expanding powered cooling can increase electricity use during the hottest hours. Efficient equipment, cooler buildings and careful demand management help limit that increase.

human.summary: Affordable, reliable ways to stay cool can protect people during dangerous heat. Access must include those unable to buy or operate cooling on their own.
consequences: Safe indoor temperatures can reduce heat illness and deaths.
People with health conditions can receive protection when heat is especially risky.

planet.summary: Safe cooling can be provided with less environmental pressure when efficient equipment and better buildings are part of the programme.
consequences: Efficient systems reduce electricity demand and the need for cooling gases.
Insulation and shade limit unnecessary energy use.

response.defaultDriver: Cooling protection depends on reliable power, efficient equipment and access during the hottest periods.
levers: Combine efficient cooling with shade and suitable home improvements.
Provide targeted bill support and plans for outages and residents with medical needs.

measurement.metric: Heat-exposed population with affordable access to safe cooling
measurement.geography: declared household population, jurisdiction, market, institution, or disaster-affected area
measurement.cadence: event-based, quarterly, or annual according to reporting

occurrences.title: Keeping cool saves thousands of lives yearly, but at a cost of worsening global warming, experts say

flood-resilient infrastructure.name: Flood-Resilient Infrastructure
flood-resilient infrastructure.description: Designing or improving buildings, roads, drains and utilities so they can better withstand high water. Measures can reduce damage and help services recover. They need to reflect local conditions and the possibility of floods larger than those seen in the past.
incoming: Repeated flooding by seawater increases the need to protect essential buildings and services. Better siting, drainage and access can reduce damage within their design limits.
outgoing: Population and Asset Exposure in Floodplains
Safer locations, drainage, water storage and protective works can reduce exposure to flooding. Maintenance and the size of future floods determine how well protection holds up.
More storage, treatment capacity and protection from floodwater can reduce sewage overflows. Separating rainwater from sewage flows can also ease pressure on the system.
Designing essential services for future floods can make failures less likely. Backup routes, spare capacity and maintenance help services continue when one part is damaged.
Keeping roads and essential services working during floods can reduce urgent rescue needs. It also helps emergency teams reach people who still need assistance.

human.summary: Services designed and maintained for flooding are more likely to keep working during an event. Protection has limits and needs to match future conditions.
consequences: Water, power, transport and health services can suffer fewer interruptions.
Households may face fewer repeated losses and outages.

planet.summary: Well-designed flood protection can reduce pollution released when essential services fail. Designs that work with natural habitats can provide additional benefits.
consequences: Restoring wetlands or floodplains can create space for water and wildlife.
Protected sewage and chemical facilities are less likely to release pollution during floods.

response.defaultDriver: Every defense has a design limit and needs maintenance. Future floods may exceed past experience.
levers: Use future conditions in design and protect natural flood-storage areas where suitable.
Combine engineered protection with land-use limits and avoid adding unsafe development.

measurement.metric: Critical assets meeting a declared flood-resilience standard
measurement.geography: named asset, operator service area, network, city, or infrastructure portfolio
measurement.cadence: event-based or operational with monthly and annual rollups

water reuse and recycling.name: Water Reuse and Recycling
water reuse and recycling.description: Cleaning used water so it can serve another purpose. Depending on the treatment, it may be used for farming, industry or drinking supplies. Health safeguards and reliable treatment are needed, and the process also uses energy.
incoming: When demand approaches available water supply, safely treating and using water again becomes more valuable. It helps most when it replaces water taken from an already stressed source.
outgoing: Treated water can replace some water pumped from underground. This reduces pressure only if total pumping actually falls.
Using treated local water again can reduce the need to remove salt from seawater. The choice depends on water quality requirements and the amount available.
Investment in collecting and treating used water can reduce releases of untreated sewage. Reuse helps when it improves the treatment system as well as finding a new use for the water.
Advanced water treatment needs energy. It can add carbon dioxide emissions when that energy comes from fossil fuels.

human.summary: Treating water so it can be used again can strengthen local supplies. Safety and benefit depend on suitable treatment and replacing demand on other sources.
consequences: A dependable local supply can become available for suitable uses.
Communities may be less exposed to drought or imported-water disruption.

planet.summary: Using treated water again can reduce pressure on rivers and groundwater when it replaces new withdrawals.
consequences: Less fresh water may need to be taken from natural sources.
Effective treatment can reduce polluted discharges.

response.defaultDriver: Required treatment depends on whether the water will be drunk, used on crops or used for another purpose.
levers: Match treatment to the intended use and monitor relevant contaminants.
Use efficient cleaner energy and protect affordability and water needed by rivers and habitats.

measurement.metric: Treated municipal and industrial wastewater reused
measurement.geography: declared basin, aquifer, utility, catchment, floodplain, or administrative reporting area
measurement.cadence: event-based to monthly with annual accounting

climate-resilient agriculture.name: Climate-Resilient Agriculture
climate-resilient agriculture.description: Helping farms keep producing under changing heat, rainfall, pests and other pressures. Options include varied crops, healthier soil, careful water use and better forecasts. The best choices depend on local conditions and farmers' resources.
incoming: Unreliable harvests increase the need for farming methods that handle heat, water shortages and other shocks. The most useful changes depend on local crops and conditions.
outgoing: A mix of crops, healthier soils, better water management and useful forecasts can make harvests more dependable. These measures reduce some risks but cannot prevent every loss.
Keeping soil covered, maintaining roots and disturbing it less can reduce erosion. Better water management can also slow the washing away of fertile ground.

More efficient farming can reduce groundwater use when limits also control total withdrawals. Saving water on each field does not help overall if irrigated production expands enough to cancel the saving.
More dependable local harvests can reduce the need to replace losses with imported food. The effect depends on which foods are grown and the shocks the farms face.

human.summary: Farming adapted to local climate risks can make food and farm incomes more dependable. Measures need to suit the crop, soil and water available.
consequences: A mix of crops and better planning can reduce some harvest shocks.
Healthier soil can hold water better and reduce dependence on costly inputs.

planet.summary: Farming methods suited to local risks can protect soil and water while supporting production. Benefits depend on management and limits on total resource use.
consequences: Keeping soil covered can reduce erosion and nutrient losses.
Healthier soil and varied habitats can support stored carbon and wildlife.

response.defaultDriver: No single practice works in every soil and climate. Water use, yields, emissions and working conditions must be considered together.
levers: Fund locally tested practices and practical advice for farmers.
Reward measured improvements in soil, water and income, with emissions cuts and worker protection.

measurement.metric: Agricultural area under a declared climate-resilience practice
measurement.geography: declared country, production region, market, fishery, farm system, or food-supply-chain segment

planned relocation.name: Planned Relocation
planned relocation.description: Organizing a move away from places that cannot be kept acceptably safe. A fair process protects people's choices, homes, livelihoods and community ties. It also requires suitable land, services and support at the destination.
incoming: Repeated flooding or other danger can make rebuilding in the same place unsafe. This increases the need to plan a move with the affected community.
outgoing: A planned move can reduce unequal disaster losses when people receive suitable housing, services, compensation and ways to earn a living. These protections need to be delivered, not just promised.
Moving a community requires organisations that can coordinate land, housing, money and public services. Experience can strengthen that ability when communities retain a voice and funding lasts.
Moving before repeated disasters destroy homes can reduce emergency displacement. The benefit depends on providing a safe, supported destination and involving the people who move.

human.summary: A planned, supported move can reduce repeated exposure to dangerous or unaffordable hazards. Residents need a real role in decisions and a viable place to live.
consequences: Moving before a disaster can reduce repeated losses.
Planning creates time to arrange housing, land, schools and income.

planet.summary: Moving development away from repeatedly hazardous areas can create room for natural recovery. The result depends on what happens to both the old site and the new one.
consequences: Floodplains or shorelines may regain space and habitat.
Less repeated rebuilding can reduce disturbance in exposed ecosystems.

response.defaultDriver: A safer site is not enough without secure rights, income opportunities and community consent.
levers: Plan voluntary moves with affected communities before an emergency forces decisions.
Guarantee fair support, services and continued cultural ties, including funding for receiving communities.

measurement.metric: Households participating in completed planned-relocation processes
measurement.geography: declared household population, jurisdiction, market, institution, or disaster-affected area
measurement.cadence: event-based, quarterly, or annual according to reporting

nature-based adaptation.name: Nature-Based Adaptation
nature-based adaptation.description: Using healthy natural places to help people cope with climate hazards. Wetlands can hold floodwater, trees can provide shade, and coastal habitats can soften waves. Their protection has limits and depends on keeping those natural systems healthy.
incoming: Healthy habitats provide the living systems needed for natural protection. Wetlands can store floodwater, while trees can provide shade and help cool their surroundings.
outgoing: Projects that use habitats to protect people can fund their recovery and care. Lasting benefits depend on maintaining those habitats after construction or planting.
Population and Asset Exposure in Floodplains
Wetlands and connected river floodplains can store water and slow its movement. This can reduce flood exposure within the limits of the land and the event.
Mangroves, marshes, dunes and reefs can reduce some coastal wave and flood impacts. They have physical limits and cannot prevent every flood.
Trees and other vegetation shade surfaces and cool the air as water evaporates. Less heat stored during the day can mean less released into nearby air at night.
Projects can help wildlife when they restore native habitats and connect them to other suitable areas. A project designed only for protection may not provide the same benefit.

human.summary: Healthy habitats can help protect people from heat, waves, floods and erosion. Their protection depends on location, condition and continued care.
consequences: Trees, wetlands and coastal habitats can reduce some harmful exposure.
Projects can provide accessible green space and local work.

planet.summary: Using healthy habitats to reduce hazards can also support wildlife and natural processes. Native species, connected space and long-term care help these benefits last.
consequences: Damaged habitats can recover their functions.
Plants and soils may store more carbon.

response.defaultDriver: Natural protection has limits and may take time to recover. It cannot make every exposed site safe.
levers: Protect existing healthy ecosystems and monitor whether restoration is working.
Combine suitable natural protection with land-use limits and engineered measures where needed.

measurement.metric: Area with implemented nature-based adaptation and monitored outcome
measurement.geography: declared habitat, ecosystem, protected area, watershed, coastline, or analysis grid

aquifer overdraft.name: Aquifer Overdraft
aquifer overdraft.description: Pumping water from an underground store faster than it is replaced. Water levels can fall, making wells less reliable. In some places, continued pumping can also pull salty water into supplies used for drinking or farming.
incoming: Water lost before it benefits crops may be replaced by extra pumping. Underground reserves decline if withdrawals keep exceeding refill and usable return flows.
Treated water can replace some water pumped from underground. This reduces pressure only if total pumping actually falls.

More efficient farming can reduce groundwater use when limits also control total withdrawals. Saving water on each field does not help overall if irrigated production expands enough to cancel the saving.
Pumping more groundwater than rain and other sources replace gradually reduces underground reserves. This can continue over years or decades.
outgoing: Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands
Excess pumping lowers the freshwater level beneath an island. Saltier water can move closer to the wells, reducing the usable reserve.
Pumping faster than water is replaced lowers underground reserves. Wells can then reach less water or stop working at their existing depth.
Heavy pumping near the sea lowers freshwater levels. This can draw salty water toward wells and reduce the usable supply.

Heavy pumping can draw salty groundwater into wells. If that water is repeatedly used on fields, evaporation can leave salt around roots. This does not happen everywhere, especially where water stays fresh and drainage removes salts.

human.summary: Excess pumping lowers the freshwater level beneath an island. Saltier water can move closer to the wells, reducing the usable reserve. A thinner freshwater reserve beneath an island can leave wells with less water or more salt. Making that supply safe to drink may become harder.
consequences: Heavy pumping near the sea lowers freshwater levels. This can draw salty water toward wells and reduce the usable supply. Saltier underground water gives utilities fewer easy-to-treat supplies. Extra treatment or replacement sources may be needed.

Heavy pumping can draw salty groundwater into wells. If that water is repeatedly used on fields, evaporation can leave salt around roots. This does not happen everywhere, especially where water stays fresh and drainage removes salts. Too much salt around roots makes it harder for crops to take in water. Harvests can fall or become less reliable, depending on the crop and how the land is managed.

planet.summary: Excess pumping lowers the freshwater level beneath an island. Saltier water can move closer to the wells, reducing the usable reserve.
consequences: Pumping faster than water is replaced lowers underground reserves. Wells can then reach less water or stop working at their existing depth.
Heavy pumping near the sea lowers freshwater levels. This can draw salty water toward wells and reduce the usable supply.

response.defaultDriver: Cheap pumping and weak limits on total withdrawals can encourage taking more water than the system can replace.
levers: Set withdrawals using evidence about recharge, connected rivers and essential needs.
Protect suitable recharge areas and reduce incentives for excessive pumping.

river flow regime change.name: River Flow Regime Change
river flow regime change.description: A lasting change in how much water a river carries, when it carries it or how variable the flow is. Earlier snowmelt or longer dry periods can change the usual seasonal pattern. This affects water supplies, wildlife and the management of dams.
incoming: Warming changes evaporation, precipitation and the timing of snowmelt. These can alter how much water rivers carry and when it arrives.
Earlier melting moves snow-fed river flows toward an earlier part of the year. Less may remain for the warm season unless storage or rainfall makes up the difference.
Less stored snow means less water released during the usual melting season. Rivers may receive water earlier in the year and less when it is most needed.
Sudden releases of stored glacier water can produce river flows far above seasonal levels. Repeated releases change the timing, size and sediment carried by downstream floods.
Storing or diverting river water changes when and how much water reaches places downstream. Operating rules can reduce seasonal peaks or create new daily fluctuations.
Narrow or poorly placed stream crossings can change water speed, depth and sediment movement nearby. These are local effects that need comparison with an unobstructed stretch of stream.
Straightening or confining rivers can move water downstream faster and separate it from floodplain storage. This changes local depths, speeds and flooding patterns.

Sustained rain from a band of moist air can sharply raise river flow, especially on wet ground or melting snow. Dry soil, reservoirs and shorter events can limit runoff and allow beneficial replenishment.
outgoing: Weaker or differently timed river flows provide less fresh water to resist the sea. Saltier water can then move farther upstream.
A dam may receive water at different times or in different amounts than expected. Stored supplies can then become less predictable under existing operating rules.
Changes in river flow can make older water-sharing rules difficult to follow. Agreements based on historical supplies may no longer match the water available.
Changed incoming river flows may no longer fit a dam's release plans. Operators can struggle to meet water, flood-control or electricity commitments.
Changes in when and how much river water arrives can make electricity from dams less dependable. Reservoirs and turbines may no longer receive the flow they were designed around.

human.summary: Changed incoming river flows may no longer fit a dam's release plans. Operators can struggle to meet water, flood-control or electricity commitments.
consequences: Changes in when and how much river water arrives can make electricity from dams less dependable. Reservoirs and turbines may no longer receive the flow they were designed around.

Weaker or differently timed river flows provide less fresh water to resist the sea. Saltier water can then move farther upstream. Saltier water reaching drinking-water intakes can exceed normal treatment capabilities. Utilities may need to change intake locations, blend supplies or use additional treatment.

planet.summary: Weaker or differently timed river flows provide less fresh water to resist the sea. Saltier water can then move farther upstream.
consequences: A dam may receive water at different times or in different amounts than expected. Stored supplies can then become less predictable under existing operating rules.
Changed incoming river flows may no longer fit a dam's release plans. Operators can struggle to meet water, flood-control or electricity commitments.

response.defaultDriver: Warming changes evaporation, precipitation and the timing of snowmelt. These can alter how much water rivers carry and when it arrives.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.

reservoir storage instability.name: Reservoir Storage Instability
reservoir storage instability.description: The amount of usable water held behind a dam becoming less predictable. A reservoir may fill at unexpected times or have too little water when it is needed. This makes it harder to plan drinking supplies, farming and electricity generation.
incoming: A dam may receive water at different times or in different amounts than expected. Stored supplies can then become less predictable under existing operating rules.
A long dry period can keep incoming river water low. Reservoirs may fail to refill enough to meet later needs.
A small winter snowpack stores less water for later in the year. This can make reservoir supplies harder to predict and manage.
Sediment carried into a reservoir settles as the water slows. Continued build-up takes up storage space and can interfere with water intakes.
outgoing: Unpredictable stored water makes it harder for dam operators to deliver the expected supply at the right time. Drinking water, flood control or electricity commitments may then be missed.

human.summary: Unpredictable stored water makes it harder for dam operators to deliver the expected supply at the right time. Drinking water, flood control or electricity commitments may then be missed.

planet.summary: Unpredictable stored water makes it harder for dam operators to deliver the expected supply at the right time. Drinking water, flood control or electricity commitments may then be missed.

response.defaultDriver: Erosion upstream and changing rainfall can add pressure to reservoirs designed for older conditions.
levers: Reduce avoidable soil erosion upstream and monitor usable storage.
Choose sediment-management methods suited to the dam and downstream river, alongside better inflow planning.

measurement.metric: Reservoir storage instability
measurement.geography: named reservoir and contributing basin
measurement.cadence: daily to seasonal operations and annual capacity review

reservoir operating shortfall.name: Reservoir Operating Shortfall
reservoir operating shortfall.description: A dam's stored water or ability to release it falling short of what people expect it to provide. Operators may be unable to meet water supply, electricity or flood-control needs. Competing demands and the timing of incoming water affect the result.
incoming: Unpredictable stored water makes it harder for dam operators to deliver the expected supply at the right time. Drinking water, flood control or electricity commitments may then be missed.
Changed incoming river flows may no longer fit a dam's release plans. Operators can struggle to meet water, flood-control or electricity commitments.
outgoing: Limited stored water or restrictions on releases can leave less water available to turn turbines. Electricity from the dam then becomes less dependable.

human.summary: Limited stored water or restrictions on releases can leave less water available to turn turbines. Electricity from the dam then becomes less dependable.

planet.summary: Changes in stored water and release timing can affect downstream flows. Effects on habitats depend on how the reservoir is operated and the water needs of the river.

response.defaultDriver: Older operating rules may no longer fit changing rainfall and snowmelt.
levers: Update release rules using present conditions and a range of future inflows.
Coordinate water supply, electricity and flood planning across the river basin.

measurement.cadence: event-based to monthly with annual accounting

shift in snowmelt timing.name: Shift in Snowmelt Timing
shift in snowmelt timing.description: Snow melting at a different time of year or at a different pace from the usual pattern. This changes when water reaches rivers and reservoirs. Earlier melting can leave less stored snow to supply water later in the warm season.
incoming: Darkened snow absorbs more sunlight than clean snow. This can make melting begin sooner or proceed faster in the affected area.

A study of 2,339 mainly undisturbed Northern Hemisphere river catchments linked each 1°C of local annual warming with an average snowmelt-flood peak 4.7 days earlier. Results varied widely between catchments, with a standard deviation of 5.0 days. The average is not a forecast for every river.
A smaller or warmer winter snowpack often melts sooner. Rivers may receive an earlier and weaker pulse of meltwater.
Warming can turn more winter precipitation into rain and bring earlier snowmelt. The timing change depends on the river basin, elevation and season.
Dark dust on snow absorbs sunlight and can bring earlier melting and runoff. Fresh snow can bury it and clouds reduce its effect, so the size of the timing change must be assessed locally.
outgoing: Snow melting earlier or faster can send a stronger pulse of water into streams. The effect is greater where the landscape has little capacity to hold the water temporarily.
Earlier melting moves snow-fed river flows toward an earlier part of the year. Less may remain for the warm season unless storage or rainfall makes up the difference.
Earlier or faster melting adds water inside mountain snow. Slopes may become unstable when wet layers lose their strength.
Earlier snowmelt can send water into a glacier before its drainage channels are ready to carry it. Blockages or sudden changes in those channels can release stored water as a flood.

Earlier snowmelt changes the seasonal mix of snow and glacier water reaching rivers. It can make the loss of late-season glacier support more noticeable, without alone proving that a basin has passed its maximum glacier runoff.
Earlier snow loss reduces the time that cool, moist patches remain on exposed mountain peaks. Specialised plants and animals may face a longer period of heat and drying.

human.summary: Snow melting earlier or faster can send a stronger pulse of water into streams. The effect is greater where the landscape has little capacity to hold the water temporarily. A surge of fast-moving water can wash material away from around a bridge's supports. Losing that material can weaken the foundations.
consequences: Earlier melting moves snow-fed river flows toward an earlier part of the year. Less may remain for the warm season unless storage or rainfall makes up the difference. Changed incoming river flows may no longer fit a dam's release plans. Operators can struggle to meet water, flood-control or electricity commitments.

Earlier or faster melting adds water inside mountain snow. Slopes may become unstable when wet layers lose their strength. Avalanches can bury or damage roads, railways, power lines and communications equipment. Repeated closures are especially disruptive where few alternative mountain routes exist.

planet.summary: Snow melting earlier or faster can send a stronger pulse of water into streams. The effect is greater where the landscape has little capacity to hold the water temporarily.
consequences: Earlier melting moves snow-fed river flows toward an earlier part of the year. Less may remain for the warm season unless storage or rainfall makes up the difference.
Earlier or faster melting adds water inside mountain snow. Slopes may become unstable when wet layers lose their strength.

response.defaultDriver: Darkened snow absorbs more sunlight than clean snow. This can make melting begin sooner or proceed faster in the affected area.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.

soil moisture collapse.name: Soil Moisture Collapse
soil moisture collapse.description: A large drop in the water held in soil. Plants then have less water available to their roots, and the land can dry out further during hot weather. How serious the effects are depends on soil depth, vegetation and how long the shortage lasts.
incoming: Little rain over a long period leaves soil water unreplenished while plants and evaporation continue using it. Soil can become exceptionally dry.

In the European models assessed, soil drought covered more land at 3°C of global warming than at 1.5°C. The estimated increase was 40%, with a spread of plus or minus 24%, so this is a model result for that region rather than a universal prediction.
Dry air draws water from soil and plants more strongly. The ground around roots dries faster when rain cannot replace the loss.
Warming increases evaporation and the water needs of plants. Soil can dry sharply when rain and irrigation do not replace the loss.
outgoing: Very dry soil leaves roots unable to obtain enough water. Crop growth and harvests can suffer, with effects that vary between crops and seasons.
When soil becomes very dry, farmers may pump more underground water for irrigation. Added pumping can lower well levels where replacement water is insufficient.
Very dry soil provides little cooling through evaporation. More energy heats the land and air, reinforcing hot, dry conditions above the ground.

human.summary: Very dry soil leaves roots unable to obtain enough water. Crop growth and harvests can suffer, with effects that vary between crops and seasons.
consequences: Very dry soil provides little cooling through evaporation. More energy heats the land and air, reinforcing hot, dry conditions above the ground. Strong drying conditions increase plants' water demand. Plants may close tiny leaf openings to conserve water, which can reduce growth and make harvests less reliable.

planet.summary: When soil becomes very dry, farmers may pump more underground water for irrigation. Added pumping can lower well levels where replacement water is insufficient.
consequences: Very dry soil provides little cooling through evaporation. More energy heats the land and air, reinforcing hot, dry conditions above the ground.

response.defaultDriver: Low rainfall, heat and poor soil management can combine to reduce water available to roots.
levers: Monitor root-zone moisture and use planting and water plans suited to local conditions.
Keep suitable ground cover and protect organic matter without increasing unsustainable water demand.

measurement.metric: Root-zone soil-moisture percentile and duration below threshold
measurement.geography: declared basin, aquifer, utility, catchment, floodplain, or administrative reporting area
measurement.cadence: event-based to monthly with annual accounting

flash flood regime.name: Flash Flood Regime
flash flood regime.description: The pattern of floods that rise very quickly after intense rain or a sudden release of water. Their speed can leave little time to respond. Damage depends on where the water travels and whether people, buildings and roads are in its path.
incoming: Intense rain can arrive faster than the ground can absorb it or drains and rivers can carry it away. Water can then rise quickly and flood nearby areas.
More moisture in the air can supply heavier bursts of rain. Fast flooding still depends on the storm, slopes, soil, drainage and how wet the ground already is.
The wetter phase of this tropical pattern can favour heavy rain in some regions. Rapid flooding still depends on local moisture, slopes and drainage.
Warmer air can support heavier short bursts of rain. Where water builds up faster than the ground and drains can handle it, sudden flooding can become more likely.
Warming can intensify short bursts of heavy rain. Sudden flood risk also depends on slopes, soil, drains and what lies in the path of the water.
outgoing: Fast-rising floodwater can exceed the capacity of sewers and treatment plants. Used water can then back up or escape into surrounding areas.
Rapid floods can wash dirt and pollution into water sources or damage intakes. Treatment plants may need extra cleaning steps or temporary interruptions.
Flooding can leave standing water, damage drains and change how people store water. In some places, this creates more breeding sites for mosquitoes and increases contact with people.
Sudden floods can contaminate drinking-water facilities and spread harmful germs. Effective treatment and hygiene can prevent exposure from becoming an outbreak.

human.summary: Rapid floods can wash dirt and pollution into water sources or damage intakes. Treatment plants may need extra cleaning steps or temporary interruptions.
consequences: Flooding can leave standing water, damage drains and change how people store water. In some places, this creates more breeding sites for mosquitoes and increases contact with people.
Sudden floods can contaminate drinking-water facilities and spread harmful germs. Effective treatment and hygiene can prevent exposure from becoming an outbreak.

consequences: Rapid floods can wash dirt and pollution into water sources or damage intakes. Treatment plants may need extra cleaning steps or temporary interruptions.

levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

drought persistence.name: Drought Persistence
drought persistence.description: Unusually dry conditions continuing for many months or across several seasons. Soil, rivers and reservoirs may not recover between dry periods. The effects build up when each new season begins with less water in reserve.
incoming: A long-lasting high-pressure pattern can divert storms and keep rain away from the same region. Dry conditions can then continue for longer.
A persistent pressure pattern can keep some North Atlantic regions short of rain. Whether it prolongs drought depends on the season and location.
Some phases of this pressure pattern can keep rain away from particular North American regions. The drought effect depends on season and location.
Slow-moving bends in high-altitude winds can keep rain away from a region. How much they contribute to a particular drought varies from event to event.

Warming increases the amount of water the air can draw from plants and soil. Where rain does not make up the loss, dry conditions can become more severe or last longer. The effect varies by region and season.

Changing air-pressure patterns around the Arctic can shift storms and temperatures farther south. In some regions and seasons, less rain and earlier snowmelt can leave dry conditions that last into the next season.
Unusually warm tropical Pacific waters can change winds and reduce rain in some regions. Dry soil, low rivers and depleted reservoirs can keep the effects going after the initial weather change.
Warming increases the air's demand for moisture. Where rain stays low, soil and plants can dry faster and drought conditions may last longer.
Long-lasting drought can be one part of a sequence or combination of climate hazards. Its causes and effects still need to be assessed for the drying region.
outgoing: A long drought reduces river flow and the flushing of river mouths. Saltier water can move farther inland and remain there longer.
A long dry period can keep incoming river water low. Reservoirs may fail to refill enough to meet later needs.
Little rain over a long period leaves soil water unreplenished while plants and evaporation continue using it. Soil can become exceptionally dry.
Repeated water shortages can make countries or regions unable to meet agreed allocations. Cooperation may come under strain as the dry period continues.
Lower water volumes during drought can leave salts and pollutants more concentrated. Utilities may need more treatment to provide safe drinking water.
A long drought reduces water reaching dams and may lower stored water levels. Less dependable flow means less dependable electricity generation.
Long dry periods can lower water levels in ground made of partly decayed plants. Exposure to air allows this stored material to break down and release carbon dioxide.
Long dry periods reduce moisture in the soil and the cooling provided by evaporation. Crops, animals and workers can then face hotter local conditions.
Long dry periods can dry vegetation across seasons. This increases the amount that can burn and can extend the time of year with high fire danger.
Long dry periods can reduce the water replenishing underground stores while increasing demand for pumping. Reserves fall faster where withdrawals already approach or exceed replacement.
Long dry periods reduce river supplies and the water replenishing underground reserves. Shortages become more likely if demand stays high.
Long dry periods leave less water in soil and less available for plants to release. More surface energy then heats the air, increasing its demand for water.

human.summary: Lower water volumes during drought can leave salts and pollutants more concentrated. Utilities may need more treatment to provide safe drinking water.
consequences: A long drought reduces water reaching dams and may lower stored water levels. Less dependable flow means less dependable electricity generation.
Long dry periods reduce river supplies and the water replenishing underground reserves. Shortages become more likely if demand stays high.

consequences: A long dry period can keep incoming river water low. Reservoirs may fail to refill enough to meet later needs.
Lower water volumes during drought can leave salts and pollutants more concentrated. Utilities may need more treatment to provide safe drinking water.

levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

freshwater lens thinning in small island.name: Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands
freshwater lens thinning in small island.description: The layer of usable fresh water beneath a small island becoming thinner. This water sits above denser salty water. Too much pumping, little rain or seawater entering the ground can reduce the amount available for wells.
incoming: Higher seawater levels can push salt into the shallow freshwater reserve beneath a small island. The usable layer may become thinner or saltier, depending on local conditions.
Excess pumping lowers the freshwater level beneath an island. Saltier water can move closer to the wells, reducing the usable reserve.
Saltwater moving inland can enter shallow freshwater stores near the coast. The layer of usable fresh water may then become thinner.
Warming contributes to rising seas and coastal flooding. On low islands, salty water can then reduce the shallow underground layer of fresh water people rely on.
outgoing: A thinner freshwater reserve beneath an island can leave wells with less water or more salt. Making that supply safe to drink may become harder.

If an island's shallow freshwater reserve cannot provide enough reliable drinking water, the community may need more salt-removal treatment or imported water. Available alternatives determine the choice.

human.summary: A shallow store of fresh groundwater can become less useful when saltwater squeezes into it. Communities may need more expensive and less dependable alternatives.
consequences: Water may still be present but too salty to use without treatment.
Households and utilities may pay more for storage, imported water or removal of salt.

planet.summary: A thinner freshwater reserve beneath an island can leave wells with less water or more salt. Making that supply safe to drink may become harder.

response.defaultDriver: Sea-level changes, drought and heavy pumping can reduce the thickness of usable freshwater.
levers: Monitor well levels and salt content and limit pumping accordingly.
Use suitable rainwater collection and storage to reduce pressure on underground supplies.

drinking water treatment stress.name: Drinking Water Treatment Stress
drinking water treatment stress.description: Water-cleaning systems having more difficulty making supplies safe to drink. Salt, dirt, harmful germs or other pollutants can require extra treatment or exceed what equipment can handle. This can increase costs or interrupt supply.
incoming: Releasing used water without normal treatment can add pollutants and suspended dirt to a river. Water plants downstream may need extra work and expense to make supplies safe.
Without forest cover, more soil can wash into streams supplying drinking water. Dirtier and less predictable source water can make treatment harder and more costly.
Saltier water reaching drinking-water intakes can exceed normal treatment capabilities. Utilities may need to change intake locations, blend supplies or use additional treatment.
Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands
A thinner freshwater reserve beneath an island can leave wells with less water or more salt. Making that supply safe to drink may become harder.
Saltier underground water gives utilities fewer easy-to-treat supplies. Extra treatment or replacement sources may be needed.
Flooding from the sea can add salt and other contamination to drinking-water sources or disrupt intakes. Water plants may then have difficulty providing safe supplies.
Rapid floods can wash dirt and pollution into water sources or damage intakes. Treatment plants may need extra cleaning steps or temporary interruptions.
Lower water volumes during drought can leave salts and pollutants more concentrated. Utilities may need more treatment to provide safe drinking water.
outgoing: Persistent salt problems can exceed ordinary water-treatment capabilities. A utility may then adopt salt-removal equipment where other suitable sources are limited.

human.summary: Water may remain available while becoming harder to make safe. Utilities and households can face higher costs and less reliable service.
consequences: Changing contamination or salt levels can require more complex treatment or different intakes.
People may face higher bills, boil-water notices or interrupted service.

planet.summary: Difficulties treating water mainly describe a service problem. Environmental effects depend on the original contamination and any treatment or waste changes, rather than treatment cost alone.

response.defaultDriver: Floods, drought and salt intrusion can make source water less predictable than the plant was designed for.
levers: Improve monitoring and treatment for the contaminants actually present.
Provide backup sources or links between systems, with support for places lacking spare capacity.

watershed forest loss.name: Watershed Forest Loss
watershed forest loss.description: Trees being removed or dying in the area that drains into a river or lake. Without their cover and roots, rain can carry more soil into the water. Water quality and the timing of flows can change.
incoming: Heat and drying can strain forests in river catchments. Greater water loss and fire risk can damage trees and change how water moves through the area.
Clearing trees within a river catchment removes canopy and roots. This can increase erosion and allow rainwater to reach streams more quickly.
Repeated severe fires can kill trees faster than forests regrow. A river catchment may then be left with less tree cover or a different type of vegetation.
outgoing: Losing trees around rivers can increase erosion and change water flow and habitat. Severe or repeated damage can reduce the ability of freshwater communities to survive and recover.
Without forest cover, more soil can wash into streams supplying drinking water. Dirtier and less predictable source water can make treatment harder and more costly.
Forest damage can change when water reaches a dam and how much sediment it carries. These changes can make electricity generation less reliable.
Forest loss can increase erosion, change river channels and remove streamside habitat. Some stretches may become unsuitable, separating populations along the river.
Losing trees can increase runoff and sediment reaching rivers. Where bank vegetation is also lost, fewer roots hold the bank in place.

human.summary: Without forest cover, more soil can wash into streams supplying drinking water. Dirtier and less predictable source water can make treatment harder and more costly.
consequences: Forest damage can change when water reaches a dam and how much sediment it carries. These changes can make electricity generation less reliable.

consequences: Without forest cover, more soil can wash into streams supplying drinking water. Dirtier and less predictable source water can make treatment harder and more costly.
Forest loss can increase erosion, change river channels and remove streamside habitat. Some stretches may become unsuitable, separating populations along the river.

wastewater infrastructure overflow.name: Wastewater Infrastructure Overflow
wastewater infrastructure overflow.description: Used water escaping from sewers, pumps or treatment plants because the system cannot contain it. Heavy rain, equipment failure or blocked drainage can contribute. The spilled water may carry pollutants and disease-causing germs into nearby areas.
incoming: Fast-rising floodwater can exceed the capacity of sewers and treatment plants. Used water can then back up or escape into surrounding areas.
When the sea rises, it can become harder for drains to carry used water away. During storms or high tides, pipes can back up and wastewater can spill into surrounding areas.
A heavy burst of rain can send more water into pipes and treatment plants than they can handle. The excess may back up or spill out.
More storage, treatment capacity and protection from floodwater can reduce sewage overflows. Separating rainwater from sewage flows can also ease pressure on the system.
outgoing: When sewers or treatment plants cannot handle the incoming water, emergency releases may bypass normal cleaning steps. The released water may be untreated or only partly treated.
Where rainwater and sewage share a pipe system, too much incoming water can escape through an overflow outlet. This connection applies only to systems built to carry both together.
Overflowing sewage systems can expose people to water carrying harmful germs. Outbreak risk rises when treatment and sanitation no longer contain that exposure.

human.summary: Overflowing sewage systems can expose people to water carrying harmful germs. Outbreak risk rises when treatment and sanitation no longer contain that exposure.
consequences: When sewers or treatment plants cannot handle the incoming water, emergency releases may bypass normal cleaning steps. The released water may be untreated or only partly treated. Releasing used water without normal treatment can add pollutants and suspended dirt to a river. Water plants downstream may need extra work and expense to make supplies safe.

planet.summary: When sewers or treatment plants cannot handle the incoming water, emergency releases may bypass normal cleaning steps. The released water may be untreated or only partly treated.
consequences: Where rainwater and sewage share a pipe system, too much incoming water can escape through an overflow outlet. This connection applies only to systems built to carry both together.
Overflowing sewage systems can expose people to water carrying harmful germs. Outbreak risk rises when treatment and sanitation no longer contain that exposure.

levers: More storage, treatment capacity and protection from floodwater can reduce sewage overflows. Separating rainwater from sewage flows can also ease pressure on the system.

wastewater bypass discharge.name: Wastewater Bypass Discharge
wastewater bypass discharge.description: Used water being released without passing through all the cleaning steps it would normally receive. This can happen during overloads, breakdowns or maintenance. The receiving river or coastal water may then receive more pollutants.
incoming: When sewers or treatment plants cannot handle the incoming water, emergency releases may bypass normal cleaning steps. The released water may be untreated or only partly treated.
Investment in collecting and treating used water can reduce releases of untreated sewage. Reuse helps when it improves the treatment system as well as finding a new use for the water.
outgoing: Releasing used water without normal treatment can add pollutants and suspended dirt to a river. Water plants downstream may need extra work and expense to make supplies safe.
Used water released without normal treatment can add nutrients that feed algae. Harmful growth is more likely where warmth, slow flushing and suitable species also occur.
Untreated water can add nutrients and decaying material near the coast. Breaking down that material uses oxygen and can contribute to shortages for marine animals.
Releasing water without normal treatment can add germs, nutrients and harmful chemicals to rivers or lakes. Severe or repeated contamination can damage their living communities and functions.
Sewage released without adequate treatment carries nitrogen and phosphorus into water. These nutrients can worsen pollution in rivers, lakes and coastal areas.
Untreated or partly treated sewage adds nutrients and organic material to receiving water. This can encourage growth and decay that use up oxygen.
Sewage pollution can harm kelp growth and reproduction where contaminated water reaches the habitat. Lasting loss requires evidence of the exposure, its duration and the plants' response.

human.summary: Releasing used water without normal treatment can add pollutants and suspended dirt to a river. Water plants downstream may need extra work and expense to make supplies safe.
consequences: Used water released without normal treatment can add nutrients that feed algae. Harmful growth is more likely where warmth, slow flushing and suitable species also occur. Toxic algae or low oxygen can kill fish or make seafood unsafe. Harvest closures and damaged stocks can then interrupt supplies arriving at ports and markets.

Untreated water can add nutrients and decaying material near the coast. Breaking down that material uses oxygen and can contribute to shortages for marine animals. Low oxygen can kill target species or push them away from fishing grounds. Local catches then become less reliable.

consequences: Used water released without normal treatment can add nutrients that feed algae. Harmful growth is more likely where warmth, slow flushing and suitable species also occur.

response.defaultDriver: Heavy runoff and worn or undersized systems can send more water to a plant than it can treat.
levers: Expand suitable storage and reduce stormwater entering overloaded sewers.
Upgrade pumps and treatment where needed and use monitoring to manage large inflows.

irrigation water inefficiency.name: Irrigation Water Inefficiency
irrigation water inefficiency.description: Water supplied to crops being lost or poorly timed, so it does not provide the intended benefit. Leaks, evaporation and excess watering can contribute. Effects on the wider water supply depend on whether unused water returns in a usable form.
incoming: Large farming systems can waste water when delivery equipment leaks or watering does not match crop needs. The problem depends on how the system is designed and managed.
outgoing: Water lost before it benefits crops may be replaced by extra pumping. Underground reserves decline if withdrawals keep exceeding refill and usable return flows.
Poorly used irrigation water can require more pumping for the same harvest. This can lower well supplies where underground water is not replaced quickly enough.
Irrigation that needs more pumping for the same harvest can drain underground reserves. The effect depends on how much of the extra water returns as usable groundwater.
Poorly managed irrigation and drainage can leave dissolved salts around plant roots. Salty groundwater rising toward the surface can add to the build-up.

human.summary: Irrigation that needs more pumping for the same harvest can drain underground reserves. The effect depends on how much of the extra water returns as usable groundwater. Falling groundwater levels reduce the reserves people can reach and make pumping more costly. Users who depend on wells may then face tighter supplies.
consequences: Poorly managed irrigation and drainage can leave dissolved salts around plant roots. Salty groundwater rising toward the surface can add to the build-up. Too much salt around roots makes it harder for crops to take in water. Harvests can fall or become less reliable, depending on the crop and how the land is managed.

Water lost before it benefits crops may be replaced by extra pumping. Underground reserves decline if withdrawals keep exceeding refill and usable return flows. Excess pumping lowers the freshwater level beneath an island. Saltier water can move closer to the wells, reducing the usable reserve.

planet.summary: Water lost before it benefits crops may be replaced by extra pumping. Underground reserves decline if withdrawals keep exceeding refill and usable return flows.
consequences: Poorly used irrigation water can require more pumping for the same harvest. This can lower well supplies where underground water is not replaced quickly enough.
Irrigation that needs more pumping for the same harvest can drain underground reserves. The effect depends on how much of the extra water returns as usable groundwater.

levers: Use farming practices suited to the local soil, water and climate, with protection for workers and livestock.
Keep soils covered where appropriate, limit avoidable nutrient and chemical losses, and manage total water use rather than efficiency alone.

hydropower reliability decline.name: Hydropower Reliability Decline
hydropower reliability decline.description: Electricity made from moving water becoming less dependable. Too little water, poorly timed flows or limits on dam releases can reduce generation when it is needed. The effects depend on the river and how the power system is managed.
incoming: Limited stored water or restrictions on releases can leave less water available to turn turbines. Electricity from the dam then becomes less dependable.
Forest damage can change when water reaches a dam and how much sediment it carries. These changes can make electricity generation less reliable.
A long drought reduces water reaching dams and may lower stored water levels. Less dependable flow means less dependable electricity generation.
Power stations that depend on water from glaciers are exposed when the amount or timing of that water changes. Electricity production may become less dependable across seasons.
Changes in when and how much river water arrives can make electricity from dams less dependable. Reservoirs and turbines may no longer receive the flow they were designed around.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Less dependable water flow can mean less dependable electricity from dams. Customers and operators may need backup supplies, with costs depending on the wider grid.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.
