basin treaty breakdown.name: Basin Treaty Breakdown
basin treaty breakdown.description: Agreements about sharing a river's water becoming harder to follow or enforce. Drought, changing flows and competing needs can strain cooperation between regions or countries. The result depends on the agreement and the ability to resolve disputes.
incoming: Changes in river flow can make older water-sharing rules difficult to follow. Agreements based on historical supplies may no longer match the water available.
Repeated water shortages can make countries or regions unable to meet agreed allocations. Cooperation may come under strain as the dry period continues.

Changing supplies of water from glaciers can put pressure on agreements between countries sharing a river. Disputes are more likely where the agreements cannot adjust to less dependable seasonal flows.
outgoing: When water-sharing agreements fail, disputes can become harder to settle. Escalation depends on institutions and wider political conditions. Violence is not inevitable.

desalination dependence.name: Desalination Dependence
desalination dependence.description: Relying on equipment that removes salt from water because other supplies are limited or unreliable. This can provide usable water, but it needs energy, maintenance and safe management of the concentrated salt left over. A breakdown can threaten supply where alternatives are scarce.
incoming: Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands

If an island's shallow freshwater reserve cannot provide enough reliable drinking water, the community may need more salt-removal treatment or imported water. Available alternatives determine the choice.
As coastal wells become saltier, ordinary supplies may be less usable. Utilities or households may turn increasingly to equipment that removes salt from water.
Persistent salt problems can exceed ordinary water-treatment capabilities. A utility may then adopt salt-removal equipment where other suitable sources are limited.
Using treated local water again can reduce the need to remove salt from seawater. The choice depends on water quality requirements and the amount available.
outgoing: Removing salt from water uses electricity. Heavy reliance on this process can add energy costs, with household effects depending on prices and support.
Salt-removal plants need energy to provide water. Where that energy comes from fossil fuels, operating the plants adds carbon dioxide releases.

human.summary: Removing salt from water uses electricity. Heavy reliance on this process can add energy costs, with household effects depending on prices and support.
consequences: Salt-removal plants need energy to provide water. Where that energy comes from fossil fuels, operating the plants adds carbon dioxide releases. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.

planet.summary: Salt-removal plants need energy to provide water. Where that energy comes from fossil fuels, operating the plants adds carbon dioxide releases.

response.defaultDriver: Shortages or salty groundwater can make coastal areas increasingly reliant on energy-intensive replacement supplies.
levers: Compare conservation, treated-water reuse and salt removal within one water plan.
Use efficient treatment and cleaner power while managing concentrated salty waste and affordability.

ice sheet mass loss.name: Ice Sheet Mass Loss
ice sheet mass loss.description: The vast ice covering Greenland or Antarctica losing more ice than it gains from snowfall. Melting and the movement of ice into the ocean both contribute. Losing ice that was on land adds water to the sea.
incoming: Warmer air melts ice at the surface, while warmer seawater can thin floating ice around the edges. Reduced support can also let ice on land flow into the sea faster.
Carbon dioxide released into the air adds to warming. Warmer air and ocean water increase pressure on the large ice masses covering Greenland and Antarctica.
Warm ocean water can melt floating ice shelves from below. Weaker shelves hold back inland ice less effectively, allowing it to move toward the sea faster.
Loss of Firn Meltwater Storage Capacity
The partly compacted snow above glacier ice can store and refreeze meltwater. When it loses empty space or forms impermeable layers, more water runs off and contributes to ice loss.
outgoing: Meltwater from Antarctic ice makes nearby seawater fresher and less dense. This can reduce the formation of water that sinks to the deepest ocean.

Faster ice movement and ice loss can be signs that floating ice is providing less support to ice inland. These observations need local evidence to identify the cause. Ice loss alone does not explain every change.
Losing ice can change where meltwater collects and how it drains. Flood hazards depend on whether water becomes trapped, how it escapes and what lies downstream.
Fresh meltwater from Greenland makes nearby surface seawater less salty and lighter. This can make it harder for water to sink and may weaken Atlantic circulation.
Fresh water from melting ice sheets forms a lighter layer near the ocean surface. This can strengthen the separation from saltier, denser water below.
Thinning and retreating ice can expose sediment and change meltwater routes. This changes when and how much material reaches nearby coastal inlets.

Ice lost from land adds water to the ocean and raises average sea level. Greenland's measured loss during 1992–2020 was equivalent to 13.5 millimetres globally, with an assessed range of 11.4–15.6 millimetres.
Water from melting ice sheets raises the sea's starting level. Coastal flooding then depends on local tides, storms, land movement and the people or buildings exposed.
Rising sea levels let waves and storm-driven water reach farther inland. Erosion can increase along coasts made of material that is easily worn away.
Sea-level rise from land-ice loss can push saltwater toward coastal underground freshwater. Pumping, rainwater replenishment and local geology affect how far it moves.
Higher sea levels raise the starting point for coastal floods. Damage can be greater when storms, high tides, heavy rain or river floods occur together.
Losing reflective land ice can expose darker surfaces that absorb more sunlight. This can reinforce local warming, depending on what surface is left behind.

Sudden releases of stored glacier water can produce river flows far above seasonal levels. Repeated releases change the timing, size and sediment carried by downstream floods.

glacial lake outburst flood risk.name: Glacial Lake Outburst Flood Risk
glacial lake outburst flood risk.description: The chance that a lake held back by ice or loose rock near a glacier suddenly releases its water. If that barrier fails, a fast flood can rush downhill. The danger depends on the lake, the barrier and what lies downstream.
incoming: At some glacier lakes, breaking ice can create waves or remove support from nearby loose rock and ice. Waves or slope failures can damage the natural barrier holding the lake, allowing water to escape suddenly.
Retreating glaciers can leave larger lakes of meltwater. Sudden flood risk increases where the barriers holding that water are weak and exposed places lie downstream.
Warming makes glaciers retreat and changes lakes of meltwater around them. Flood danger increases where unstable barriers hold back water above exposed communities.
outgoing: If a lake held beside a glacier breaks through its barrier, stored water can rush downstream. The flood can also carry large amounts of sediment.
A sudden glacier-lake flood can send fast, powerful flows past bridges. These can wash away the material supporting their foundations.
If ice or loose rock holding back a glacier lake fails, stored water can escape quickly. The flood can carry large amounts of water and sediment downstream.

human.summary: A sudden glacier-lake flood can send fast, powerful flows past bridges. These can wash away the material supporting their foundations.
consequences: If a lake held beside a glacier breaks through its barrier, stored water can rush downstream. The flood can also carry large amounts of sediment. A surge of fast-moving water can wash material away from around a bridge's supports. Losing that material can weaken the foundations.

If ice or loose rock holding back a glacier lake fails, stored water can escape quickly. The flood can carry large amounts of water and sediment downstream. Sudden releases of stored glacier water can produce river flows far above seasonal levels. Repeated releases change the timing, size and sediment carried by downstream floods.

sea ice season loss.name: Sea Ice Season Loss
sea ice season loss.description: A region of ocean staying frozen for a shorter part of the year. Ice may form later or melt earlier. This changes conditions for wildlife, coastal protection and travel. The area covered in one month does not tell us the full season's length.
incoming: More global warming makes an Arctic September with almost no sea ice more likely. The assessment puts the yearly chance by the end of the century at about 1% with 1.5°C of warming, compared with 10–35% with 2°C.
Warm ocean water can melt sea ice from below and delay freezing in autumn. This shortens the time that sea ice covers the water.
Faster warming in the Arctic can bring earlier spring melting and later autumn freezing. Sea ice then remains for less of the year.

The cited study found that Arctic September sea-ice area fell roughly in step with accumulated human carbon dioxide emissions. Over its assessed record, each extra metric tonne was associated with about 3 square metres less ice, with an uncertainty of plus or minus 0.3 square metres.
outgoing: A longer ice-free season can allow vessels to use northern routes for more of the year. Moving ice, storms, ports, insurance and rules still determine whether traffic actually increases.
Less time covered by bright sea ice leaves darker water exposed to sunlight for longer. More absorbed energy contributes to faster warming in the Arctic.
A shorter season of sea ice leaves Arctic coasts more exposed to waves and erosion. It can also shorten periods when people can safely use ice-based access routes.
A shorter ice season can leave thinner and less connected Arctic sea ice. Winds and currents can move this ice more readily through areas used by ships.
A shorter ice season reduces stable growing space for algae living in sea ice. Earlier melting can change bloom timing and wash away some of this material.
A longer open-water season gives waves more time and space to attack Arctic coasts. Shores made of thawing, ice-rich ground can erode especially quickly.
Losing sea ice during the sunlit season exposes darker ocean water. The water absorbs more sunlight, adding heat that can encourage further melting.

coastal inundation risk.name: Coastal Inundation Risk
coastal inundation risk.description: How likely seawater is to spread onto nearby land, and how serious the flooding could be. Storms can push water inland, while high tides and rising sea levels make it easier for water to reach homes, roads and other low-lying places.
incoming: Mangroves, marshes, dunes and reefs can reduce some coastal wave and flood impacts. They have physical limits and cannot prevent every flood.
Warming expands seawater and melts ice on land, raising sea levels. A higher starting water level makes it easier for seawater to flood nearby land.
Carbon dioxide adds to warming and the resulting rise in sea level. This increases the background pressure behind coastal flooding and erosion.
Changes in Atlantic ocean circulation can raise or lower sea levels along parts of the North Atlantic coast. Flooding there also depends on tides, storms, waves and the longer-term rise in sea level.

A weaker current through the Florida Straits is associated with higher sea levels along nearby Atlantic coasts. Many other factors control flooding there, so a rising tide gauge alone does not identify a change in the current.
Water from melting ice sheets raises the sea's starting level. Coastal flooding then depends on local tides, storms, land movement and the people or buildings exposed.

Higher sea levels make previously rare coastal water levels easier to reach. Across the assessed tide-gauge locations, relative sea-level rise is projected to make recent extreme still-water levels occur roughly 20–30 times as often by 2050. Local tides, storms and land movement affect the result.
outgoing: When the sea rises, it can become harder for drains to carry used water away. During storms or high tides, pipes can back up and wastewater can spill into surrounding areas.
Higher seawater levels can push salty water farther inland through river mouths and connected underground stores. This is especially important when river flow is too weak to push it back.
Repeated flooding by the sea can add salt to connected underground freshwater stores. Shallow or exposed stores may become less suitable for drinking or farming.
Flooding from the sea can add salt and other contamination to drinking-water sources or disrupt intakes. Water plants may then have difficulty providing safe supplies.
Seawater can reach low-lying airports near the coast. Flooded runways, access roads or equipment can interrupt flights and damage the airport.
Repeated flooding by seawater can increase expected insurance losses. Insurers may raise prices, limit coverage or stop offering policies in exposed areas.
Rising water can damage coastal wetlands if they cannot build up soil or move inland fast enough. Losing plants and soils can put their stored carbon at risk of release.
Repeated flooding by seawater increases the need to protect essential buildings and services. Better siting, drainage and access can reduce damage within their design limits.
Storms, tides and rising sea levels can bring seawater onto low-lying buildings and services. Whether they fail depends on flood depth, protection, equipment design and available backups.
Repeated coastal floods can increase expected insurance claims and the cost of covering them. Insurers may raise prices, limit policies or leave exposed markets.
Coastal floods can close ports, damage access roads and stop cargo handling. Sea routes can be disrupted even when the open water remains navigable.
Rising seawater can change salt levels in estuaries. This may make particular places more or less suitable for disease-causing organisms, depending on the salt range they tolerate.

thermokarst expansion.name: Thermokarst Expansion
thermokarst expansion.description: More land sinking or becoming uneven as ice inside frozen ground melts. The changes can create ponds, damage structures and alter drainage. Wet, thawed plant material can also decay and release gases that warm the planet.
incoming: When ice inside frozen soil melts, the ground can sink and become uneven. More thaw can create additional hollows, ponds and unstable surfaces.
Warming melts ice within frozen ground. The land can sink unevenly, creating hollows, ponds and unstable surfaces.
Severe northern fires can remove moss, plants and organic soil that insulate frozen ground. Where the ground contains much ice, later thaw can make it sink and form new hollows or ponds.
outgoing: Sinking ground and new ponds can damage roads, pipes and building foundations in cold regions. Structures may no longer have the stable support they were designed for.
When frozen ground thaws and sinks, water can collect in the new hollows. The breakdown of previously frozen material in this wet ground can release methane.
Sinking thawed ground can form ponds and wet hollows. Plant material decaying there with little oxygen can become a local source of methane.

Damage to roads, power lines or utilities in remote polar areas can interrupt essential services. Difficult access and limited alternatives can make recovery harder.
consequences: When frozen ground thaws and sinks, water can collect in the new hollows. The breakdown of previously frozen material in this wet ground can release methane. Methane traps heat and has contributed to the warming already observed. The cited assessment estimates its contribution over a particular historical period, with an uncertainty range rather than one exact value.

arctic shipping expansion.name: Arctic Shipping Expansion
arctic shipping expansion.description: More vessels travelling through northern polar waters, or using them for a longer season. Less sea ice can open routes, but moving ice, severe weather and limited ports still create hazards. Less ice alone does not guarantee more vessel traffic.
incoming: A longer ice-free season can allow vessels to use northern routes for more of the year. Moving ice, storms, ports, insurance and rules still determine whether traffic actually increases.
A shorter sea-ice season can make some Arctic routes open to ships for longer. Actual use still depends on safety, facilities and whether the journey is economically worthwhile.
outgoing: More ships using Arctic routes means more journeys exposed to changing ice conditions. Remote locations and limited rescue or repair services can make disruptions harder to manage.
Additional ship journeys burn fuel and release carbon dioxide. The total depends on the number of journeys, their length and the fuels used.

polar infrastructure failure.name: Polar Infrastructure Failure
polar infrastructure failure.description: Roads, buildings, power supplies or other essential structures in polar regions becoming unable to do their job. Thawing ground, erosion and severe conditions can cause damage. Remote locations can make repairs and replacement supplies difficult.
incoming: Sinking ground and new ponds can damage roads, pipes and building foundations in cold regions. Structures may no longer have the stable support they were designed for.
A shorter season of sea ice leaves Arctic coasts more exposed to waves and erosion. It can also shorten periods when people can safely use ice-based access routes.
Thawing ice within the ground can make land sink or shift unevenly. Buildings, roads and pipes built on susceptible frozen ground can lose support or become distorted.
Rapid erosion and collapsing coastal slopes can remove support beneath buildings, roads and pipes. Communities may lose reliable access and essential services.
Warming contributes to thawing frozen ground and losing protective sea ice. These changes can damage buildings, roads and services in polar regions.
Ice loss and related changes to coasts and frozen ground can threaten polar buildings and transport. The risk is greatest where facilities depend on stable ice or land.
outgoing: Damage to roads, power lines or utilities in remote polar areas can interrupt essential services. Difficult access and limited alternatives can make recovery harder.

planet.summary: Damaged pipes or industrial equipment can release pollutants into northern environments. A failing road or building does not always cause a spill, so the environmental effect needs site-specific evidence.

response.defaultDriver: Buildings and roads may be based on ground conditions that no longer hold as northern regions warm.
levers: Monitor ground movement and inspect vulnerable structures.
Adapt foundations or relocate assets where needed, using engineering suited to the specific ground.

snow drought.name: Snow Drought
snow drought.description: Less water being stored as seasonal snow than usual. This can happen because too little snow falls, more precipitation falls as rain, or snow melts early. Rivers and reservoirs may then receive less water during the season when it is needed.
incoming: Warmer weather can cause more rain instead of snow and melt existing snow sooner. Less water then remains stored as snow for later in the year.
Warming can shift snowfall toward rain and speed melting. Mountain areas may then store much less water in winter snow than expected.
outgoing: Less stored snow means less water released during the usual melting season. Rivers may receive water earlier in the year and less when it is most needed.
A small winter snowpack stores less water for later in the year. This can make reservoir supplies harder to predict and manage.
A smaller or warmer winter snowpack often melts sooner. Rivers may receive an earlier and weaker pulse of meltwater.
Less stored winter snow can make a river basin more dependent on glacier melt. Once that glacier contribution begins declining, late-season water supplies become more exposed.
A season with little snowfall or unusually early melting leaves less water stored in mountain snow. The change differs with elevation, season and river basin.
Repeated winters with too little snow leave small ice caps with less new ice to replace melting. Their summits and connecting ice can thin until a once-continuous cap breaks apart.

human.summary: Less stored snow means less water released during the usual melting season. Rivers may receive water earlier in the year and less when it is most needed. Changed incoming river flows may no longer fit a dam's release plans. Operators can struggle to meet water, flood-control or electricity commitments.
consequences: A small winter snowpack stores less water for later in the year. This can make reservoir supplies harder to predict and manage. Unpredictable stored water makes it harder for dam operators to deliver the expected supply at the right time. Drinking water, flood control or electricity commitments may then be missed.

Less stored winter snow can make a river basin more dependent on glacier melt. Once that glacier contribution begins declining, late-season water supplies become more exposed. After a glacier basin passes its period of greatest meltwater supply, the contribution can decline over time. People and power systems relying on that water may face less dependable dry-season flows.

loss of firn meltwater storage capacity.name: Loss of Firn Meltwater Storage Capacity
loss of firn meltwater storage capacity.description: Older, partly compressed snow losing the small spaces that can hold meltwater. If these spaces fill with ice or disappear, less water can be stored or frozen again. More meltwater may then drain off an ice sheet.
incoming: Warmer conditions melt more of the partly compacted snow above glacier ice. Over time, this layer can lose space that would otherwise hold and refreeze meltwater.
outgoing: The partly compacted snow above glacier ice can temporarily hold meltwater. Losing that storage changes when water reaches rivers, making supplies less dependable for users downstream.
The partly compacted snow above glacier ice can store and refreeze meltwater. When it loses empty space or forms impermeable layers, more water runs off and contributes to ice loss.

human.summary: The partly compacted snow above glacier ice can temporarily hold meltwater. Losing that storage changes when water reaches rivers, making supplies less dependable for users downstream.
consequences: The partly compacted snow above glacier ice can store and refreeze meltwater. When it loses empty space or forms impermeable layers, more water runs off and contributes to ice loss. Water from melting ice sheets raises the sea's starting level. Coastal flooding then depends on local tides, storms, land movement and the people or buildings exposed.

planet.summary: The partly compacted snow above glacier ice can store and refreeze meltwater. When it loses empty space or forms impermeable layers, more water runs off and contributes to ice loss.

levers: Include changing snow storage in ice and sea-level projections.

incoming: Loss of Firn Meltwater Storage Capacity
The partly compacted snow above glacier ice can temporarily hold meltwater. Losing that storage changes when water reaches rivers, making supplies less dependable for users downstream.
After a glacier basin passes its period of greatest meltwater supply, the contribution can decline over time. People and power systems relying on that water may face less dependable dry-season flows.
Warming changes glacier size and when meltwater reaches rivers. People, farms and power systems that depend on that water can face less reliable supplies.
outgoing: Power stations that depend on water from glaciers are exposed when the amount or timing of that water changes. Electricity production may become less dependable across seasons.

Changing supplies of water from glaciers can put pressure on agreements between countries sharing a river. Disputes are more likely where the agreements cannot adjust to less dependable seasonal flows.

oceanic deoxygenation.name: Oceanic Deoxygenation
oceanic deoxygenation.description: Seawater losing some of the oxygen that marine animals need to live. Warming and changes in water mixing can contribute. Animals may have less suitable living space, particularly where oxygen was already scarce.
incoming: Warmer seawater holds less oxygen, and stronger layering can reduce the supply reaching deeper water. Together these processes can lower ocean oxygen. Projections depend on the future climate scenario.
Strongly separated water layers can slow mixing from the surface. Less oxygen then reaches deeper water to replace what living things use.

Less sinking and renewal of deep water can reduce oxygen delivery far below the surface. The cited observations describe this connection in a particular Antarctic ocean basin, not an identical change everywhere.
Warming makes seawater hold less oxygen and can reduce mixing between surface and deep water. These processes contribute to declining oxygen in parts of the ocean.
outgoing: As oxygen falls, sensitive animals may leave or die while more tolerant ones remain. This changes local feeding relationships and the habitat available.
Reduced oxygen can shrink suitable fish habitat, move stocks or cause deaths. These changes add to fishery risks, alongside fishing pressure and other local conditions.
Water arriving with less oxygen gives a shallow sea less protection against further oxygen loss. A smaller additional loss may then be enough to harm local marine life.

Less oxygen can reduce the depths and temperatures fish can tolerate and change where their food lives. Responses differ between species, and local oxygen loss may come from nutrient pollution as well as climate change.

human.summary: As oxygen falls, sensitive animals may leave or die while more tolerant ones remain. This changes local feeding relationships and the habitat available. Changes in feeding relationships can alter which fish are available and when. Fishing businesses may receive a less predictable mix or quantity of seafood.
consequences: Reduced oxygen can shrink suitable fish habitat, move stocks or cause deaths. These changes add to fishery risks, alongside fishing pressure and other local conditions. Severely depleted fish stocks leave fewer fish available to catch. Ports and markets may then receive smaller or less reliable supplies.

Water arriving with less oxygen gives a shallow sea less protection against further oxygen loss. A smaller additional loss may then be enough to harm local marine life. Long periods of low oxygen can kill sensitive seabed animals and push fish elsewhere. Species that tolerate these conditions may become more common, changing the food web.

planet.summary: Less oxygen leaves fewer suitable places for many marine animals. Species may need to move or compete within a narrower band of water.
consequences: Fish and other animals can lose usable habitat.
Warmer, more separated water layers can limit the mixing that replaces oxygen.

response.defaultDriver: Warming reduces how much oxygen water holds and can weaken mixing. Excess nutrients add pressure in some coastal waters.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions and excess nutrients reaching vulnerable waters.
Monitor oxygen at relevant depths and adjust habitat and fishing management to the observed changes.

antarctic bottom water decline.name: Antarctic Bottom Water Decline
antarctic bottom water decline.description: Less cold, dense water forming near Antarctica and sinking to the deepest ocean. This movement helps renew deep water and carry oxygen into it. A reduction can change conditions far below the surface.
incoming: Warming and added freshwater around Antarctica can make it harder for very dense water to form and sink. The response varies by region and also depends on winds and other conditions.
Meltwater from Antarctic ice makes nearby seawater fresher and less dense. This can reduce the formation of water that sinks to the deepest ocean.
Winds around Antarctica influence how coastal and offshore waters mix. Along with temperature and fresh water, this affects the formation of dense water that sinks into the deep ocean.

Warming and additional meltwater change water conditions around Antarctica. Lighter surface water may sink less readily, weakening the formation of dense water that spreads along the deep ocean floor.

ocean acidification.name: Ocean Acidification
ocean acidification.description: Seawater becoming more acidic as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air. The chemical change makes some of the materials used to build shells and coral skeletons less available. The ocean does not need to become an acid overall for these effects to matter.
incoming: The ocean absorbs some of the carbon dioxide people release into the air. This changes seawater chemistry and makes the water more acidic.

Warmer water and changing currents affect how carbon dioxide is absorbed and moved through the ocean. They change where seawater chemistry shifts, while absorbed carbon dioxide remains the main cause of increasing acidity.

Some carbon dioxide from burning coal to make electricity is eventually absorbed by the ocean. It changes seawater chemistry as part of the combined global total. A particular local change cannot be assigned to this source alone.

outgoing: Changing seawater chemistry can make the materials for shells and coral skeletons less available. Some organisms then have more difficulty building or maintaining them, with large differences between species and conditions.
Changes in seawater chemistry affect species differently. If some organisms grow or survive less well, animals that depend on them can also be affected, changing feeding relationships.
Changing seawater chemistry can slow the building and repair of coral skeletons. If losses outpace replacement, the reef framework can weaken.

Changes in seawater chemistry can harm the growth or survival of some young fish and shell-forming animals. Effects differ between species. Evidence of exposure alone does not show that an entire estuary has lost its nursery role.
Changing seawater chemistry can reduce coral growth and recovery. It can make heat stress harder to withstand, but it is not itself a measure of heat-related bleaching.
Coral Larval Survival and Recruitment Failure
Changing seawater chemistry can interfere with early coral growth and the signals young corals use to find a place to settle. Sensitive species may have lower survival.
Changes in seawater chemistry can slow reef building and increase erosion. Weaker structures can become more vulnerable when waves or other disturbances strike.

Changing seawater chemistry can affect growth, reproduction, prey and habitat. It may contribute to changes in where fish live, but direct evidence is generally weaker than for warming and numbers can change without movement.

human.summary: Changes in seawater chemistry can make it harder for some marine animals to build shells or reefs. People depending on seafood and coastal habitats may feel the effects.
consequences: Shellfish hatcheries and reef communities can become less productive.
Fishing households may face lower income or less dependable food supplies.

planet.summary: Changing seawater chemistry makes shell and reef building harder for some organisms. Effects can spread to the animals and habitats that depend on them.
consequences: Sensitive shell-building species may use more energy or grow and survive less well.

pacific decadal oscillation.name: Pacific Decadal Oscillation
pacific decadal oscillation.description: A broad pattern of warmer and cooler surface waters in the North Pacific that varies over years and decades. It is linked to changes in regional rainfall and marine conditions. It describes natural climate variability rather than a simple rise in temperature everywhere.
incoming: Unusually warm tropical Pacific conditions can leave a lasting effect on North Pacific temperatures and currents. These effects contribute to longer-lived patterns alongside the ocean's own changes.
Unusually cool tropical Pacific conditions can reinforce some cool patterns farther north. The longer-lived North Pacific pattern also has other causes.
outgoing: Longer-term North Pacific temperature patterns can change where unusually warm ocean episodes are more likely or intense. Individual events still depend on additional conditions.
This recurring North Pacific pattern changes the background distribution of ocean warmth and regional weather. It can influence unusual conditions without determining every event.
North Pacific temperature and habitat changes can make open-water species more available in some places and less in others. Responses differ by species and region.

Longer-lived North Pacific temperature patterns can affect how changes in air pressure travel through the atmosphere. This can alter the chance of particular weather patterns over the Pacific and North America.

Long-lasting North Pacific sea-temperature patterns can influence winds high in the atmosphere. This can affect the jet stream over the Pacific and North America, alongside its own natural variability.

outgoing: Long-term North Atlantic temperature patterns vary alongside regional climate conditions. The association does not establish that people control the pattern's phase or that it alone causes a particular event.

outgoing: Warm and cool phases in the tropical Atlantic are linked with shifts in winds and rainfall. These can influence unusual conditions in connected regions.
Tropical Atlantic temperature patterns can influence seasonal rains in nearby and connected regions. Whether rain increases or decreases depends on the phase, season and place.
Changes in tropical Atlantic water conditions can move suitable habitat for open-water species. Different species and regions respond differently.

indian ocean dipole.name: Indian Ocean Dipole
indian ocean dipole.description: A difference in surface temperature between the western and eastern tropical Indian Ocean that becomes stronger or reverses. This contrast changes winds and where rain tends to fall. Its effects depend on the season and other climate patterns happening at the same time.
incoming: Unusually warm tropical Pacific water changes tropical winds. This can alter the temperature difference between the eastern and western Indian Ocean.
outgoing: An east-west temperature contrast in the Indian Ocean shifts where moist air rises and rain falls. This can change rainy-season behaviour in particular regions, without one uniform effect everywhere.
Changing temperature contrasts across the Indian Ocean can shift rainfall and warmth in connected regions. The phase and season affect which places are wetter, drier or hotter.

Temperature differences across the Indian Ocean affect tropical winds and storm activity. These conditions can influence how the eastward-moving band of tropical rain develops and travels.

marine fisheries collapse.name: Marine Fisheries Collapse
marine fisheries collapse.description: Fish populations becoming so depleted that they can no longer support normal catches or their usual role in the sea. Fishing pressure, habitat damage and environmental changes can contribute. Recovery depends on the species and whether the pressures are reduced.
incoming: Losing sheltered habitat for young fish can mean fewer survive to adulthood. Where this stage limits population recovery, the chance of a serious decline in catches increases.
Prolonged unusually warm seawater can kill sensitive animals, damage habitat or move fish away. These changes can undermine fisheries, with effects that vary between places and species.
Reduced oxygen can shrink suitable fish habitat, move stocks or cause deaths. These changes add to fishery risks, alongside fishing pressure and other local conditions.
Losing feeding links or suitable prey can reduce the survival of young fish and the ability of stocks to recover. Catch outcomes also depend on fishing and management.
Repeated oxygen shortages can kill fish, reduce living space and harm young animals. Where sensitive stocks are exposed, fisheries face a greater risk of decline.
Losing reef structure removes shelter, feeding areas and places for young fish to grow. Fisheries depending on those habitats can become less able to sustain catches.

Under the high-emissions pathway RCP8.5, Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projects global maximum fish catch potential to fall by 20.5–24.1% in 2081–2100 compared with 1986–2005. This is a scenario-based estimate of potential catch, not a prediction that every fishery will change by the same amount.
Large oil spills can harm fish and shellfish or force fishing closures. Longer-term population effects depend on exposure, life stage and recovery.
outgoing: Severely depleted fish stocks leave fewer fish available to catch. Ports and markets may then receive smaller or less reliable supplies.
Falling catches create greater food and income risks where communities already depend heavily on fish. The consequences depend on affordable alternatives and trade.

Fewer accessible fish can increase competition over catches and income where access is contested. Scarcity does not inevitably cause conflict. Good agreements and recovery plans can reduce the pressure.
Losing large numbers of harvested predators or other consumers can change the species they eat and those below them. A chain reaction needs evidence at several levels, not just one declining species.

human.summary: Large losses of fish stocks can remove food and income from coastal communities. Replacing those supplies and jobs may take time.
consequences: Fishing families can lose income when fish become scarce or move beyond reach.

Changes in east-to-west tropical Pacific winds affect how surface water moves and how cold water rises from below. The direction of the wind change determines the response.

coastal hypoxia.name: Coastal Hypoxia
coastal hypoxia.description: Water near the shore containing too little oxygen for many animals to live normally. Warm water, limited mixing and the decay of excess algae can contribute. Fish may leave the area, while animals unable to move can be harmed.
incoming: Extra nitrogen carried to the coast can fuel algae growth. As the algae decay, they use oxygen and can leave too little for other marine life.
More strongly separated water layers slow the replacement of oxygen below the surface. Low-oxygen conditions are more likely where excess organic material is also using up oxygen as it decays.
Untreated water can add nutrients and decaying material near the coast. Breaking down that material uses oxygen and can contribute to shortages for marine animals.
Large growths of algae can use up oxygen as they live and decay. In some coastal waters, this leaves too little oxygen for other living things.
Warmer seawater holds less oxygen and can mix less with deeper water. This can worsen oxygen shortages near some coasts, although nutrient pollution and local currents may have a larger influence.
Warming can reduce oxygen in coastal water and limit mixing with deeper layers. In nutrient-rich areas, faster decay and weaker mixing can worsen oxygen shortages.
Nutrients lost from farms can reach coastal water and encourage growth that later uses up oxygen. The connection depends on transport downstream and the actual oxygen response.

marine food-web reorganization.description: Changes in which sea creatures eat which, and in how energy passes between them. Some species or feeding links may disappear while others become more common. This can change fish catches and make the system less able to cope with further disturbance.
incoming: When open-water species move, predators and prey may no longer meet in the same places. These changes can reorganize who eats whom in the sea.
More strongly separated saltwater layers can change how nutrients reach the surface. This affects the organisms that grow there and the animals that depend on them.

As oxygen falls, sensitive animals may leave or die while more tolerant ones remain. This changes local feeding relationships and the habitat available.
Changes in seawater chemistry affect species differently. If some organisms grow or survive less well, animals that depend on them can also be affected, changing feeding relationships.
Changes in currents move heat and nutrients differently. This can change which organisms grow in an area and the animals that feed on them.
Long periods of unusually warm seawater affect marine species differently. Changes in survival, feeding and energy transfer can disrupt food chains, and larger predators may recover more slowly.

When warm surface water mixes less with deeper water, fewer nutrients may reach sunlit waters. At a Gulf of Lions study site, the less productive season also showed a narrower range of food resources used by bottom-living animals.

Changes in algae growing in sea ice affect when and how much food becomes available to small marine animals. Too little food, or food arriving at the wrong time, can affect animals farther up the food chain.
When shellfish and shell-forming plankton grow less well or die, animals feeding on them may lose food. Habitats and food chains can change where these species play an important role.

Carbon dioxide changes ocean temperature and chemistry, with further effects on oxygen and currents. Some species lose suitable conditions or food, and repeated losses can leave a less varied food web.

ocean salinity stratification.name: Ocean Salinity Stratification
ocean salinity stratification.description: Seawater forming layers because some water is saltier and denser than the water above it. Stronger separation can make the layers mix less easily. This affects how oxygen, heat, nutrients and carbon move between shallow and deep water.
incoming: Warming and added freshwater from melting land ice can make surface water lighter than the water below. Stronger separation can reduce mixing, depending on local circulation.
Fresh water from melting ice sheets forms a lighter layer near the ocean surface. This can strengthen the separation from saltier, denser water below.
Heavy rain and runoff can make local surface seawater fresher and lighter. This can briefly reduce mixing with deeper water when winds and currents are weak.
Warming changes rain, evaporation and ice melt. In some ocean regions, the resulting differences in salt content and temperature strengthen the separation between surface and deeper water.
outgoing: Salt content changes how dense seawater is and how strongly it forms separate layers. These differences help influence the movement and mixing of ocean water.

Layers caused by differences in seawater salt content can change surface temperature in the tropical Atlantic. This can influence its warm and cool phases, alongside other ocean and wind processes.
A lighter, fresher surface layer in the North Atlantic can limit mixing and sinking. This weakens a process that helps drive the ocean's large circulation.

incoming: Losing coastal trees and roots removes some resistance to waves and moving water. Nearby people and buildings can become more exposed during storms.

outgoing: Low-lying shores exposed to storm-driven seawater face greater danger when high tides, waves or river flow occur at the same time. The combined water can overwhelm drainage or protection.
High storm water levels let waves reach and wear away beaches, dunes or cliffs. Erosion can be greater where little new sediment arrives to replace what is lost.

incoming: Heat, drought and fire can damage plants and increase the release of carbon from living things and soils. This can reduce how much carbon dioxide land ecosystems remove from the air overall.

Recovering vegetation and healthier soils can increase the carbon taken up and stored on land. The benefit depends on lasting recovery and protection from renewed damage.

peat oxidation pulse.description: A burst of carbon release when long-stored, partly decayed plant material is exposed to air and breaks down. Draining or drying the ground can allow this to happen. Carbon that accumulated over a long time can then return to the atmosphere.

Draining wet ground lowers its water level and exposes buried plant material to air. Microbes can then break it down faster, releasing stored carbon.
Damaged peatland can lose the high water table that keeps buried plant material wet. Exposure to air allows faster decay and greater carbon loss.
outgoing: When dried peat breaks down in air, it releases carbon dioxide. Fires can release this long-stored carbon much more quickly.

nocturnal heat stress.name: Nocturnal Heat Stress
nocturnal heat stress.description: Nights staying hot enough to make recovery from daytime heat difficult. Homes may remain warm and people may struggle to cool down or rest. The effect depends on humidity, housing, health and access to cooling.
incoming: Losing trees removes shade and some natural cooling. Neighbourhoods can store more daytime heat and remain warmer at night, leaving less relief for residents.
Warming can raise nighttime temperatures and increase exposure to hot, humid conditions. The loss of cool hours can reduce the relief available after a hot day.
Warming raises nighttime temperatures and can reduce relief after hot days. Repeated hot nights give the body less chance to cool and recover.
outgoing: Hot nights can prevent the body and the home from cooling down. Health risks can therefore be greater than an average daily temperature alone would suggest.

Studies link hot nights with increased risk of death, but estimates differ and can be uncertain. In the cited Chinese study, the uncertainty range for nighttime-only heat also allowed for no increase.

incoming: Human-caused warming raises the starting point for daytime and nighttime temperatures. This can make very hot days followed by unusually hot nights more likely, with regional differences.

outgoing: When nights remain hot after very hot days, people have less time to cool down and recover. Observed studies find that this continuous exposure can create greater health burdens than heat limited to the day.

incoming: Wind patterns high above the equator are linked with changes in a travelling pattern of tropical clouds and rain. Researchers are still studying how the two interact.

outgoing: A travelling pattern of tropical clouds and winds can influence active and dry spells within a rainy season. The effect depends on its location and the region involved.
This moving tropical weather pattern influences winds and rainfall over several weeks. It can contribute to unusual conditions but does not uniquely determine them.

incoming: Hot, humid weather can cause many people to use cooling equipment at once. The resulting jump in electricity demand can strain a power system that has little spare capacity.

Rapid growth in computing for artificial intelligence can add concentrated electricity demand. Power connections and supply may struggle when this grows faster than the network's capacity or flexibility.
Delayed power-line upgrades can stop electricity from reaching places that need it during busy periods. A region can therefore face shortages even when power is available elsewhere.
Substations cannot always expand on time when key electrical equipment is unavailable. That can leave the network with too little capacity to meet busy periods.
Power stations that need cooling water may have to limit output when water is scarce or unsuitable. This can tighten electricity supply during hot periods when demand is high.
Stored electricity can be released when demand is high and supply is tight. This helps only while enough stored energy and delivery capacity remain available.
Reducing or moving flexible electricity use during busy hours eases pressure on the power system. The benefit depends on how much demand actually changes.
Buildings that need less heating and cooling use less electricity during temperature extremes. This can reduce pressure during the busiest hours.
Switching many buildings to electric heating and cooling can increase electricity demand at busy times. Building efficiency and power-system planning help manage the extra load.
Buildings designed to stay cooler need less powered cooling during hot hours. This can ease pressure on electricity supplies.
Many vehicles charging during already busy hours can put extra pressure on electricity supplies. Managing charging times can reduce that pressure.

energy affordability crisis.name: Energy Affordability Crisis
energy affordability crisis.description: Households or essential services being unable to reliably pay for the power or fuel they need. People may have to cut back on heating, cooling or other necessities. The problem depends on prices, income, housing and available support.
incoming: A strained power system may need expensive extra generation or face price spikes. These costs can add to household energy bills, depending on how prices are set.
Expensive electricity production during busy periods can add to customer costs. How much reaches household bills depends on pricing and market rules.
Electricity systems that rely on gas are exposed to changes in fuel prices. Those changes can affect customer bills, depending on market arrangements and protections.
Leaving available low-cost wind or solar power unused can add costs to the electricity system. The effect on household bills depends on how the market and tariffs work.
Removing salt from water uses electricity. Heavy reliance on this process can add energy costs, with household effects depending on prices and support.
outgoing: When households cannot afford energy bills, unpaid balances can put them at risk of losing service. Consumer protections and support affect whether disconnection occurs.
People who cannot afford to run cooling may face unsafe indoor temperatures. This can increase heat illness, especially where housing offers little natural protection.
High energy costs can stop households from buying or running enough cooling. Having an electricity connection or an air conditioner does not ensure that using it is affordable.

human.summary: When energy is too expensive, people may be unable to keep homes at safe temperatures or reach essential places. Bills can compete with other basic needs.
consequences: Households may use too little heating or cooling during dangerous weather.

airport operational disruption.name: Airport Operational Disruption
airport operational disruption.description: Flights, ground services or passenger movements being delayed or stopped. Heavy rain, heat or damaged equipment can contribute. Effects may spread to other places when aircraft, staff or cargo cannot continue their journeys.
incoming: Heat, flooding or other hazards can interrupt runways, access roads and ground equipment. Flights may then be delayed or cancelled, depending on the airport's protection and response.
Very heavy rain can overwhelm airport drains and reduce visibility. Flights and ground operations may be delayed or cancelled.
Hot, humid conditions can reduce aircraft takeoff performance and the time staff can safely work outside. This can limit airport operations and schedules.
outgoing: When an airport stops operating, a region may lose an important route for people, supplies and emergency help. The effects are greater where few alternative routes are available.

human.summary: When an airport stops operating, a region may lose an important route for people, supplies and emergency help. The effects are greater where few alternative routes are available.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

response.defaultDriver: Tightly packed schedules leave little spare capacity to recover from repeated disruptions.
levers: Prepare heat, smoke and flood operating plans and alternative arrangements.
Protect drainage, backup power and critical ground equipment at exposed sites.

bridge scour exposure.name: Bridge Scour Exposure
bridge scour exposure.description: Flowing water being able to wash away soil or rock around a bridge's supports. Losing this material can weaken the foundations. The risk depends on river flow, the riverbed and the design and condition of the bridge.
incoming: A surge of fast-moving water can wash material away from around a bridge's supports. Losing that material can weaken the foundations.
A sudden glacier-lake flood can send fast, powerful flows past bridges. These can wash away the material supporting their foundations.
outgoing: Fast-moving water can wash material away from around bridge foundations. A weakened or closed bridge can cut an important transport link.
Damage to a bridge foundation can close roads used to carry goods to and from a port. This can add delays even when the port itself is working.

human.summary: Fast-moving water can wash material away from around bridge foundations. A weakened or closed bridge can cut an important transport link.
consequences: Damage to a bridge foundation can close roads used to carry goods to and from a port. This can add delays even when the port itself is working.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

response.defaultDriver: Older design assumptions or inspections may miss changes in flood flows and the riverbed.
levers: Inspect and monitor vulnerable foundations and nearby riverbed levels.
Use site-specific protection or foundation upgrades and prepare safe closure procedures.

rail heat buckling.name: Rail Heat Buckling
rail heat buckling.description: Train tracks bending out of position as the metal expands in hot weather. Where that expansion is constrained, forces can build up in the rails. Inspections, slower trains or closures may be needed to keep services safe.
incoming: Heat makes steel rails expand. Rails can bend out of shape if the heat exceeds what the track's design, installation and maintenance can safely handle.
Intense fire close to a railway can deform rails and damage track components. Smoke or a nearby line closure alone does not show that rails have bent.
outgoing: Hot rails can expand and bend sideways when the track cannot contain the force. Inspections, speed limits or closures can interrupt passenger and freight services, while severe failures can cause derailments.

human.summary: Hot rails can expand and bend sideways when the track cannot contain the force. Inspections, speed limits or closures can interrupt passenger and freight services, while severe failures can cause derailments.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

response.defaultDriver: Heat makes steel rails expand. Rails can bend out of shape if the heat exceeds what the track's design, installation and maintenance can safely handle.
levers: Maintain transport assets and plan alternative routes for the hazards they actually face.
Use efficient and lower-emissions travel options where practical, with reliable public transport and cleaner power.

biodiversity intactness loss.name: Biodiversity Intactness Loss
biodiversity intactness loss.description: An area's original mix and abundance of living things declining compared with a reference condition. Some species may disappear while others become much less common. The measure concerns the wider living community, rather than just counting how many species remain.
incoming: Severe damage to rivers, lakes or wetlands can remove species and reduce the abundance of those remaining. Their living communities become less like the earlier reference condition.
Removing water from wetlands changes or removes habitat for species adapted to wet conditions. Some populations may decline or disappear locally.
Species with less suitable, connected living space can become less abundant or disappear locally. This changes the area's original mix of life.
Small, separated populations can lose access to mates and resources. This can reduce abundance and increase local extinction risk for species that cannot cross the gaps.
Repairing damaged habitats can help native plants and animals recover. Recovery depends on removing the original pressures and maintaining a diverse, connected habitat.
Projects can help wildlife when they restore native habitats and connect them to other suitable areas. A project designed only for protection may not provide the same benefit.

Losing suitable cold habitat on isolated rocky peaks leaves specialised plants and animals with fewer places to survive. Small, separated populations may face a greater chance of disappearing locally.
Warming shifts the conditions that plants and animals can tolerate and the places where they can survive. These pressures add to habitat loss, harvesting and other human activities.

Replacing tropical forest with oil palms removes and separates habitats used by forest species. Keeping forest patches and improving plantation management can help, but does not recreate the original forest community.

Harmful introduced species can displace native wildlife and change habitats or food webs. Being non-native alone does not establish harm. The effects need evidence for the species and place concerned.
Removing older trees can reduce nesting holes, dead wood and layered habitats used by specialised wildlife. Effects differ between forests, and some managed areas retain or regain important features.

A lasting shift to more open vegetation removes conditions needed by many forest species. The new landscape may support other wildlife, so the loss concerns the original forest community rather than all biodiversity.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Changes in species and habitats can weaken benefits such as pollination, useful plants and reliable local resources. A loss in an index does not by itself measure how many people are harmed.

planet.summary: Fewer native species or lower abundance can change how an ecosystem functions. The response depends on which species and interactions are lost, not just the total count.

response.defaultDriver: Land clearing, roads, pollution and other pressures can break habitats into smaller, less connected pieces.
levers: Protect places where native plants and animals can still thrive. Restore links between suitable places so wildlife can move between them.
Include measured habitat and species outcomes in land-use decisions and restoration.

measurement.metric: Quality-controlled species occurrence coverage
measurement.geography: global, country, or bounded region
measurement.cadence: monthly

wildfire regime shift.name: Wildfire Regime Shift
wildfire regime shift.description: Changes in how often fires occur, when they burn, how intense they are or how much land they affect. Weather, vegetation and human activity all influence these patterns. A change can affect habitats, communities and smoke exposure.
incoming: Warming can create hotter, drier conditions and longer periods suitable for burning. Actual fires still depend on fuel, ignition and local management.
Changing air-pressure patterns over the Pacific and North America can shift heat, rain and drought. Fire danger may then change in particular regions, sometimes days or weeks later.
Dry air removes moisture from living plants and dead vegetation. Fires can start and spread more easily when dry material, wind and a source of ignition come together.
Long dry periods can dry vegetation across seasons. This increases the amount that can burn and can extend the time of year with high fire danger.
Warming can increase heat and drying, changing when and how intensely fires burn. Fires still need burnable material and a source of ignition.
Damaged or cleared forests can interact with drying and human ignitions to change fire patterns. The result also depends on available vegetation and land management.
Heat and drought can dry vegetation before a fire starts, creating a sequence of connected hazards. Fire still needs burnable material and an ignition source.
outgoing: Very intense fires can create towering storm clouds. These can carry smoke much higher than ordinary fire plumes, allowing it to travel farther or remain aloft longer.
Repeated severe fires can leave surviving forest in separate patches. Connectivity depends on the pattern of burning and later regrowth.
Larger or longer-lasting fires can produce more persistent smoke. Health exposure increases where winds carry that smoke to people.
Larger or longer fire seasons can expose people to more smoke and fine particles. Breathing this pollution can harm the lungs and heart and increase illness and death risks.
More destructive fires can increase losses beyond what insurers planned for. Prices may rise, renewals may be restricted and some insurers may leave exposed areas.
Repeated severe fires can kill trees faster than forests regrow. A river catchment may then be left with less tree cover or a different type of vegetation.
Intense fire close to a railway can deform rails and damage track components. Smoke or a nearby line closure alone does not show that rails have bent.
Large or severe fires can release soot that travels downwind. Some may settle on snow and ice, depending on transport and weather conditions.
Wildfires produce carbon monoxide as material burns incompletely. The amount varies with the fuel and burning conditions.
Severe or repeated fires can burn peat, kill plants and change how water moves through the land. Recovery can become more difficult after repeated damage.
Longer or more severe fire seasons increase the chance that fire reaches dry peat. Repeated burning can occur before the wetland has recovered.
Mountain Forest Cover and Treeline Contraction
Severe fires can remove mountain trees and seed sources. Lasting forest loss occurs when trees cannot regrow. Many forests normally recover from fire, and some lower-intensity fires support renewal.

human.summary: Larger or longer fire seasons can expose people to more smoke and fine particles. Breathing this pollution can harm the lungs and heart and increase illness and death risks.
consequences: More destructive fires can increase losses beyond what insurers planned for. Prices may rise, renewals may be restricted and some insurers may leave exposed areas.
More smoke-producing fires create more opportunities for people to breathe fine particles. Winds, where people live and how they reduce exposure determine the actual amount inhaled.

planet.summary: Very intense fires can create towering storm clouds. These can carry smoke much higher than ordinary fire plumes, allowing it to travel farther or remain aloft longer.
consequences: Repeated severe fires can leave surviving forest in separate patches. Connectivity depends on the pattern of burning and later regrowth.
Larger or longer-lasting fires can produce more persistent smoke. Health exposure increases where winds carry that smoke to people.

response.defaultDriver: Warming, land management and building in exposed areas can combine. Their importance varies across landscapes.
levers: Use locally appropriate fuel management, including carefully managed fire where suitable.
Reduce exposure of homes and protect water supplies from runoff after severe burns.

forest fragmentation.name: Forest Fragmentation
forest fragmentation.description: A large wooded area being broken into smaller, separated patches. Roads, clearing and other disturbances can make it harder for wildlife to move between them. Effects depend on the species and whether the spaces between patches can be crossed.
incoming: Clearing sections of a forest can split continuous habitat into smaller pieces. More exposed edges and larger gaps can make those pieces harder for wildlife to use.
Repeated severe fires can leave surviving forest in separate patches. Connectivity depends on the pattern of burning and later regrowth.
Logging and access roads can create gaps and edges in older forests. The amount of separation depends on how harvesting is done and must be assessed across the wider landscape.
outgoing: Breaking up a forest leaves smaller or more isolated places for wildlife. Their value depends on size, quality and whether animals can move between them.
Gaps between forest patches can stop species reaching suitable cooler habitat. Their occupied area may shrink when movement cannot keep pace with changing conditions.
Breaking a forest into smaller patches can leave insect populations isolated. Smaller populations may struggle when they cannot move between suitable habitats.

Splitting forests into separate patches can make it harder for some species to move, breed or recolonise an area. Other species can cross the gaps, so a map alone does not prove that movement has stopped.
Splitting habitat into smaller pieces can leave fewer animals or plants breeding in each area. With less movement between groups, inherited variety may decline over generations.

human.summary: Breaking a forest into smaller patches can leave insect populations isolated. Smaller populations may struggle when they cannot move between suitable habitats. If declining insect numbers include pollinating species, fewer animals may be available to transfer pollen. Effects depend on which insects are lost and whether others can replace their work.

planet.summary: Breaking up a forest leaves smaller or more isolated places for wildlife. Their value depends on size, quality and whether animals can move between them.
consequences: Gaps between forest patches can stop species reaching suitable cooler habitat. Their occupied area may shrink when movement cannot keep pace with changing conditions.
Breaking a forest into smaller patches can leave insect populations isolated. Smaller populations may struggle when they cannot move between suitable habitats.

response.defaultDriver: Clearing sections of a forest can split continuous habitat into smaller pieces. More exposed edges and larger gaps can make those pieces harder for wildlife to use.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.

mangrove buffer loss.name: Mangrove Buffer Loss
mangrove buffer loss.description: The loss of coastal trees and roots that help soften waves and hold shorelines together. Nearby communities can become more exposed to water and erosion. These habitats also support wildlife and store carbon.
incoming: Rising seas can overwhelm mangroves if soil does not build up fast enough. They are especially exposed where buildings or steep ground prevent them from moving inland.
Erosion can remove the soil and stable shoreline that support mangrove roots. Losing these trees also weakens the natural barrier they form against storms.
outgoing: Losing coastal trees and roots removes some resistance to waves and moving water. Nearby people and buildings can become more exposed during storms.
Without mangrove roots to hold sediment and slow water, a shoreline can lose material more easily. Local wave conditions and sediment supply affect the rate.
Clearing or eroding mangroves removes trees and can disturb deep organic soils. Both hold carbon that may no longer remain stored after the damage.

human.summary: Clearing or eroding mangroves removes trees and can disturb deep organic soils. Both hold carbon that may no longer remain stored after the damage. Damage to coastal habitats can release stored carbon and reduce future uptake. Carbon actually released must be counted separately from carbon that is no longer being absorbed.

planet.summary: Losing coastal trees and roots removes some resistance to waves and moving water. Nearby people and buildings can become more exposed during storms.
consequences: Without mangrove roots to hold sediment and slow water, a shoreline can lose material more easily. Local wave conditions and sediment supply affect the rate.
Clearing or eroding mangroves removes trees and can disturb deep organic soils. Both hold carbon that may no longer remain stored after the damage.

response.defaultDriver: Rising seas can overwhelm mangroves if soil does not build up fast enough. They are especially exposed where buildings or steep ground prevent them from moving inland.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.

reef structural collapse.name: Reef Structural Collapse
reef structural collapse.description: The hard framework built by corals breaking down faster than it is maintained. This removes shelter for marine life and can reduce protection from waves. Heat damage and conditions that hinder skeleton growth can contribute.
incoming: Severe or repeated warm-water episodes can kill corals after stress and bleaching. If recovery is too slow, the reef's hard framework can lose complexity and break down.
Changing seawater chemistry can slow the building and repair of coral skeletons. If losses outpace replacement, the reef framework can weaken.
Coral Larval Survival and Recruitment Failure
If too few young corals survive and establish themselves, they cannot replace lost adults. Over time this can weaken the living cover and solid structure of a reef.
Repeated breakage can remove the connected, three-dimensional structure of a reef. If growth and repair cannot keep up, habitat complexity and resistance to waves decline.
outgoing: Losing reef structure removes shelter, feeding areas and places for young fish to grow. Fisheries depending on those habitats can become less able to sustain catches.
Repeated damage can weaken the solid structure built by corals. As that structure breaks down, reef habitat can become smaller, separated and less stable.
Coral Larval Survival and Recruitment Failure
Heat and other stresses can reduce the survival of young corals and their ability to settle on a reef. This makes recovery harder where the reef is already damaged.

human.summary: Losing reef structure removes shelter, feeding areas and places for young fish to grow. Fisheries depending on those habitats can become less able to sustain catches. Severely depleted fish stocks leave fewer fish available to catch. Ports and markets may then receive smaller or less reliable supplies.

planet.summary: Losing reef structure removes shelter, feeding areas and places for young fish to grow. Fisheries depending on those habitats can become less able to sustain catches.
consequences: Repeated damage can weaken the solid structure built by corals. As that structure breaks down, reef habitat can become smaller, separated and less stable.
Heat and other stresses can reduce the survival of young corals and their ability to settle on a reef. This makes recovery harder where the reef is already damaged.

response.defaultDriver: Severe or repeated warm-water episodes can kill corals after stress and bleaching. If recovery is too slow, the reef's hard framework can lose complexity and break down.
levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

pollinator service decline.name: Pollinator Service Decline
pollinator service decline.description: Bees and other animals becoming less able to transfer pollen between flowers. Many plants need this help to produce seeds or fruit. The effects depend on the crops or wild plants involved and what other pollinating species remain.
incoming: If declining insect numbers include pollinating species, fewer animals may be available to transfer pollen. Effects depend on which insects are lost and whether others can replace their work.

Chemicals drifting off a field can reach flowers, water or nesting sites used by pollinating insects. Detecting them does not prove declining pollination. Effects depend on the product, species, amount and timing.
Large areas of one crop, fewer habitats and pesticide exposure can reduce food and safety for pollinating insects. Farm management and the surrounding landscape affect the outcome.
outgoing: Crops that need animals to transfer pollen may set less fruit or seed when that help declines. Harvests can become smaller or less reliable.

human.summary: Crops that need animals to transfer pollen may set less fruit or seed when that help declines. Harvests can become smaller or less reliable.

planet.summary: Fewer successful visits to flowers can reduce reproduction in plants that depend on animals to move pollen. Effects vary across plants and available pollinating species.

response.defaultDriver: Loss of varied flowering habitat and harmful chemical exposure can weaken populations.
levers: Protect flowering habitat across seasons and reduce harmful pesticide exposure.
Monitor wild and managed populations and test whether crop pollination is improving.

measurement.metric: Pollinator visitation or fruit-set deficit for a declared pollinator-dependent crop
measurement.geography: declared habitat, ecosystem, protected area, watershed, coastline, or analysis grid
measurement.cadence: seasonal or annual with event updates where applicable

freshwater ecosystem collapse.name: Freshwater Ecosystem Collapse
freshwater ecosystem collapse.description: Rivers, lakes or wetlands losing much of their living community or their ability to function. Pollution, altered flows and barriers can contribute. The term describes severe damage, not simply any change in a waterway.
incoming: Losing trees around rivers can increase erosion and change water flow and habitat. Severe or repeated damage can reduce the ability of freshwater communities to survive and recover.
Releasing water without normal treatment can add germs, nutrients and harmful chemicals to rivers or lakes. Severe or repeated contamination can damage their living communities and functions.
Barriers can isolate aquatic populations and prevent access to breeding sites or refuge. Repeated or widespread isolation can weaken the river's living community.
Draining wetland areas changes water storage, natural filtering and habitat. Severe changes can undermine nearby freshwater communities and their functions.
Barriers at stream crossings can stop animals reaching shelter or breeding areas. Repeated isolation can reduce populations and make recovery after damage harder.
Removing side channels and floodplain connections reduces the variety of river habitats. Fish and other wildlife may lose places to feed, breed or shelter.
Warming changes water temperatures, river flow and flood or drought extremes. These changes can put freshwater plants and animals under pressure.

Some farm chemicals can harm aquatic plants and animals when exposure is high enough or repeated. Detection alone does not prove harm, and crossing a screening threshold does not establish that a whole ecosystem has failed.
Continued river-bank loss can add fine sediment, bury habitat and remove shade. River plants and animals may lose suitable places to live.
Large, lasting mussel losses remove animals that filter water and help stabilise riverbeds. Nutrient movement and habitats supported by dense mussel groups may also change.
Forest loss can change river flows, water quality and stream habitats. Freshwater wildlife may be harmed where these catchment changes reach the water.
Acid entering poorly protected waters can harm sensitive species and release harmful aluminium from surrounding materials. Food webs can change where the water and soil cannot neutralise the acid.
outgoing: Severe damage to rivers, lakes or wetlands can remove species and reduce the abundance of those remaining. Their living communities become less like the earlier reference condition.

human.summary: Damaged rivers and lakes can become less useful for fishing, recreation and dependable water supplies. The current measurements describe particular ecological conditions, not a global count of people affected.

planet.summary: Severe damage to rivers, lakes or wetlands can remove species and reduce the abundance of those remaining. Their living communities become less like the earlier reference condition.

response.defaultDriver: Losing trees around rivers can increase erosion and change water flow and habitat. Severe or repeated damage can reduce the ability of freshwater communities to survive and recover.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.
