species range contraction.name: Species Range Contraction
species range contraction.description: The area where a plant or animal can live becoming smaller. Conditions may become unsuitable at one edge while barriers prevent movement into better areas. Smaller living areas can make populations more vulnerable to further disturbance.
incoming: Gaps between forest patches can stop species reaching suitable cooler habitat. Their occupied area may shrink when movement cannot keep pace with changing conditions.
Small isolated habitat patches may prevent animals or plants from reaching new suitable places. Their occupied range can then become smaller as conditions change.
Warming can make the warm edge of a species' habitat unsuitable. Its overall range shrinks if it cannot establish enough new habitat in cooler places to make up the loss.
outgoing: Species with less suitable, connected living space can become less abundant or disappear locally. This changes the area's original mix of life.

human.summary: When suitable living space for a species shrinks, communities relying on that species may lose food, income or cultural benefits. The effect on people depends on the species and available alternatives.

planet.summary: Species with less suitable, connected living space can become less abundant or disappear locally. This changes the area's original mix of life.

response.defaultDriver: Gaps between forest patches can stop species reaching suitable cooler habitat. Their occupied area may shrink when movement cannot keep pace with changing conditions.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.

insect biomass decline.name: Insect Biomass Decline
insect biomass decline.description: A reduction in the total mass of insects in a defined place and period. This can reflect fewer insects, smaller insects or changes in which kinds are present. It can affect animals that eat insects and the work insects do in natural systems.
incoming: Extreme heat and changes to habitats can put insects under pressure. Some populations may shrink, although the effects differ between species and places.
Removing varied habitats and exposing insects to farm chemicals can reduce their numbers. The effect depends on farming practices and the species involved.
Clearing forests removes food, shelter and stable local conditions for insects. Populations can decline where the remaining habitat cannot support them.
Breaking a forest into smaller patches can leave insect populations isolated. Smaller populations may struggle when they cannot move between suitable habitats.
outgoing: If declining insect numbers include pollinating species, fewer animals may be available to transfer pollen. Effects depend on which insects are lost and whether others can replace their work.

human.summary: If declining insect numbers include pollinating species, fewer animals may be available to transfer pollen. Effects depend on which insects are lost and whether others can replace their work. Crops that need animals to transfer pollen may set less fruit or seed when that help declines. Harvests can become smaller or less reliable.

planet.summary: If declining insect numbers include pollinating species, fewer animals may be available to transfer pollen. Effects depend on which insects are lost and whether others can replace their work.

response.defaultDriver: Extreme heat and changes to habitats can put insects under pressure. Some populations may shrink, although the effects differ between species and places.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.

soil humus decline.name: Soil Humus Decline
soil humus decline.description: Soil losing the well-decayed plant and animal material that helps it hold water and nutrients. Erosion and changes in land management can contribute. With less of this material, soil can become less able to support plants during dry conditions.
incoming: Erosion carries away the carbon-rich upper soil. If that loss is faster than new organic material builds up, less well-decayed plant matter remains.
Intensive soil disturbance and too little return of organic material can reduce the soil's stored plant matter. The outcome depends on the farming practices used.
Removing trees reduces fallen leaves and roots that replenish soil. Exposed ground can then lose organic material through erosion, heat and faster decay.
Warmer conditions can speed the breakdown of dead plant material in soil. Where losses exceed new inputs, soil can hold less water and support plants less well.
outgoing: With less organic material, soil can hold less water and nutrients. Crops may then be more sensitive to dry periods and other growing conditions.

human.summary: With less organic material, soil can hold less water and nutrients. Crops may then be more sensitive to dry periods and other growing conditions.

planet.summary: Loss of decomposed organic material can weaken soil structure, nutrient storage and its ability to hold water. The rate and consequences vary across soils and land uses.

response.defaultDriver: Erosion carries away the carbon-rich upper soil. If that loss is faster than new organic material builds up, less well-decayed plant matter remains.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.

urban tree canopy loss.name: Urban Tree Canopy Loss
urban tree canopy loss.description: A city losing the cover provided by tree leaves and branches. Streets and buildings receive less shade, and less water is released by trees to cool the air. The loss can make already hot neighbourhoods harder to keep cool.
incoming: Heat and drought can weaken or kill city trees. Losses are more likely where other pressures combine and trees receive insufficient water or care.
Building outward can remove trees and cover soil with roads and buildings. Tree cover can shrink if development does not protect existing trees or provide suitable space for replacements.
outgoing: Losing trees removes shade and some natural cooling. Neighbourhoods can store more daytime heat and remain warmer at night, leaving less relief for residents.
Losing city trees removes shade and cooling from water released by leaves. Nearby streets, buildings and air can become hotter.

human.summary: Losing street and neighbourhood trees can remove shade and make hot conditions harder to manage. It can also reduce the comfort and use of outdoor spaces.

planet.summary: Losing trees removes shade and some natural cooling. Neighbourhoods can store more daytime heat and remain warmer at night, leaving less relief for residents.
consequences: Losing city trees removes shade and cooling from water released by leaves. Nearby streets, buildings and air can become hotter.

response.defaultDriver: Heat and drought can weaken or kill city trees. Losses are more likely where other pressures combine and trees receive insufficient water or care.
levers: Include affected communities in decisions about protection, services and recovery.
Fund practical support and monitor who can actually access it, especially where people have few alternatives.

crop yield volatility.name: Crop Yield Volatility
crop yield volatility.description: Harvest amounts changing more unpredictably between seasons or places. Heat, water shortages, heavy rain and other pressures can contribute. This makes planning food supplies and farm income harder, even when average production has not fallen.
incoming: Too much salt around roots makes it harder for crops to take in water. Harvests can fall or become less reliable, depending on the crop and how the land is managed.
Strong drying conditions increase plants' water demand. Plants may close tiny leaf openings to conserve water, which can reduce growth and make harvests less reliable.
Ozone entering leaves can damage plant tissues and reduce growth. Harvest effects depend on the crop, exposure and region. An estimate for one crop cannot be assumed to apply to all others.
Hail can physically damage crops. Changes in where and when hail occurs alter harvest risk, with different outcomes for crops at different growth stages.
Very dry soil leaves roots unable to obtain enough water. Crop growth and harvests can suffer, with effects that vary between crops and seasons.
Crops that need animals to transfer pollen may set less fruit or seed when that help declines. Harvests can become smaller or less reliable.
With less organic material, soil can hold less water and nutrients. Crops may then be more sensitive to dry periods and other growing conditions.
Excessive heat can damage flowering, seed formation and the way plants use sunlight to grow. Harvests can become smaller or less dependable.
When plant nutrients become much more expensive, farmers may use less or apply them at the wrong time. This can make harvests smaller or less dependable.
Livestock farms that depend on crops for animal feed are exposed when those harvests change sharply. A poor crop harvest can mean less feed or higher feed prices.
Dangerous working conditions can reduce the time available for planting, tending or harvesting crops. Missing these time-sensitive jobs can make harvests less dependable.
Losing the upper layer of soil removes nutrients and reduces the ground's ability to hold water. Crops may then produce smaller or less dependable harvests.
outgoing: Unreliable harvests increase the need for farming methods that handle heat, water shortages and other shocks. The most useful changes depend on local crops and conditions.
Unreliable harvests can reduce local food supplies and increase prices. Households may then find it harder to obtain enough nutritious food.
Poor harvests of major food crops can tighten supplies and make prices less stable. Stored reserves and substitute foods can soften the effect.

human.summary: Unreliable harvests can affect farm income, debt and the cost of basic foods. Widespread losses can also increase the need for imports or aid.
consequences: Farmers may struggle to repay costs when harvests vary sharply between seasons.
Higher food prices put particular pressure on households already spending much of their income on staples.

planet.summary: Variable harvests describe food production, rather than a direct measure of ecosystem condition. Environmental effects depend on the climate pressures and farming responses behind the changes.

response.defaultDriver: Too much salt around roots makes it harder for crops to take in water. Harvests can fall or become less reliable, depending on the crop and how the land is managed.
levers: A mix of crops, healthier soils, better water management and useful forecasts can make harvests more dependable. These measures reduce some risks but cannot prevent every loss.

farm heat stress.name: Farm Heat Stress
farm heat stress.description: Hot conditions making agricultural work harder or less safe. Physical effort, humidity and long hours can add to the strain. Reduced safe working time can affect both workers' health and the work needed to produce food.
incoming: Higher temperatures make damaging heat more likely during the growing season. Crops can struggle when conditions exceed the temperatures they can tolerate.
Hot, humid air makes it harder for livestock and workers to lose body heat. This adds to the strain farms face during hot weather.
Long dry periods reduce moisture in the soil and the cooling provided by evaporation. Crops, animals and workers can then face hotter local conditions.
Warmer growing seasons can strain crops, livestock and farm workers. Reproduction, safe working time and farm output may all be affected.
outgoing: Excessive heat can damage flowering, seed formation and the way plants use sunlight to grow. Harvests can become smaller or less dependable.
The same hot conditions that strain crops can make field work unsafe. Farm workers may need more breaks or fewer working hours.

human.summary: Excessive heat can damage flowering, seed formation and the way plants use sunlight to grow. Harvests can become smaller or less dependable.
consequences: The same hot conditions that strain crops can make field work unsafe. Farm workers may need more breaks or fewer working hours.

livestock disease pressure.name: Livestock Disease Pressure
livestock disease pressure.description: Conditions making farm animals more likely to become ill. Germs, biting insects, heat, crowding and care practices can all matter. Illness can reduce production, cause deaths or require restrictions on animal movement.
incoming: Warmer conditions can stress farm animals and change where some germs and disease-carrying insects survive. The effect depends on the disease, location and animal care.
Hot, humid conditions can stress farm animals and weaken their ability to resist illness. They may also favour some germs and disease-carrying insects.
Limited water can bring animals together around fewer drinking places and make cleaning harder. Poorer water quality and closer contact can increase the spread of disease.
Warming changes heat stress and conditions for some disease-carrying insects. Livestock disease also depends on animal care, movement and trade.
outgoing: Animal illness can reduce milk, meat and egg production or kill livestock. Restrictions on moving animals can also interrupt food supplies.
Disease can make local meat, milk and egg supplies less dependable. A country may then need to buy more of these foods from elsewhere.

human.summary: Animal illness can reduce milk, meat and egg production or kill livestock. Restrictions on moving animals can also interrupt food supplies.
consequences: Disease can make local meat, milk and egg supplies less dependable. A country may then need to buy more of these foods from elsewhere.

planet.summary: Disease can affect farm-animal health and production. Effects on wildlife or wider habitats depend on the disease, species and management. They are not automatic.

fertilizer price shock.name: Fertilizer Price Shock
fertilizer price shock.description: A sudden rise in the cost of products used to supply crops with nutrients. Farmers may face higher bills or use less, affecting later harvests. The result depends on crop needs, other available nutrients and farmers' finances.
incoming: Producing plant nutrients requires energy and raw materials. Shortages of these inputs can raise production costs and prices paid by farmers.
Farms that depend heavily on manufactured plant nutrients are exposed to energy prices and supply disruptions. Sudden cost increases can affect planting decisions and farm income.

Natural gas is both a raw material and a major cost in making ammonia and urea fertilisers. A sharp gas-price rise can reduce production and raise prices. This is a shared dependence on gas, not an effect of electricity demand alone.
outgoing: When plant nutrients become much more expensive, farmers may use less or apply them at the wrong time. This can make harvests smaller or less dependable.
More expensive plant nutrients raise farming costs. If farmers cannot afford enough, food production may also fall.
Higher farming costs can reduce local food production. Places facing such losses may become more dependent on food bought from other countries.
Higher fertiliser prices raise farming costs and may lead to lower use. Smaller later harvests can add pressure to prices of basic foods.

human.summary: When plant nutrients become much more expensive, farmers may use less or apply them at the wrong time. This can make harvests smaller or less dependable.
consequences: More expensive plant nutrients raise farming costs. If farmers cannot afford enough, food production may also fall.
Higher farming costs can reduce local food production. Places facing such losses may become more dependent on food bought from other countries.

feed crop dependency.name: Feed Crop Dependency
feed crop dependency.description: Animal farming relying on dedicated supplies of crops such as maize and soy. Producing that feed uses land, water and other resources. Poor harvests or supply interruptions can then raise costs or limit livestock production.
incoming: Large livestock operations need steady supplies of crops such as maize and soy for feed. This ties animal production to the land, water, nutrients and trade used to grow those crops.
outgoing: Livestock farms that depend on crops for animal feed are exposed when those harvests change sharply. A poor crop harvest can mean less feed or higher feed prices.
Livestock raised on imported feed depend on supplies from other countries. Disrupted deliveries or higher prices can affect local meat, milk and egg production.
A shortage of crops used as animal feed can reduce livestock production. This can affect the availability and price of meat, milk and eggs.
Livestock production based on purchased feed needs large, steady supplies of crops such as maize and soy. This can support more concentrated and intensive farming systems.

human.summary: Livestock farms that depend on crops for animal feed are exposed when those harvests change sharply. A poor crop harvest can mean less feed or higher feed prices.
consequences: Livestock raised on imported feed depend on supplies from other countries. Disrupted deliveries or higher prices can affect local meat, milk and egg production.
A shortage of crops used as animal feed can reduce livestock production. This can affect the availability and price of meat, milk and eggs.

planet.summary: Growing crops to feed livestock uses land, water and nutrients. The environmental burden depends on where and how the feed is produced and whether new land is cleared.

food import exposure.name: Food Import Exposure
food import exposure.description: A place relying on food brought in from elsewhere, leaving it affected by problems beyond its borders. Poor harvests, trade restrictions or transport delays can change availability and prices. The effect depends on alternative suppliers and local reserves.
incoming: Where people rely heavily on local fish, falling supplies may require more food from elsewhere. That can expose households to overseas prices and transport interruptions.
Disrupted sea routes can delay food deliveries or make them more expensive. Places that rely heavily on food brought in by ship are more exposed.
Disease can make local meat, milk and egg supplies less dependable. A country may then need to buy more of these foods from elsewhere.
Livestock raised on imported feed depend on supplies from other countries. Disrupted deliveries or higher prices can affect local meat, milk and egg production.
Higher farming costs can reduce local food production. Places facing such losses may become more dependent on food bought from other countries.
Unreliable refrigeration can waste locally produced food before it reaches people. Replacing those losses may increase reliance on food from elsewhere.
More dependable local harvests can reduce the need to replace losses with imported food. The effect depends on which foods are grown and the shocks the farms face.
outgoing: Food brought from far away often relies on cooling throughout transport and storage. Delays or broken refrigeration can spoil temperature-sensitive supplies before they reach consumers.
An interruption in imported food or a sharp price rise can increase the need for aid. Shortfalls are more likely where local reserves, household income and aid capacity are limited.
Imported food becoming scarce or expensive affects households unevenly. People with fewer savings and supply alternatives can find it harder to recover after a disaster.
Disrupted food imports or sharp price rises can add pressure where people already face insecurity and inequality. These pressures can contribute to conflict, but they do not make conflict inevitable.
Reliance on imported food exposes households to supply and price changes elsewhere. Disruptions can make enough nutritious food harder to afford or obtain.

cold chain failure risk.name: Cold Chain Failure Risk
cold chain failure risk.description: The chance that food or other temperature-sensitive goods become too warm during storage or transport. A power cut, equipment fault or delay can break the required cooling. Goods may spoil before reaching the people who need them.
incoming: Food brought from far away often relies on cooling throughout transport and storage. Delays or broken refrigeration can spoil temperature-sensitive supplies before they reach consumers.
Very high electricity demand can lead to outages where supply cannot keep up. Refrigerators and refrigerated transport may then fail to keep food cold.
Too little investment can leave refrigerated food and medicine storage poorly protected from heat and power cuts. Transport problems can make the losses worse.
outgoing: Food can spoil or become unsafe when it is not kept cold enough during storage and transport. This reduces the amount available to eat.
Unreliable refrigeration can waste locally produced food before it reaches people. Replacing those losses may increase reliance on food from elsewhere.
Broken refrigeration can leave perishable food at unsafe temperatures. Food may spoil before it can be sold or eaten.

human.summary: Food can spoil or become unsafe when it is not kept cold enough during storage and transport. This reduces the amount available to eat.
consequences: Unreliable refrigeration can waste locally produced food before it reaches people. Replacing those losses may increase reliance on food from elsewhere.
Broken refrigeration can leave perishable food at unsafe temperatures. Food may spoil before it can be sold or eaten.

planet.summary: Food can spoil or become unsafe when it is not kept cold enough during storage and transport. This reduces the amount available to eat. Demand for meat, animal feed and other farm products can encourage expansion onto forest land. This is less likely when existing farmland, higher yields or effective protection meet the demand without new clearing.
consequences: Broken refrigeration can leave perishable food at unsafe temperatures. Food may spoil before it can be sold or eaten. Food in landfill can decay with little oxygen and produce methane. The amount released depends on waste handling and whether the gas is captured.

fishery protein dependence.name: Fishery Protein Dependence
fishery protein dependence.description: People relying heavily on fish and other harvested seafood for nourishment. If catches or access decline, suitable replacement foods may be costly or unavailable. The effects depend on local diets, incomes and alternatives.
incoming: Unreliable fish deliveries matter especially where seafood is a major source of nourishment. This connection describes how existing dependence makes a supply interruption more serious. It does not mean the interruption itself creates that dependence.
Falling catches create greater food and income risks where communities already depend heavily on fish. The consequences depend on affordable alternatives and trade.
outgoing: Where people rely heavily on local fish, falling supplies may require more food from elsewhere. That can expose households to overseas prices and transport interruptions.
Communities heavily dependent on fish face higher costs when access is lost. This can make catch-sharing changes difficult, but dependence can also encourage cooperation rather than conflict.

human.summary: Where people rely heavily on local fish, falling supplies may require more food from elsewhere. That can expose households to overseas prices and transport interruptions.

agricultural labor exposure.name: Agricultural Labor Exposure
agricultural labor exposure.description: Farm workers coming into contact with hazards such as heat, smoke and chemicals. The type of task and time spent working affect the dose or strain they receive. Protection, rest and access to services influence the resulting harm.
incoming: The same hot conditions that strain crops can make field work unsafe. Farm workers may need more breaks or fewer working hours.
High humidity makes sweating less effective during hot weather. Farm workers may be unable to keep working safely through the hottest hours.
outgoing: Dangerous working conditions can reduce the time available for planting, tending or harvesting crops. Missing these time-sensitive jobs can make harvests less dependable.
When heat reduces the hours people can safely work on farms, less food may be produced or collected. The effect depends on the timing of the heat and the protection workers have.

consequences: When heat reduces the hours people can safely work on farms, less food may be produced or collected. The effect depends on the timing of the heat and the protection workers have.

topsoil erosion acceleration.name: Topsoil Erosion Acceleration
topsoil erosion acceleration.description: The fertile upper layer of soil being removed faster by water, wind or farming activities. This carries away material that holds nutrients and water. Plants can become harder to grow, and the displaced soil can enter nearby waterways.
incoming: Frequent ploughing, removing crop remains and leaving fields bare can expose soil. Wind and heavy rain can then carry away the fertile upper layer more easily.
Plant cover and roots help hold soil in place. Restoring them can reduce the amount of fertile ground carried away by wind and water.
Keeping soil covered, maintaining roots and disturbing it less can reduce erosion. Better water management can also slow the washing away of fertile ground.
Removing trees leaves soil with less protection from rain and fewer roots holding it. Erosion can increase on vulnerable slopes during heavy rain.
Ground tightly packed by cattle absorbs water less easily and may support fewer plants. Rain can then create more runoff and erosion where slopes and soil are vulnerable.
Tightly packed soil lets less water soak in and restricts roots. More runoff can carry away topsoil where rainfall and slopes create enough force.
outgoing: Erosion carries away the carbon-rich upper soil. If that loss is faster than new organic material builds up, less well-decayed plant matter remains.
Losing the upper layer of soil removes nutrients and reduces the ground's ability to hold water. Crops may then produce smaller or less dependable harvests.

human.summary: Losing the upper layer of soil removes nutrients and reduces the ground's ability to hold water. Crops may then produce smaller or less dependable harvests.
consequences: Erosion carries away the carbon-rich upper soil. If that loss is faster than new organic material builds up, less well-decayed plant matter remains. With less organic material, soil can hold less water and nutrients. Crops may then be more sensitive to dry periods and other growing conditions.

planet.summary: Erosion carries away the carbon-rich upper soil. If that loss is faster than new organic material builds up, less well-decayed plant matter remains.

response.defaultDriver: Bare ground and unsuitable farming practices can leave soil exposed to wind and runoff.
levers: Use locally suitable cover, crop rotations and reduced soil disturbance.

insurance retreat.name: Insurance Retreat
insurance retreat.description: Insurers reducing the cover they offer, raising prices or leaving markets where losses are difficult to manage. Repeated climate-related damage can contribute. Households and businesses may then have fewer affordable ways to protect themselves financially.
incoming: Repeated hail damage can add to insurance costs and influence whether companies offer cover. Regulation and the wider mix of insured risks also affect those decisions.
Repeated coastal floods can increase expected insurance claims and the cost of covering them. Insurers may raise prices, limit policies or leave exposed markets.
More destructive fires can increase losses beyond what insurers planned for. Prices may rise, renewals may be restricted and some insurers may leave exposed areas.
outgoing: As insurers reduce cover in hazardous areas, coastal households may face higher prices or policies that are not renewed. The effect varies with local losses and insurance arrangements.
Reduced insurance cover can leave disputes over losses and responsibility unresolved. Some disputes may move into court, depending on local law and the circumstances.
When home insurance becomes expensive or unavailable, borrowers have less protection from disaster losses. This can affect housing costs, property values and the ability to repay a home loan.
When insurance is unavailable or unaffordable, households and governments pay more disaster costs themselves. This can leave less money to reduce future risks.
Losing affordable insurance can make it harder to stay in or finance an exposed home. Public insurance arrangements may either support a planned move or delay it.

human.summary: When home insurance becomes unavailable or unaffordable, households face more disaster costs themselves. Financial pressure can begin before physical damage occurs.
consequences: A home may become difficult to insure while it is still usable.
Lenders may make borrowing harder when long-term protection is uncertain.

mortgage market exposure.description: Home loans, borrowers and lenders being vulnerable to damage, falling property values or loss of insurance. Repeated hazards can make a property more costly to own or harder to sell. These effects depend on local markets and lending arrangements.
incoming: Losing affordable property insurance can make it harder to obtain or renew a home loan. It can also affect property values and the finances of borrowers and lenders.
When home insurance becomes expensive or unavailable, borrowers have less protection from disaster losses. This can affect housing costs, property values and the ability to repay a home loan.
outgoing: Repeated damage, difficult loans or homes that are hard to sell can increase pressure for a supported move. Local institutions then need to address housing, funding and community needs.

public health heat burden.name: Public Health Heat Burden
public health heat burden.description: The combined illness, deaths and demand for care associated with dangerously hot conditions. Hospitals and support services may face extra pressure at the same time. Housing, income, health and access to cooling influence who is most affected.
incoming: Losing electricity can stop cooling and essential equipment during hot weather. People may face greater illness and difficulty staying safe at home.
Working cooling systems can help prevent hot conditions from becoming a health emergency. Their protection depends on access, affordability and reliable power.
Humid heat limits cooling through sweat. This can increase heat illness and strain the heart, lungs and kidneys, especially during prolonged exposure.

When nights remain hot after very hot days, people have less time to cool down and recover. Observed studies find that this continuous exposure can create greater health burdens than heat limited to the day.
Hot nights can prevent the body and the home from cooling down. Health risks can therefore be greater than an average daily temperature alone would suggest.
If a strained electricity system fails during extreme heat, cooling and medical equipment can stop. The interruption can increase illness and demand for care.
People who cannot afford to run cooling may face unsafe indoor temperatures. This can increase heat illness, especially where housing offers little natural protection.

Replacing coal power with lower-emissions electricity reduces a source of future warming. This can ease future heat-related health risks, alongside the more immediate benefit of less combustion pollution.
Well-designed building upgrades can slow indoor overheating. This can keep temperatures safer for longer, including when cooling is limited.
Heat pumps that provide cooling as well as heating can help keep indoor temperatures safe. Protection depends on access, affordability and reliable electricity.
Shade, suitable ventilation and reflective surfaces can reduce the heat entering or staying inside buildings. This can lower people's exposure to dangerous indoor temperatures.
Coordinating cooling spaces, health services and contact with vulnerable residents can reduce illness during hot weather. The plan needs staff, funding and follow-through.
outgoing: Heat-related illness and demand for care can slow recovery after a disaster. Households and health services with fewer resources may struggle for longer.
Growing illness during hot weather shows where cities need stronger preparation. Plans can connect forecasts with cooling, health services and support for people at greatest risk.
Repeated severe heat illness can increase pressure to consider moving people or services. That becomes more likely where safe housing, cooling and health care cannot be maintained locally.

human.summary: Heat-related illness and demand for care can slow recovery after a disaster. Households and health services with fewer resources may struggle for longer.

vector-borne disease expansion.name: Vector-Borne Disease Expansion
vector-borne disease expansion.description: Illnesses carried by insects or other animals becoming able to spread in new places or seasons. Temperature and moisture affect the carriers and the germs they carry. Suitable conditions alone do not guarantee an outbreak. Exposure and public-health protection matter too.
incoming: Temperature changes can affect where disease-carrying insects survive and how quickly germs develop inside them. Some places may become more suitable for transmission, while excessive heat can make others less suitable.
Flooding can leave standing water, damage drains and change how people store water. In some places, this creates more breeding sites for mosquitoes and increases contact with people.

Clearing forests changes shade, standing water, wildlife and contact between people and insects. In some tropical settings, these changes favour mosquitoes that carry disease, but the effect is not universal.
Rapid city growth without adequate drains, waste services or water supplies can create breeding places for some disease-carrying insects. Dense populations and travel can increase contact and spread.
Changes in temperature and rain can make some places suitable for disease-carrying insects for longer. Effects vary by disease and can reverse where conditions become too hot or dry.
outgoing: Illness carried by insects can slow recovery after a disaster. People with less access to prevention and treatment may face a larger burden.

human.summary: Changing temperatures and rain can make some places or seasons more suitable for disease-carrying insects. People may face infections where preparation is limited.
consequences: Mosquito- or tick-borne diseases can create new demands on local prevention systems.
Health services may need longer periods of monitoring and treatment.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

response.defaultDriver: Temperature changes can affect where disease-carrying insects survive and how quickly germs develop inside them. Some places may become more suitable for transmission, while excessive heat can make others less suitable.
levers: Connect useful warnings with accessible health services and practical protection for exposed people.
Improve access to safe housing, water or cooling where the documented exposure requires it.

adaptation capital shortfall.name: Adaptation Capital Shortfall
adaptation capital shortfall.description: Too little funding being available to prepare for climate hazards and reduce their damage. Projects such as safer housing, drainage or cooling may be delayed. A funding gap is different from proving that any particular project will work.
incoming: Court cases can expose disagreements about who should pay for protection and recovery. They may draw attention to funding gaps without necessarily closing them.
Households and governments struggling to replace disaster losses may have little money left for future protection. Unequal recovery can therefore deepen gaps in preparation for the next hazard.
When insurance is unavailable or unaffordable, households and governments pay more disaster costs themselves. This can leave less money to reduce future risks.
outgoing: Too little investment can leave refrigerated food and medicine storage poorly protected from heat and power cuts. Transport problems can make the losses worse.
Too little funding can limit the planning, housing, compensation and services needed for a fair move. Good decision-making still matters even when money is available.
Funding shortages can leave gaps in hazard monitoring, useful alerts and preparation. People may receive less warning or have fewer ways to act on it.
Too little investment can delay cooler housing, shaded spaces and public cooling facilities. Communities already receiving fewer services may remain less protected.

human.summary: Too little investment can leave refrigerated food and medicine storage poorly protected from heat and power cuts. Transport problems can make the losses worse.

planet.summary: Too little investment can leave refrigerated food and medicine storage poorly protected from heat and power cuts. Transport problems can make the losses worse. Food can spoil or become unsafe when it is not kept cold enough during storage and transport. This reduces the amount available to eat.

response.defaultDriver: Short budgets and difficulty showing long-term benefits can delay investment.
levers: Direct funding using exposure, need and fair access rather than property values alone.
Plan improvements in stages and include maintenance and community participation in budgets.

critical infrastructure fragility.name: Critical Infrastructure Fragility
critical infrastructure fragility.description: Essential systems such as electricity, water and transport being easily disrupted or slow to recover. Damage in one system can interrupt others that depend on it. Maintenance, backup capacity and local hazards affect how fragile the network is.
incoming: Damage to roads, power lines or utilities in remote polar areas can interrupt essential services. Difficult access and limited alternatives can make recovery harder.
A shortage of voltage-changing equipment can delay repairs and power-network upgrades. Essential services may remain exposed to outages for longer.
Heat can interrupt a port's work when equipment or workers cannot operate safely. The disruption is harder to contain where backup equipment and alternative routes are limited.
When an airport stops operating, a region may lose an important route for people, supplies and emergency help. The effects are greater where few alternative routes are available.
Fast-moving water can wash material away from around bridge foundations. A weakened or closed bridge can cut an important transport link.
A blocked sea passage can interrupt many deliveries at once. This reveals how dependent a transport system is on a small number of routes.
Designing essential services for future floods can make failures less likely. Backup routes, spare capacity and maintenance help services continue when one part is damaged.
An electricity failure during high demand can interrupt water supplies, transport and communications. Emergency services may also lose equipment or access they depend on.
Facilities that need water for cooling may struggle when other users need the same limited supply. Essential services can be affected if reliable cooling water is unavailable.
Frequent reliance on backup generators can reveal weaknesses in normal electricity supply. Services may remain vulnerable if backup fuel, equipment or delivery also fails.
Storms, tides and rising sea levels can bring seawater onto low-lying buildings and services. Whether they fail depends on flood depth, protection, equipment design and available backups.
Warming and related changes in moisture and salt exposure can speed damage to concrete and steel. Some structures may need earlier repair or have a shorter useful life.
outgoing: Failures in transport, water or health services can prevent people from getting protection during extreme heat. Several failures together can increase the risk of death.
Failures of essential services can lead to legal disputes about foreseeable climate risks. These disputes may concern whether operators disclosed risks or took reasonable steps to protect people.
Weak power and communication systems can interrupt warnings. Alerts may fail to reach the people who need them, especially in the final step to homes and communities.

Broken roads, ports, storage or power supplies can delay food and increase transport or spoilage costs. Food reserves and alternative routes can prevent those disruptions from turning into price rises.
Damaged roads, power, water or communications can prevent aid from reaching people. Funding, security and coordination can also block help even when physical systems still work.

Unreliable power and poorly protected buildings can leave people without safe indoor temperatures. Those unable to afford better housing or backup options face greater exposure, although cost barriers can exist even with reliable power.
Failure of a fuel tank, pipe, hose or protective barrier can allow fuel to reach nearby water. The risk depends on the damaged equipment and its connection to the waterway.

human.summary: Failures in transport, water or health services can prevent people from getting protection during extreme heat. Several failures together can increase the risk of death.
consequences: Broken roads, ports, storage or power supplies can delay food and increase transport or spoilage costs. Food reserves and alternative routes can prevent those disruptions from turning into price rises.
Damaged roads, power, water or communications can prevent aid from reaching people. Funding, security and coordination can also block help even when physical systems still work.

levers: Designing essential services for future floods can make failures less likely. Backup routes, spare capacity and maintenance help services continue when one part is damaged.

disaster recovery inequality.name: Disaster Recovery Inequality
disaster recovery inequality.description: People having unequal chances to rebuild after a damaging event. Those with less money, insurance, secure housing or access to aid may take longer to recover. Repeated losses can leave them with fewer resources to prepare for the next event.
incoming: Imported food becoming scarce or expensive affects households unevenly. People with fewer savings and supply alternatives can find it harder to recover after a disaster.
Heat-related illness and demand for care can slow recovery after a disaster. Households and health services with fewer resources may struggle for longer.
Illness carried by insects can slow recovery after a disaster. People with less access to prevention and treatment may face a larger burden.
People who receive no useful warning have less chance to prepare or reach safety. The resulting losses can make recovery harder for groups already facing disadvantages.
Warnings can reduce unequal disaster losses when they reach vulnerable groups and come with real options for protection. Access to transport, shelter and support matters.
A planned move can reduce unequal disaster losses when people receive suitable housing, services, compensation and ways to earn a living. These protections need to be delivered, not just promised.
People forced to move have unequal access to savings, housing, documents and aid. These differences can widen the gap between households able to recover and those left behind.
outgoing: Communities unable to rebuild may face pressure to move. Unequal access to recovery funds then becomes a challenge for decisions about land, housing and public support.
Households and governments struggling to replace disaster losses may have little money left for future protection. Unequal recovery can therefore deepen gaps in preparation for the next hazard.

levers: Warnings can reduce unequal disaster losses when they reach vulnerable groups and come with real options for protection. Access to transport, shelter and support matters.

relocation governance capacity.name: Relocation Governance Capacity
relocation governance capacity.description: The ability of public institutions to organize and support a fair move away from unsafe places. This includes planning, funding, community choice and protection of rights. Suitable housing, services and livelihoods are needed at the destination.
incoming: Repeated damage, difficult loans or homes that are hard to sell can increase pressure for a supported move. Local institutions then need to address housing, funding and community needs.
Moving a community requires organisations that can coordinate land, housing, money and public services. Experience can strengthen that ability when communities retain a voice and funding lasts.
Repeated severe heat illness can increase pressure to consider moving people or services. That becomes more likely where safe housing, cooling and health care cannot be maintained locally.
Too little funding can limit the planning, housing, compensation and services needed for a fair move. Good decision-making still matters even when money is available.
Communities unable to rebuild may face pressure to move. Unequal access to recovery funds then becomes a challenge for decisions about land, housing and public support.
Large or repeated movements of people can overwhelm housing and public services. Authorities need enough capacity to coordinate land access, legal arrangements and community participation.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: People moving from dangerous places need clear decisions, fair compensation and access to homes, jobs and services. Weak planning can turn a safety measure into lasting hardship.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

levers: Moving a community requires organisations that can coordinate land, housing, money and public services. Experience can strengthen that ability when communities retain a voice and funding lasts.

climate litigation pressure.name: Climate Litigation Pressure
climate litigation pressure.description: Lawsuits creating demands to address climate-related harm, pollution or failures to prepare. Cases can raise questions about responsibility, disclosure and funding. Their outcomes depend on the legal setting and the evidence in each case.
incoming: Reduced insurance cover can leave disputes over losses and responsibility unresolved. Some disputes may move into court, depending on local law and the circumstances.
Failures of essential services can lead to legal disputes about foreseeable climate risks. These disputes may concern whether operators disclosed risks or took reasonable steps to protect people.
outgoing: Court cases can expose disagreements about who should pay for protection and recovery. They may draw attention to funding gaps without necessarily closing them.

human.summary: Court cases can expose disagreements about who should pay for protection and recovery. They may draw attention to funding gaps without necessarily closing them.

levers: Include affected communities in decisions about protection, services and recovery.
Fund practical support and monitor who can actually access it, especially where people have few alternatives.

conflict risk escalation.name: Conflict Risk Escalation
conflict risk escalation.description: Conditions making disputes or violence more likely or harder to resolve. Climate hazards can worsen existing pressures through lost livelihoods, food shortages or displacement. They are one possible influence among many, not a direct or inevitable cause of conflict.
incoming: When water-sharing agreements fail, disputes can become harder to settle. Escalation depends on institutions and wider political conditions. Violence is not inevitable.
Disrupted food imports or sharp price rises can add pressure where people already face insecurity and inequality. These pressures can contribute to conflict, but they do not make conflict inevitable.
Shortages of important resources can worsen existing tensions. Conflict risk depends strongly on how resources are shared and whether institutions can resolve disputes fairly.

Repeated confrontations or failed fishing agreements can worsen political tensions. Most disputes remain within negotiation, and existing tensions may cause fishing incidents rather than result from them.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Pressure on food, water or income can add to existing tensions. Conflict is shaped by politics, institutions and other factors. Climate pressure alone does not determine whether violence occurs.

levers: Include affected communities in decisions about protection, services and recovery.

talik expansion.name: Talik Expansion
talik expansion.description: Unfrozen areas inside or beneath otherwise frozen ground becoming larger. These areas can let water move through places that were previously blocked by ice. Where thawed plant material and low-oxygen conditions occur, they can also enable releases of methane.
incoming: Continued warming can enlarge unfrozen pockets or layers within otherwise frozen ground. These openings can change water movement and ground stability.
Sustained ground warming can enlarge areas that stay unfrozen within otherwise frozen terrain. Snow, water, soil and plants determine where these areas develop.
outgoing: Permanently unfrozen ground can provide places for methane to form or routes for it to escape. Organic material and low-oxygen conditions are needed for this pathway.

human.summary: Permanently unfrozen ground can provide places for methane to form or routes for it to escape. Organic material and low-oxygen conditions are needed for this pathway. Methane traps heat and has contributed to the warming already observed. The cited assessment estimates its contribution over a particular historical period, with an uncertainty range rather than one exact value.

planet.summary: Permanently unfrozen ground can provide places for methane to form or routes for it to escape. Organic material and low-oxygen conditions are needed for this pathway.

response.defaultDriver: Warmer conditions and local changes to drainage, snow or construction can keep ground from refreezing.
levers: Monitor ground temperature and water movement near exposed infrastructure.
Protect building foundations in ways suited to the site. Avoid disturbing ground that contains a lot of ice and could be badly damaged by thawing.

measurement.metric: Talik extent change
measurement.geography: named permafrost profile, lake setting, or infrastructure corridor
measurement.cadence: seasonal to annual monitoring interval

pollinator colony collapse.name: Pollinator Colony Collapse
pollinator colony collapse.description: A community of bees or other pollinating insects losing so many members that it can no longer function normally. Disease, parasites, poor nutrition, chemicals and weather can contribute. Losing colonies can reduce the help that nearby plants receive in producing seeds and fruit.
incoming: Pesticides and a lack of varied flowers or habitat can contribute to losses of pollinating insects or colonies. Parasites, disease, nutrition and weather also matter, so the affected species and exposure need to be identified.
Heat and changing seasonal timing can stress some pollinating insects. Population or colony losses usually involve several pressures, including food, habitat, chemicals and disease.

Losing forests and other natural habitat removes flowers, nesting sites and shelter used by pollinating insects. This can add to pressures from chemicals, disease and climate rather than acting as the only cause of colony loss.

Farm chemicals drifting beyond their target can reach bees directly or through contaminated food brought back to a colony. Colony harm depends on the chemical, dose and exposure, alongside other stresses.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Losses of pollinating insects can make production less reliable for crops that need their visits. The effect differs across crops and depends on wild pollinators and farming practices too.

planet.summary: Loss of pollinating animals can reduce reproduction in plants that rely on them. Managed colony losses and changes in wild populations need to be assessed separately.

response.defaultDriver: Pesticides and a lack of varied flowers or habitat can contribute to losses of pollinating insects or colonies. Parasites, disease, nutrition and weather also matter, so the affected species and exposure need to be identified.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.

measurement.metric: Pollinator population or colony loss
measurement.geography: named pollinator population, colony system, or monitored landscape
measurement.cadence: seasonal to annual monitoring

nitrogen fertilizer runoff.name: Nitrogen Fertilizer Runoff
nitrogen fertilizer runoff.description: Rain or irrigation carrying unused crop nutrients off fields into drains, rivers and lakes. Those nutrients can encourage excessive algae growth. The effects depend on the amount reaching the water and the conditions there.
incoming: Adding crop nutrients faster than plants can use them leaves material that rain or irrigation can wash away. It can then reach rivers and other waterways.
outgoing: Extra nitrogen carried to the coast can fuel algae growth. As the algae decay, they use oxygen and can leave too little for other marine life.
Nitrogen that crops do not absorb can wash or drain into waterways. It can encourage excessive algae growth and the oxygen loss that follows.
Nitrogen washed from fields can be changed by microbes in downstream soils and water. Some is released as nitrous oxide, adding an indirect source of emissions.
Nutrients washed from fields can travel through rivers into estuaries. They can feed extra algae growth and the oxygen-consuming decay that follows.

human.summary: Extra nitrogen carried to the coast can fuel algae growth. As the algae decay, they use oxygen and can leave too little for other marine life. Low oxygen can kill target species or push them away from fishing grounds. Local catches then become less reliable.
consequences: Nitrogen that crops do not absorb can wash or drain into waterways. It can encourage excessive algae growth and the oxygen loss that follows. Extra nutrients can help harmful algae grow rapidly. Light, water movement and temperature also determine whether a harmful bloom develops.

Nitrogen washed from fields can be changed by microbes in downstream soils and water. Some is released as nitrous oxide, adding an indirect source of emissions. Nitrous oxide traps heat and remains in the air for a long time. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimates its past emissions contributed about 0.09°C of warming in 2010–2019 compared with 1850–1900, with a very likely range of about 0.05–0.16°C.

planet.summary: Extra nitrogen carried to the coast can fuel algae growth. As the algae decay, they use oxygen and can leave too little for other marine life.
consequences: Nitrogen that crops do not absorb can wash or drain into waterways. It can encourage excessive algae growth and the oxygen loss that follows.
Nitrogen washed from fields can be changed by microbes in downstream soils and water. Some is released as nitrous oxide, adding an indirect source of emissions.

response.defaultDriver: Adding crop nutrients faster than plants can use them leaves material that rain or irrigation can wash away. It can then reach rivers and other waterways.
levers: Use farming practices suited to the local soil, water and climate, with protection for workers and livestock.
Keep soils covered where appropriate, limit avoidable nutrient and chemical losses, and manage total water use rather than efficiency alone.

tropospheric ozone.name: Tropospheric Ozone
tropospheric ozone.description: A reactive gas in the lower atmosphere that forms when other pollutants react in sunlight. Near the ground it can harm lungs and plants, and it also traps heat. It is distinct from the protective layer of the same gas much higher in the atmosphere.
incoming: Sunlight allows certain polluting gases to react and form ozone near the ground. It is formed in the air rather than released directly, and the outcome depends on the mix of gases and local conditions.
Some carbon-containing gases react with other pollutants in sunlight to form ozone near the ground. How much forms depends on the mix of gases and the local air conditions.
Hot, sunny weather with little air movement can help ground-level ozone build up. The gases that form it, clouds and air mixing also matter, so temperature alone does not determine pollution.
outgoing: Ozone entering leaves can damage plant tissues and reduce growth. Harvest effects depend on the crop, exposure and region. An estimate for one crop cannot be assumed to apply to all others.

Breathing ground-level ozone irritates and damages airways, especially in exposed or vulnerable people. Studies reviewed for World Health Organization guidelines also link short-term outdoor increases with a small rise in daily deaths from all causes.

human.summary: Ozone entering leaves can damage plant tissues and reduce growth. Harvest effects depend on the crop, exposure and region. An estimate for one crop cannot be assumed to apply to all others.
consequences: Breathing ground-level ozone irritates and damages airways, especially in exposed or vulnerable people. Studies reviewed for World Health Organization guidelines also link short-term outdoor increases with a small rise in daily deaths from all causes.

planet.summary: The gas can enter leaves and damage plant tissues, reducing growth in sensitive species. Effects depend on concentration, duration and growing conditions.

response.defaultDriver: Sunlight drives reactions between pollution from transport, industry and other sources. Winds can carry the resulting gas beyond cities.
levers: Reduce the pollutants that form the gas, including nitrogen oxides and suitable sources of other reactive gases.
Monitor exposure and use locally tested crop and air-quality protection measures.

measurement.metric: Ground-level ozone concentration and exposure
measurement.geography: named regulatory monitor, airshed, urban area, agricultural region, or gridded model domain
measurement.cadence: hourly observations with daily and seasonal summaries

marine heatwaves.name: Marine Heatwaves
marine heatwaves.description: Seawater staying unusually warm for a prolonged period compared with the normal conditions for that place and season. This can stress corals, fish and other marine life. The effects depend on how hot the water becomes, how long it stays warm and which species are present.
incoming: Longer-term North Pacific temperature patterns can change where unusually warm ocean episodes are more likely or intense. Individual events still depend on additional conditions.
Multi-decade Atlantic temperature changes can make regional seas warmer or cooler as a starting point. Unusually warm episodes still depend on several immediate causes.

Under the very high-emissions scenario SSP5-8.5, marine heatwaves are projected to occur eight times as often globally in 2081–2100 as in 1995–2014. The assessed likely range is three to fifteen times. This is a scenario estimate, not a guaranteed outcome.
outgoing: Prolonged unusually warm seawater can kill sensitive animals, damage habitat or move fish away. These changes can undermine fisheries, with effects that vary between places and species.
Unusually warm seawater can favour some harmful algae when nutrients and other suitable conditions are present. Warmth alone does not guarantee a harmful outbreak.
Prolonged warm seawater can help some disease-causing germs grow in new places or seasons. Salt content, human or animal contact and other local conditions also matter.
Severe or repeated warm-water episodes can kill corals after stress and bleaching. If recovery is too slow, the reef's hard framework can lose complexity and break down.
Unusually warm surface and upper-ocean water can supply energy to a tropical cyclone and limit cooling beneath it. Rapid strengthening still depends on winds, humidity, storm structure and its path.
Long periods of unusually warm seawater affect marine species differently. Changes in survival, feeding and energy transfer can disrupt food chains, and larger predators may recover more slowly.
Unusually hot seawater can damage seagrass and kill plants. Severe or repeated events can reduce the area and condition of these underwater meadows.
Unusually hot seawater can make it harder for young shellfish to grow and form shells. This may add to stress from changing water chemistry, with different limits for each species.
Prolonged unusually warm seawater can disrupt the partnership between corals and the tiny algae living inside them. Corals may turn pale, with responses differing between species and reefs.
Coral Larval Survival and Recruitment Failure
Seawater above the temperatures young corals can tolerate can reduce survival and successful settlement. Effects vary by species and stage of growth.

Long periods of unusually warm sea water can harm kelp and reduce supplies of cool, nutrient-rich water. Brief events do not always cause lasting loss, and some forests recover when other pressures are limited.
Unusually hot seawater can move suitable habitat farther away, deeper or toward the poles. Some fish move, while others stay, adjust or return after the event.

human.summary: Prolonged unusually warm seawater can kill sensitive animals, damage habitat or move fish away. These changes can undermine fisheries, with effects that vary between places and species. Severely depleted fish stocks leave fewer fish available to catch. Ports and markets may then receive smaller or less reliable supplies.
consequences: Unusually warm seawater can favour some harmful algae when nutrients and other suitable conditions are present. Warmth alone does not guarantee a harmful outbreak. Toxic algae or low oxygen can kill fish or make seafood unsafe. Harvest closures and damaged stocks can then interrupt supplies arriving at ports and markets.

Prolonged warm seawater can help some disease-causing germs grow in new places or seasons. Salt content, human or animal contact and other local conditions also matter. Some marine germs can cause illness through seafood or contact with open wounds. Their spread can add pressure to coastal health services. This is an infection pathway, rather than heat injury itself.

planet.summary: Prolonged unusually warm seawater can kill sensitive animals, damage habitat or move fish away. These changes can undermine fisheries, with effects that vary between places and species.
consequences: Unusually warm seawater can favour some harmful algae when nutrients and other suitable conditions are present. Warmth alone does not guarantee a harmful outbreak.
Prolonged warm seawater can help some disease-causing germs grow in new places or seasons. Salt content, human or animal contact and other local conditions also matter.

response.defaultDriver: Background ocean warming raises the chance of extreme temperatures, while local weather and currents shape individual events.
levers: Use ocean forecasts and habitat monitoring to guide temporary fishing or conservation measures.
Reduce other local pressures and assess restoration methods against the likely future climate.

measurement.cadence: daily classification with monthly and annual rollups

fracking wastewater lakes.name: Fracking Wastewater Lakes
fracking wastewater lakes.description: Ponds used to hold contaminated water from operations that extract oil or gas by fracturing rock. Leaks, spills or poor handling can threaten nearby water supplies. The risks depend on the stored material, site and protection in place.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Poorly managed oil and gas wastewater can contaminate fresh supplies, while extraction also uses water. These pressures matter especially where usable freshwater is already limited.
Spills or poorly contained wastewater can carry salts, metals and other contaminants into streams or groundwater. Aquatic life can be harmed within the area reached by the release.
Salty or toxic wastewater reaching surface water can injure organisms and damage habitat. Effects depend on its contents, concentration, movement and the ability of the ecosystem to recover.

human.summary: Poorly managed oil and gas wastewater can contaminate fresh supplies, while extraction also uses water. These pressures matter especially where usable freshwater is already limited.

consequences: Spills or poorly contained wastewater can carry salts, metals and other contaminants into streams or groundwater. Aquatic life can be harmed within the area reached by the release.
Salty or toxic wastewater reaching surface water can injure organisms and damage habitat. Effects depend on its contents, concentration, movement and the ability of the ecosystem to recover.

response.defaultDriver: Ponds used to hold contaminated water from operations that extract oil or gas by fracturing rock. Leaks, spills or poor handling can threaten nearby water supplies. The risks depend on the stored material, site and protection in place.
levers: Plan electricity supply, networks and demand together so cleaner options remain dependable.
Improve efficiency and maintain equipment, with backup arrangements suited to essential services and local hazards.

cattle grazing overcompaction.name: Cattle Grazing Overcompaction
cattle grazing overcompaction.description: Repeated movement of farm animals pressing soil together so tightly that it loses spaces for air and water. This can make it harder for roots to grow and rain to soak in. The effect depends on animal numbers, soil conditions and how grazing is managed.
incoming: Too many grazing animals, or repeated trampling on wet ground, can press soil tightly together. Water and roots may then find it harder to move through the soil.
More cattle on the same land create more hoof pressure. Soil can become tightly packed where wetness, soil type and limited recovery make it vulnerable.
outgoing: Ground tightly packed by cattle absorbs water less easily and may support fewer plants. Rain can then create more runoff and erosion where slopes and soil are vulnerable.
Persistent heavy trampling reduces the spaces that let air, water and roots move through soil. This can damage the habitat used by soil organisms.

human.summary: Ground tightly packed by cattle absorbs water less easily and may support fewer plants. Rain can then create more runoff and erosion where slopes and soil are vulnerable. Losing the upper layer of soil removes nutrients and reduces the ground's ability to hold water. Crops may then produce smaller or less dependable harvests.

planet.summary: Persistent heavy trampling reduces the spaces that let air, water and roots move through soil. This can damage the habitat used by soil organisms.

response.defaultDriver: Too many grazing animals, or repeated trampling on wet ground, can press soil tightly together. Water and roots may then find it harder to move through the soil.
levers: Use farming practices suited to the local soil, water and climate, with protection for workers and livestock.
Keep soils covered where appropriate, limit avoidable nutrient and chemical losses, and manage total water use rather than efficiency alone.

measurement.metric: Grazing-related soil compaction
measurement.geography: named paddock or pasture
measurement.cadence: pre/post season or repeated soil survey

nitrous oxide.name: Nitrous Oxide
nitrous oxide.description: A long-lasting gas that traps heat in the atmosphere. It is released by natural processes and human activities, particularly where soil microbes process added nutrients or manure. It contributes to warming alongside other heat-trapping gases.
incoming: Microbes can turn some nitrogen added to farm soil into nitrous oxide, a heat-trapping gas. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's basic method estimates 0.010 kilograms of nitrogen released in this gas per kilogram of qualifying nitrogen added, with a default uncertainty range of 0.002–0.018.
Nitrogen washed from fields can be changed by microbes in downstream soils and water. Some is released as nitrous oxide, adding an indirect source of emissions.

Manure, crop remains and other nitrogen inputs can release nitrous oxide through soil processes. Emissions depend on the practices and conditions. The basic Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimate for qualifying managed-soil inputs is 1% of added nitrogen, with a default range of 0.2–1.8%.
Making nitric acid for some fertilisers produces nitrous oxide as a by-product. This link applies to that manufacturing process, not to every type of fertiliser production.
outgoing: Nitrous oxide traps heat and remains in the air for a long time. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimates its past emissions contributed about 0.09°C of warming in 2010–2019 compared with 1850–1900, with a very likely range of about 0.05–0.16°C.

Nitrous oxide lasts long enough to spread through the atmosphere and add to heat trapping. Its effect is assessed from global abundance with other gases accounted for, so a sector's emissions cannot directly replace that measurement.

human.summary: Nitrous oxide traps heat and remains in the air for a long time. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimates its past emissions contributed about 0.09°C of warming in 2010–2019 compared with 1850–1900, with a very likely range of about 0.05–0.16°C. Hotter air can make aircraft takeoff more difficult and put extra strain on runways and ground operations. The effects depend on the aircraft, airport and conditions.

consequences: Nitrous oxide lasts long enough to spread through the atmosphere and add to heat trapping. Its effect is assessed from global abundance with other gases accounted for, so a sector's emissions cannot directly replace that measurement.

phytoplankton decline.name: Phytoplankton Decline
phytoplankton decline.description: A reduction in the tiny drifting organisms that use sunlight to grow in water. They support many marine food chains. Changes in their abundance or growth can affect the animals that feed on them and, later, fish catches.
incoming: When less deep water reaches the surface, fewer nutrients may be available to tiny sunlit-water organisms. Their growth can decline, reducing food at the base of marine food chains.
Stronger separation between surface and deep ocean water can keep nutrients below the sunlit layer. Tiny drifting plants may grow less where they already lack nutrients.
Marine heatwaves can occur with wind and current changes that bring fewer nutrients to the surface. This can reduce the amount of drifting plant life or change which sizes are most common.
outgoing: Less growth by tiny drifting organisms can leave less food for the animals above them in the food chain. Fisheries that depend on this production may receive less reliable catches.
Changes in the tiny organisms that grow using sunlight alter the food available to other sea life. Different species and feeding relationships may then become dominant.

human.summary: Less growth by tiny drifting organisms can leave less food for the animals above them in the food chain. Fisheries that depend on this production may receive less reliable catches.
consequences: Changes in the tiny organisms that grow using sunlight alter the food available to other sea life. Different species and feeding relationships may then become dominant. Changes in feeding relationships can alter which fish are available and when. Fishing businesses may receive a less predictable mix or quantity of seafood.

planet.summary: Changes in the tiny organisms that grow using sunlight alter the food available to other sea life. Different species and feeding relationships may then become dominant.

response.defaultDriver: When less deep water reaches the surface, fewer nutrients may be available to tiny sunlit-water organisms. Their growth can decline, reducing food at the base of marine food chains.
levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

antarctic shelf instability.name: Antarctic Shelf Instability
antarctic shelf instability.description: Floating platforms of ice around Antarctica thinning, cracking or retreating. These platforms help hold back ice flowing from land. When their support weakens, some inland ice can move toward the sea more quickly.
incoming: Faster ice movement and ice loss can be signs that floating ice is providing less support to ice inland. These observations need local evidence to identify the cause. Ice loss alone does not explain every change.
Warmer water beneath Antarctic ice shelves melts them from below. Thinner shelves provide less support to the land ice behind them.
Warming can destabilise Antarctic ice shelves through warmer surrounding seas. In some places, surface meltwater can also widen cracks and contribute to break-up.
outgoing: Floating shelves help hold back ice on land. When they weaken, inland ice can flow into the ocean faster and add to sea-level rise.

human.summary: Floating shelves help hold back ice on land. When they weaken, inland ice can flow into the ocean faster and add to sea-level rise. Higher seawater levels can push salt into the shallow freshwater reserve beneath a small island. The usable layer may become thinner or saltier, depending on local conditions.

planet.summary: Floating shelves help hold back ice on land. When they weaken, inland ice can flow into the ocean faster and add to sea-level rise.

wildlife habitat patches.name: Wildlife Habitat Patches
wildlife habitat patches.description: Separate pieces of land or water where wild plants and animals can live. Their size, quality and connections influence whether populations can find food, shelter and mates. A patch may remain present while becoming too isolated for some species.
incoming: Breaking up a forest leaves smaller or more isolated places for wildlife. Their value depends on size, quality and whether animals can move between them.
outgoing: Small isolated habitat patches may prevent animals or plants from reaching new suitable places. Their occupied range can then become smaller as conditions change.
Small, separated populations can lose access to mates and resources. This can reduce abundance and increase local extinction risk for species that cannot cross the gaps.
Small or shrinking habitat patches may support fewer breeding individuals. Genetic variety can fall if too few newcomers join the population.

human.summary: Smaller, isolated living areas can make wildlife populations harder to sustain. People who depend on those species or places may lose benefits, but the available habitat measure does not quantify that human loss.

consequences: Small, separated populations can lose access to mates and resources. This can reduce abundance and increase local extinction risk for species that cannot cross the gaps.
Small or shrinking habitat patches may support fewer breeding individuals. Genetic variety can fall if too few newcomers join the population.

levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.

topsoil salinization fields.name: Topsoil Salinization Fields
topsoil salinization fields.description: Salt building up in the upper soil where crops grow. Excess salt can make it harder for roots to take in water and can damage soil structure. The effect depends on the crop, water supply and drainage.
incoming: Heavy pumping can draw salty groundwater into wells. If that water is repeatedly used on fields, evaporation can leave salt around roots. This does not happen everywhere, especially where water stays fresh and drainage removes salts.
Poorly managed irrigation and drainage can leave dissolved salts around plant roots. Salty groundwater rising toward the surface can add to the build-up.
Falling groundwater supplies can force use of poorer-quality water or change how salty water moves. Soil salt levels can rise where irrigation and drainage allow salts to collect.
Seawater entering fields or freshwater supplies brings dissolved salts with it. Salt left around crop roots can make farming more difficult on low-lying land.
outgoing: Too much salt around roots makes it harder for crops to take in water. Harvests can fall or become less reliable, depending on the crop and how the land is managed.

human.summary: Too much salt around roots makes it harder for crops to take in water. Harvests can fall or become less reliable, depending on the crop and how the land is managed.

planet.summary: Excess salt makes it harder for many roots to draw water and can change soil conditions. Tolerance differs between plants and soils.

response.defaultDriver: Heavy pumping can draw salty groundwater into wells. If that water is repeatedly used on fields, evaporation can leave salt around roots. This does not happen everywhere, especially where water stays fresh and drainage removes salts.
levers: Use farming practices suited to the local soil, water and climate, with protection for workers and livestock.
Keep soils covered where appropriate, limit avoidable nutrient and chemical losses, and manage total water use rather than efficiency alone.
