staple food price volatility.name: Staple Food Price Volatility
staple food price volatility.description: The cost of everyday foods such as rice, wheat or maize swinging sharply or unpredictably. This makes household spending and farm planning harder. People with low incomes or few reserves may struggle when prices rise.
incoming: Broken roads, ports, storage or power supplies can delay food and increase transport or spoilage costs. Food reserves and alternative routes can prevent those disruptions from turning into price rises.
Poor harvests of major food crops can tighten supplies and make prices less stable. Stored reserves and substitute foods can soften the effect.
Higher fertiliser prices raise farming costs and may lead to lower use. Smaller later harvests can add pressure to prices of basic foods.
Disrupted sea routes can delay food and farming supplies or make delivery more expensive. These changes can increase swings in market prices.
outgoing: Sharp or unpredictable changes in basic food prices make household budgets harder to manage. Families with little income or stored food can struggle to buy enough.

human.summary: Sharp or unpredictable changes in basic food prices make household budgets harder to manage. Families with little income or stored food can struggle to buy enough.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

levers: Include affected communities in decisions about protection, services and recovery.

sulfur dioxide.name: Sulfur Dioxide
sulfur dioxide.description: A gas released by burning sulfur-containing fuels, processing some metals and volcanic activity. It can harm air quality and form tiny particles that reflect sunlight. Reducing the gas improves air quality while also changing that short-lived cooling influence.
incoming: Sulfur in coal forms sulfur dioxide when the fuel burns. The amount released depends on the fuel and how effectively the plant cleans its exhaust.
Sulfur in ship fuel can form sulfur dioxide during burning. Fuel standards and exhaust-cleaning equipment determine how much escapes.
Sulfur in steelmaking fuels and raw materials can be released as sulfur dioxide. Capture and treatment equipment affect the final amount emitted.
outgoing: Sulfur pollution can form particles that reflect sunlight and briefly cool the climate. Reducing that pollution improves air quality but also removes some of the cooling that had partly hidden warming from other gases.
Sulfur dioxide reacts in the air to form sulfuric acid. It can then reach the ground in rain, snow or dry particles, sometimes far from its source.
Some sulfur dioxide changes into tiny sulfate-containing particles in the air. These become part of fine-particle pollution.

human.summary: Some sulfur dioxide changes into tiny sulfate-containing particles in the air. These become part of fine-particle pollution. Very small airborne particles can reach deep into the lungs. Studies following people over time link greater long-term exposure with a higher risk of death from natural causes.
consequences: Sulfur pollution can form particles that reflect sunlight and briefly cool the climate. Reducing that pollution improves air quality but also removes some of the cooling that had partly hidden warming from other gases. Some airborne particles have partly offset warming by reflecting sunlight. Removing that cooling influence can add near-term warming unless the warming influence of other gases also falls enough.

consequences: Sulfur dioxide reacts in the air to form sulfuric acid. It can then reach the ground in rain, snow or dry particles, sometimes far from its source.
Some sulfur dioxide changes into tiny sulfate-containing particles in the air. These become part of fine-particle pollution.

coral bleaching.name: Coral Bleaching
coral bleaching.description: Stressed corals losing the tiny algae that live inside them and supply much of their food. The corals become pale and have less energy. They may recover if conditions improve, so turning white does not necessarily mean they have died.
incoming: Prolonged unusually warm seawater can disrupt the partnership between corals and the tiny algae living inside them. Corals may turn pale, with responses differing between species and reefs.
Changing seawater chemistry can reduce coral growth and recovery. It can make heat stress harder to withstand, but it is not itself a measure of heat-related bleaching.
Excess nutrients and organic matter can add stress to coastal reefs. This may make heat-related bleaching and recovery worse, depending on local conditions.
Warmer seawater can disrupt the tiny algae that live inside corals and provide much of their food. Corals may turn pale, and prolonged stress can kill colonies.
outgoing: Coral Larval Survival and Recruitment Failure
Stressed adult corals may have less energy to reproduce and support their young. Fewer larvae may be produced, or fewer may survive and settle successfully.
Repeated severe heat stress can kill or weaken corals. Their remaining structures may then break or erode more easily during later disturbances.

human.summary: Heat-stressed reefs can become less able to support fishing and tourism if damage lasts or repeats. A bleaching event does not mean every coral has died. Recovery depends on later conditions.

planet.summary: Stressed adult corals may have less energy to reproduce and support their young. Fewer larvae may be produced, or fewer may survive and settle successfully.
consequences: Repeated severe heat stress can kill or weaken corals. Their remaining structures may then break or erode more easily during later disturbances.

levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.

invasive species encroachment.name: Invasive Species Encroachment
invasive species encroachment.description: Plants, animals or other organisms spreading outside their native range and causing harm. They can crowd out local species or change habitats and feeding relationships. Not every species introduced to a new place becomes harmful.
incoming: Ships can carry organisms in stored water, on their hulls or with cargo. An introduced species becomes invasive only if it establishes, spreads and causes harm. Transport or detection alone does not prove that.
Aircraft and cargo can move living organisms to places they would not normally reach. Most do not establish harmful populations, so flight numbers cannot be treated as a count of invasions.
Warming can make new places suitable for some introduced species or help them survive longer seasons. It can also make conditions worse for other invaders, so effects differ by species and region.
outgoing: Harmful introduced species can displace native wildlife and change habitats or food webs. Being non-native alone does not establish harm. The effects need evidence for the species and place concerned.
Amphibian Chytrid Infection Prevalence and Mortality
Introduced animals carrying the fungus can expose native amphibians as they move between waters. Finding both together does not prove transmission. Timing, movement or genetic evidence is needed.
An introduced predator or competitor can change who eats what in a food web. These changes may spread through several connected groups of organisms.

Persistent losses or imbalances between predators and prey can remove feeding relationships. The remaining community may have fewer species able to perform similar roles.

deepwater petroleum operations.name: Deepwater Petroleum Operations
deepwater petroleum operations.description: Oil and gas operations far below the sea surface. High pressure, distance from shore and difficult access can make accidents harder to prevent or manage. Released oil can harm marine life, depending on where it spreads and how long exposure lasts.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: A large offshore oil release can harm young animals, contaminate food and damage habitats. Feeding relationships can change within the area reached by the spill.
Large oil spills can harm fish and shellfish or force fishing closures. Longer-term population effects depend on exposure, life stage and recovery.
Oil contamination can harm many species and damage habitats from deep water to shore. The extent of biodiversity loss depends on the spill's reach and the organisms exposed.

consequences: Large oil spills can harm fish and shellfish or force fishing closures. Longer-term population effects depend on exposure, life stage and recovery. Severely depleted fish stocks leave fewer fish available to catch. Ports and markets may then receive smaller or less reliable supplies.

volatile organic compounds.description: Carbon-containing chemicals that readily enter the air as gases. Sources include fuels, solvents, plants and industrial processes. Some are harmful to breathe or take part in reactions that produce other air pollution.
incoming: Making and handling petrochemical products can release gases from processing, storage and evaporation. The type and amount depend on the product and pollution controls.
outgoing: Some carbon-containing gases react with other pollutants in sunlight to form ozone near the ground. How much forms depends on the mix of gases and the local air conditions.
Some organic gases react with nitrogen oxides in sunlight to form ground-level ozone. The response depends on the mix of gases and local atmospheric conditions.

consequences: Some organic gases react with nitrogen oxides in sunlight to form ground-level ozone. The response depends on the mix of gases and local atmospheric conditions. sea-level rise.name: Sea-Level Rise
sea-level rise.description: The average height of the ocean increasing over time. Warming makes seawater expand, while melting ice on land adds more water. Local changes also depend on currents and whether the land itself is rising or sinking.
incoming: Seawater expands as it warms. As the ocean stores more heat, this expansion directly contributes to the rise in average sea level.

Warming makes seawater expand, contributing to the rise in average sea level. Melting land ice and changes in water storage add separate contributions, while local land movement affects what a coastline experiences.
When more coastal ice loses contact with the ground, there may be less resistance to glacier movement. Faster movement of land ice into the ocean raises sea level.
Losing an ice cap's summit removes stored land ice and may expose darker ground that speeds further melting. Water from the shrinking ice cap contributes to rising sea level.
Floating shelves help hold back ice on land. When they weaken, inland ice can flow into the ocean faster and add to sea-level rise.
Warming makes seawater expand and melts ice stored on land. Both processes raise average sea level.
Ice moving from land into the ocean adds water mass and raises sea level. The loss of already-floating ice matters mainly when it lets ice on land flow faster.

Ice lost from land adds water to the ocean and raises average sea level. Greenland's measured loss during 1992–2020 was equivalent to 13.5 millimetres globally, with an assessed range of 11.4–15.6 millimetres.
outgoing: Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands
Higher seawater levels can push salt into the shallow freshwater reserve beneath a small island. The usable layer may become thinner or saltier, depending on local conditions.
Rising seas can overwhelm mangroves if soil does not build up fast enough. They are especially exposed where buildings or steep ground prevent them from moving inland.
Higher coastal sea levels can push salty water toward underground freshwater. Pumping, replenishment, geology and connected canals or rivers determine the local response.

Higher sea levels make previously rare coastal water levels easier to reach. Across the assessed tide-gauge locations, relative sea-level rise is projected to make recent extreme still-water levels occur roughly 20–30 times as often by 2050. Local tides, storms and land movement affect the result.

consequences: Higher sea levels make previously rare coastal water levels easier to reach. Across the assessed tide-gauge locations, relative sea-level rise is projected to make recent extreme still-water levels occur roughly 20–30 times as often by 2050. Local tides, storms and land movement affect the result. Flooding from the sea can add salt and other contamination to drinking-water sources or disrupt intakes. Water plants may then have difficulty providing safe supplies.

tundra methane outgassing.name: Tundra Methane Outgassing
tundra methane outgassing.description: A heat-trapping gas escaping from cold northern soils, wetlands and lakes. Microbes can produce it when thawed plant material decays with little oxygen. The amount released depends on both production and processes that break the gas down before it reaches the air.
incoming: Warmer air and ground can lengthen the thaw season and speed decay in northern soils. Wet areas with little oxygen may release more methane.
Thawing ground exposes previously frozen plant material to decay. Where the soil stays waterlogged, this can produce methane that escapes into the air.
Sinking thawed ground can form ponds and wet hollows. Plant material decaying there with little oxygen can become a local source of methane.
outgoing: Methane made in thawing northern soils and lakes can escape into the air if it is not broken down first. The amount varies greatly with temperature, wetness and the route the gas takes.

human.summary: Methane made in thawing northern soils and lakes can escape into the air if it is not broken down first. The amount varies greatly with temperature, wetness and the route the gas takes. Methane traps heat and has contributed to the warming already observed. The cited assessment estimates its contribution over a particular historical period, with an uncertainty range rather than one exact value.

soil microbial depletion.name: Soil Microbial Depletion
soil microbial depletion.description: Soil losing some of its tiny living organisms or their ability to do useful work. These organisms help break down material and make nutrients available to plants. Compaction, chemicals and changing water conditions can affect them.
incoming: Tightly packed farm soil restricts the movement of air and water. This can make conditions less suitable for some of the microbes that support healthy soil.
Frequent soil disturbance, few crop types and chemical pressures can change the communities living in farm soil. Local measurements are needed to show which organisms and functions are affected.
Long periods of dry soil can damage plants and reduce soil fertility. Microbes and the functions they perform may come under pressure.
Persistent heavy trampling reduces the spaces that let air, water and roots move through soil. This can damage the habitat used by soil organisms.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Soil organisms help recycle nutrients and support plant growth. Changes in them can affect farming, but one laboratory measure does not directly show a farm's yield or income loss.

surface water storage instability.name: Surface Water Storage Instability
surface water storage instability.description: Water held in lakes and reservoirs becoming less predictable or reliable. Changing inflows, evaporation and withdrawals can cause larger swings. These changes matter most where users have little spare supply to cope with a low-water period.
incoming: When water use is already close to available supply, seasonal or drought-related changes can leave lakes and reservoirs short. Imports, lower demand and careful operation can sometimes keep storage stable.
Less rain, runoff or river inflow means less water entering lakes, wetlands and reservoirs. Storage can fall if other inflows do not make up the loss.
Evaporation removes water from lakes and reservoirs. Their levels can fall when incoming water does not replace it.
Some lakes and wetlands exchange water with underground reserves. Changes in that exchange can raise or lower the amount stored at the surface.
Taking or diverting water can reduce lake and reservoir storage. The effect depends on how withdrawals compare with incoming water and operating rules.
Long periods of little rain reduce water entering lakes and reservoirs. Storage can fall or become less dependable if withdrawals continue.
Warming can increase evaporation and change when snowmelt and river water arrive. This can alter how much surface water remains stored through the year.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Changing amounts of water in lakes and reservoirs can make household, farm and industrial supplies harder to plan. Effects depend on timing, local demand and backup sources.

planet.summary: Changing water levels can alter the extent and timing of aquatic habitat. Natural seasonal variation must be distinguished from lasting or unusual changes.

response.defaultDriver: When water use is already close to available supply, seasonal or drought-related changes can leave lakes and reservoirs short. Imports, lower demand and careful operation can sometimes keep storage stable.
levers: Limit water withdrawals to what the connected water system can support, while protecting essential human and environmental needs.
Reduce pollution and improve storage, drainage or treatment where local evidence shows these are the relevant problems.

measurement.metric: Surface-water storage instability
measurement.geography: global basin assessment or named surface-water body with aggregation retained
measurement.cadence: major UN-Water assessment cycle or daily-to-seasonal water-balance interval

occurrences.title: Clouds have a surprising effect on surface warming, climate researchers find

persistent pesticide residues in sedimen.name: Persistent Pesticide Residues in Sediment and Biota
persistent pesticide residues in sedimen.description: Long-lasting pest-control chemicals remaining in bottom sediments or inside living things. Repeated exposure can allow some chemicals to build up in tissues or pass through food chains. Effects depend on the chemical, dose and species.
incoming: Some farm chemicals remain in soil and sediment long after use and can enter living things. Current farming alone does not prove where an older chemical came from, and not all pesticides persist or enter food chains.

Some chemicals in water bind to sediment and enter animals through water or food. Many break down quickly or do not build up appreciably, while older contaminated sediment can remain a source after water levels fall.
outgoing: Chemicals stored in animal tissues can affect survival, reproduction or development if the dose is harmful. Finding a residue alone does not prove population damage, and effects differ between chemicals and food webs.

human.summary: Some chemicals can remain in organisms and pass through food chains, potentially exposing people through food or work. Risk depends on the chemical, dose and route of exposure.

planet.summary: Chemicals stored in animal tissues can affect survival, reproduction or development if the dose is harmful. Finding a residue alone does not prove population damage, and effects differ between chemicals and food webs.

response.defaultDriver: Some farm chemicals remain in soil and sediment long after use and can enter living things. Current farming alone does not prove where an older chemical came from, and not all pesticides persist or enter food chains.
levers: Use farming practices suited to the local soil, water and climate, with protection for workers and livestock.
Keep soils covered where appropriate, limit avoidable nutrient and chemical losses, and manage total water use rather than efficiency alone.

measurement.metric: Persistent pesticide residue in sediment and biota
measurement.geography: named water body, sediment reach, species, tissue, food-web sample, watershed, and reference site
measurement.cadence: seasonal or annual sediment and tissue sampling with multi-year persistence review

occurrences.title: Transboundary impacts of pesticide use in food production

pm2.5 particulates.name: PM2.5 Particulates
pm2.5 particulates.description: Tiny airborne particles no wider than 2.5 micrometres, much smaller than the width of a human hair. They can reach deep into the lungs when breathed in. Their health effects depend on concentration, composition and the length of exposure.
incoming: Some sulfur dioxide changes into tiny sulfate-containing particles in the air. These become part of fine-particle pollution.
outgoing: Very small airborne particles can reach deep into the lungs. Studies following people over time link greater long-term exposure with a higher risk of death from natural causes.
Tiny particles are a major health hazard in wildfire smoke because they can reach deep into the lungs. Pollution level and time exposed help determine the harm.

human.summary: Very small airborne particles can reach deep into the lungs. Studies following people over time link greater long-term exposure with a higher risk of death from natural causes.

planet.summary: Tiny particles are a major health hazard in wildfire smoke because they can reach deep into the lungs. Pollution level and time exposed help determine the harm.

response.defaultDriver: Combustion from vehicles, industry and other sources contributes, while location and weather shape exposure.
levers: Reduce emissions at their sources and monitor exposure where people live, study and work.
Use suitable indoor filtration as additional protection, alongside cleaner outdoor air.

measurement.metric: Population-weighted global mean annual ambient fine particulate matter exposure
measurement.geography: declared monitoring site, airshed, waterbody, facility, region, or emissions inventory boundary
measurement.cadence: hourly or event-based with monthly and annual rollups

occurrences.title: Wildfire smoke far more dangerous to health than thought, say scientists

coastal hypoxic dead zones.name: Coastal Hypoxic Dead Zones
coastal hypoxic dead zones.description: Areas of coastal water with too little oxygen for many fish and bottom-dwelling animals. Excess nutrients can fuel algae growth whose decay uses up oxygen. Some animals leave, while those that cannot move may die.
incoming: If low oxygen near the coast becomes severe and persistent, some areas may lose nearly all usable oxygen. Many animals cannot remain in those conditions.
Farm nutrients can contribute to coastal areas with very little oxygen after extra algae decay. Evidence is needed that the nutrients reached the water and helped cause the oxygen loss.
Extra nitrogen and phosphorus can fuel algae growth. As the algae decay, they may use up enough oxygen to create persistent low-oxygen areas in vulnerable waters.
Warmer water holds less oxygen and may mix less. Severe oxygen loss is more likely where extra nutrients and weak circulation already create pressure. Temperature alone does not establish it.
Extra nutrients from fields can travel downstream and encourage algae growth. Decay can then use up oxygen in vulnerable receiving waters.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Very low oxygen can drive fish away or kill organisms unable to move. Fishing and coastal livelihoods may suffer where important habitats or catches are affected.

planet.summary: Very low oxygen leaves less usable habitat for many animals. Some move away while others may die. The outcome depends on oxygen levels, duration and species.

response.defaultDriver: If low oxygen near the coast becomes severe and persistent, some areas may lose nearly all usable oxygen. Many animals cannot remain in those conditions.
levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

measurement.metric: Coastal dissolved oxygen
measurement.geography: named estuary, coastal shelf, or marine basin
measurement.cadence: event to seasonal

occurrences.title: Scientists forecast milder Chesapeake Bay dead zone in 2026

ice albedo feedback loops.name: Ice Albedo Feedback Loops
ice albedo feedback loops.description: A cycle in which melting snow or ice exposes darker land or water. The darker surface absorbs more sunlight, causing more warming and further melting. This can strengthen an initial temperature increase.
incoming: Melting snow and sea ice expose darker surfaces that absorb more sunlight. This adds heat and can encourage further melting, with the strength of the effect varying by place and season.
Losing sea ice during the sunlit season exposes darker ocean water. The water absorbs more sunlight, adding heat that can encourage further melting.
Dark sediment and living material on snow or ice can reduce the sunlight reflected away. Exposed dark patches may then melt more quickly.
Losing reflective land ice can expose darker surfaces that absorb more sunlight. This can reinforce local warming, depending on what surface is left behind.
outgoing: As reflective snow and ice disappear, the Arctic absorbs more sunlight. This is one of the processes that helps the region warm faster than the global average.

human.summary: As reflective snow and ice disappear, the Arctic absorbs more sunlight. This is one of the processes that helps the region warm faster than the global average. Rapid Arctic warming heats the ground and deepens the layer that thaws each summer. This can accelerate the loss of ground that used to remain frozen year-round.

planet.summary: As reflective snow and ice disappear, the Arctic absorbs more sunlight. This is one of the processes that helps the region warm faster than the global average.

response.defaultDriver: Melting snow and sea ice expose darker surfaces that absorb more sunlight. This adds heat and can encourage further melting, with the strength of the effect varying by place and season.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.

measurement.metric: Sea-ice and snow albedo anomaly with absorbed shortwave radiation
measurement.geography: bounded Arctic sea-ice or snow-covered region
measurement.cadence: monthly seasonal cycle

occurrences.title: Surface darkening by abundant and diverse algae on an Antarctic ice cap

forest dieback areas.name: Forest Dieback Areas
forest dieback areas.description: Wooded landscapes where many trees are dying because they cannot recover from the pressures they face. Drought, heat, pests and fire can combine. The effects depend on which trees are lost and whether the forest can regrow.
incoming: Clearing and splitting forests can make the remaining trees less able to withstand heat, drought, pests and fire. Trees may die where several of these pressures occur together.
When many dominant trees die across adjoining areas, the losses form a wider episode of forest die-off. Mapping the pattern helps distinguish it from isolated tree deaths.

Large beetle populations can overwhelm susceptible trees and disrupt their water and nutrient supply. Wide areas may die, but other stresses often contribute and delayed surveys can make the cause difficult to separate.
Warming can add heat and drying stress to forests. Large-scale tree loss depends on other pressures and uncertain local limits, so it cannot be inferred from temperature alone.
Long water shortages can stop trees moving enough water to survive. Heat, pests, fire injury and the condition of the forest can add to the stress.

Acidic pollution can wash useful nutrients from soil and make aluminium more available. This can weaken some trees against cold, pests and other stresses, rather than acting as a universal sole cause of forest loss.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Widespread tree deaths can reduce forest products, shade and cultural benefits and change local fire conditions. Human effects depend on the forest and what nearby communities rely on it for.

planet.summary: Tree deaths change canopy cover, stored carbon and living space for other species. Regrowth, decay, fire and remaining vegetation shape the longer-term result.

response.defaultDriver: Clearing and splitting forests can make the remaining trees less able to withstand heat, drought, pests and fire. Trees may die where several of these pressures occur together.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.

measurement.metric: Forest dieback area and mortality
measurement.geography: named forest stand, landscape, or host population
measurement.cadence: seasonal to annual field, remote-sensing, or survey interval

occurrences.title: Can satellites detect when forests lose resilience?

combined sewer overflow.name: Combined Sewer Overflow
combined sewer overflow.description: Rainwater and sewage spilling out of a shared pipe system when it becomes too full. The released mixture may not receive normal treatment. This can carry pollution and germs into nearby rivers or coastal waters.
incoming: Where rainwater and sewage share a pipe system, too much incoming water can escape through an overflow outlet. This connection applies only to systems built to carry both together.
Heavy rain can send more runoff into pipes that carry both rainwater and sewage. Overflow occurs only where such a combined system exists and the incoming water exceeds its capacity.
Hard urban surfaces can send rainwater quickly into combined rainwater and sewage pipes. Overflow risk rises where storage and pipe capacity cannot handle the flow.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Heavy flows can release sewage into nearby waters when the system cannot treat it all. People may lose safe recreation or face contaminated water until conditions improve.

planet.summary: Untreated sewage can add germs, nutrients and material that uses oxygen as it breaks down. Effects depend on the receiving water and how much is released.

response.defaultDriver: Where rainwater and sewage share a pipe system, too much incoming water can escape through an overflow outlet. This connection applies only to systems built to carry both together.
levers: Limit water withdrawals to what the connected water system can support, while protecting essential human and environmental needs.
Reduce pollution and improve storage, drainage or treatment where local evidence shows these are the relevant problems.

measurement.metric: Combined sewer overflow event and volume
measurement.geography: named CSO outfall, sewer shed, municipality, or reporting jurisdiction
measurement.cadence: event-based monitoring with annual permit reporting

occurrences.title: Dry weather sewage discharges soar as water companies face scrutiny

humanitarian response capacity gap.name: Humanitarian Response Capacity Gap
humanitarian response capacity gap.description: The difference between the help people need in a crisis and what aid services can actually deliver. Staff, money, supplies, transport or access may be insufficient. A promise of funding alone does not ensure that help reaches people.
incoming: An interruption in imported food or a sharp price rise can increase the need for aid. Shortfalls are more likely where local reserves, household income and aid capacity are limited.
Damaged roads, power, water or communications can prevent aid from reaching people. Funding, security and coordination can also block help even when physical systems still work.
Insufficient funding can force aid organisations to delay, reduce or close programmes. The effect depends on each operation's needs, access and freedom to use the funds.
Conflict, restrictions and attacks can stop aid workers reaching people. Supplies and funding cannot meet needs if access remains blocked.
Several disasters or conflicts occurring together can create more needs than aid services can meet. The shortfall depends on the capacity and circumstances of each response.
An expanding animal-to-human disease outbreak can increase needs for testing, care and containment at the same time. A resource gap occurs only if these needs exceed available response capacity.
More people facing acute hunger increases demand for food assistance. Funding and access limits can leave part of that need unmet.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: When aid lacks money, staff or supplies, people may wait longer for shelter, food, water or healthcare. A recorded funding gap does not directly count everyone who missed help.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

response.defaultDriver: An interruption in imported food or a sharp price rise can increase the need for aid. Shortfalls are more likely where local reserves, household income and aid capacity are limited.
levers: Include affected communities in decisions about protection, services and recovery.
Fund practical support and monitor who can actually access it, especially where people have few alternatives.

measurement.metric: OCHA FTS reported response-plan resource gap
measurement.geography: named released OCHA Humanitarian Programme Cycle plan and its declared locations
measurement.cadence: monthly during the plan year; retain completed-year revisions

occurrences.title: It Has Never Been Harder to Be a Humanitarian

carbon monoxide.name: Carbon Monoxide
carbon monoxide.description: A poisonous, colourless gas produced when fuels do not burn completely. Breathing it reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen. The danger depends on the concentration, time exposed and the person's health and activity.
incoming: Diesel trucks can release carbon monoxide when fuel does not burn completely. Engine condition, controls and operating load affect how much is produced.
Ship engines can produce carbon monoxide when fuel burns incompletely. A useful estimate needs details about the engine, fuel and how the vessel operates.
Wildfires produce carbon monoxide as material burns incompletely. The amount varies with the fuel and burning conditions.
outgoing: Breathing carbon monoxide reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen. Risk depends on the amount breathed, exposure time and the person's condition. Detecting the gas alone does not measure health harm.

Carbon monoxide also reacts with hydroxyl radicals, which help remove methane. More carbon monoxide can leave less removal capacity, although other reactions can recycle these chemicals and change the result.

human.summary: Breathing carbon monoxide reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen. Risk depends on the amount breathed, exposure time and the person's condition. Detecting the gas alone does not measure health harm.

planet.summary: Carbon monoxide also reacts with hydroxyl radicals, which help remove methane. More carbon monoxide can leave less removal capacity, although other reactions can recycle these chemicals and change the result.

response.defaultDriver: Diesel trucks can release carbon monoxide when fuel does not burn completely. Engine condition, controls and operating load affect how much is produced.
levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

measurement.metric: Carbon-monoxide emission or concentration
measurement.geography: named inventory source, monitor, or indoor setting
measurement.cadence: continuous to triennial inventory

occurrences.title: Warming winters weaken New Hampshire forest's carbon sink over 20 years

gulf stream transport and position.name: Gulf Stream Transport and Position
gulf stream transport and position.description: Changes in the strength and route of the powerful current carrying warm water through the western North Atlantic. Its movement affects regional ocean conditions and nearby coastal water levels. This current is related to, but is not the same as, the entire Atlantic overturning circulation.
incoming: Part of the strong northward Atlantic surface current belongs to the ocean's wider overturning circulation. Changes in that wider system can affect it, but winds also drive the current, so the two are not interchangeable.

Long-lasting North Atlantic pressure and wind changes can influence the position of the current farther downstream. Relationships vary by place and time, and matching patterns alone do not prove one direct cause.
outgoing: A weaker current through the Florida Straits is associated with higher sea levels along nearby Atlantic coasts. Many other factors control flooding there, so a rising tide gauge alone does not identify a change in the current.

human.summary: A weaker current through the Florida Straits is associated with higher sea levels along nearby Atlantic coasts. Many other factors control flooding there, so a rising tide gauge alone does not identify a change in the current. Flooding from the sea can add salt and other contamination to drinking-water sources or disrupt intakes. Water plants may then have difficulty providing safe supplies.

planet.summary: A weaker current through the Florida Straits is associated with higher sea levels along nearby Atlantic coasts. Many other factors control flooding there, so a rising tide gauge alone does not identify a change in the current.

response.defaultDriver: Part of the strong northward Atlantic surface current belongs to the ocean's wider overturning circulation. Changes in that wider system can affect it, but winds also drive the current, so the two are not interchangeable.
levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

measurement.metric: Gulf Stream section transport and path position
measurement.geography: named current segment and cross-stream section such as the Florida Straits at 27 degrees north, Cape Hatteras separation region, or downstream longitude band with depth and contour definitions
measurement.cadence: daily transport and altimetry observation with monthly, annual, and multi-decadal method-consistent assessment

occurrences.title: The seven best shows to stream this week

rapid runoff response.name: Rapid Runoff Response
rapid runoff response.description: Water suddenly flowing off land or out of melting snow into streams much faster than usual. Rapid flows can carry soil and pollutants and raise river levels. The outcome depends on the landscape, ground conditions and drainage.
incoming: Snow melting earlier or faster can send a stronger pulse of water into streams. The effect is greater where the landscape has little capacity to hold the water temporarily.
If a lake held beside a glacier breaks through its barrier, stored water can rush downstream. The flood can also carry large amounts of sediment.

Faster snowmelt can send stored water into streams over a shorter spring period. Earlier melting does not always mean damaging floods: reservoirs can slow the flow, and total runoff may fall as exposed land loses more water to the air.
outgoing: A surge of fast-moving water can wash material away from around a bridge's supports. Losing that material can weaken the foundations.
Large runoff events can quickly carry nutrients from land into an estuary. The effect depends on nutrients being present in the upstream area.
A rapid rise in runoff can increase river depth and speed. Banks erode when the force of moving water exceeds the ground's resistance.

human.summary: A surge of fast-moving water can wash material away from around a bridge's supports. Losing that material can weaken the foundations.

planet.summary: Large runoff events can quickly carry nutrients from land into an estuary. The effect depends on nutrients being present in the upstream area.
consequences: A rapid rise in runoff can increase river depth and speed. Banks erode when the force of moving water exceeds the ground's resistance.

response.defaultDriver: Snow melting earlier or faster can send a stronger pulse of water into streams. The effect is greater where the landscape has little capacity to hold the water temporarily.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.

measurement.metric: Peak runoff response relative to antecedent baseline flow
measurement.geography: declared basin, aquifer, utility, catchment, floodplain, or administrative reporting area
measurement.cadence: event-based to monthly with annual accounting

occurrences.title: Human-induced climate change amplification on storm dynamics in Valencia's 2024 catastrophic flash flood

population and asset exposure in floodpl.name: Population and Asset Exposure in Floodplains
population and asset exposure in floodpl.description: People, homes, roads and other assets located on land that a river can cover when it overflows. Being in this area creates potential exposure. Actual damage depends on the flood and the protection in place.
incoming: Restored wetlands, forests and river floodplains can hold or slow water. This can reduce some flood exposure, depending on their location, size and the flood itself.
Wetlands and connected river floodplains can store water and slow its movement. This can reduce flood exposure within the limits of the land and the event.
Safer locations, drainage, water storage and protective works can reduce exposure to flooding. Maintenance and the size of future floods determine how well protection holds up.
Heavier rain can increase flood hazards. Risk rises where homes, people and important services occupy land that rivers can flood.
Forest loss can increase sediment and rapid runoff reaching rivers. Flood risk depends on how the water moves downstream and whether people or buildings are exposed.
Repeated heavy rain and flooding can threaten people and buildings on flood-prone land. Exposure depends on what occupies the affected area.
outgoing: Repeated flood damage can make buying out, removing or relocating exposed buildings a useful protection option. The choice depends on households' needs and public decisions.

human.summary: People and buildings in areas reached by floods can face damage and interrupted services. Being inside a mapped flood area describes exposure, not a prediction that everyone there will be harmed.

planet.summary: The measure counts people or assets in mapped flood areas. Floodplains also have natural ecological roles, so human exposure is not itself proof of environmental damage.

response.defaultDriver: Heavier rain can increase flood hazards. Risk rises where homes, people and important services occupy land that rivers can flood.
levers: Restored wetlands, forests and river floodplains can hold or slow water. This can reduce some flood exposure, depending on their location, size and the flood itself.
Wetlands and connected river floodplains can store water and slow its movement. This can reduce flood exposure within the limits of the land and the event.

measurement.metric: Population and assets within a declared flood-probability zone
measurement.geography: declared basin, aquifer, utility, catchment, floodplain, or administrative reporting area
measurement.cadence: event-based to monthly with annual accounting

occurrences.title: European birds with narrow climate tolerance face population declines

groundwater depletion wells.name: Groundwater Depletion Wells
groundwater depletion wells.description: Wells reaching less usable water because the underground water level has fallen. Continued pumping can lower levels faster than they recover. A well may become more expensive to use or stop supplying water altogether.
incoming: Pumping faster than water is replaced lowers underground reserves. Wells can then reach less water or stop working at their existing depth.
When soil becomes very dry, farmers may pump more underground water for irrigation. Added pumping can lower well levels where replacement water is insufficient.
Poorly used irrigation water can require more pumping for the same harvest. This can lower well supplies where underground water is not replaced quickly enough.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Falling underground water levels can leave shallow wells dry or make pumping more expensive. People with fewer alternative supplies may be affected sooner.

planet.summary: Falling underground water can reduce flows to connected rivers, springs or wetlands. Whether this occurs depends on the local connections and pumping pattern.

response.defaultDriver: Pumping faster than water is replaced lowers underground reserves. Wells can then reach less water or stop working at their existing depth.
levers: Limit water withdrawals to what the connected water system can support, while protecting essential human and environmental needs.
Reduce pollution and improve storage, drainage or treatment where local evidence shows these are the relevant problems.

measurement.metric: Monitoring wells with groundwater-level decline beyond a declared threshold
measurement.geography: declared basin, aquifer, utility, catchment, floodplain, or administrative reporting area
measurement.cadence: event-based to monthly with annual accounting

occurrences.title: Groundwater crisis deepens in Karnataka’s hard rock terrain

greenhouse gas effective radiative forci.name: Greenhouse Gas Effective Radiative Forcing
greenhouse gas effective radiative forci.description: The extra heat kept in Earth's climate system by gases such as carbon dioxide and methane. These gases reduce how easily heat escapes to space. When more energy stays in than leaves, the land and oceans warm as the system adjusts.
incoming: Persistent aircraft ice clouds both reflect sunlight and trap outgoing heat. The assessed global net effect is warming, but uncertainty is large and individual trails can have little effect or cause cooling depending on place and time.

If the air's chemical ability to remove methane weakens, methane can remain longer and trap more heat. Other removal processes can offset this, and the size of the effect is difficult to measure directly everywhere.

Carbon dioxide accumulating in the air reduces the heat Earth can release to space. Yearly emissions alone do not determine the change because oceans and land absorb a varying share. The assessment uses global concentration relative to a stated baseline.

More methane across the atmosphere traps additional heat and also affects ozone and water vapour high above Earth. A local leak or brief concentration spike is not equivalent to a change in the global annual heat balance.

Nitrous oxide lasts long enough to spread through the atmosphere and add to heat trapping. Its effect is assessed from global abundance with other gases accounted for, so a sector's emissions cannot directly replace that measurement.

Using less powerful heat-trapping cooling gases and preventing leaks reduces their contribution to warming. The benefit is measured against what would happen if those releases continued without controls.
outgoing: When more energy stays in Earth's climate system than leaves it, the land and oceans warm as the system adjusts. Short-term regional temperatures can still move in the opposite direction, and the energy measure is not a temperature observation.

human.summary: When more energy stays in Earth's climate system than leaves it, the land and oceans warm as the system adjusts. Short-term regional temperatures can still move in the opposite direction, and the energy measure is not a temperature observation. Hotter air can make aircraft takeoff more difficult and put extra strain on runways and ground operations. The effects depend on the aircraft, airport and conditions.

planet.summary: When more energy stays in Earth's climate system than leaves it, the land and oceans warm as the system adjusts. Short-term regional temperatures can still move in the opposite direction, and the energy measure is not a temperature observation.

response.defaultDriver: Carbon dioxide, methane and other long-lived gases trap more outgoing heat as their amounts rise. Aircraft trails also affect Earth’s energy balance, but they are separate from the long-lived-gas measurement shown here.
levers: Using less powerful heat-trapping cooling gases and preventing leaks reduces their contribution to warming. The benefit is measured against what would happen if those releases continued without controls.

measurement.metric: Long-lived greenhouse-gas effective radiative forcing
measurement.geography: global atmosphere, with the observing network and forcing calculation stated
measurement.cadence: annual concentration update with assessment-method revision tracking

occurrences.title: Research news on greenhouse gases

ocean heat content.name: Ocean Heat Content
ocean heat content.description: The amount of heat stored in seawater within a stated depth and area. It describes more than the temperature at the surface. As the sea stores more heat, the water can expand and conditions for marine life can change.
incoming: Carbon dioxide reduces how easily Earth loses heat to space. The ocean takes up most of the extra heat, storing it from the surface into deeper water.
outgoing: Seawater expands as it warms. As the ocean stores more heat, this expansion directly contributes to the rise in average sea level.
Added ocean heat makes seawater lighter. In the North Atlantic, this can reduce the sinking of water that helps sustain its large ocean circulation.
Warm ocean water can melt sea ice from below and delay freezing in autumn. This shortens the time that sea ice covers the water.

Warmer water and changing currents affect how carbon dioxide is absorbed and moved through the ocean. They change where seawater chemistry shifts, while absorbed carbon dioxide remains the main cause of increasing acidity.
Warm ocean water can melt floating ice shelves from below. Weaker shelves hold back inland ice less effectively, allowing it to move toward the sea faster.
Warmer water near the ocean surface can support more evaporation. How much moisture enters the air also depends on wind and how humid the air already is.
Warm water beneath floating ice can melt and thin it near the coast. Where the land shape allows, the boundary between grounded and floating ice can retreat inland.
A deep layer of warm ocean water can keep supplying heat as a cyclone stirs the sea. This reduces cooling beneath the storm and can support rapid strengthening when other conditions are favourable.
Extra heat stored beneath the equatorial Pacific can help prepare the ocean for a warm phase. Suitable wind changes are still needed. Stored heat alone does not guarantee it.
Less heat stored in the equatorial Pacific makes cold water below the surface easier to bring upward. This favours a later cool phase.
Warmer water beneath Antarctic ice shelves melts them from below. Thinner shelves provide less support to the land ice behind them.
Warm water reaching a glacier's ocean-facing edge can melt and undercut it. The weakened front may crack and release icebergs.

human.summary: Warmer water near the ocean surface can support more evaporation. How much moisture enters the air also depends on wind and how humid the air already is. Humid heat limits cooling through sweat. This can increase heat illness and strain the heart, lungs and kidneys, especially during prolonged exposure.
consequences: A deep layer of warm ocean water can keep supplying heat as a cyclone stirs the sea. This reduces cooling beneath the storm and can support rapid strengthening when other conditions are favourable. A rapidly strengthening cyclone gives ships and ports less time to prepare. Closures, changed routes and delays may increase.

Extra heat stored beneath the equatorial Pacific can help prepare the ocean for a warm phase. Suitable wind changes are still needed. Stored heat alone does not guarantee it. Changes in Pacific ocean temperatures can bring heat, drought or flooding to farming regions. These conditions can damage harvests and interrupt food supplies.

planet.summary: Seawater expands as it warms. As the ocean stores more heat, this expansion directly contributes to the rise in average sea level.
consequences: Added ocean heat makes seawater lighter. In the North Atlantic, this can reduce the sinking of water that helps sustain its large ocean circulation.
Warm ocean water can melt sea ice from below and delay freezing in autumn. This shortens the time that sea ice covers the water.

response.defaultDriver: Carbon dioxide reduces how easily Earth loses heat to space. The ocean takes up most of the extra heat, storing it from the surface into deeper water.
levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

measurement.metric: Ocean heat-content anomaly over a declared depth layer
measurement.geography: global ocean, basin, or bounded grid and depth layer
measurement.cadence: monthly with quarterly and annual synthesis

occurrences.title: Antarctic sea ice defied global warming for decades – now, hidden ocean heat is breaking through

peatland degradation.name: Peatland Degradation
peatland degradation.description: Damage to wet ground that contains deep stores of partly decayed plant material. Draining or drying it lets that material break down more quickly. This can release stored carbon, lower the ground surface and damage wildlife habitat.
incoming: Draining peatland exposes wet organic soil to air. The soil can decay, sink and lose the water conditions and plants that support a healthy wetland.
Clearing plants from peatland often comes with drainage or conversion to another use. This can expose stored peat and remove plants that help build and protect it.
Severe or repeated fires can burn peat, kill plants and change how water moves through the land. Recovery can become more difficult after repeated damage.
outgoing: Draining peat exposes partly decayed plant material to air, allowing it to release carbon dioxide as it breaks down. Fires and the loss of plants can add to these carbon losses.
Damaged peatland can lose the high water table that keeps buried plant material wet. Exposure to air allows faster decay and greater carbon loss.
Damage to wetland plants and water flow can leave peat dry and exposed. Fires may start more easily, burn deeper and become harder to put out.

Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.

waterborne pathogen outbreaks.name: Waterborne Pathogen Outbreaks
waterborne pathogen outbreaks.description: Groups of people getting sick after contact with water that contains harmful germs. People may drink the water, swim in it or touch it during a flood. The risk depends on which germs are present and whether water and sewage systems keep people safe.
incoming: Warming and heavy rain can favour some germs, overwhelm sanitation and wash pollution into water. Disease outbreaks depend on whether treatment and public-health systems contain the exposure.
Floods and heat can increase contact with contaminated water when water treatment and sanitation fail. Disease risk depends on the germs present and the protection people have.
Overflowing sewage systems can expose people to water carrying harmful germs. Outbreak risk rises when treatment and sanitation no longer contain that exposure.
Sudden floods can contaminate drinking-water facilities and spread harmful germs. Effective treatment and hygiene can prevent exposure from becoming an outbreak.
Water treatment that cannot handle contamination may allow harmful germs to reach users. Outbreak risk depends on actual exposure and whether other protections work.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Germs carried by contaminated water can cause illness and increase demand for care. Investigations must establish the germ and exposure route before linking an outbreak to a particular water event.

planet.summary: An outbreak record concerns disease in people. It does not alone establish ecosystem damage or identify the original environmental source of the germs.

response.defaultDriver: Warming and heavy rain can favour some germs, overwhelm sanitation and wash pollution into water. Disease outbreaks depend on whether treatment and public-health systems contain the exposure.
levers: Limit water withdrawals to what the connected water system can support, while protecting essential human and environmental needs.
Reduce pollution and improve storage, drainage or treatment where local evidence shows these are the relevant problems.

emergency response capacity exceedance.name: Emergency Response Capacity Exceedance
emergency response capacity exceedance.description: More people needing urgent help than available staff, vehicles, beds or equipment can serve in time. Several problems can happen at once during a disaster. Delays depend on both the size of the emergency and the resources available locally.
incoming: Earlier warnings give services time to prepare and help people move before danger arrives. This can reduce the number of urgent rescues needed at once.
Keeping roads and essential services working during floods can reduce urgent rescue needs. It also helps emergency teams reach people who still need assistance.

A surge in heat illness and deaths may occur alongside overwhelming demand for ambulances and hospitals. Death counts alone do not show whether services were overloaded. Their workload and capacity need separate evidence.
Restricted access delays help and leaves more needs unmet. Responders who can still reach affected places may face growing pressure.
Too little funding limits staff, supplies and transport for emergency services. Demand may then exceed what they can deliver.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: When calls exceed available staff, vehicles or supplies, people may wait longer for help. The consequences depend on the emergency, available alternatives and how services prioritize needs.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

response.defaultDriver: A surge in heat illness and deaths may occur alongside overwhelming demand for ambulances and hospitals. Death counts alone do not show whether services were overloaded. Their workload and capacity need separate evidence.
levers: Earlier warnings give services time to prepare and help people move before danger arrives. This can reduce the number of urgent rescues needed at once.

zoonotic disease outbreaks.name: Zoonotic Disease Outbreaks
zoonotic disease outbreaks.description: Clusters of illness caused by germs that can pass between animals and people. An outbreak may require both human and animal health services. Its spread depends on the germ, contacts and measures used to detect and contain it.
incoming: Forest clearing changes contact between wildlife, domestic animals and people. This can create opportunities for germs to cross species, but most clearing does not cause an outbreak and the transmission route needs evidence.

Crowded animals, frequent movement and poor disease controls can help germs persist or reach workers and food. Effective controls can reduce some risks, and outcomes differ by germ and farming system.
Urban growth can change contact with animals through habitat expansion, waste and food systems. It does not identify an outbreak's source by itself, and better services can reduce risk.
outgoing: An expanding animal-to-human disease outbreak can increase needs for testing, care and containment at the same time. A resource gap occurs only if these needs exceed available response capacity.

human.summary: An expanding animal-to-human disease outbreak can increase needs for testing, care and containment at the same time. A resource gap occurs only if these needs exceed available response capacity.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

response.defaultDriver: Forest clearing changes contact between wildlife, domestic animals and people. This can create opportunities for germs to cross species, but most clearing does not cause an outbreak and the transmission route needs evidence.
levers: Include affected communities in decisions about protection, services and recovery.

coastal erosion.name: Coastal Erosion
coastal erosion.description: Waves, currents and storms wearing away the land at the sea's edge. Beaches, cliffs and wetlands can lose material. Homes, roads and habitats may become more exposed as the shoreline moves inland.
incoming: High storm water levels let waves reach and wear away beaches, dunes or cliffs. Erosion can be greater where little new sediment arrives to replace what is lost.
Without mangrove roots to hold sediment and slow water, a shoreline can lose material more easily. Local wave conditions and sediment supply affect the rate.
Dams can trap sediment that would otherwise reach a river delta or beach. Waves and currents may then remove coastal material faster than it is replaced.
Rising sea levels let waves and storm-driven water reach farther inland. Erosion can increase along coasts made of material that is easily worn away.
outgoing: Erosion can remove the soil and stable shoreline that support mangrove roots. Losing these trees also weakens the natural barrier they form against storms.
Erosion and shifting sediment can wash away or bury seagrass habitat. Meadows may shrink where roots cannot remain established.

human.summary: Land lost along a shore can threaten homes, roads and places important to local communities. Damage depends on how fast the shore changes and what lies in its path.

planet.summary: Erosion can remove the soil and stable shoreline that support mangrove roots. Losing these trees also weakens the natural barrier they form against storms.
consequences: Erosion and shifting sediment can wash away or bury seagrass habitat. Meadows may shrink where roots cannot remain established.

response.defaultDriver: High storm water levels let waves reach and wear away beaches, dunes or cliffs. Erosion can be greater where little new sediment arrives to replace what is lost.
levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

alpine snowpack declines.name: Alpine Snowpack Declines
alpine snowpack declines.description: Mountain snow becoming thinner, covering less area, holding less water or lasting for a shorter time. Warming can turn some snowfall into rain and bring earlier melting. This changes the water stored for later in the year.
incoming: Warmer mountain weather can turn snowfall into rain and bring earlier melting. The effect is especially strong where winter temperatures are already close to freezing.
A season with little snowfall or unusually early melting leaves less water stored in mountain snow. The change differs with elevation, season and river basin.
Soot darkens snow so it absorbs more sunlight. Enough soot and sunshine can speed melting, with effects varying between mountain areas and seasons.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Less water stored as mountain snow can change the timing and amount reaching farms, reservoirs and households. Effects vary by basin and by the other water sources available.

planet.summary: Less stored snow can change when water reaches streams and how long nearby ground remains covered. Habitats may face different seasonal water and temperature conditions.

response.defaultDriver: Warmer mountain weather can turn snowfall into rain and bring earlier melting. The effect is especially strong where winter temperatures are already close to freezing.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.

wetland drainage.name: Wetland Drainage
wetland drainage.description: Removing or redirecting water from naturally wet land. This changes the plants and animals that can live there and can reduce natural floodwater storage. Where the soil contains long-stored plant material, drying can also release carbon.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Removing water from wetlands changes or removes habitat for species adapted to wet conditions. Some populations may decline or disappear locally.
Draining wetland areas changes water storage, natural filtering and habitat. Severe changes can undermine nearby freshwater communities and their functions.
Draining carbon-rich wetland soil exposes stored plant material to air. Its decay can continue releasing carbon dioxide. The rate depends on soil, climate and land use.
Draining wet ground lowers its water level and exposes buried plant material to air. Microbes can then break it down faster, releasing stored carbon.
Draining a coastal wetland changes its water supply and exposes wet soils to air. This can release carbon that the plants and soils had stored.
Draining peatland exposes wet organic soil to air. The soil can decay, sink and lose the water conditions and plants that support a healthy wetland.
Draining peat lowers its moisture and makes it easier to ignite. Once burning, dry peat can smoulder for a long time below the surface.
Draining coastal wetlands removes wet conditions that protect plants and organic soils. Stored carbon becomes more exposed to decay and erosion.

human.summary: Draining carbon-rich wetland soil exposes stored plant material to air. Its decay can continue releasing carbon dioxide. The rate depends on soil, climate and land use. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.

planet.summary: Removing water from wetlands changes or removes habitat for species adapted to wet conditions. Some populations may decline or disappear locally.
consequences: Draining wetland areas changes water storage, natural filtering and habitat. Severe changes can undermine nearby freshwater communities and their functions.
Draining carbon-rich wetland soil exposes stored plant material to air. Its decay can continue releasing carbon dioxide. The rate depends on soil, climate and land use.

submarine cable landing-site concentrati.name: Submarine Cable Landing-Site Concentration and Exposure
submarine cable landing-site concentrati.description: Many undersea communication lines reaching land through a small number of coastal sites. Shared power or onward connections can create a common weak point. Damage at one such site may interrupt several routes at once.
incoming: Several cables sharing a landing area, power supply or land connection may fail together. More cables provide protection only when these supporting routes and services are sufficiently independent.

Coastal flooding can affect cable landing stations and their power or land connections. Shared locations increase the risk of several links failing together, while protection, backup power and separated routes can prevent disruption.
outgoing: Losing shared cable landing or power facilities can remove several communication paths at once. Essential services are less affected where traffic can switch to independent routes with enough spare capacity.

human.summary: Losing shared cable landing or power facilities can remove several communication paths at once. Essential services are less affected where traffic can switch to independent routes with enough spare capacity.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

response.defaultDriver: Shorter, cheaper routes and existing facilities can encourage links to cluster in the same places.
levers: Create independent routes and landing locations where practical.
Protect vulnerable shore connections and test recovery plans for more than one simultaneous failure.

rice paddy methane emissions.name: Rice Paddy Methane Emissions
rice paddy methane emissions.description: A heat-trapping gas being released as plant material breaks down in flooded crop fields with little oxygen. It can escape through plants, bubbles or the water surface. Releases depend on water management, soil and the growing season.
incoming: Flooded rice fields create soil conditions with little oxygen. Decaying organic material can then produce methane.
Demand for rice can increase the area or intensity of flooded cultivation. The response also depends on yields, trade, diets and available water.
outgoing: Plant material breaking down in flooded fields can produce methane, which escapes through plants, bubbles and the water surface. The amount varies with water management, soil, added organic material and the growing season.

human.summary: Plant material breaking down in flooded fields can produce methane, which escapes through plants, bubbles and the water surface. The amount varies with water management, soil, added organic material and the growing season. Methane traps heat and has contributed to the warming already observed. The cited assessment estimates its contribution over a particular historical period, with an uncertainty range rather than one exact value.

planet.summary: Plant material breaking down in flooded fields can produce methane, which escapes through plants, bubbles and the water surface. The amount varies with water management, soil, added organic material and the growing season.

response.defaultDriver: Keeping fields continuously flooded can favour methane production, though practices differ across rice-growing areas.
levers: Use locally suitable wetting and drying schedules where water control allows them.

managed-retreat decision pressure.name: Managed-Retreat Decision Pressure
managed-retreat decision pressure.description: A growing need to decide whether staying in a hazardous place is still safe or affordable. Repeated flooding or erosion may make protection and rebuilding increasingly difficult. Decisions involve homes, livelihoods, public costs and community choice.
incoming: Repeated or expected coastal floods can make continued protection and rebuilding impractical. Communities may need to consider a planned move that protects residents' rights and livelihoods.
Losing affordable insurance can make it harder to stay in or finance an exposed home. Public insurance arrangements may either support a planned move or delay it.
Population and Asset Exposure in Floodplains
Repeated flood damage can make buying out, removing or relocating exposed buildings a useful protection option. The choice depends on households' needs and public decisions.
outgoing: Repeated flooding or other danger can make rebuilding in the same place unsafe. This increases the need to plan a move with the affected community.

human.summary: Repeated hazards can make remaining in a place more costly or dangerous. Moving can improve safety but also disrupt housing, jobs and community ties unless people have meaningful support and choice.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

jet stream volatility.name: Jet Stream Volatility
jet stream volatility.description: Changes in the position, speed or bends of the fast-moving winds high in the atmosphere. These winds help guide weather systems. Large or slow-moving bends can contribute to conditions lingering over a region.
incoming: Pressure differences between the Arctic and farther south can shift high-altitude winds and storm routes. This influences variability without making every future wind change predictable.

Faster Arctic warming can reduce the temperature contrast with lower latitudes near the surface. This may favour some weaker or more winding jet-stream patterns in certain seasons, but it does not determine their behaviour.

Long-lasting North Pacific sea-temperature patterns can influence winds high in the atmosphere. This can affect the jet stream over the Pacific and North America, alongside its own natural variability.
Alternating winds high above the equator can influence how atmospheric waves and polar winds behave. In some seasons, this changes the likelihood of shifts in the jet stream farther from the equator.
outgoing: A slow or strongly winding jet stream can help weather patterns remain in place. Other atmospheric conditions still determine whether a long-lasting block develops.

human.summary: A slow or strongly winding jet stream can help weather patterns remain in place. Other atmospheric conditions still determine whether a long-lasting block develops. A long-lasting high-pressure pattern can divert storms and keep rain away from the same region. Dry conditions can then continue for longer.

planet.summary: A slow or strongly winding jet stream can help weather patterns remain in place. Other atmospheric conditions still determine whether a long-lasting block develops.

response.defaultDriver: Pressure differences between the Arctic and farther south can shift high-altitude winds and storm routes. This influences variability without making every future wind change predictable.
levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

glacier calving events.name: Glacier Calving Events
glacier calving events.description: Chunks of ice breaking away from the edge of a glacier into a lake or the sea. This forms icebergs and removes ice from the glacier. Large events can also disturb nearby water and create local hazards.
incoming: Warm water reaching a glacier's ocean-facing edge can melt and undercut it. The weakened front may crack and release icebergs.
Warmer air creates more meltwater on ice surfaces. Water entering cracks can deepen them and destabilise ice that is already vulnerable.
When a glacier's grounded edge retreats into deeper water, it can lose support from the seabed. A taller, less stable ice front may then become more prone to cracking and iceberg release.
outgoing: At some glacier lakes, breaking ice can create waves or remove support from nearby loose rock and ice. Waves or slope failures can damage the natural barrier holding the lake, allowing water to escape suddenly.
Breaking ice and falling icebergs can disturb sediment near a glacier front. Underwater slides and cloudy currents may move material that had already settled.
Ice moving from land into the ocean adds water mass and raises sea level. The loss of already-floating ice matters mainly when it lets ice on land flow faster.

human.summary: At some glacier lakes, breaking ice can create waves or remove support from nearby loose rock and ice. Waves or slope failures can damage the natural barrier holding the lake, allowing water to escape suddenly. A sudden glacier-lake flood can send fast, powerful flows past bridges. These can wash away the material supporting their foundations.
consequences: Ice moving from land into the ocean adds water mass and raises sea level. The loss of already-floating ice matters mainly when it lets ice on land flow faster. Higher seawater levels can push salt into the shallow freshwater reserve beneath a small island. The usable layer may become thinner or saltier, depending on local conditions.

planet.summary: At some glacier lakes, breaking ice can create waves or remove support from nearby loose rock and ice. Waves or slope failures can damage the natural barrier holding the lake, allowing water to escape suddenly.
consequences: Breaking ice and falling icebergs can disturb sediment near a glacier front. Underwater slides and cloudy currents may move material that had already settled.

wildfire smoke hospitalization burden.name: Wildfire Smoke Hospitalization Burden
wildfire smoke hospitalization burden.description: Hospital admissions linked to breathing pollution from vegetation fires. These admissions reflect serious health effects and add to demand for care. They are one part of the total harm caused by polluted air.
incoming: Fine particles in wildfire smoke can worsen heart and lung illness and increase hospital visits. Actual admissions depend on exposure and the population affected, not just the presence of smoke.
Longer or repeated smoke exposure gives more time for harmful effects on the heart and lungs. Hospital admissions still need to be measured rather than assumed from the smoke alone.
More severe or frequent fires can expose nearby or downwind populations to more smoke. Hospital use may rise where that exposure worsens illness.
outgoing: Hospital admissions attributed to wildfire smoke are one measured part of the health effects of polluted air. They do not include every symptom, illness or effect outside hospital care.

human.summary: Hospital admissions attributed to wildfire smoke are one measured part of the health effects of polluted air. They do not include every symptom, illness or effect outside hospital care.
