cooling equity gaps.name: Cooling Equity Gaps
cooling equity gaps.description: Some people having much less access than others to shade, safe indoor temperatures and affordable ways to cool down. Poor housing, high electricity costs or unreliable power can contribute. The same hot day can therefore create very different risks for different households.
incoming: Unreliable power and poorly protected buildings can leave people without safe indoor temperatures. Those unable to afford better housing or backup options face greater exposure, although cost barriers can exist even with reliable power.
Dangerous hot and humid conditions increase the need for effective cooling. People who cannot afford or reach safe indoor spaces face a wider protection gap.
High energy costs can stop households from buying or running enough cooling. Having an electricity connection or an air conditioner does not ensure that using it is affordable.
An electricity shutoff stops powered cooling when people may need it most. Households with health conditions can be especially vulnerable during dangerous heat.
Too little investment can delay cooler housing, shaded spaces and public cooling facilities. Communities already receiving fewer services may remain less protected.
outgoing: People unable to keep indoor temperatures safe face greater heat illness risks. Older people, those with existing illness and households with limited resources may be especially exposed.

human.summary: People unable to keep indoor temperatures safe face greater heat illness risks. Older people, those with existing illness and households with limited resources may be especially exposed.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

levers: Include affected communities in decisions about protection, services and recovery.

kelp forest collapse.name: Kelp Forest Collapse
kelp forest collapse.description: Underwater stands of large seaweed losing so much cover and new growth that they cannot recover normally. These habitats provide food and shelter for many animals. Their loss can change coastal wildlife and fisheries.
incoming: Long periods of unusually warm sea water can harm kelp and reduce supplies of cool, nutrient-rich water. Brief events do not always cause lasting loss, and some forests recover when other pressures are limited.
Some warm Pacific events bring both warmer coastal water and powerful waves that damage kelp. Effects vary greatly by location, and nearby forests can respond differently to the same event.
Sewage pollution can harm kelp growth and reproduction where contaminated water reaches the habitat. Lasting loss requires evidence of the exposure, its duration and the plants' response.
outgoing: Losing kelp removes food and complex shelter used by many marine animals. The food web may change, but temporary loss can recover before lasting changes occur.

human.summary: Losing kelp removes food and complex shelter used by many marine animals. The food web may change, but temporary loss can recover before lasting changes occur. Changes in feeding relationships can alter which fish are available and when. Fishing businesses may receive a less predictable mix or quantity of seafood.

trophic cascade disruption.name: Trophic Cascade Disruption
trophic cascade disruption.description: A major change in one part of a food chain spreading to other parts. For example, losing a predator can change the animals it eats and then the organisms those animals feed on. The effects depend on the local feeding relationships.
incoming: Losing large numbers of harvested predators or other consumers can change the species they eat and those below them. A chain reaction needs evidence at several levels, not just one declining species.
An introduced predator or competitor can change who eats what in a food web. These changes may spread through several connected groups of organisms.
Broken reef habitat can remove shelter and feeding areas. This changes how predators and prey encounter each other and may affect the wider food web.
outgoing: Persistent losses or imbalances between predators and prey can remove feeding relationships. The remaining community may have fewer species able to perform similar roles.

human.summary: Persistent losses or imbalances between predators and prey can remove feeding relationships. The remaining community may have fewer species able to perform similar roles. Changes in feeding relationships can alter which fish are available and when. Fishing businesses may receive a less predictable mix or quantity of seafood.

planet.summary: Persistent losses or imbalances between predators and prey can remove feeding relationships. The remaining community may have fewer species able to perform similar roles.

response.defaultDriver: Losing large numbers of harvested predators or other consumers can change the species they eat and those below them. A chain reaction needs evidence at several levels, not just one declining species.

groundwater recharge decline.name: Groundwater Recharge Decline
groundwater recharge decline.description: Less water reaching underground stores to replace what has been removed or naturally drained away. Rainfall, land cover and soil conditions affect this refill. A sustained reduction can make wells and other dependent water supplies less reliable.
incoming: Long dry periods leave less water to move through soil and replenish underground stores. The response can be delayed, and falling groundwater may also reflect extra pumping rather than reduced replenishment alone.
Paved surfaces and drains can send rainwater to rivers before it soaks underground. Local leaks, storage basins and designs that let water soak in can offset or reverse that effect.

Removing forests changes roots, soil and water use. It can reduce groundwater replenishment where runoff increases, but can increase it where trees previously used much of the water. Local evidence is needed.
outgoing: Less water replenishing underground stores can reduce dependable supplies and increase saltwater intrusion near coasts. Large reserves or lower pumping can protect users from short-term shortages.

human.summary: Less water replenishing underground stores can reduce dependable supplies and increase saltwater intrusion near coasts. Large reserves or lower pumping can protect users from short-term shortages.

Reduce pollution and improve storage, drainage or treatment where local evidence shows these are the relevant problems.

supply chain port bottlenecks.name: Supply Chain Port Bottlenecks
supply chain port bottlenecks.description: Goods getting held up because a harbour cannot move ships or cargo through quickly enough. Limits may involve workers, storage, equipment or onward transport. Delays can spread to businesses and consumers far from the port.
incoming: Delays and detours at sea can make ships arrive together or disrupt planned schedules. Ports may then struggle to unload, store and move the accumulated cargo.
Dangerous heat can slow outdoor work and affect port equipment. Ships and goods may then wait longer to be handled.
Damage to a bridge foundation can close roads used to carry goods to and from a port. This can add delays even when the port itself is working.
Blocked or unsafe sea routes can force ships to change course. Delayed ships may arrive together at alternative ports, creating queues and slowing deliveries.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Slow or closed ports can delay goods, reduce working hours and raise delivery costs. The impact depends on stored supplies, alternative routes and how long the disruption lasts.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

levers: Maintain transport assets and plan alternative routes for the hazards they actually face.

coastal property insurance nonrenewal.name: Coastal Property Insurance Nonrenewal
coastal property insurance nonrenewal.description: Insurers declining to renew or offer cover for homes and buildings exposed to hazards near the sea. Repeated flood losses or rising expected costs can contribute. Losing cover can also complicate home loans and property sales.
incoming: As insurers reduce cover in hazardous areas, coastal households may face higher prices or policies that are not renewed. The effect varies with local losses and insurance arrangements.
Repeated flooding by seawater can increase expected insurance losses. Insurers may raise prices, limit coverage or stop offering policies in exposed areas.
outgoing: Losing affordable property insurance can make it harder to obtain or renew a home loan. It can also affect property values and the finances of borrowers and lenders.

human.summary: Losing affordable property insurance can make it harder to obtain or renew a home loan. It can also affect property values and the finances of borrowers and lenders.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

response.defaultDriver: Long-lived buildings and mortgages face hazards that can change faster than annually renewed insurance terms.
levers: Disclose long-term flood and coverage risks clearly in property decisions.
Plan fair protection or voluntary moves where appropriate, including support for people with few financial options.

cloud radiative effect change.name: Cloud Radiative Effect Change
cloud radiative effect change.description: Clouds changing how much sunlight Earth reflects and how much heat it keeps. These effects can oppose one another. Whether the overall change warms or cools the planet depends on the cloud type, height, location and amount.
incoming: Fewer low clouds over the sea can mean less sunlight reflected back to space. Their contribution to cooling then weakens in affected regions.
Changes in airborne particles can change cloud droplets, brightness and lifetime. This affects reflected sunlight where the particle-cloud connection is established.
Some aircraft trails spread into thin ice clouds, changing reflected sunlight and escaping heat. Most disappear quickly, and their warming and cooling effects can partly offset each other.
outgoing: Cloud changes affect both sunlight reflected away and heat kept near Earth. The combined effect can warm or cool the planet, so the direction must be checked rather than assumed.

human.summary: Cloud changes affect both sunlight reflected away and heat kept near Earth. The combined effect can warm or cool the planet, so the direction must be checked rather than assumed. Hotter air can make aircraft takeoff more difficult and put extra strain on runways and ground operations. The effects depend on the aircraft, airport and conditions.

planet.summary: Cloud changes affect both sunlight reflected away and heat kept near Earth. The combined effect can warm or cool the planet, so the direction must be checked rather than assumed.

response.defaultDriver: Fewer low clouds over the sea can mean less sunlight reflected back to space. Their contribution to cooling then weakens in affected regions.
levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

deep-sea mining sediment plumes.name: Deep-Sea Mining Sediment Plumes
deep-sea mining sediment plumes.description: Clouds of fine seabed material stirred into the water by mineral extraction or waste disposal. The particles can settle on animals and habitats or affect feeding. The area and duration of exposure depend on currents and the operation.
incoming: Collecting material from the seabed and releasing processing water can stir up fine particles. These form cloudy plumes near the bottom or within the water above it.
outgoing: Particles from seabed mining can settle over habitats or interfere with feeding. Effects depend on the organisms and the area reached by the plume.
Mining plumes can carry metal-containing particles or dissolved metals to deep-water organisms. This creates a possible exposure route near the affected area.

human.summary: Sediment clouds from seabed mining can affect marine habitats whose links to human benefits are still being studied. The evidence here does not establish a measured direct health or livelihood loss for nearby people.

planet.summary: Particles from seabed mining can settle over habitats or interfere with feeding. Effects depend on the organisms and the area reached by the plume.
consequences: Mining plumes can carry metal-containing particles or dissolved metals to deep-water organisms. This creates a possible exposure route near the affected area.

response.defaultDriver: Collecting material from the seabed and releasing processing water can stir up fine particles. These form cloudy plumes near the bottom or within the water above it.
levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

pesticide residues in surface water.name: Pesticide Residues in Surface Water
pesticide residues in surface water.description: Chemicals used to control pests, or the substances they break down into, remaining in rivers and lakes. They can affect fish, plants and other water-living organisms. Effects depend on the chemical, concentration and length of exposure.
incoming: Farm chemicals can reach streams through runoff, drains or water moving through soil. Whether they arrive depends on the chemical, weather and farm practices. Use on a field does not by itself prove water contamination.

Drifting farm chemicals can settle directly on water or on surfaces that later drain into it. A drift event does not prove contamination at a particular site, and detected residues may have other sources.
outgoing: Some farm chemicals can harm aquatic plants and animals when exposure is high enough or repeated. Detection alone does not prove harm, and crossing a screening threshold does not establish that a whole ecosystem has failed.
Persistent Pesticide Residues in Sediment and Biota

Some chemicals in water bind to sediment and enter animals through water or food. Many break down quickly or do not build up appreciably, while older contaminated sediment can remain a source after water levels fall.

human.summary: Farm chemicals reaching water can add treatment costs and limit uses of that water. Health effects depend on which substances are present and the amount people encounter.

planet.summary: Some farm chemicals can harm aquatic plants and animals when exposure is high enough or repeated. Detection alone does not prove harm, and crossing a screening threshold does not establish that a whole ecosystem has failed.

response.defaultDriver: Farm chemicals can reach streams through runoff, drains or water moving through soil. Whether they arrive depends on the chemical, weather and farm practices. Use on a field does not by itself prove water contamination.
levers: Use farming practices suited to the local soil, water and climate, with protection for workers and livestock.
Keep soils covered where appropriate, limit avoidable nutrient and chemical losses, and manage total water use rather than efficiency alone.

acid rain deposition.name: Acid Rain Deposition
acid rain deposition.description: Acid-forming pollution reaching land and water through rain, snow, gases or particles. It can change soil and water chemistry and affect living things. Local soils, water and pollutant sources determine how much damage occurs.
incoming: Sulfur dioxide reacts in the air to form sulfuric acid. It can then reach the ground in rain, snow or dry particles, sometimes far from its source.
Coal-burning releases sulfur dioxide, which can turn into acid and settle downwind. Emissions at a power station do not by themselves show how much reaches a particular place.
outgoing: More acidic conditions can make some metals easier to dissolve and move. Exposure may increase where those metals are already present in soil or water.
Acid entering poorly protected waters can harm sensitive species and release harmful aluminium from surrounding materials. Food webs can change where the water and soil cannot neutralise the acid.
Repeated acidic pollution can remove sensitive species from waters and nearby land. Effects are greater where soils and water have little ability to neutralise the acid.

Acidic pollution can wash useful nutrients from soil and make aluminium more available. This can weaken some trees against cold, pests and other stresses, rather than acting as a universal sole cause of forest loss.

human.summary: Pollutants returning to land in rain or other deposits can damage forests, waters and materials. Those changes can create repair costs or reduce resources people use.

planet.summary: More acidic conditions can make some metals easier to dissolve and move. Exposure may increase where those metals are already present in soil or water.
consequences: Acid entering poorly protected waters can harm sensitive species and release harmful aluminium from surrounding materials. Food webs can change where the water and soil cannot neutralise the acid.
Repeated acidic pollution can remove sensitive species from waters and nearby land. Effects are greater where soils and water have little ability to neutralise the acid.

response.defaultDriver: Sulfur dioxide reacts in the air to form sulfuric acid. It can then reach the ground in rain, snow or dry particles, sometimes far from its source.
levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

dryland degradation.name: Dryland Degradation
dryland degradation.description: Dry regions losing healthy soil, vegetation or their ability to support people and wildlife. This can happen through unsuitable land use, drought and other pressures. The result may be less reliable crop or livestock production. It does not simply mean sand dunes spreading.
incoming: Warming can increase drying and erosion pressures on dryland soil and plants. It does not prove lasting land damage on its own. Rain, management and several measures of land condition need to be considered.
Repeated drought can reduce plant cover and leave soil exposed to erosion. Healthy or restored land may recover when rain returns, so a dry period is not automatically permanent degradation.

Poorly suited farming can remove protective plants, erode soil, drain water reserves or leave salts behind. Well-managed crops, irrigation and restoration can instead maintain or improve dryland condition.
outgoing: Long-lasting damage to soil, vegetation and water supplies can make food production less reliable. Income, imports, technology and public support can protect households from some of the resulting losses.
Bare or damaged dryland can expose loose soil that strong winds lift into the air. Degraded land does not create a storm without suitable winds, and many dust sources are natural.
Damaged dryland can supply loose dust, but reaching snow also requires the right winds and route. Some dust sources are natural, so identifying the source needs evidence beyond nearby land damage.

human.summary: Long-lasting damage to soil, vegetation and water supplies can make food production less reliable. Income, imports, technology and public support can protect households from some of the resulting losses.
consequences: Bare or damaged dryland can expose loose soil that strong winds lift into the air. Degraded land does not create a storm without suitable winds, and many dust sources are natural. Windblown mineral particles can worsen air quality near their source and far downwind. Health effects depend on the particles and actual exposure. A visible dust plume alone does not establish illness.

Damaged dryland can supply loose dust, but reaching snow also requires the right winds and route. Some dust sources are natural, so identifying the source needs evidence beyond nearby land damage. Faster snowmelt can send stored water into streams over a shorter spring period. Earlier melting does not always mean damaging floods: reservoirs can slow the flow, and total runoff may fall as exposed land loses more water to the air.

planet.summary: Bare or damaged dryland can expose loose soil that strong winds lift into the air. Degraded land does not create a storm without suitable winds, and many dust sources are natural.
consequences: Damaged dryland can supply loose dust, but reaching snow also requires the right winds and route. Some dust sources are natural, so identifying the source needs evidence beyond nearby land damage.

response.defaultDriver: Warming can increase drying and erosion pressures on dryland soil and plants. It does not prove lasting land damage on its own. Rain, management and several measures of land condition need to be considered.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.

atmospheric ozone-depleting substance bu.name: Atmospheric Ozone-Depleting Substance Burden
atmospheric ozone-depleting substance bu.description: Long-lasting gases in the air that can release chemicals which destroy the protective ozone layer high above Earth. Many contain chlorine or bromine. Their effects can continue long after release because they remain in the atmosphere for years.
incoming: Older cooling equipment can leak CFCs or HCFCs that damage the ozone layer. This pathway excludes modern replacement gases that contain no ozone-damaging chlorine or bromine, and equipment counts alone do not measure leaks.

Controls on old ozone-damaging gases reduce new supply, while recovery and destruction prevent releases from existing equipment. Improvement is slow because stored gases can still leak and some remain in the air for many decades.
outgoing: Stratospheric Ozone Column Depletion and Recovery

High in the atmosphere, sunlight breaks down certain gases and releases chemicals containing chlorine or bromine that destroy ozone. Cold polar clouds can speed the process, but gas levels alone do not predict each season's ozone loss.

human.summary: Certain long-lived industrial gases can damage the upper-air layer that filters harmful sunlight. Human consequences arise through that loss of protection, rather than from this atmospheric measure alone.

planet.summary: High in the atmosphere, sunlight breaks down certain gases and releases chemicals containing chlorine or bromine that destroy ozone. Cold polar clouds can speed the process, but gas levels alone do not predict each season's ozone loss.

response.defaultDriver: Older cooling equipment can leak CFCs or HCFCs that damage the ozone layer. This pathway excludes modern replacement gases that contain no ozone-damaging chlorine or bromine, and equipment counts alone do not measure leaks.
levers: Controls on old ozone-damaging gases reduce new supply, while recovery and destruction prevent releases from existing equipment. Improvement is slow because stored gases can still leak and some remain in the air for many decades.

arctic amplification.name: Arctic Amplification
arctic amplification.description: The northern polar region warming faster than the planet as a whole. Losing reflective snow and ice is one of the processes involved. Faster warming changes frozen ground, sea ice and the conditions faced by northern communities and wildlife.
incoming: Less time covered by bright sea ice leaves darker water exposed to sunlight for longer. More absorbed energy contributes to faster warming in the Arctic.
Loss of reflective snow and ice, along with changes in clouds and heat movement, can speed Arctic warming. These interacting changes help explain why the region warms faster than the global average.
As reflective snow and ice disappear, the Arctic absorbs more sunlight. This is one of the processes that helps the region warm faster than the global average.
outgoing: Faster warming in the Arctic can bring earlier spring melting and later autumn freezing. Sea ice then remains for less of the year.
Rapid Arctic warming heats the ground and deepens the layer that thaws each summer. This can accelerate the loss of ground that used to remain frozen year-round.

Faster Arctic warming can reduce the temperature contrast with lower latitudes near the surface. This may favour some weaker or more winding jet-stream patterns in certain seasons, but it does not determine their behaviour.

human.summary: Rapid Arctic warming heats the ground and deepens the layer that thaws each summer. This can accelerate the loss of ground that used to remain frozen year-round. Thawing frozen ground can damage buildings, roads and essential services. People may need to move when repairs or continued protection become too difficult.
consequences: Faster warming in the Arctic can bring earlier spring melting and later autumn freezing. Sea ice then remains for less of the year. A longer ice-free season can allow vessels to use northern routes for more of the year. Moving ice, storms, ports, insurance and rules still determine whether traffic actually increases.

planet.summary: Faster warming in the Arctic can bring earlier spring melting and later autumn freezing. Sea ice then remains for less of the year.
consequences: Rapid Arctic warming heats the ground and deepens the layer that thaws each summer. This can accelerate the loss of ground that used to remain frozen year-round.

Faster Arctic warming can reduce the temperature contrast with lower latitudes near the surface. This may favour some weaker or more winding jet-stream patterns in certain seasons, but it does not determine their behaviour.

response.defaultDriver: Less time covered by bright sea ice leaves darker water exposed to sunlight for longer. More absorbed energy contributes to faster warming in the Arctic.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.

rainforest savannization.name: Rainforest Savannization
rainforest savannization.description: A moist, densely wooded landscape shifting toward a drier, more open one with fewer trees. Repeated drying, fire and forest loss can contribute. This changes the habitat, water cycle and carbon stored in the landscape.
incoming: Clearing and splitting tropical forests can reduce moisture recycling and increase fire exposure. Combined with climate change, this may favour a more open landscape, but the scale of change is uncertain and some damaged areas can regrow.

Heat increases plants' demand for water and can add to stress from drought, fire and land use. It may favour a more open tropical landscape, but temperature alone does not determine the outcome and the thresholds remain uncertain.
Repeated drought can kill trees, increase fire risk and favour plants adapted to drier conditions. A single drought does not prove a permanent change from forest to open vegetation.
outgoing: A lasting shift to more open vegetation removes conditions needed by many forest species. The new landscape may support other wildlife, so the loss concerns the original forest community rather than all biodiversity.

human.summary: A shift away from dense, moist forest can change the food, water and cultural resources available to forest communities. The outcome varies across regions and is not inevitable for every rainforest.

planet.summary: A lasting shift to more open vegetation removes conditions needed by many forest species. The new landscape may support other wildlife, so the loss concerns the original forest community rather than all biodiversity.

response.defaultDriver: Clearing and splitting tropical forests can reduce moisture recycling and increase fire exposure. Combined with climate change, this may favour a more open landscape, but the scale of change is uncertain and some damaged areas can regrow.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.

urban water rationing.name: Urban Water Rationing
urban water rationing.description: Limits on when or how much water homes and businesses may use during shortages. Restrictions can help conserve a scarce supply, but interruptions can also create hardship. Saving water successfully should not itself be treated as worsening danger.
incoming: Growing cities may use water faster than supplies and pipes can expand. Restrictions become more likely during shortages, but growth need not lead to rationing when efficiency, reuse and services keep pace.
When water supplies fall short of demand, utilities may limit use to protect essential needs. Restrictions are an operating decision, not an automatic result of a dry period.
High demand can use up the spare capacity in a city's water supply. Utilities may impose restrictions, especially during drought, depending on their operating choices.
Leaks and other physical losses reduce the water that reaches customers. When supply is tight, this can contribute to stronger restrictions on use.
Poor source-water quality can reduce how much a treatment plant can safely supply. Utilities may restrict use while dealing with the problem, but the decision depends on local conditions.
When reliable water supply cannot meet normal demand, utilities may ask or require people to use less. The restrictions depend on local operating decisions.
A long drought can reduce a city's source-water supply and lead to restrictions. Storage, transfers, leaks and conservation affect how much use must be limited.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Limits on water delivery can make washing, cooking and business operations harder. Households with little storage or money for other supplies may face greater difficulty.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

response.defaultDriver: Growing cities may use water faster than supplies and pipes can expand. Restrictions become more likely during shortages, but growth need not lead to rationing when efficiency, reuse and services keep pace.
levers: Include affected communities in decisions about protection, services and recovery.
Fund practical support and monitor who can actually access it, especially where people have few alternatives.

asphalt surface heat storage.name: Asphalt Surface Heat Storage
asphalt surface heat storage.description: Dark road and pavement surfaces absorbing sunlight and storing heat. They can release that heat after the sun goes down. Large paved areas can therefore help keep neighbourhoods warm into the night.
incoming: Outward housing growth often adds roads and other paved areas. Dark pavement absorbs sunlight and stores heat that is later released into the surroundings.
Car-oriented development often needs large areas of roads and parking. Dark paved surfaces can store daytime heat, although shade, reflective materials and compact design can reduce this effect.
outgoing: Dark asphalt absorbs sunlight during the day and releases stored heat later. Large paved areas can keep nearby places warmer after sunset.

human.summary: Dark asphalt absorbs sunlight during the day and releases stored heat later. Large paved areas can keep nearby places warmer after sunset. Extra daytime and nighttime heat in cities increases people's exposure to high temperatures. This can add to illness risks, especially where cooling is limited.

heat-attributable excess mortality.name: Heat-Attributable Excess Mortality
heat-attributable excess mortality.description: Additional deaths attributed to unusually hot conditions, compared with what would have been expected otherwise. Estimating this requires a defined comparison and evidence linking heat to the deaths. It is not simply the total number of deaths during a hot period.
incoming: High humidity makes it harder for sweat to evaporate and cool the body. During extreme heat, this can increase illness and deaths attributed to hot conditions.

A study of Chinese communities linked sustained hot days and nights with a larger increase in deaths than hot nights alone. The size of the effect is specific to the studied places and methods, with uncertainty in the estimates.

Studies link hot nights with increased risk of death, but estimates differ and can be uncertain. In the cited Chinese study, the uncertainty range for nighttime-only heat also allowed for no increase.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Very hot periods can increase deaths, particularly where people lack protection or have existing health problems. The estimate compares observed outcomes with a modelled expectation. It does not identify a cause for every individual death.

ambient air-quality standard exceedance.name: Ambient Air-Quality Standard Exceedance
ambient air-quality standard exceedance.description: Outdoor pollution exceeding a stated guideline or legal limit. The comparison must identify the pollutant and the period over which it is measured. Different standards serve different purposes, and exceeding one does not describe every aspect of air quality.
incoming: Fuel-burning plants used during busy hours can release pollutants near surrounding communities. The amount depends on the fuel and pollution controls.
Keeping diesel trucks in service means people near roads continue to breathe their exhaust. Replacing them with electric trucks can reduce this local source of air pollution.
Replacing local fuel-burning power stations with cleaner electricity can reduce nearby air pollution. The improvement depends on which plants reduce output or close.
Closing coal-fired power stations removes a source of smoke and other harmful air pollutants. Cleaner replacement power helps preserve that improvement.
Finding and repairing gas leaks may also reduce harmful pollutants released alongside methane. Local air-quality benefits depend on what the leaking gas contains.
Cleaner buses and trains can reduce local air pollution when they replace traffic that burns fuel. The benefit depends on the vehicles used and the car journeys avoided.
More walking and cycling can reduce road exhaust when vehicle journeys fall. A connected network matters because isolated routes may change little traffic overall.
Electric vehicles remove exhaust emissions from the vehicles they replace. Pollution from tyres, brakes and electricity or material production still needs attention.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: People spending time in polluted air face increased health risks. Measurements need to retain the pollutant and exposure period because different substances affect people differently.

planet.summary: Different air pollutants can affect plants, soil, water or climate in different ways. A general exposure statistic must retain the pollutant and location to support an environmental claim.

response.defaultDriver: Fuel-burning plants used during busy hours can release pollutants near surrounding communities. The amount depends on the fuel and pollution controls.
levers: Replacing local fuel-burning power stations with cleaner electricity can reduce nearby air pollution. The improvement depends on which plants reduce output or close.
Closing coal-fired power stations removes a source of smoke and other harmful air pollutants. Cleaner replacement power helps preserve that improvement.

population genetic bottlenecks.name: Population Genetic Bottlenecks
population genetic bottlenecks.description: A population shrinking so sharply that it loses some of its inherited variety. With fewer breeding individuals, close relatives may breed more often. This can reduce the population's ability to cope with disease or changing conditions.
incoming: Splitting habitat into smaller pieces can leave fewer animals or plants breeding in each area. With less movement between groups, inherited variety may decline over generations.
Losing usable routes between habitats can reduce breeding between separated groups. Small, isolated populations can then lose genetic variety more easily.
Small or shrinking habitat patches may support fewer breeding individuals. Genetic variety can fall if too few newcomers join the population.
outgoing: Less inherited variety and more breeding between close relatives can reduce a population's ability to adjust to change. Some affected populations may become less likely to persist.

human.summary: Less variety within a population can reduce its ability to cope with new conditions. Human effects depend on whether people rely on the affected species. The genetic measure is not a direct count of human harm.

planet.summary: Less inherited variety and more breeding between close relatives can reduce a population's ability to adjust to change. Some affected populations may become less likely to persist.

palm oil-driven forest clearance.name: Palm Oil-Driven Forest Clearance
palm oil-driven forest clearance.description: Forests being permanently cleared to make room for oil-palm plantations. The loss removes habitat and stored carbon. This explanation applies where evidence links the clearing to that crop, rather than assuming every nearby forest loss has the same cause.
incoming: Demand for palm-containing products can encourage more production. Forest loss occurs only when the extra supply comes from clearing forest, rather than higher yields or land that was already cleared. This differs greatly between regions.
Establishing an oil-palm plantation can remove forest if it expands onto forested land. A plantation's presence alone does not prove recent clearing. Earlier land cover and timing need to be checked.

Road-fuel demand can add pressure for palm-oil production where fuel contains palm-based biodiesel. Forest impacts depend on where extra supply comes from, yields and land protection. The link does not apply where palm oil is not used in transport fuel.
outgoing: Replacing an existing forest with an oil-palm plantation is one form of permanent forest clearance. Evidence must establish that sequence. Nearby plantations alone do not prove why a forest was lost.

Replacing tropical forest with oil palms removes and separates habitats used by forest species. Keeping forest patches and improving plantation management can help, but does not recreate the original forest community.

human.summary: Replacing an existing forest with an oil-palm plantation is one form of permanent forest clearance. Evidence must establish that sequence. Nearby plantations alone do not prove why a forest was lost. Clearing forests changes shade, standing water, wildlife and contact between people and insects. In some tropical settings, these changes favour mosquitoes that carry disease, but the effect is not universal.

planet.summary: Replacing an existing forest with an oil-palm plantation is one form of permanent forest clearance. Evidence must establish that sequence. Nearby plantations alone do not prove why a forest was lost.
consequences: Replacing tropical forest with oil palms removes and separates habitats used by forest species. Keeping forest patches and improving plantation management can help, but does not recreate the original forest community.

response.defaultDriver: Demand for palm-containing products can encourage more production. Forest loss occurs only when the extra supply comes from clearing forest, rather than higher yields or land that was already cleared. This differs greatly between regions.
levers: Use farming practices suited to the local soil, water and climate, with protection for workers and livestock.
Keep soils covered where appropriate, limit avoidable nutrient and chemical losses, and manage total water use rather than efficiency alone.

transboundary fisheries conflict.name: Transboundary Fisheries Conflict
transboundary fisheries conflict.description: Disagreements between countries or fishing fleets over fish that move across political boundaries. Shifting stocks or catches can strain existing access agreements. Whether a dispute becomes more serious depends on cooperation, enforcement and alternatives.
incoming: Fish moving across borders can change which fleets can reach them and challenge existing catch agreements. Shared surveys and flexible agreements can manage the change without conflict.

Fewer accessible fish can increase competition over catches and income where access is contested. Scarcity does not inevitably cause conflict. Good agreements and recovery plans can reduce the pressure.
Communities heavily dependent on fish face higher costs when access is lost. This can make catch-sharing changes difficult, but dependence can also encourage cooperation rather than conflict.
outgoing: Repeated confrontations or failed fishing agreements can worsen political tensions. Most disputes remain within negotiation, and existing tensions may cause fishing incidents rather than result from them.

human.summary: Repeated confrontations or failed fishing agreements can worsen political tensions. Most disputes remain within negotiation, and existing tensions may cause fishing incidents rather than result from them.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

response.defaultDriver: Fish moving across borders can change which fleets can reach them and challenge existing catch agreements. Shared surveys and flexible agreements can manage the change without conflict.
levers: Include affected communities in decisions about protection, services and recovery.
Fund practical support and monitor who can actually access it, especially where people have few alternatives.

stratospheric cooling.name: Stratospheric Cooling
stratospheric cooling.description: Temperatures falling in the layer of air above most clouds and ordinary weather. Changes in heat-trapping gases and ozone can affect this layer differently from the surface. Cooling high above Earth can occur while the surface warms.
incoming: Alternating wind directions high above the equator are linked with temperature changes in that atmospheric layer. This describes recurring variability, not a claim that the pattern causes long-term cooling.
Stratospheric Ozone Column Depletion and Recovery
Ozone absorbs energy and warms the upper atmosphere. Losing it can cool the affected layer, although carbon dioxide also causes cooling there and cold conditions can themselves encourage ozone loss.
outgoing: Cooling high above Antarctica can strengthen the winds circling the pole. This can also shift the belt of west-to-east winds closer to Earth's surface.

human.summary: Cooling high above Antarctica can strengthen the winds circling the pole. This can also shift the belt of west-to-east winds closer to Earth's surface. The southern belt of strong westerly winds shifting north or south changes storm routes and rainfall. Regional effects depend on the phase and season.

planet.summary: Cooling high above Antarctica can strengthen the winds circling the pole. This can also shift the belt of west-to-east winds closer to Earth's surface.

response.defaultDriver: Alternating wind directions high above the equator are linked with temperature changes in that atmospheric layer. This describes recurring variability, not a claim that the pattern causes long-term cooling.
levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

measurement.geography: declared station, reanalysis grid, climate region, or global domain

inland waterway fuel spills.name: Inland Waterway Fuel Spills
inland waterway fuel spills.description: Oil-based fuel accidentally entering rivers, canals or lakes. Damaged vessels, refuelling accidents or broken tanks can cause releases. Effects depend on the amount spilled, how it spreads and which habitats or water users are exposed.
incoming: Collisions, running aground and fuel transfers can damage a vessel or its fuel lines. Spilled fuel can then enter a river, canal or nearby shore.
Failure of a fuel tank, pipe, hose or protective barrier can allow fuel to reach nearby water. The risk depends on the damaged equipment and its connection to the waterway.
Floods can expose or damage fuel pipes and overwhelm barriers around storage. High flows can also carry an existing spill into a river more quickly.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Spilled fuel can make water unsafe or unusable for a time and disrupt fishing and recreation. The effects depend on the fuel, amount, water flow and cleanup.

planet.summary: Fuel in rivers can harm aquatic organisms and contaminate banks. Effects depend on fuel type, quantity, flow, spread and cleanup.

response.defaultDriver: Collisions, running aground and fuel transfers can damage a vessel or its fuel lines. Spilled fuel can then enter a river, canal or nearby shore.
levers: Maintain transport assets and plan alternative routes for the hazards they actually face.
Use efficient and lower-emissions travel options where practical, with reliable public transport and cleaner power.

measurement.geography: named inland waterway or adjoining shoreline
measurement.cadence: incident to annual

coral reef fragmentation.name: Coral Reef Fragmentation
coral reef fragmentation.description: Connected coral habitat being broken into smaller, separated pieces. Damage can remove shelter and make it harder for organisms to move between suitable areas. The consequences depend on whether growth and recovery can keep pace with the loss.
incoming: Repeated damage can weaken the solid structure built by corals. As that structure breaks down, reef habitat can become smaller, separated and less stable.
Powerful cyclone waves and currents can break or overturn corals and move reef rubble. Damage depends on the storm's path and the reef exposed to it.
Repeated severe heat stress can kill or weaken corals. Their remaining structures may then break or erode more easily during later disturbances.
Changes in seawater chemistry can slow reef building and increase erosion. Weaker structures can become more vulnerable when waves or other disturbances strike.
Ships running aground or dropping anchors can crush, break or bury corals. The damage is concentrated around the incident and any removal work.
outgoing: Repeated breakage can remove the connected, three-dimensional structure of a reef. If growth and repair cannot keep up, habitat complexity and resistance to waves decline.
Broken reef habitat can remove shelter and feeding areas. This changes how predators and prey encounter each other and may affect the wider food web.

human.summary: Repeated breakage can remove the connected, three-dimensional structure of a reef. If growth and repair cannot keep up, habitat complexity and resistance to waves decline. Losing reef structure removes shelter, feeding areas and places for young fish to grow. Fisheries depending on those habitats can become less able to sustain catches.
consequences: Broken reef habitat can remove shelter and feeding areas. This changes how predators and prey encounter each other and may affect the wider food web. Persistent losses or imbalances between predators and prey can remove feeding relationships. The remaining community may have fewer species able to perform similar roles.

planet.summary: Repeated breakage can remove the connected, three-dimensional structure of a reef. If growth and repair cannot keep up, habitat complexity and resistance to waves decline.
consequences: Broken reef habitat can remove shelter and feeding areas. This changes how predators and prey encounter each other and may affect the wider food web.

response.defaultDriver: Repeated damage can weaken the solid structure built by corals. As that structure breaks down, reef habitat can become smaller, separated and less stable.
levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

measurement.geography: named reef tract, incident perimeter, survey transect, or restoration site
measurement.cadence: event-based and annual repeat survey

mountain pass avalanches.name: Mountain Pass Avalanches
mountain pass avalanches.description: Masses of snow or ice moving quickly downhill through mountain routes. They can bury roads, railways or power and communication lines. People and services are at risk where these routes cross the path of a slide.
incoming: Warming changes how mountain snow builds up and how often rain or meltwater enters it. These changes can alter snow stability and the timing of avalanches near mountain routes.
Rain adds weight and liquid water to existing snow and can weaken its layers. On steep slopes, this may trigger a slide of wet snow.
Earlier or faster melting adds water inside mountain snow. Slopes may become unstable when wet layers lose their strength.
outgoing: Avalanches can bury or damage roads, railways, power lines and communications equipment. Repeated closures are especially disruptive where few alternative mountain routes exist.

human.summary: Avalanches can bury or damage roads, railways, power lines and communications equipment. Repeated closures are especially disruptive where few alternative mountain routes exist.

planet.summary: Moving snow can disturb vegetation and slopes, but avalanches are also natural mountain processes. Road closures alone do not measure ecosystem damage.

response.defaultDriver: Warming changes how mountain snow builds up and how often rain or meltwater enters it. These changes can alter snow stability and the timing of avalanches near mountain routes.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.

dust storm frequency.name: Dust Storm Frequency
dust storm frequency.description: How often wind lifts enough loose soil or sand to create a major cloud of dust. Dry ground, exposed soil and strong winds influence these events. Airborne particles can reduce visibility and affect health far from their source.
incoming: Bare or damaged dryland can expose loose soil that strong winds lift into the air. Degraded land does not create a storm without suitable winds, and many dust sources are natural.
Drought can dry the surface and reduce plant cover, leaving more material available for wind to lift. Strong winds and loose sediment are still needed, and protective soil crusts can limit dust.
Disturbing dry soil and removing cover can make farmland more vulnerable to wind erosion. Keeping plants, windbreaks and suitable grazing or ploughing practices can instead reduce dust losses.
outgoing: Windblown mineral particles can worsen air quality near their source and far downwind. Health effects depend on the particles and actual exposure. A visible dust plume alone does not establish illness.

Dust storms can carry mineral particles to mountain snow, where they settle in layers. A storm elsewhere does not prove deposition at a particular site, and buried dust may not reach the surface until later melting.

human.summary: Windblown mineral particles can worsen air quality near their source and far downwind. Health effects depend on the particles and actual exposure. A visible dust plume alone does not establish illness.
consequences: Dust storms can carry mineral particles to mountain snow, where they settle in layers. A storm elsewhere does not prove deposition at a particular site, and buried dust may not reach the surface until later melting. Faster snowmelt can send stored water into streams over a shorter spring period. Earlier melting does not always mean damaging floods: reservoirs can slow the flow, and total runoff may fall as exposed land loses more water to the air.

planet.summary: Dust storms can carry mineral particles to mountain snow, where they settle in layers. A storm elsewhere does not prove deposition at a particular site, and buried dust may not reach the surface until later melting.

levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.

ice shelf grounding line retreat.name: Ice Shelf Grounding Line Retreat
ice shelf grounding line retreat.description: The point where a large body of ice leaves the ground and begins floating moving farther inland. Losing contact with the bed can change the resistance to ice flow. In some settings this allows more land ice to move toward the sea.
incoming: Warmer air and ocean water can thin Antarctic glaciers near the coast. The point where ice lifts off the ground and starts floating may move inland.
Warm water beneath floating ice can melt and thin it near the coast. Where the land shape allows, the boundary between grounded and floating ice can retreat inland.
Changing ocean currents can bring more warm water beneath floating ice shelves. Extra melting can reduce support and encourage inland retreat where the shape of the seabed makes the ice vulnerable.
outgoing: When more coastal ice loses contact with the ground, there may be less resistance to glacier movement. Faster movement of land ice into the ocean raises sea level.
When a glacier's grounded edge retreats into deeper water, it can lose support from the seabed. A taller, less stable ice front may then become more prone to cracking and iceberg release.

human.summary: When more coastal ice loses contact with the ground, there may be less resistance to glacier movement. Faster movement of land ice into the ocean raises sea level. Higher seawater levels can push salt into the shallow freshwater reserve beneath a small island. The usable layer may become thinner or saltier, depending on local conditions.
consequences: When a glacier's grounded edge retreats into deeper water, it can lose support from the seabed. A taller, less stable ice front may then become more prone to cracking and iceberg release. At some glacier lakes, breaking ice can create waves or remove support from nearby loose rock and ice. Waves or slope failures can damage the natural barrier holding the lake, allowing water to escape suddenly.

planet.summary: When more coastal ice loses contact with the ground, there may be less resistance to glacier movement. Faster movement of land ice into the ocean raises sea level.
consequences: When a glacier's grounded edge retreats into deeper water, it can lose support from the seabed. A taller, less stable ice front may then become more prone to cracking and iceberg release.

response.defaultDriver: Warmer air and ocean water can thin Antarctic glaciers near the coast. The point where ice lifts off the ground and starts floating may move inland.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.

pollen allergen spikes.name: Pollen Allergen Spikes
pollen allergen spikes.description: Short periods with unusually high amounts of allergy-causing plant material in the air. People who are sensitive to it can develop symptoms or worsening asthma. Effects depend on the plant species, weather and individual sensitivity.
incoming: Warmer seasons and later autumn frost can let some plants release pollen for longer. The cited monitoring covers a limited network and measures season length, not every person's exposure or the total pollen produced.

Carbon dioxide building up in the air can increase pollen or allergen production in some plants. Responses vary by species and conditions. Nearby emissions do not directly establish nearby pollen levels.
outgoing: Pollen can irritate the nose and eyes or worsen asthma in people who are sensitive to it. Outdoor counts do not measure each person's exposure, and many exposed people have no symptoms.

human.summary: Pollen can irritate the nose and eyes or worsen asthma in people who are sensitive to it. Outdoor counts do not measure each person's exposure, and many exposed people have no symptoms.

planet.summary: The record concerns airborne material that can trigger allergies in people. Higher counts are not by themselves evidence that vegetation or pollinator health has improved or worsened.

response.defaultDriver: Warmer seasons and later autumn frost can let some plants release pollen for longer. The cited monitoring covers a limited network and measures season length, not every person's exposure or the total pollen produced.
levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

measurement.geography: named pollen-monitoring station and its stated representativeness area

estuary eutrophication.name: Estuary Eutrophication
estuary eutrophication.description: Too many nutrients entering the water where a river meets the sea. This can encourage excessive algae growth, reduce light and use up oxygen during decay. The resulting changes can harm seagrass, fish and other wildlife.
incoming: Nutrients washed from fields can travel through rivers into estuaries. They can feed extra algae growth and the oxygen-consuming decay that follows.
Untreated or partly treated sewage adds nutrients and organic material to receiving water. This can encourage growth and decay that use up oxygen.
Large runoff events can quickly carry nutrients from land into an estuary. The effect depends on nutrients being present in the upstream area.
outgoing: Excess nutrients encourage algae to grow in the water and on seagrass leaves. This can block the light that seagrass needs to survive.
Excess nutrients can encourage growth and decay that use oxygen and release carbon dioxide into coastal water. The resulting conditions can make shell formation harder for vulnerable animals.

human.summary: Excess nutrients can encourage growth and decay that use oxygen and release carbon dioxide into coastal water. The resulting conditions can make shell formation harder for vulnerable animals. When shellfish and shell-forming plankton grow less well or die, animals feeding on them may lose food. Habitats and food chains can change where these species play an important role.

planet.summary: Excess nutrients encourage algae to grow in the water and on seagrass leaves. This can block the light that seagrass needs to survive.
consequences: Excess nutrients can encourage growth and decay that use oxygen and release carbon dioxide into coastal water. The resulting conditions can make shell formation harder for vulnerable animals.

response.defaultDriver: Nutrients washed from fields can travel through rivers into estuaries. They can feed extra algae growth and the oxygen-consuming decay that follows.
levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

migratory bird timing, route, and stopov.name: Migratory Bird Timing, Route, and Stopover Disruption
migratory bird timing, route, and stopov.description: Birds travelling between seasonal homes at the wrong time, by altered routes or with fewer suitable stopping places. They may miss food or arrive too late to breed successfully. Repeated problems can reduce survival and population size.
incoming: Warmer seasons can change when food becomes available along bird migration routes. Some birds adjust successfully while others do not. An early arrival in one year does not prove a lasting mismatch.

Losing resting or seasonal habitats can force migrating birds to travel farther or leave them with less food. Some use alternative sites, so fewer birds at one stop does not by itself prove a failing route.
outgoing: Repeated difficulty finding food or suitable habitat during migration can reduce survival and breeding success. A changed route or date can also be a useful adjustment, so population effects need evidence across the birds' full yearly cycle.

human.summary: Changes in bird journeys can affect wildlife-related livelihoods and cultural activities. The evidence here does not establish a single direct health or income effect for all disrupted routes.

planet.summary: Repeated difficulty finding food or suitable habitat during migration can reduce survival and breeding success. A changed route or date can also be a useful adjustment, so population effects need evidence across the birds' full yearly cycle.

response.defaultDriver: Warmer seasons can change when food becomes available along bird migration routes. Some birds adjust successfully while others do not. An early arrival in one year does not prove a lasting mismatch.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.

shell calcification failures.name: Shell Calcification Failures
shell calcification failures.description: Animals having difficulty building or maintaining hard shells and skeletons. Water chemistry and other conditions can affect the materials and energy available for growth. Poor growth or survival can also affect animals that depend on them for food or habitat.
incoming: Changing seawater chemistry can make the materials for shells and coral skeletons less available. Some organisms then have more difficulty building or maintaining them, with large differences between species and conditions.
Unusually hot seawater can make it harder for young shellfish to grow and form shells. This may add to stress from changing water chemistry, with different limits for each species.
Excess nutrients can encourage growth and decay that use oxygen and release carbon dioxide into coastal water. The resulting conditions can make shell formation harder for vulnerable animals.
outgoing: When shellfish and shell-forming plankton grow less well or die, animals feeding on them may lose food. Habitats and food chains can change where these species play an important role.

human.summary: When shellfish and shell-forming plankton grow less well or die, animals feeding on them may lose food. Habitats and food chains can change where these species play an important role. Changes in feeding relationships can alter which fish are available and when. Fishing businesses may receive a less predictable mix or quantity of seafood.

planet.summary: When shellfish and shell-forming plankton grow less well or die, animals feeding on them may lose food. Habitats and food chains can change where these species play an important role.

levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.

arctic pack ice drift.name: Arctic Pack Ice Drift
arctic pack ice drift.description: Floating sea ice in the north being moved by winds and ocean currents. It can gather in some places and leave others open. Moving ice can obstruct vessel routes even when the region has less ice overall.
incoming: A shorter ice season can leave thinner and less connected Arctic sea ice. Winds and currents can move this ice more readily through areas used by ships.
Changing Arctic surface currents can carry sea ice in different directions or at different speeds. Ice may move into coastal areas or routes that ships planned to use.
Warming makes Arctic sea ice thinner and more broken up. This can change how readily winds and currents move it.
outgoing: Moving sea ice can enter planned ship routes and narrow safe passages. Ships may need to wait, change course or seek icebreaker support even when total ice cover is low.

human.summary: Moving sea ice can enter planned ship routes and narrow safe passages. Ships may need to wait, change course or seek icebreaker support even when total ice cover is low.

planet.summary: Moving sea ice changes where ice habitat and freshwater are carried. Local effects depend on drift direction, thickness and the wider ice conditions.

response.defaultDriver: A shorter ice season can leave thinner and less connected Arctic sea ice. Winds and currents can move this ice more readily through areas used by ships.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.

amphibian chytrid infection prevalence a.name: Amphibian Chytrid Infection Prevalence and Mortality
amphibian chytrid infection prevalence a.description: Fungal infection affecting the skin of frogs, salamanders and related animals. Severe infection can disrupt functions they need to survive and cause deaths. The impact varies between species, places and infection levels.
incoming: Temperature affects both amphibians and the fungus that infects their skin. Infection can be greatest at intermediate temperatures, so warming may increase suitability in cold places but reduce it in already hot places.
Introduced animals carrying the fungus can expose native amphibians as they move between waters. Finding both together does not prove transmission. Timing, movement or genetic evidence is needed.
outgoing: Severe fungal infection can damage amphibian skin function and cause death. Many infections do not cause visible disease, and some populations recover despite continued exposure. Deaths need a confirmed cause.

human.summary: Disease in amphibians can damage species that people value and the food webs they help support. This measure concerns wildlife disease. It does not show an outbreak of the same illness in humans.

planet.summary: Severe fungal infection can damage amphibian skin function and cause death. Many infections do not cause visible disease, and some populations recover despite continued exposure. Deaths need a confirmed cause.

early-warning coverage gap.name: Early-Warning Coverage Gap
early-warning coverage gap.description: People not getting a clear alert in time before danger arrives, or not having a way to act on it. Sensors may miss the danger, messages may not reach everyone, or people may lack help to leave. Having an alert system does not mean everyone is protected.
incoming: Better monitoring and accessible alerts can reach people who previously lacked useful warnings. People also need to trust the warning and have practical ways to act.
Funding shortages can leave gaps in hazard monitoring, useful alerts and preparation. People may receive less warning or have fewer ways to act on it.
Weak power and communication systems can interrupt warnings. Alerts may fail to reach the people who need them, especially in the final step to homes and communities.
outgoing: People who receive no useful warning have less chance to prepare or reach safety. The resulting losses can make recovery harder for groups already facing disadvantages.
Missing observations or alerts leave people with less time to prepare. These gaps show where better monitoring, communication and response plans are needed.

black carbon deposition.name: Black Carbon Deposition
black carbon deposition.description: Dark soot from burning fuel or vegetation settling out of the air onto surfaces. On snow and ice it can reduce the sunlight reflected away. This can increase absorbed heat and speed local melting.
incoming: More soot in the air provides more material that can settle onto snow and ice. Rain, snow and air movement affect where it is deposited.
Large or severe fires can release soot that travels downwind. Some may settle on snow and ice, depending on transport and weather conditions.
Ship engines can release soot when they burn fuel. Winds may carry some of it to snow and ice, especially in nearby regions.
outgoing: Dark soot settling on snow makes the surface reflect less sunlight. More energy is absorbed, which can increase melting where enough material accumulates.

human.summary: Soot on snow and ice can increase melting and change water or ice conditions people depend on. This deposit measure should not be treated as a direct measure of the particles people breathe.

planet.summary: Dark soot settling on snow makes the surface reflect less sunlight. More energy is absorbed, which can increase melting where enough material accumulates.

response.defaultDriver: More soot in the air provides more material that can settle onto snow and ice. Rain, snow and air movement affect where it is deposited.
levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.

glacial siltation streams.name: Glacial Siltation Streams
glacial siltation streams.description: Streams carrying large amounts of fine rock particles ground up by moving ice. The particles can cloud the water or settle downstream. Continued buildup may affect river habitats, reservoir capacity and water intakes.
incoming: Strong seasonal meltwater flows carry fine rock particles from glaciers. The amount and timing of sediment depend on the flow, rather than simply on whether a basin has passed its maximum glacier runoff.
Sudden releases of glacier water can sweep up sediment from beneath the ice and river banks. Short bursts may carry far more material than normal seasonal flows.
Heavy rain can wash recently exposed sediment and river-bank material into glacier-fed streams. It can add to the sediment already carried by meltwater.
outgoing: Sediment carried into a reservoir settles as the water slows. Continued build-up takes up storage space and can interfere with water intakes.

human.summary: Sediment carried into a reservoir settles as the water slows. Continued build-up takes up storage space and can interfere with water intakes. Unpredictable stored water makes it harder for dam operators to deliver the expected supply at the right time. Drinking water, flood control or electricity commitments may then be missed.

planet.summary: Sediment carried into a reservoir settles as the water slows. Continued build-up takes up storage space and can interfere with water intakes.

response.defaultDriver: Strong seasonal meltwater flows carry fine rock particles from glaciers. The amount and timing of sediment depend on the flow, rather than simply on whether a basin has passed its maximum glacier runoff.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.

jellyfish bloom frequency and biomass.name: Jellyfish Bloom Frequency and Biomass
jellyfish bloom frequency and biomass.description: Changes in how often very large gatherings of jellyfish occur and how much living material they contain. Dense gatherings can interfere with fishing nets and fish farms. Effects depend on the species and where the animals collect.
incoming: Nutrient-rich coastal water can increase food for some jellyfish and create conditions they tolerate well. The response depends on the species and local water conditions.
Some jellyfish tolerate low oxygen better than fish and other competitors. Oxygen-poor conditions may therefore shift the balance in their favour.
Piers, seawalls and other underwater structures can provide places for the attached life stage of some jellyfish. More suitable surfaces can support later releases of free-swimming animals.
outgoing: Dense jellyfish groups can clog fishing nets, harm catches or affect fish-farm enclosures. Local fishing operations may be interrupted while the event lasts.

human.summary: Dense jellyfish groups can clog fishing nets, harm catches or affect fish-farm enclosures. Local fishing operations may be interrupted while the event lasts.

planet.summary: Large gatherings can change local feeding interactions and competition for food. Species, currents and observation effort matter, so sightings do not prove a uniform global increase.

response.defaultDriver: Nutrient-rich coastal water can increase food for some jellyfish and create conditions they tolerate well. The response depends on the species and local water conditions.
levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

cryoconite hole expansion.name: Cryoconite Hole Expansion
cryoconite hole expansion.description: Small melt holes on glacier surfaces growing or becoming more numerous around dark dirt and microbes. The dark material absorbs sunlight more readily than clean ice. This can speed melting in the areas where it collects.
incoming: Dark sediment on glacier surfaces absorbs sunlight and encourages local melting. Warmer conditions can enlarge the small melt holes around these patches.
Soot settling on glacier ice darkens the surface and helps it absorb sunlight. Where dark particles collect, small melt holes can grow.
Soot on snow and ice reduces the sunlight reflected away. Dark particles gathering in small patches can encourage deeper local melting.
outgoing: Dark sediment and living material on snow or ice can reduce the sunlight reflected away. Exposed dark patches may then melt more quickly.

human.summary: Dark material and melt holes can change how an ice surface absorbs sunlight and drains water. A local increase alone does not establish a measured loss for nearby communities.

planet.summary: Dark sediment and living material on snow or ice can reduce the sunlight reflected away. Exposed dark patches may then melt more quickly.

response.defaultDriver: Dark sediment on glacier surfaces absorbs sunlight and encourages local melting. Warmer conditions can enlarge the small melt holes around these patches.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.

bark beetle epidemics.name: Bark Beetle Epidemics
bark beetle epidemics.description: Large outbreaks of insects that live and feed beneath tree bark. When attacks overwhelm tree defences, many trees can die. The scale of damage depends on the insects, host trees and surrounding conditions.
incoming: Warmer seasons can let some bark beetles develop faster and survive winter in greater numbers. Excessive heat or a lack of suitable trees can instead limit outbreaks.
Severe drought can weaken a tree's protective sap and other defences against beetles. The response varies: moderate dryness can hinder some beetles, and drought links are weak for some species.
Trees injured but not killed by fire may become suitable hosts for some beetles. Fire can also kill the insects or their hosts, so a burned area does not automatically predict an outbreak.
outgoing: Large bark-beetle populations can attack and kill host trees. The trees selected are not always simply the ones that were already most stressed.

Large beetle populations can overwhelm susceptible trees and disrupt their water and nutrient supply. Wide areas may die, but other stresses often contribute and delayed surveys can make the cause difficult to separate.

human.summary: Large beetle outbreaks can kill trees, affecting forest products, tourism and valued landscapes. The effects depend on the tree species, outbreak size and forest management.

planet.summary: Large bark-beetle populations can attack and kill host trees. The trees selected are not always simply the ones that were already most stressed.
consequences: Large beetle populations can overwhelm susceptible trees and disrupt their water and nutrient supply. Wide areas may die, but other stresses often contribute and delayed surveys can make the cause difficult to separate.

response.defaultDriver: Warmer seasons can let some bark beetles develop faster and survive winter in greater numbers. Excessive heat or a lack of suitable trees can instead limit outbreaks.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.
