old-growth forest logging.name: Old-Growth Forest Logging
old-growth forest logging.description: Cutting trees in forests that have developed over many decades or centuries. Removing large trees and adding access roads can change habitat and stored carbon. Even selective cutting can disturb nearby trees and break up continuous cover.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Logging and access roads can create gaps and edges in older forests. The amount of separation depends on how harvesting is done and must be assessed across the wider landscape.
Removing older trees can reduce nesting holes, dead wood and layered habitats used by specialised wildlife. Effects differ between forests, and some managed areas retain or regain important features.

Logging moves carbon from living trees into wood products and material that may decay. The overall emissions depend on regrowth, product lifespan and the time assessed. Harvested wood is not automatically equal to carbon released.

human.summary: Logging moves carbon from living trees into wood products and material that may decay. The overall emissions depend on regrowth, product lifespan and the time assessed. Harvested wood is not automatically equal to carbon released. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.

planet.summary: Logging and access roads can create gaps and edges in older forests. The amount of separation depends on how harvesting is done and must be assessed across the wider landscape.
consequences: Removing older trees can reduce nesting holes, dead wood and layered habitats used by specialised wildlife. Effects differ between forests, and some managed areas retain or regain important features.

Logging moves carbon from living trees into wood products and material that may decay. The overall emissions depend on regrowth, product lifespan and the time assessed. Harvested wood is not automatically equal to carbon released.

levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.

savanna tree-cover decline.name: Savanna Tree-Cover Decline
savanna tree-cover decline.description: Open grassland landscapes losing some of their trees and shrubs. These woody plants provide shade, food and nesting places. Their loss can change the mix of wildlife and how the landscape functions.
incoming: Repeated dry periods can make it harder for savanna trees to establish and survive. Effects are greater where rain and soil already limit growth.
Frequent or severe fire can kill young woody plants before they grow large enough to withstand burning. This can reduce tree cover over time.
Clearing land for crops or heavy livestock pressure can reduce trees in savannas. The link applies where those activities overlap the vegetation being measured.
outgoing: Lasting loss of savanna trees removes shade, food, nesting sites and shelter. Species that depend on that woody layer may decline.

human.summary: Fewer trees can change shade, fuelwood and other resources used by nearby communities. The consequences depend on the landscape. Open grassland is not automatically damaged habitat.

planet.summary: Lasting loss of savanna trees removes shade, food, nesting sites and shelter. Species that depend on that woody layer may decline.

response.defaultDriver: Repeated dry periods can make it harder for savanna trees to establish and survive. Effects are greater where rain and soil already limit growth.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.

particulate soot levels.name: Particulate Soot Levels
particulate soot levels.description: The amount of fine, dark material from burning fuel or vegetation present in the air. It contributes to particle pollution. Where it later settles on snow or ice, it can also darken the surface and increase melting.
incoming: Incomplete burning in wildfires releases soot and other dark fine particles. Larger or more frequent smoke events increase opportunities for elevated soot downwind, depending on transport.
outgoing: Soot in the air can be carried to snowy regions and settle on the surface. Winds and precipitation determine where it lands and how strongly it darkens the snow.
Soot settling on glacier ice darkens the surface and helps it absorb sunlight. Where dark particles collect, small melt holes can grow.
More soot in the air provides more material that can settle onto snow and ice. Rain, snow and air movement affect where it is deposited.

human.summary: Breathing soot-containing air can add to health risks from fine particles. Exposure, particle mixtures and time spent in polluted places affect the burden.

planet.summary: Soot in the air can be carried to snowy regions and settle on the surface. Winds and precipitation determine where it lands and how strongly it darkens the snow.
consequences: Soot settling on glacier ice darkens the surface and helps it absorb sunlight. Where dark particles collect, small melt holes can grow.
More soot in the air provides more material that can settle onto snow and ice. Rain, snow and air movement affect where it is deposited.

response.defaultDriver: Incomplete burning in wildfires releases soot and other dark fine particles. Larger or more frequent smoke events increase opportunities for elevated soot downwind, depending on transport.
levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

measurement.geography: declared monitoring site, airshed, waterbody, facility, region, or emissions inventory boundary
measurement.cadence: hourly or event-based with monthly and annual rollups

pesticide spray drift.name: Pesticide Spray Drift
pesticide spray drift.description: Pest-control chemicals travelling through the air beyond the place where they were applied. Droplets, dust or vapour can reach nearby people, plants and water. Harm depends on the chemical and the amount and route of exposure.
incoming: Spraying farm chemicals can send droplets or dust beyond the intended field, and some chemicals can move through the air later. Suitable weather, equipment and buffer areas can greatly reduce this movement.
outgoing: Drifting farm chemicals can reach workers, homes and schools through air or direct contact. Harm depends on the chemical and dose. Detecting drift alone does not establish a health effect.

Chemicals drifting off a field can reach flowers, water or nesting sites used by pollinating insects. Detecting them does not prove declining pollination. Effects depend on the product, species, amount and timing.

Drifting farm chemicals can settle directly on water or on surfaces that later drain into it. A drift event does not prove contamination at a particular site, and detected residues may have other sources.

Farm chemicals drifting beyond their target can reach bees directly or through contaminated food brought back to a colony. Colony harm depends on the chemical, dose and exposure, alongside other stresses.

human.summary: Drifting farm chemicals can reach workers, homes and schools through air or direct contact. Harm depends on the chemical and dose. Detecting drift alone does not establish a health effect.
consequences: Chemicals drifting off a field can reach flowers, water or nesting sites used by pollinating insects. Detecting them does not prove declining pollination. Effects depend on the product, species, amount and timing. Crops that need animals to transfer pollen may set less fruit or seed when that help declines. Harvests can become smaller or less reliable.

planet.summary: Chemicals drifting off a field can reach flowers, water or nesting sites used by pollinating insects. Detecting them does not prove declining pollination. Effects depend on the product, species, amount and timing.
consequences: Farm chemicals drifting beyond their target can reach bees directly or through contaminated food brought back to a colony. Colony harm depends on the chemical, dose and exposure, alongside other stresses.

response.defaultDriver: Spraying farm chemicals can send droplets or dust beyond the intended field, and some chemicals can move through the air later. Suitable weather, equipment and buffer areas can greatly reduce this movement.
levers: Use farming practices suited to the local soil, water and climate, with protection for workers and livestock.
Keep soils covered where appropriate, limit avoidable nutrient and chemical losses, and manage total water use rather than efficiency alone.

estuarine nursery loss.name: Estuarine Nursery Loss
estuarine nursery loss.description: Sheltered areas where rivers meet the sea becoming less suitable for young fish and other animals. These places provide food and protection while the animals grow. Losing them can reduce the number that survive to join adult populations.
incoming: Too little oxygen makes sheltered coastal water less suitable for young fish and shellfish. Fewer may survive to join the adult populations caught nearby.
Separated layers in warm river-mouth waters can make oxygen shortages worse. Young fish and shellfish may then have less suitable sheltered habitat.

Changes in seawater chemistry can harm the growth or survival of some young fish and shell-forming animals. Effects differ between species. Evidence of exposure alone does not show that an entire estuary has lost its nursery role.
outgoing: Losing sheltered habitat for young fish can mean fewer survive to adulthood. Where this stage limits population recovery, the chance of a serious decline in catches increases.
Damage to places where young fish grow can reduce future adult populations. Coastal fishing communities may then receive smaller or less predictable catches.

human.summary: Damage to places where young fish grow can affect catches later, after those fish would have reached harvestable size. Coastal food and income effects may therefore be delayed.
consequences: A fishery can decline without an obvious sudden die-off of adults.
Less successful breeding and survival of young fish can make future catches less dependable.

planet.summary: Losing sheltered habitat for young fish can mean fewer survive to adulthood. Where this stage limits population recovery, the chance of a serious decline in catches increases.

response.defaultDriver: Development and pollution may harm nursery areas whose value is not visible in current catch totals.
levers: Protect and restore important nursery habitats and reduce the pressures damaging them.
Track young fish survival and habitat conditions alongside adult catches.

measurement.metric: Estuarine and coastal nursery-habitat extent, historical loss, and fisheries dependence
measurement.geography: declared habitat, ecosystem, protected area, watershed, coastline, or analysis grid
measurement.cadence: seasonal or annual with event updates where applicable

ice algae pigmentation.name: Ice Algae Pigmentation
ice algae pigmentation.description: Tiny organisms growing on or near snow and ice adding colour to the surface. Their pigments can change how much sunlight is absorbed. These organisms can also form part of polar food systems, depending on where they grow.
incoming: Warming changes meltwater, salty water pockets and light inside snow and sea ice. This can change when ice-dwelling algae grow and how much coloured material they produce.
A shorter ice season reduces stable growing space for algae living in sea ice. Earlier melting can change bloom timing and wash away some of this material.
outgoing: Changes in algae growing in sea ice affect when and how much food becomes available to small marine animals. Too little food, or food arriving at the wrong time, can affect animals farther up the food chain.

human.summary: Changes in algae growing in sea ice affect when and how much food becomes available to small marine animals. Too little food, or food arriving at the wrong time, can affect animals farther up the food chain. Changes in feeding relationships can alter which fish are available and when. Fishing businesses may receive a less predictable mix or quantity of seafood.

planet.summary: Changes in algae growing in sea ice affect when and how much food becomes available to small marine animals. Too little food, or food arriving at the wrong time, can affect animals farther up the food chain.

response.defaultDriver: Warming changes meltwater, salty water pockets and light inside snow and sea ice. This can change when ice-dwelling algae grow and how much coloured material they produce.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.

measurement.geography: named glacier, ice sheet sector, snow basin, permafrost region, or polar analysis grid
measurement.cadence: daily to monthly with seasonal and annual rollups

mineral dust deposition on snow.name: Mineral Dust Deposition on Snow
mineral dust deposition on snow.description: Mineral particles settling on snow and making its surface darker. Darkened snow absorbs more sunlight and can melt earlier. This changes when stored snow-water reaches rivers and exposes the ground beneath.
incoming: Dust storms can carry mineral particles to mountain snow, where they settle in layers. A storm elsewhere does not prove deposition at a particular site, and buried dust may not reach the surface until later melting.
Damaged dryland can supply loose dust, but reaching snow also requires the right winds and route. Some dust sources are natural, so identifying the source needs evidence beyond nearby land damage.
outgoing: Dark dust on snow absorbs sunlight and can bring earlier melting and runoff. Fresh snow can bury it and clouds reduce its effect, so the size of the timing change must be assessed locally.

Faster snowmelt can send stored water into streams over a shorter spring period. Earlier melting does not always mean damaging floods: reservoirs can slow the flow, and total runoff may fall as exposed land loses more water to the air.

human.summary: Faster snowmelt can send stored water into streams over a shorter spring period. Earlier melting does not always mean damaging floods: reservoirs can slow the flow, and total runoff may fall as exposed land loses more water to the air. A surge of fast-moving water can wash material away from around a bridge's supports. Losing that material can weaken the foundations.
consequences: Dark dust on snow absorbs sunlight and can bring earlier melting and runoff. Fresh snow can bury it and clouds reduce its effect, so the size of the timing change must be assessed locally. Snow melting earlier or faster can send a stronger pulse of water into streams. The effect is greater where the landscape has little capacity to hold the water temporarily.

planet.summary: Dark dust on snow absorbs sunlight and can bring earlier melting and runoff. Fresh snow can bury it and clouds reduce its effect, so the size of the timing change must be assessed locally.
consequences: Faster snowmelt can send stored water into streams over a shorter spring period. Earlier melting does not always mean damaging floods: reservoirs can slow the flow, and total runoff may fall as exposed land loses more water to the air.

response.defaultDriver: Dust storms can carry mineral particles to mountain snow, where they settle in layers. A storm elsewhere does not prove deposition at a particular site, and buried dust may not reach the surface until later melting.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.

heavy-metal bioaccumulation.name: Heavy-Metal Bioaccumulation
heavy-metal bioaccumulation.description: Metals building up inside living things when they are taken in faster than they are removed. Some can harm growth, reproduction or survival at sufficient doses. Effects depend on the metal, its chemical form and the exposed organism.
incoming: Mining and processing can release metals from waste, drainage and disturbed material. Some can enter water, food and animal tissues.
More acidic conditions can make some metals easier to dissolve and move. Exposure may increase where those metals are already present in soil or water.
Mining plumes can carry metal-containing particles or dissolved metals to deep-water organisms. This creates a possible exposure route near the affected area.
outgoing: Enough metal building up in tissues can harm survival, reproduction or behaviour. Effects depend on the metal, dose and species exposed.

human.summary: Some metals can build up in organisms and expose people through contaminated food. Harm depends on the metal, chemical form and amount consumed or otherwise encountered.

planet.summary: Enough metal building up in tissues can harm survival, reproduction or behaviour. Effects depend on the metal, dose and species exposed.

response.defaultDriver: Mining and processing can release metals from waste, drainage and disturbed material. Some can enter water, food and animal tissues.
levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

glacier hydrologic system floods.name: Glacier Hydrologic System Floods
glacier hydrologic system floods.description: Water stored inside, underneath or beside a glacier being released quickly. A sudden release can send a large surge down a valley. Its danger depends on the amount of water and what lies in the flow path.
incoming: Losing ice can change where meltwater collects and how it drains. Flood hazards depend on whether water becomes trapped, how it escapes and what lies downstream.
Warming can increase meltwater stored in or beside glaciers. If that stored water drains suddenly, a large flood can follow downstream.
Earlier snowmelt can send water into a glacier before its drainage channels are ready to carry it. Blockages or sudden changes in those channels can release stored water as a flood.
If ice or loose rock holding back a glacier lake fails, stored water can escape quickly. The flood can carry large amounts of water and sediment downstream.
outgoing: Sudden releases of stored glacier water can produce river flows far above seasonal levels. Repeated releases change the timing, size and sediment carried by downstream floods.
Sudden releases of glacier water can sweep up sediment from beneath the ice and river banks. Short bursts may carry far more material than normal seasonal flows.

human.summary: Sudden releases of stored glacier water can produce river flows far above seasonal levels. Repeated releases change the timing, size and sediment carried by downstream floods. Changed incoming river flows may no longer fit a dam's release plans. Operators can struggle to meet water, flood-control or electricity commitments.
consequences: Sudden releases of glacier water can sweep up sediment from beneath the ice and river banks. Short bursts may carry far more material than normal seasonal flows. Sediment carried into a reservoir settles as the water slows. Continued build-up takes up storage space and can interfere with water intakes.

consequences: Sudden releases of glacier water can sweep up sediment from beneath the ice and river banks. Short bursts may carry far more material than normal seasonal flows.

wetland peat fires.name: Wetland Peat Fires
wetland peat fires.description: Fire burning into the carbon-rich soil of wetlands that have become dry. It can smoulder below the surface and consume material built up over long periods. Burning releases carbon dioxide and smoke, with the amount depending on the area and depth burned.
incoming: Draining peat lowers its moisture and makes it easier to ignite. Once burning, dry peat can smoulder for a long time below the surface.
Longer or more severe fire seasons increase the chance that fire reaches dry peat. Repeated burning can occur before the wetland has recovered.
Damage to wetland plants and water flow can leave peat dry and exposed. Fires may start more easily, burn deeper and become harder to put out.
outgoing: Burning peat releases carbon stored over long periods as carbon dioxide and other pollutants. The amount depends partly on the area burned and how deep the fire reaches.

human.summary: Burning peat releases carbon stored over long periods as carbon dioxide and other pollutants. The amount depends partly on the area burned and how deep the fire reaches. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.

convective available potential energy an.name: Convective Available Potential Energy and Inhibition Anomaly
convective available potential energy an.description: Changes in how readily warm, moist air can rise and form strong storm clouds. Both the energy available for rising air and the barriers holding it down matter. Storms still require suitable moisture and a way to get started.
incoming: Warm, moist air near the ground can rise more strongly if the air above allows it. Warming higher up, dryness or a layer that blocks rising air can prevent this potential from becoming a storm.
outgoing: More strongly rising air can support heavier rain, but moisture, storm movement and organisation also matter. High potential energy can remain unused, while very moist storms can produce extreme rain with little of it.
Lightning Flash Density and Seasonality Anomaly
Strong rising air can move water and ice through clouds in ways that help generate lightning. Other cloud conditions matter, so one measure of atmospheric energy is not a lightning forecast.

High potential energy can remain unused, while very moist storms can produce extreme rain with little of it. Very heavy rain can overwhelm airport drains and reduce visibility. Flights and ground operations may be delayed or cancelled.

ice cap decapitation.name: Ice Cap Decapitation
ice cap decapitation.description: A small ice-covered region losing its high-elevation area where snow normally builds up. The remaining lower ice may no longer receive enough new snow to replace what melts. Exposed darker ground can also absorb more sunlight.
incoming: Sustained warming can raise the height at which snow lasts through summer above an ice cap's summit. The cap then loses its remaining area where snow can build up over the long term.
Repeated winters with too little snow leave small ice caps with less new ice to replace melting. Their summits and connecting ice can thin until a once-continuous cap breaks apart.
Soot makes snow and ice absorb more sunlight. Persistent extra melting can help thin and break up an already vulnerable small ice cap.
outgoing: Losing an ice cap's summit removes stored land ice and may expose darker ground that speeds further melting. Water from the shrinking ice cap contributes to rising sea level.

human.summary: Losing an ice cap's summit removes stored land ice and may expose darker ground that speeds further melting. Water from the shrinking ice cap contributes to rising sea level. Higher seawater levels can push salt into the shallow freshwater reserve beneath a small island. The usable layer may become thinner or saltier, depending on local conditions.

riparian bank erosion.name: Riparian Bank Erosion
riparian bank erosion.description: Flowing water wearing away riverbanks and the soil beside streams. This can remove plants and shade and add sediment to the water. Persistent loss changes habitats along the river and can threaten nearby land or structures.
incoming: Heavy rain and flood peaks can increase water force against river banks. Saturated or undercut banks may collapse where they are vulnerable.
A rapid rise in runoff can increase river depth and speed. Banks erode when the force of moving water exceeds the ground's resistance.
Losing trees can increase runoff and sediment reaching rivers. Where bank vegetation is also lost, fewer roots hold the bank in place.
outgoing: Continued river-bank loss can add fine sediment, bury habitat and remove shade. River plants and animals may lose suitable places to live.

human.summary: Eroding riverbanks can remove land and damage nearby routes or property. Extra sediment can also complicate water use downstream, depending on where it travels.

planet.summary: Continued river-bank loss can add fine sediment, bury habitat and remove shade. River plants and animals may lose suitable places to live.

nighttime heat retention.name: Nighttime Heat Retention
nighttime heat retention.description: Heat stored by buildings, roads and other surfaces being released slowly after sunset. The surrounding area can remain warm when it would normally cool down. Limited vegetation and local air conditions can add to the effect.
incoming: Designs that limit heat storage and allow heat to escape can keep places cooler after sunset. The result depends on local materials, building layout and airflow.
Trees and other vegetation shade surfaces and cool the air as water evaporates. Less heat stored during the day can mean less released into nearby air at night.
Dense buildings and paved surfaces store daytime heat and release it slowly after sunset. Limited vegetation also reduces cooling from evaporation.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Heat stored in city surfaces can keep homes and streets warm after sunset. This can disturb sleep and increase cooling needs, particularly where housing offers little protection.

planet.summary: This measure compares urban temperatures with a stated reference at night. It does not directly quantify separate damage to plants, animals or the wider climate.

nunatak habitat shrinkage.name: Nunatak Habitat Shrinkage
nunatak habitat shrinkage.description: Suitable living space becoming smaller or more isolated on rocky mountain areas that rise above surrounding ice. Cold-adapted plants and animals may have fewer places to survive as conditions change. Changes in ice cover alone do not establish how much suitable habitat remains.
incoming: Warming may expose more bare mountain ground while reducing the cold, snowy conditions some species need. Suitable habitat can shrink even where the total ice-free area grows.
Thawing frozen ground on exposed rocky peaks changes moisture, stability and cold local conditions. Specialised species can lose suitable habitat even as the total area of bare rock grows.
Earlier snow loss reduces the time that cool, moist patches remain on exposed mountain peaks. Specialised plants and animals may face a longer period of heat and drying.
outgoing: Losing suitable cold habitat on isolated rocky peaks leaves specialised plants and animals with fewer places to survive. Small, separated populations may face a greater chance of disappearing locally.

human.summary: Changes to isolated mountain habitats can threaten specialised wildlife and valued natural places. The available evidence does not establish a direct, measured health or income burden on people.

planet.summary: Losing suitable cold habitat on isolated rocky peaks leaves specialised plants and animals with fewer places to survive. Small, separated populations may face a greater chance of disappearing locally.

functional habitat connectivity loss.name: Functional Habitat Connectivity Loss
functional habitat connectivity loss.description: Living things becoming less able to move between the places they need for food, shelter or breeding. Roads, damaged habitat and other barriers can interrupt these routes. Isolated populations may struggle to recover after losses or reach cooler places as conditions change.
incoming: Splitting forests into separate patches can make it harder for some species to move, breed or recolonise an area. Other species can cross the gaps, so a map alone does not prove that movement has stopped.
Development can remove habitat and add roads, noise or light that interfere with wildlife movement. Parks, gardens and safe crossings can preserve useful links for some species.
outgoing: Less movement between habitats can isolate populations and limit access to food or cooler places. Connections are not always the main constraint, and they can also spread disease or invasive species.
Migratory Bird Timing, Route, and Stopover Disruption

Losing resting or seasonal habitats can force migrating birds to travel farther or leave them with less food. Some use alternative sites, so fewer birds at one stop does not by itself prove a failing route.
Losing usable routes between habitats can reduce breeding between separated groups. Small, isolated populations can then lose genetic variety more easily.

human.summary: Breaking connections between habitats can make wildlife populations harder to sustain. Human effects depend on local uses and values. They cannot be calculated from a broken route alone.

planet.summary: Less movement between habitats can isolate populations and limit access to food or cooler places. Connections are not always the main constraint, and they can also spread disease or invasive species.
consequences: Losing resting or seasonal habitats can force migrating birds to travel farther or leave them with less food. Some use alternative sites, so fewer birds at one stop does not by itself prove a failing route.

pacific walker circulation variability.name: Pacific Walker Circulation Variability
pacific walker circulation variability.description: Changes in the loop of air moving east and west across the tropical Pacific. Air rises over some warm, rainy areas and sinks over drier areas. Shifts in this loop change winds, ocean conditions and where rainfall tends to occur.
incoming: Warmer central and eastern Pacific water shifts rising air and tropical storms eastward. This can weaken or move the usual east-to-west circulation, but one event does not establish a long-term trend.

Cooler central and eastern Pacific water can strengthen the usual pattern of rising air in the west and sinking air in the east. The response differs between events and does not by itself explain a decades-long trend.
outgoing: Changes in tropical rising and sinking air can shift where rain falls. Some monsoon regions respond, while local weather processes can outweigh the distant influence.

human.summary: Changes in tropical rising and sinking air can shift where rain falls. Some monsoon regions respond, while local weather processes can outweigh the distant influence. Unreliable seasonal rains can disrupt planting, watering and harvesting. Farms that depend heavily on these rains may produce less food.

planet.summary: Changes in tropical rising and sinking air can shift where rain falls. Some monsoon regions respond, while local weather processes can outweigh the distant influence.

response.defaultDriver: Warmer central and eastern Pacific water shifts rising air and tropical storms eastward. This can weaken or move the usual east-to-west circulation, but one event does not establish a long-term trend.
levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

fjord sedimentation pulses.name: Fjord Sedimentation Pulses
fjord sedimentation pulses.description: Bursts of mud, sand and other particles entering a narrow sea inlet between steep sides. Melting or retreating glaciers can change the supply and timing of this material. It can cloud the water and build up on the bottom.
incoming: Thinning and retreating ice can expose sediment and change meltwater routes. This changes when and how much material reaches nearby coastal inlets.
Meltwater carries fine rock and soil into the water below glaciers. How much arrives, and at what depth, depends on the amount of water and how it enters the basin.
Heavy rain can wash loose material from glacier-fed rivers and deltas. Short bursts of flow may carry fine particles and larger sediment into nearby coastal waters.
Breaking ice and falling icebergs can disturb sediment near a glacier front. Underwater slides and cloudy currents may move material that had already settled.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Large amounts of sediment entering a narrow coastal inlet can change water conditions and seabed habitats. Consequences for fishing or other uses depend on the event and location.

planet.summary: A sudden sediment supply can cloud water or cover seabed habitats. The effect depends on grain size, amount and where currents deposit the material.

response.defaultDriver: Thinning and retreating ice can expose sediment and change meltwater routes. This changes when and how much material reaches nearby coastal inlets.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.

transformer heat failure risk.name: Transformer Heat Failure Risk
transformer heat failure risk.description: The chance that equipment used to change electricity voltage overheats and stops working. Heavy electrical loads and hot surroundings can add to the strain. Failure can interrupt power, and replacement may take time.
incoming: Hot air makes it harder for an electrical transformer to release the heat it produces. Its hottest parts can become hotter still, ageing insulation faster and increasing failure risk.
Carrying more electricity creates more heat inside a transformer. High demand combined with hot weather can shorten insulation life and increase the chance of failure.
outgoing: A failed transformer can interrupt electricity to essential services. Replacements can take a long time, leaving connected facilities more vulnerable until supply is restored.

human.summary: A failed transformer can interrupt electricity to essential services. Replacements can take a long time, leaving connected facilities more vulnerable until supply is restored.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

response.defaultDriver: Hot air makes it harder for an electrical transformer to release the heat it produces. Its hottest parts can become hotter still, ageing insulation faster and increasing failure risk.
levers: Plan electricity supply, networks and demand together so cleaner options remain dependable.

freeze-thaw rock fracturing.name: Freeze-Thaw Rock Fracturing
freeze-thaw rock fracturing.description: Water inside cracks in rock repeatedly freezing and thawing. Ice formation can widen or weaken existing cracks over time. This can make rock less stable, depending on the water supply, temperatures and structure of the rock.
incoming: Repeated changes around freezing can make water in existing rock cracks freeze and thaw. The resulting pressure can gradually loosen or move pieces of rock.
Heavy rain or rapid snowmelt can fill cracks in rock. Later freezing and thawing, together with water pressure, can weaken blocks that are already vulnerable.
Ice in rock cracks can help hold pieces in place. When it thaws, the rock loses support and becomes more exposed to seasonal water and temperature changes.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Water freezing and thawing in cracks can help loosen rock. Falling rock may threaten nearby routes or buildings, but local slopes and other triggers determine the actual hazard.

planet.summary: Changes in cracks can loosen rock and add material to slopes below. Rock movement also depends on local geology and other forces.

response.defaultDriver: Repeated changes around freezing can make water in existing rock cracks freeze and thaw. The resulting pressure can gradually loosen or move pieces of rock.

overstory tree mortality.name: Overstory Tree Mortality
overstory tree mortality.description: The death of large trees that form a forest's upper leafy layer. Losing them changes shade, habitat and the forest's structure. When many die across an area, the wider forest can struggle to maintain its usual functions.
incoming: Heat and dry soil together can make it harder for trees to move enough water and keep growing. Earlier damage and pests can add to this pressure and contribute to tree death.

In western North American pine forests, warming can help some bark beetles develop faster and survive winter. During severe drought, weakened trees may be less able to resist the increased beetle pressure.
Long water shortages can disrupt a tree's water transport and weaken its defences. The air's demand for moisture also matters, so temperature alone is not enough to describe the exposure.
Severe fires can kill tall canopy trees by burning crowns or damaging bark and roots. Some injured trees die later, including after insect attack.
Large bark-beetle populations can attack and kill host trees. The trees selected are not always simply the ones that were already most stressed.
outgoing: When many dominant trees die across adjoining areas, the losses form a wider episode of forest die-off. Mapping the pattern helps distinguish it from isolated tree deaths.

human.summary: Losing large upper-layer trees can remove shade, forest products and valued habitat. Effects on people vary with the forest and the resources they depend on.

planet.summary: When many dominant trees die across adjoining areas, the losses form a wider episode of forest die-off. Mapping the pattern helps distinguish it from isolated tree deaths.

airborne microplastic concentration and.name: Airborne Microplastic Concentration and Deposition
airborne microplastic concentration and.description: Tiny plastic fibres and fragments floating in the air or settling out of it. Wear, manufacturing and waste handling can release them, and wind can lift previously settled particles. Their presence is different from a demonstrated health effect at a particular dose.
incoming: Wear, processing and weathering can release tiny plastic fibres or fragments that enter the air. Plastic use alone does not measure airborne releases, and suspected particles need chemical confirmation.

Dense urban activity creates opportunities for small plastic particles to enter or re-enter the air from wear, handling and dust. Cities also receive particles from elsewhere, so location alone does not identify the source.

Heavy road use wears tyres and can release tiny fragments containing synthetic materials. Not every dark roadside particle comes from tyres, and freight-specific claims need evidence about vehicle types.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: People can encounter tiny airborne plastic particles, but measuring their presence does not establish a specific health effect. Particle size, composition and exposure remain important uncertainties.

planet.summary: Wind can carry small plastic particles and deposit them on land or water. Detecting particles does not by itself establish the size of ecological harm at the receiving site.

coastal saltwater intrusion.name: Coastal Saltwater Intrusion
coastal saltwater intrusion.description: Seawater moving inland or upward into places that previously held fresher water. Rivers, soil and underground supplies can be affected. Higher sea levels or heavy pumping of fresh water can contribute, making some supplies less suitable for use.
incoming: Heavy pumping near a coast can reduce the freshwater flowing toward the sea. Saltwater may then move into areas that previously held fresh groundwater.
Sea-level rise from land-ice loss can push saltwater toward coastal underground freshwater. Pumping, rainwater replenishment and local geology affect how far it moves.
Higher coastal sea levels can push salty water toward underground freshwater. Pumping, replenishment, geology and connected canals or rivers determine the local response.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Salt entering underground freshwater can make wells less useful for drinking or irrigation. Households and farms may need treatment or another supply.

planet.summary: Salt entering freshwater changes conditions for plants and organisms that depend on low-salt water. The affected area depends on local underground flow and geology.

response.defaultDriver: Heavy pumping near a coast can reduce the freshwater flowing toward the sea. Saltwater may then move into areas that previously held fresh groundwater.

tundra shrub expansion.name: Tundra Shrub Expansion
tundra shrub expansion.description: Shrubs spreading across northern landscapes previously dominated by lower-growing plants. Warmer growing conditions can favour some species. The pace and effects also depend on snow, soil moisture, grazing and disturbance.
incoming: A longer Arctic growing season can help some shrubs spread. The response depends on the species, moisture, snow, grazing animals and disturbance.
Thawing ground changes drainage, nutrients and the shape of the land. These changes can favour shrubs in some tundra areas, but not everywhere.
Tundra fires change vegetation, soil warmth and frozen-ground conditions. This can alter whether shrubs establish successfully after the disturbance.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: More or taller shrubs can change northern landscapes and wildlife habitat used by local communities. Benefits and difficulties vary by place and by how people use the land.

planet.summary: More shrubs change shade, snow trapping and habitat in northern landscapes. Effects on ground warmth and other species differ by region and shrub type.

north atlantic subpolar gyre circulation.name: North Atlantic Subpolar Gyre Circulation Strength
north atlantic subpolar gyre circulation.description: Changes in the strength and reach of a large rotating system of currents in the northern Atlantic. Winds and exchanges of heat with the air help shape it. The circulation can strengthen or weaken, affecting the movement of water and heat.
incoming: North Atlantic pressure patterns change winds and heat exchange over the ocean. These can strengthen, weaken or shift its northern circular flow, but no atmospheric phase gives one fixed response everywhere.

Changes in salt content alter seawater density and can change northern Atlantic circulation. Fresher water does not automatically mean weaker flow because temperature, winds and the water carried by currents also matter.

Warmer or less strongly cooled surface water may sink less and change northern Atlantic flow. Temperature alone cannot determine the response because salt content and transported heat also affect density and circulation.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Changes in the broad North Atlantic circulation can alter the movement of heat and nutrients. Local effects on people need separate evidence. One circulation index does not directly measure fishing or coastal losses.

planet.summary: Changes in this broad circulation alter the transport of heat, salt and nutrients in the North Atlantic. Different regions can change differently, and this is not the same as the ocean's deep overturning circulation.

response.defaultDriver: North Atlantic pressure patterns change winds and heat exchange over the ocean. These can strengthen, weaken or shift its northern circular flow, but no atmospheric phase gives one fixed response everywhere.

shelf-sea hypoxia.name: Shelf-Sea Hypoxia
shelf-sea hypoxia.description: Shallow seas beside continents containing too little dissolved oxygen for many animals. Poor mixing and the breakdown of excess organic material can contribute. Less-tolerant animals may die or move away, changing the local food web.
incoming: Strongly separated water layers mix less easily, slowing the oxygen supply to the bottom. Oxygen can run low as organisms continue to use it, especially where much organic material is decaying.
Extra nutrients can produce more algae in shallow seas. As this material decays, it can use oxygen faster than fresh water movement replaces it near the seabed.
Water arriving with less oxygen gives a shallow sea less protection against further oxygen loss. A smaller additional loss may then be enough to harm local marine life.
outgoing: Long periods of low oxygen can kill sensitive seabed animals and push fish elsewhere. Species that tolerate these conditions may become more common, changing the food web.

human.summary: Long periods of low oxygen can kill sensitive seabed animals and push fish elsewhere. Species that tolerate these conditions may become more common, changing the food web. Changes in feeding relationships can alter which fish are available and when. Fishing businesses may receive a less predictable mix or quantity of seafood.

planet.summary: Long periods of low oxygen can kill sensitive seabed animals and push fish elsewhere. Species that tolerate these conditions may become more common, changing the food web.

freshwater mussel population decline.name: Freshwater Mussel Population Decline
freshwater mussel population decline.description: Fewer river and lake mussels, fewer kinds of them or fewer places where they live. These shellfish filter water and contribute to habitats on the bottom. Large, lasting losses can therefore affect more than the mussels themselves.
incoming: Excess nutrients can change oxygen, algae and ammonia levels in freshwater. Sensitive young mussels may be harmed where exposure becomes high enough.
Dams and other barriers can change flow and prevent movement of fish that carry young mussels during part of their life cycle. This can limit mussel spread and recovery.
Long periods of low water can expose mussel beds, increase heat and concentrate pollution. Fish needed for the mussels' life cycle may also lose access.
outgoing: Large, lasting mussel losses remove animals that filter water and help stabilise riverbeds. Nutrient movement and habitats supported by dense mussel groups may also change.

human.summary: Losing mussels can change river ecosystems and species valued by local communities. Population counts alone do not establish a direct drinking-water or financial loss.

lightning flash density and seasonality.name: Lightning Flash Density and Seasonality Anomaly
lightning flash density and seasonality.description: Changes in how often lightning occurs, where flashes are concentrated or which seasons they occur in. A flash reaching dry vegetation can start a fire under suitable conditions. Changes in lightning do not by themselves determine how much land burns.
incoming: Convective Available Potential Energy and Inhibition Anomaly
Strong rising air can move water and ice through clouds in ways that help generate lightning. Other cloud conditions matter, so one measure of atmospheric energy is not a lightning forecast.

Warming changes moisture, rising air and the ice processes involved in lightning. Models disagree on how these effects combine, so the direction of future lightning change remains uncertain in many regions.
outgoing: Lightning Ignition under Fire Weather Conditions

Lightning reaching the ground can ignite vegetation when it is dry enough and rain does not put the fire out. Most flashes do not start a recorded fire, and later spread depends on weather and response.

human.summary: Changes in where and when lightning occurs can affect people outdoors and exposed equipment. Risk also depends on protection, activity and whether strikes reach vulnerable places.

coral larval survival and recruitment fa.name: Coral Larval Survival and Recruitment Failure
coral larval survival and recruitment fa.description: Young corals failing to survive, settle on a suitable surface or grow into new colonies. Adults then have fewer replacements when they die. Persistent failure can reduce long-term coral cover and the maintenance of reef structure.
incoming: Heat and other stresses can reduce the survival of young corals and their ability to settle on a reef. This makes recovery harder where the reef is already damaged.
Seawater above the temperatures young corals can tolerate can reduce survival and successful settlement. Effects vary by species and stage of growth.
Stressed adult corals may have less energy to reproduce and support their young. Fewer larvae may be produced, or fewer may survive and settle successfully.
Changing seawater chemistry can interfere with early coral growth and the signals young corals use to find a place to settle. Sensitive species may have lower survival.
outgoing: If too few young corals survive and establish themselves, they cannot replace lost adults. Over time this can weaken the living cover and solid structure of a reef.

human.summary: If too few young corals survive and establish themselves, they cannot replace lost adults. Over time this can weaken the living cover and solid structure of a reef. Losing reef structure removes shelter, feeding areas and places for young fish to grow. Fisheries depending on those habitats can become less able to sustain catches.

planet.summary: If too few young corals survive and establish themselves, they cannot replace lost adults. Over time this can weaken the living cover and solid structure of a reef.

response.defaultDriver: Heat and other stresses can reduce the survival of young corals and their ability to settle on a reef. This makes recovery harder where the reef is already damaged.

river network fragmentation.name: River Network Fragmentation
river network fragmentation.description: Rivers being divided into sections that aquatic animals cannot easily travel between. Dams, road crossings, low flows or damaged stretches can create barriers. Animals may lose access to breeding places, food or refuge during harsh conditions.
incoming: Forest loss can increase erosion, change river channels and remove streamside habitat. Some stretches may become unsuitable, separating populations along the river.
Dams and water diversions can block movement and separate river habitats. Their effects need evidence about the actual barriers and the species trying to pass them.
Poorly designed pipes, crossings and gates can stop aquatic animals moving along streams. Whether a crossing acts as a barrier depends on its design and the species involved.
Embankments and straightened channels can cut rivers off from nearby floodplains and side habitats. Documented barriers are needed to assess how much wildlife movement is restricted.
outgoing: Barriers can isolate aquatic populations and prevent access to breeding sites or refuge. Repeated or widespread isolation can weaken the river's living community.
Dams and other barriers can change flow and prevent movement of fish that carry young mussels during part of their life cycle. This can limit mussel spread and recovery.

human.summary: Barriers can interrupt fish movement and affect communities relying on connected river habitats. Effects differ across species and river uses, and need local assessment.

planet.summary: Barriers can isolate aquatic populations and prevent access to breeding sites or refuge. Repeated or widespread isolation can weaken the river's living community.
consequences: Dams and other barriers can change flow and prevent movement of fish that carry young mussels during part of their life cycle. This can limit mussel spread and recovery.

response.defaultDriver: Forest loss can increase erosion, change river channels and remove streamside habitat. Some stretches may become unsuitable, separating populations along the river.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.

mountain forest cover and treeline contr.name: Mountain Forest Cover and Treeline Contraction
mountain forest cover and treeline contr.description: Wooded areas high in the mountains becoming smaller or less connected. Changes in tree survival and where trees can grow alter shade, food and shelter. Species that depend on these cool, high places may have limited alternatives.
incoming: Warming can dry lower forest margins and prevent young trees from establishing, while allowing trees to grow higher where cold once limited them. Both boundaries and local moisture need to be checked before claiming the forest is shrinking overall.
Long dry periods can weaken mountain trees and prevent regrowth after damage. Some forests recover when moisture returns, so a short decline in greenness is not proof of permanent loss.
Severe fires can remove mountain trees and seed sources. Lasting forest loss occurs when trees cannot regrow. Many forests normally recover from fire, and some lower-intensity fires support renewal.
outgoing: Lasting changes in mountain forests alter shelter, food and connections used by wildlife. Some species lose habitat while others benefit from openings or forest expansion, so population changes need separate evidence.

human.summary: Changes in mountain forests can affect local resources, recreation and valued habitats. Human effects depend on which forest areas are lost and what communities rely on them for.

atmospheric river intensification.name: Atmospheric River Intensification
atmospheric river intensification.description: Long bands of moist air carrying more water toward a region, lasting longer or producing heavier rain and snow. When the air rises over mountains or weather fronts, moisture can fall out rapidly. Effects depend on the route, duration and local conditions.
incoming: Warmer air can carry more water vapour, allowing long bands of moist air to transport more water. This does not guarantee more events or stronger winds in every place, and historical trends depend on the available record.
outgoing: A strong, long-lasting stream of moist air can produce heavy rain or snow when mountains or fronts lift it. Without suitable lifting, direction or duration, it may mainly provide useful water rather than an extreme event.

Sustained rain from a band of moist air can sharply raise river flow, especially on wet ground or melting snow. Dry soil, reservoirs and shorter events can limit runoff and allow beneficial replenishment.

human.summary: A strong, long-lasting stream of moist air can produce heavy rain or snow when mountains or fronts lift it. Without suitable lifting, direction or duration, it may mainly provide useful water rather than an extreme event. Very heavy rain can overwhelm airport drains and reduce visibility. Flights and ground operations may be delayed or cancelled.
consequences: Sustained rain from a band of moist air can sharply raise river flow, especially on wet ground or melting snow. Dry soil, reservoirs and shorter events can limit runoff and allow beneficial replenishment. Changed incoming river flows may no longer fit a dam's release plans. Operators can struggle to meet water, flood-control or electricity commitments.

planet.summary: A strong, long-lasting stream of moist air can produce heavy rain or snow when mountains or fronts lift it. Without suitable lifting, direction or duration, it may mainly provide useful water rather than an extreme event.

equatorial pacific trade-wind anomaly.name: Equatorial Pacific Trade-Wind Anomaly
equatorial pacific trade-wind anomaly.description: The usual east-to-west winds near the equator in the Pacific becoming stronger or weaker than their seasonal pattern. These winds influence ocean surface water and tropical rainfall. The sign of the change matters: an unusual reading does not always mean weakening.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Weaker east-to-west winds over the equatorial Pacific allow warm surface water to move east. This can reinforce warming in the central and eastern Pacific.

Stronger, rather than weaker, east-to-west Pacific winds push warm water west and bring colder water up in the east. That opposite phase of the wind measure supports cooler tropical Pacific conditions.
Changes in east-to-west tropical Pacific winds affect how surface water moves and how cold water rises from below. The direction of the wind change determines the response.

human.summary: Weaker east-to-west winds over the equatorial Pacific allow warm surface water to move east. This can reinforce warming in the central and eastern Pacific. Changes in Pacific ocean temperatures can bring heat, drought or flooding to farming regions. These conditions can damage harvests and interrupt food supplies.
consequences: Stronger, rather than weaker, east-to-west Pacific winds push warm water west and bring colder water up in the east. That opposite phase of the wind measure supports cooler tropical Pacific conditions. Changes linked to unusually cool Pacific waters can bring destructive rain to some regions and drought to others. Harvests and fisheries may be affected in different ways across regions.

consequences: Stronger, rather than weaker, east-to-west Pacific winds push warm water west and bring colder water up in the east. That opposite phase of the wind measure supports cooler tropical Pacific conditions.

blue carbon habitat loss.name: Blue Carbon Habitat Loss
blue carbon habitat loss.description: Coastal habitats such as mangroves, salt marshes and seagrass beds being damaged or removed. These places store carbon in plants and soils. Their loss can release stored carbon and reduce future uptake, which are two different effects.
incoming: Losing seagrass removes plants that take up carbon and can expose carbon-rich seabed to erosion and decay. Stored carbon may then be lost.
Clearing or eroding mangroves removes trees and can disturb deep organic soils. Both hold carbon that may no longer remain stored after the damage.
Draining coastal wetlands removes wet conditions that protect plants and organic soils. Stored carbon becomes more exposed to decay and erosion.
outgoing: Damage to coastal habitats can release stored carbon and reduce future uptake. Carbon actually released must be counted separately from carbon that is no longer being absorbed.

human.summary: Damage to coastal habitats can release stored carbon and reduce future uptake. Carbon actually released must be counted separately from carbon that is no longer being absorbed. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.

planet.summary: Damage to coastal habitats can release stored carbon and reduce future uptake. Carbon actually released must be counted separately from carbon that is no longer being absorbed.

atmospheric hydroxyl sink weakening.name: Atmospheric Hydroxyl Sink Weakening
atmospheric hydroxyl sink weakening.description: The air becoming less able to break down methane and some other gases through chemical reactions. Highly reactive molecules normally help remove them. If that cleaning capacity weakens, the gases can remain in the air longer for the same amount released.
incoming: Removing methane from air uses highly reactive chemicals called hydroxyl radicals. More methane can use some of that capacity and stay longer, but other chemical and weather changes can increase removal instead.

Carbon monoxide also reacts with hydroxyl radicals, which help remove methane. More carbon monoxide can leave less removal capacity, although other reactions can recycle these chemicals and change the result.
outgoing: If the air's chemical ability to remove methane weakens, methane can remain longer and trap more heat. Other removal processes can offset this, and the size of the effect is difficult to measure directly everywhere.

human.summary: If the air's chemical ability to remove methane weakens, methane can remain longer and trap more heat. Other removal processes can offset this, and the size of the effect is difficult to measure directly everywhere. When more energy stays in Earth's climate system than leaves it, the land and oceans warm as the system adjusts. Short-term regional temperatures can still move in the opposite direction, and the energy measure is not a temperature observation.

stratospheric ozone column depletion and.name: Stratospheric Ozone Column Depletion and Recovery
stratospheric ozone column depletion and.description: Changes in the amount of ozone high in the atmosphere, including its loss and recovery. This gas absorbs harmful ultraviolet sunlight and helps warm that layer of air. Recovery depends on the chemicals present and atmospheric conditions.
incoming: High in the atmosphere, sunlight breaks down certain gases and releases chemicals containing chlorine or bromine that destroy ozone. Cold polar clouds can speed the process, but gas levels alone do not predict each season's ozone loss.

Reducing ozone-damaging cooling gases lowers the future supply of reactive chlorine and bromine high in the atmosphere. Recovery is slow and uneven because old equipment, long gas lifetimes and weather still matter.
outgoing: Ozone absorbs energy and warms the upper atmosphere. Losing it can cool the affected layer, although carbon dioxide also causes cooling there and cold conditions can themselves encourage ozone loss.

human.summary: The protective layer high in the atmosphere filters harmful ultraviolet sunlight. Changes in that protection can affect exposure, but a seasonal polar measurement does not directly describe everyone's local risk.

planet.summary: Ozone absorbs energy and warms the upper atmosphere. Losing it can cool the affected layer, although carbon dioxide also causes cooling there and cold conditions can themselves encourage ozone loss.

aviation condensation trails.name: Aviation Condensation Trails
aviation condensation trails.description: Thin lines of ice cloud forming when aircraft exhaust mixes with cold, moist air high above the ground. Some disappear quickly. Others spread and last longer. They change both reflected sunlight and escaping heat, so their effects depend on the conditions.
incoming: More flights create more opportunities for exhaust to form ice clouds at cruising height. Persistent trails form only in suitable cold, humid air. Flight numbers alone cannot predict them.
outgoing: Some aircraft trails spread into thin ice clouds, changing reflected sunlight and escaping heat. Most disappear quickly, and their warming and cooling effects can partly offset each other.

Persistent aircraft ice clouds both reflect sunlight and trap outgoing heat. The assessed global net effect is warming, but uncertainty is large and individual trails can have little effect or cause cooling depending on place and time.

human.summary: Some aircraft trails spread into thin ice clouds, changing reflected sunlight and escaping heat. Most disappear quickly, and their warming and cooling effects can partly offset each other. Cloud changes affect both sunlight reflected away and heat kept near Earth. The combined effect can warm or cool the planet, so the direction must be checked rather than assumed.
consequences: Persistent aircraft ice clouds both reflect sunlight and trap outgoing heat. The assessed global net effect is warming, but uncertainty is large and individual trails can have little effect or cause cooling depending on place and time. When more energy stays in Earth's climate system than leaves it, the land and oceans warm as the system adjusts. Short-term regional temperatures can still move in the opposite direction, and the energy measure is not a temperature observation.

consequences: Persistent aircraft ice clouds both reflect sunlight and trap outgoing heat. The assessed global net effect is warming, but uncertainty is large and individual trails can have little effect or cause cooling depending on place and time.

compound coastal flooding.name: Compound Coastal Flooding
compound coastal flooding.description: Several sources of high water combining near the sea, such as storm-driven seawater, high tides and heavy river flow. Together they can make drainage harder or flooding deeper. The outcome depends on their timing and the local landscape.
incoming: Low-lying shores exposed to storm-driven seawater face greater danger when high tides, waves or river flow occur at the same time. The combined water can overwhelm drainage or protection.
A storm that strengthens quickly near land can leave less preparation time. Strong winds, heavy rain and high seawater levels may then combine to produce flooding.
Higher sea levels raise the starting point for coastal floods. Damage can be greater when storms, high tides, heavy rain or river floods occur together.
outgoing: Submarine Cable Landing-Site Concentration and Exposure

Coastal flooding can affect cable landing stations and their power or land connections. Shared locations increase the risk of several links failing together, while protection, backup power and separated routes can prevent disruption.

human.summary: Coastal flooding can affect cable landing stations and their power or land connections. Shared locations increase the risk of several links failing together, while protection, backup power and separated routes can prevent disruption. Losing shared cable landing or power facilities can remove several communication paths at once. Essential services are less affected where traffic can switch to independent routes with enough spare capacity.

planet.summary: Seawater, river flow and heavy rain arriving together can change flooding and salt exposure near coasts. Effects on habitats depend on the mix, depth and duration of water.

response.defaultDriver: Low-lying shores exposed to storm-driven seawater face greater danger when high tides, waves or river flow occur at the same time. The combined water can overwhelm drainage or protection.

fisheries range redistribution.name: Fisheries Range Redistribution
fisheries range redistribution.description: Fish that people catch moving to different places, depths or seasons. Fishing communities may find familiar stocks less accessible, while other places gain access. When fish cross national boundaries, existing sharing agreements may become harder to apply.
incoming: Unusually hot seawater can move suitable habitat farther away, deeper or toward the poles. Some fish move, while others stay, adjust or return after the event.

Less oxygen can reduce the depths and temperatures fish can tolerate and change where their food lives. Responses differ between species, and local oxygen loss may come from nutrient pollution as well as climate change.

Changing seawater chemistry can affect growth, reproduction, prey and habitat. It may contribute to changes in where fish live, but direct evidence is generally weaker than for warming and numbers can change without movement.
outgoing: Fish moving across borders can change which fleets can reach them and challenge existing catch agreements. Shared surveys and flexible agreements can manage the change without conflict.

human.summary: Fish moving across borders can change which fleets can reach them and challenge existing catch agreements. Shared surveys and flexible agreements can manage the change without conflict. Repeated confrontations or failed fishing agreements can worsen political tensions. Most disputes remain within negotiation, and existing tensions may cause fishing incidents rather than result from them.

planet.summary: Fish moving toward different temperatures or depths can change local food webs and overlap between species. Movement alone does not show whether total populations have grown or declined.

levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.

coastal aquifer salinization.name: Coastal Aquifer Salinization
coastal aquifer salinization.description: An underground freshwater store near the sea becoming saltier. Water that was suitable for drinking or farming may then need extra treatment or replacement. The causes and effects depend on pumping, seawater movement and the local ground.
incoming: Heavy pumping near the sea lowers freshwater levels. This can draw salty water toward wells and reduce the usable supply.
Repeated flooding by the sea can add salt to connected underground freshwater stores. Shallow or exposed stores may become less suitable for drinking or farming.
Salt moving through river mouths can also reach connected underground water. This can make coastal wells and reserves saltier.
outgoing: Saltier underground water gives utilities fewer easy-to-treat supplies. Extra treatment or replacement sources may be needed.
As coastal wells become saltier, ordinary supplies may be less usable. Utilities or households may turn increasingly to equipment that removes salt from water.

human.summary: Salt or other contamination in coastal groundwater can make wells less dependable. The amount of water underground may hide a decline in its usefulness.
consequences: Wells may still contain water that has become too salty for normal use.
Farms and utilities lose flexibility when a formerly reliable freshwater source deteriorates.

planet.summary: Saltier underground water gives utilities fewer easy-to-treat supplies. Extra treatment or replacement sources may be needed.

response.defaultDriver: Heavy pumping and seawater movement can worsen quality where management tracks only the quantity withdrawn.
levers: Monitor salt levels as well as water levels and limit damaging withdrawals.
Plan alternative supplies before existing wells become unreliable.

food insecurity.name: Food Insecurity
food insecurity.description: Not having reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food. A household may face shortages, unaffordable prices or difficulty obtaining suitable meals. Producing enough food overall does not guarantee that everyone can get it.
incoming: Unreliable harvests can reduce local food supplies and increase prices. Households may then find it harder to obtain enough nutritious food.
Reliance on imported food exposes households to supply and price changes elsewhere. Disruptions can make enough nutritious food harder to afford or obtain.
Sharp or unpredictable changes in basic food prices make household budgets harder to manage. Families with little income or stored food can struggle to buy enough.
Warming-related heat, drought and floods can damage harvests and food transport. Higher prices or reduced supplies make adequate food harder to obtain for households with little money or reserves.

Long-lasting damage to soil, vegetation and water supplies can make food production less reliable. Income, imports, technology and public support can protect households from some of the resulting losses.
Farms dependent on costly inputs or facing damaged soil and limited water can become less reliable. Food access is affected when these pressures change harvests, prices or household income.
Several hazards can disrupt food production, income and access at the same time. Conflict, inequality and market conditions can make the resulting hardship better or worse.
Blocked routes, conflict or restrictions can stop food aid reaching people in crisis. Households may go without adequate food even when supplies exist elsewhere.
Funding cuts can mean food aid reaches fewer people or provides smaller rations. Hunger can worsen among households depending on that support.
outgoing: Long-lasting difficulty obtaining enough food can push people to leave their homes. Jobs, conflict and other economic conditions also influence whether people move.
More people facing acute hunger increases demand for food assistance. Funding and access limits can leave part of that need unmet.
More people facing severe hunger increases the need for urgent food, nutrition and delivery support. Response services must expand quickly enough to meet it.

human.summary: Long-lasting difficulty obtaining enough food can push people to leave their homes. Jobs, conflict and other economic conditions also influence whether people move.
consequences: More people facing acute hunger increases demand for food assistance. Funding and access limits can leave part of that need unmet.
More people facing severe hunger increases the need for urgent food, nutrition and delivery support. Response services must expand quickly enough to meet it.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

levers: Connect useful warnings with accessible health services and practical protection for exposed people.
Improve access to safe housing, water or cooling where the documented exposure requires it.

nutrient pollution.name: Nutrient Pollution
nutrient pollution.description: Too much nitrogen or phosphorus entering rivers, lakes or coastal water. These substances help plants grow, but an excess can trigger algae growth and oxygen loss. The damage depends on the receiving water and the amount and timing of the input.
incoming: Making and using fertilisers increases the amount of nitrogen and phosphorus available in the environment. Some can escape into rivers and coastal waters if losses are not controlled.
Nitrogen that crops do not absorb can wash or drain into waterways. It can encourage excessive algae growth and the oxygen loss that follows.
Sewage released without adequate treatment carries nitrogen and phosphorus into water. These nutrients can worsen pollution in rivers, lakes and coastal areas.
Producing large amounts of short-lived clothing creates more wastewater and waste to manage. Pollution reaching rivers or coasts depends on what that waste contains and how effectively it is treated.
Nitrogen applied to fields but not absorbed by crops can wash away or move through soil. It may then pollute rivers, lakes or groundwater.
Leaking or overflowing manure stores can send nitrogen and phosphorus into water. Applying the manure to fields at unsuitable times can create another route for losses.
outgoing: Extra nutrients can help harmful algae grow rapidly. Light, water movement and temperature also determine whether a harmful bloom develops.
Excess nutrients and organic matter can add stress to coastal reefs. This may make heat-related bleaching and recovery worse, depending on local conditions.
Extra nutrients can produce more algae in shallow seas. As this material decays, it can use oxygen faster than fresh water movement replaces it near the seabed.
Nutrient-rich coastal water can increase food for some jellyfish and create conditions they tolerate well. The response depends on the species and local water conditions.
Excess nutrients can change oxygen, algae and ammonia levels in freshwater. Sensitive young mussels may be harmed where exposure becomes high enough.
Extra nitrogen and phosphorus can fuel algae growth. As the algae decay, they may use up enough oxygen to create persistent low-oxygen areas in vulnerable waters.

human.summary: Extra nutrients can help harmful algae grow rapidly. Light, water movement and temperature also determine whether a harmful bloom develops. Toxic algae or low oxygen can kill fish or make seafood unsafe. Harvest closures and damaged stocks can then interrupt supplies arriving at ports and markets.
consequences: Nutrient-rich coastal water can increase food for some jellyfish and create conditions they tolerate well. The response depends on the species and local water conditions. Dense jellyfish groups can clog fishing nets, harm catches or affect fish-farm enclosures. Local fishing operations may be interrupted while the event lasts.

Extra nutrients can produce more algae in shallow seas. As this material decays, it can use oxygen faster than fresh water movement replaces it near the seabed. Long periods of low oxygen can kill sensitive seabed animals and push fish elsewhere. Species that tolerate these conditions may become more common, changing the food web.

consequences: Excess nutrients and organic matter can add stress to coastal reefs. This may make heat-related bleaching and recovery worse, depending on local conditions.

levers: Limit water withdrawals to what the connected water system can support, while protecting essential human and environmental needs.

seagrass meadow decline.name: Seagrass Meadow Decline
seagrass meadow decline.description: Underwater flowering plants losing area or becoming less healthy. Their beds provide habitat, store carbon and help stabilize the seabed. Less cover can weaken these functions even before a bed disappears completely.
incoming: Unusually hot seawater can damage seagrass and kill plants. Severe or repeated events can reduce the area and condition of these underwater meadows.
Excess nutrients encourage algae to grow in the water and on seagrass leaves. This can block the light that seagrass needs to survive.
Erosion and shifting sediment can wash away or bury seagrass habitat. Meadows may shrink where roots cannot remain established.
outgoing: Losing seagrass removes plants that take up carbon and can expose carbon-rich seabed to erosion and decay. Stored carbon may then be lost.

human.summary: Losing seagrass removes plants that take up carbon and can expose carbon-rich seabed to erosion and decay. Stored carbon may then be lost. Damage to coastal habitats can release stored carbon and reduce future uptake. Carbon actually released must be counted separately from carbon that is no longer being absorbed.

urban heat island.name: Urban Heat Island
urban heat island.description: A town or city being warmer than a defined nearby non-urban area. Buildings and roads store heat, while limited vegetation provides less shade and cooling. The size of the difference varies by weather, time of day and neighbourhood.
incoming: Losing city trees removes shade and cooling from water released by leaves. Nearby streets, buildings and air can become hotter.
Outward housing growth can replace vegetation with roofs, roads and other surfaces that store heat. This can increase local warming within built-up areas.
Dark asphalt absorbs sunlight during the day and releases stored heat later. Large paved areas can keep nearby places warmer after sunset.
outgoing: Extra daytime and nighttime heat in cities increases people's exposure to high temperatures. This can add to illness risks, especially where cooling is limited.
Dense buildings and paved surfaces store daytime heat and release it slowly after sunset. Limited vegetation also reduces cooling from evaporation.

human.summary: Extra daytime and nighttime heat in cities increases people's exposure to high temperatures. This can add to illness risks, especially where cooling is limited.

humanitarian response funding shortfall.name: Humanitarian Response Funding Shortfall
