incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Insufficient funding can force aid organisations to delay, reduce or close programmes. The effect depends on each operation's needs, access and freedom to use the funds.
Funding cuts can mean food aid reaches fewer people or provides smaller rations. Hunger can worsen among households depending on that support.
Too little funding limits staff, supplies and transport for emergency services. Demand may then exceed what they can deliver.

incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Pumping groundwater for irrigation lowers reserves when withdrawals keep exceeding replacement. A record of water use alone does not show that an underground store is shrinking.
Irrigation pumping can reduce underground reserves when use exceeds replacement from rain, rivers or managed replenishment. Other users then have less dependable water available.
Farm pumping can intercept groundwater that would otherwise feed springs, streams or wetlands. Connected habitats may lose water during dry periods.

consequences: Pumping groundwater for irrigation lowers reserves when withdrawals keep exceeding replacement. A record of water use alone does not show that an underground store is shrinking. Falling groundwater levels reduce the reserves people can reach and make pumping more costly. Users who depend on wells may then face tighter supplies.

agricultural nitrogen application.name: Agricultural Nitrogen Application
agricultural nitrogen application.description: Adding nitrogen-containing products or organic material to farmland to help crops grow. The amount, timing and crop needs influence how much is used by plants. Unused nutrients can be lost to water or air.
incoming: Farms seeking high crop output may apply more nitrogen nutrients. Actual use depends on the crop, existing soil fertility and how precisely nutrients are managed.
outgoing: Microbes can turn some nitrogen added to farm soil into nitrous oxide, a heat-trapping gas. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's basic method estimates 0.010 kilograms of nitrogen released in this gas per kilogram of qualifying nitrogen added, with a default uncertainty range of 0.002–0.018.
Nitrogen applied to fields but not absorbed by crops can wash away or move through soil. It may then pollute rivers, lakes or groundwater.
Extra nutrients from fields can travel downstream and encourage algae growth. Decay can then use up oxygen in vulnerable receiving waters.

human.summary: Microbes can turn some nitrogen added to farm soil into nitrous oxide, a heat-trapping gas. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's basic method estimates 0.010 kilograms of nitrogen released in this gas per kilogram of qualifying nitrogen added, with a default uncertainty range of 0.002–0.018. Nitrous oxide traps heat and remains in the air for a long time. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimates its past emissions contributed about 0.09°C of warming in 2010–2019 compared with 1850–1900, with a very likely range of about 0.05–0.16°C.
consequences: Nitrogen applied to fields but not absorbed by crops can wash away or move through soil. It may then pollute rivers, lakes or groundwater. Extra nutrients can help harmful algae grow rapidly. Light, water movement and temperature also determine whether a harmful bloom develops.

anaerobic manure lagoon operation.name: Anaerobic Manure Lagoon Operation
anaerobic manure lagoon operation.description: Keeping animal waste in a pond where it breaks down with little oxygen. This can produce methane, a gas that traps heat. Releases depend on the animals, amount of waste, temperature, storage time and treatment.

outgoing: Liquid manure breaking down without oxygen produces methane. Capturing and using or destroying the gas can reduce how much escapes.
Leaking or overflowing manure stores can send nitrogen and phosphorus into water. Applying the manure to fields at unsuitable times can create another route for losses.

cattle stocking density.name: Cattle Stocking Density

outgoing: More cattle on the same land create more hoof pressure. Soil can become tightly packed where wetness, soil type and limited recovery make it vulnerable.

coal-power sulfur emissions.name: Coal-Power Sulfur Emissions
coal-power sulfur emissions.description: Sulfur-containing pollution released when power stations burn coal. The amount depends on the fuel and pollution-control equipment. It can affect air quality and contribute to acid-forming pollution downwind.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Sulfur in coal forms sulfur dioxide when the fuel burns. The amount released depends on the fuel and how effectively the plant cleans its exhaust.
Coal-burning releases sulfur dioxide, which can turn into acid and settle downwind. Emissions at a power station do not by themselves show how much reaches a particular place.
Sulfur dioxide from coal burning can form fine particles downwind. Exposure to these pollutants can harm the lungs and heart, with controls affecting how much is released.

Sulfur particles formed after coal burning reflect some sunlight and temporarily mask part of greenhouse warming. They also cause serious air pollution. Reducing them removes some cooling while improving air quality.

Sulfur particles formed after coal burning reflect some sunlight and temporarily mask part of greenhouse warming. They also cause serious air pollution. urban hydrologic supply shortfall.name: Urban Hydrologic Supply Shortfall
urban hydrologic supply shortfall.description: A city's available water falling below what its users and operating rules require. Rivers, reservoirs or underground stores may provide too little. The size of the gap depends on demand, stored reserves and other usable supplies.
incoming: A long drought can reduce reservoir inflow, river supply and groundwater replenishment available to a city. The resulting shortfall depends on demand and remaining reserves.
outgoing: When water supplies fall short of demand, utilities may limit use to protect essential needs. Restrictions are an operating decision, not an automatic result of a dry period.
A continuing gap between dependable city water supplies and demand directly indicates a strained system. The size of the gap depends on local sources and operating rules.

urban water-demand peak.name: Urban Water-Demand Peak

incoming: More people and buildings can increase water use at the same time of day. Efficiency, prices, climate and network design affect how large those peaks become.
outgoing: High demand can use up the spare capacity in a city's water supply. Utilities may impose restrictions, especially during drought, depending on their operating choices.

incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Leaks and other physical losses reduce the water that reaches customers. When supply is tight, this can contribute to stronger restrictions on use.

surface-water inflow deficit.name: Surface-Water Inflow Deficit

incoming: Long periods of low rain and runoff reduce water entering rivers and reservoirs. Snow and groundwater can delay or soften the effect where enough reserves remain.
outgoing: Less rain, runoff or river inflow means less water entering lakes, wetlands and reservoirs. Storage can fall if other inflows do not make up the loss.

outgoing: Some lakes and wetlands exchange water with underground reserves. Changes in that exchange can raise or lower the amount stored at the surface.

coal power co2 output.name: Coal Power CO2 Output
coal power co2 output.description: The heat-trapping gas released when coal is burned to generate electricity. The total depends on fuel use and how efficiently stations produce power. This describes releases from the specified power sector, place and period.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Carbon dioxide from burning coal to make electricity adds to the total released into the air. This record covers only the activities, places and years specified in its source, so it should not be counted again in an overlapping total. The cited assessment gives a median direct climate impact of 760 grams of CO₂-equivalent per kilowatt-hour for the assessed coal technology, with a range of 670–870. CO₂-equivalent combines gases by their warming effect. It is not a measurement of carbon dioxide alone.

Carbon dioxide from burning coal to make electricity joins emissions from other sources and builds up in the atmosphere. Its contribution to warming accumulates over time, rather than staying near the place where it was released.

Some carbon dioxide from burning coal to make electricity is eventually absorbed by the ocean. It changes seawater chemistry as part of the combined global total. A particular local change cannot be assigned to this source alone.
